items.title: Gold Surges Along With US Treasuries as Oil Price Slide Deepens
body: Gold held a decline after the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in three years and signaled another hike was likely before year-end.

Bullion was trading around $4,270 an ounce, after falling 2% over the previous three sessions as traders priced in the Fed’s widely expected move. The Federal Open Market Committee voted unanimously late Wednesday to increase the benchmark federal funds rate by a quarter percentage point. Its median outlook for rates at the end of 2026 was 4.1%, up from 3.8% earlier, indicating support for more hikes.
Markets interpreted the Fed’s guidance as hawkish. Treasury yields fell along the curve, while the dollar rose. Higher rates are typically negative for gold as it pays no interest.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh used his post-decision briefing to reaffirm the threat posed by inflation to the US economy, saying too many categories of products and services were showing annualized price gains above 3% on a 6- and 12-month basis.
Read More: Bond Traders Signal Warsh Credibility Growing in Inflation Fight

The hike defied the wishes of President Donald Trump, who recently threatened to escalate his trade wars if the Fed didn’t drop rates. He said on social media that US interest rates should be 1% or lower, but stopped short of calling out Warsh.

Data released last week showed core US inflation rose at a hotter-than-expected pace in August, which added to concerns that price pressures may be broadening beyond the temporary effect of tariffs and the Iran war’s impact on energy costs.

Oil dropped on signs of supply pressure easing. Saudi Arabia is seeking to return about half the capacity of its damaged East-West pipeline within days, and full operations in about six weeks, a person familiar with the matter said.

Spot gold was up 0.2% at $4,273.82 an ounce at 7:52 a.m. in Singapore. Silver rose 0.5% to $63.28 an ounce. Platinum and palladium edged higher. The Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index, a gauge of the US currency, was steady after rising 0.5% the previous session.

items.title: Trump Floats EU Tariffs If Canada Invite Deemed Hostile Act
body: President Donald Trump floated hitting goods imported from the European Union with fresh tariffs or even cutting off some trade if he determined that a push to make Canada a potential associate of the bloc was harmful to the US.
“If they do that, if I think it’s at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things,” Trump told reporters Wednesday when asked about the proposal.
“If Europe does that with a bad intention — if it’s a good intention, that’s fine — if it’s a bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe,” he added.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has proposed Canada becoming the first associate member of the European Union, saying she would like to work with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on the idea. She offered the invitation during her state of the union address in Strasbourg, France, Wednesday, with Carney in attendance.

Trump’s comments risk further inflaming a simmering trade war between the US and Canada, two longtime allies whose economies are closely linked. After trade talks collapsed last month, Trump imposed 50% tariffs on $20 billion of goods imported from Canada, and Carney retaliated with roughly equal levies on US-made products.
The president on Wednesday slapped yet another escalation on the US’s northern neighbor by making good on a threat to restrict Canadian goods from federal government purchases.

Canada’s government has made clear it is eager to boost economic ties with the rest of the world, including the EU, in a multi-year strategic shift to reorient trade flows more to the east and west, rather than being primarily focused southbound toward the US.
Yet there is much uncertainty over the offer to make the country an “associate member” of the EU, including what that would entail. Negotiations could also take years.
And the move, as Trump’s comments indicate, could draw blowback from the US, which Carney has said sought greater input over Ottawa’s trade deals with other economies.

Trump over the weekend had expressed optimism about resolving the trade fight between the US and its northern neighbor, saying he saw a deal coming “fairly soon,” even as he offered no details on any resumption of formal talks between the two countries. It’s unclear what legal authority Trump would use to impose his fresh threat of penalties.
“I think it’s laughable,” Trump said Wednesday of the EU’s invite to Canada. “Canada has been a terrible trade partner,” he added.

items.title: Snap Shares More Details About $2,195 Specs AR Glasses, Plus Verizon Partnership
body: Snap Inc. revealed new partnership and software details about its forthcoming Specs augmented reality glasses, pitching the $2,195 device to early adopters ahead of a launch planned for later this year.

The social media company, which believes it has found a design that could make consumers more comfortable with donning a computer on their face, announced a partnership Wednesday with Verizon Communications Inc. that will allow people to try Specs at select Verizon stores and purchase custom wireless data plans for the wearable device.

A higher-priced $2,395 version of the Specs will include a carrying case that features built-in cellular data connectivity, allowing the glasses to move beyond Wi-Fi networks and function anywhere a user can get Verizon reception. There will be a separate monthly fee for users who want that level of freedom.

Snap, best known for the Snapchat social media app, sold quirky camera-equipped “Spectacles” glasses a decade ago. It is now reentering a smart glasses market currently dominated by Meta Platforms Inc. But Ray-Ban Meta glasses have faced growing pushback from consumers who are wary of being recorded in public without their knowledge or consent.

“Success for this product is showing people that we can build a totally different type of computer that makes computing feel way more human,” Snap Chief Executive Officer Evan Spiegel said in an interview ahead of the announcement. “I think if we can land that vision and people understand it, then they understand the next 20 years of what we’re trying to accomplish.”

The Snap Specs are more technically advanced than Meta’s highest-end $799 glasses that feature an integrated display, though they fall short of the visual clarity and immersion offered by larger, bulkier headsets like   Apple Inc.’s $3,699 Vision Pro, which has failed to find significant momentum with consumers.

Along with the ability to understand three-dimensional space and layer digital effects onto the real world, the most compelling aspect of Snap’s hardware is that it’s fully untethered, with all of the computing technology fully contained inside the glasses. There’s no dangling puck or battery, which can’t be said for Apple’s headset or the upcoming “Aura” AR glasses developed by Xreal Inc. and Alphabet Inc’s Google.

But this style isn’t without compromise: Some parts of the design — like the temples — are quite thick. Snap’s June unveiling of its consumer Specs, which followed several years of testing developer-focused AR models, was ridiculed by some on social media when Spiegel’s ears seemed to fold under their weight.
Read More: Snap Launches $2,195 Specs, Declaring Glasses the Next Computer

During a roughly half-hour hands-on session ahead of Wednesday’s keynote, the Specs felt mostly comfortable, though they still feel hefty compared with conventional glasses. Users can bring up the virtual interface’s home screen by looking at their open palm. From there, the glasses’ hand tracking allows for making selections. This approach to navigation worked well enough, but there wasn’t enough time to assess how intuitive it really is over extended use or if the glasses cause fatigue when worn for long stretches.

Spiegel said Specs are designed for intermittent use and not something people are meant to have on their face all day, which is partially a reflection of their limited battery life: They last for around four hours of mixed usage factoring in both video and audio playback.

Users can stream video from services such as YouTube and HBO Max through the included web browser on Specs, resizing the content and placing it wherever they’d like in nearby three-dimensional space. The glasses can dim their lenses to make entertainment easier to focus on.

Some popular apps like Spotify won’t be available until after the glasses go on sale, the company said. Others, like Shopify, will allow users to preview the actual size of furniture and other items in their personal space — though this is something most smartphones can replicate with software AR features.

Different “lenses,” another word for apps in Snap parlance, will allow users to see navigation directions mapped into their actual view or provide live translation functionality in as many as 60 supported languages. The glasses also allow for standard-fare tricks like setting up a virtual secondary display for a laptop or privately watching a movie on the go.

Snap is building a social element into Specs, letting two owners play games like dominoes together. Other experiences can help people improve upon their golf swing or basketball skills by blending virtual lessons and challenges with a user’s real-world view.

“I think right now, the narrative is computers are replacing us and we think people are going to spend more time in virtual worlds,” Spiegel said. “And we’re saying, ‘No, we don’t agree with that vision. We think computers should enhance human capability and skill.’” Since few people are likely to purchase $2,000-plus glasses sight unseen, Snap plans to open a pop-up experience in Los Angeles as another way for consumers to test out Specs as they evolve over time. Other locations could later follow, the company said.

The company is also introducing its own artificial intelligence platform, called Specs Intelligence, that is being framed as a proactive assistant meant to present information exactly when it’s most helpful. Specs Intelligence will be available for the iPhone and Apple’s macOS operating system, so users don’t need to splurge on the AR glasses just to give Snap’s personalized AI helper a try.

In the interview, Spiegel shrugged off the idea that the backlash around camera glasses could taint the Specs launch. With his product, he said, “you can see them from a mile away,” since the hardware is unmistakable to bystanders. “They’ve got iridescent lenses. And they're a computer, so people aren't using them to primarily record videos. They're watching videos, right? Or playing a game or working on their golf swing or getting work done.”

The “misstep” that Meta and others made, he added, was pursuing a conventional glasses style while building in cameras that can often be hard to see. Spiegel is confident consumers will understand “that we built something really different and they’re not a pair of spy glasses.”

Spiegel said the Specs have the best odds with early adopters and tech enthusiasts, but declined to comment on how many units the company is aiming to sell or what would constitute a commercial success.  For now, he said, the company is able to fully back Specs Inc., a standalone subsidiary formed earlier this year, through the broader Snap business. But Spiegel said there could be room for outside investment if the effort takes off.

“What’ll be interesting is, let’s say the opportunity is way bigger than we thought and we really want to accelerate. Then I think we have an opportunity to look at raising more capital for whatever that may be,” he said.

items.title: CATL Bulls Reject 'De‑CATLization' Fear After $100 Billion Rout
body: Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Ltd. bulls are unfazed by a $100 billion market value wipeout over just four months, arguing the Chinese battery leader’s technology moat makes it a clear winner in the long-term global energy transition.

Its Shenzhen‑listed shares have slid 34% from their May record high, tracking weakness in global electric vehicle and battery peers as investors fret over profitability and demand. CATL’s selloff accelerated this week on concerns over its outlook as the domestic industry struggles with excess capacity and tough competition.

Such difficulties have renewed long-standing market fears of Chinese EV makers diversifying battery supply away from CATL’s higher-priced offerings. The sell-side remains positive on CATL, with a unanimous 47 buy ratings among analysts touting its superior technology and product quality.

“Many automakers in the past have pushed for ‘de-CATLization’ but none succeeded” said Bing Yuan, a fund manager at Edmond de Rothschild Asset Management. “Replicating CATL’s technology and reliability is extremely difficult. Smaller suppliers may serve mass‑market models, but flagship and premium lines will still rely on CATL.”
Read more: CATL Shares Drop 10% in Two Days as Outlook Worries Mount

Among recent headlines stirring investor unease, Chinese EV maker Li Auto Inc. announced plans to switch to self-developed batteries from CATL products. And Xiaomi Corp. forged pacts with rivals Sunwoda Electronic Co. and CALB Group Co., looking to add battery suppliers beyond CATL.

Such stories have overshadowed news of supply deal wins that help even the score, according to UBS Group AG. “On carmakers’ de-CATLization, despite multi-year discussion, CATL’s domestic market share remains stable at more than 40%,” analysts including Paul Gong wrote in a Sept. 9 note.

In fact, even though Volkswagen AG is the largest shareholder in battery maker Gotion High-tech Co., CATL continues to increase its share of the German car giant’s business, according to Morgan Stanley analysts including Jack Lu.

“Several automakers have reported quality-related issues in the past, including recalls, warranty costs, and damage to brand equity, highlighting the significant opportunity cost of moving away from the industry leader,” they wrote in a report last week.

Investors have somewhat pared bearish bets against CATL, with short interest in its Hong Kong-listed shares down to 19.2% of the free float, compared with 21% in July, according to data from S3 Partners.

Despite confidence in its technology leadership, CATL is facing a domestic market struggling with weak auto demand. Overseas EV sales have been strong, but momentum is clouded by geopolitical and trade uncertainties.

“Continued pressure on vehicle sales could weigh on CATL’s demand outlook and raise questions around capacity utilization, making some of the market’s concerns understandable,” said Gareth Pan, senior investment manager at Pictet Asset Management. “While near-term uncertainty is likely to persist, the risk-reward profile may be becoming more balanced at current levels.”
For bulls, the recent slump offers a buying opportunity after a multi-year run higher as the artificial intelligence boom spurred a surge in energy-storage system demand at data centers.

Mainland-listed shares are cheaper now at about 12 times forward earnings estimates, less than half the five-year average. At the same time, prospects for shareholder returns have improved with the company launching its first-ever buyback this week.

“CATL is and will be the dominant player, not only as a battery maker but also an AI electrification infra-player,” said Wooho Rho, an analyst at Meritz Securities Co. “If you could invest in CATL for more than 10 years, there are few business risks, and still a good chance to buy it.”

items.title: Laissez-Faire Hong Kong Meets the Five-Year Plan
body: Milton Friedman was baffled by Hong Kong. During his second visit in 1963, there was pulsating activity all around him — but no official data. Why wasn’t the colonial administration crowing about its achievements, he asked. The absence of a gross domestic product series wasn’t an oversight, as John Cowperthwaite, Hong Kong’s financial secretary at the time, explained to the celebrated American economist: “If I let them compute those statistics, they’ll want to use them for planning.”

That aversion to state intervention, long believed to be the mantra of Hong Kong’s capitalist success, was consigned to history Wednesday with the unveiling of the financial center’s first five-year plan.

It’s natural to view this as more evidence that the city is hewing its policy apparatus closer to the mainland ahead of the 30th anniversary of its handover to China next year. (Beijing just launched its 15th five-year plan.) However, the larger significance of the move is that Chief Executive John Lee is jumping on a global bandwagon.

Planning in a 21st-century market economy is a far cry from the Soviet Union where the state was (or pretended to be) in total control of production, pricing, and distribution. What Hong Kong is attempting to do is better understood as industrial policy. Once a part of the standard playbook, state intervention fell out of favor in the Reagan-Thatcher era and was practically mothballed after the 1989 Washington Consensus put deregulation and free trade at the top of the global agenda.

But industrial policy is back in fashion — this time as a tool to make the private sector commit to long-gestation investments that it may otherwise avoid given the enormous uncertainties along the way.

Instead of command-and-control, the modern state planner employs incentives like subsidies, tax credits, and cheap land to nudge entrepreneurial energies toward desired outcomes. For instance, the Chips and Science Act in the US is trying to rebuild a domestic semiconductor-fabrication industry with $39 billion in federal grants. China has responded with a $50 billion Big Fund III to ease bottlenecks in areas like lithography and chip design. India recently unveiled a fresh $20 billion package of production-linked incentives to boost local manufacturing of smartphones and semiconductors.

Friedrich Hayek, the 20th-century prophet of free markets, famously argued that central planners’ pretense of knowledge is no match for the information contained in prices. Modern industrial policy tacitly concedes his point. Since it’s impossible for policymakers to conceive of everything that needs to go right to realize their ambitions, the state sets high-level targets and lets markets work out the details.

That’s why embedding goals within plans helps. The end results don't have to be spelled out to the last technological detail. China’s 15th plan merely says that it wants to develop capabilities in quantum computing and multimodal intelligence — AI that processes text, speech, images, and sensory signals simultaneously. For startups in these areas, that’s enough: Once something is in the plan, universities will come up with research grants, municipalities will fast-track permits, and state-backed venture funds will mark them as priority investments.

Hong Kong’s first five-year plan fits this new variant. There are no numerical goals around the GDP growth rate, labor productivity, worker wages, public health expenditure, or foreign trade. The targets, where they exist — for instance, on the share of its innovation economy or the value added in manufacturing — are described as “anticipatory.” The binding commitment is only on environmental protection — and, most importantly, on making available spade-ready land parcels to developers in Northern Metropolis, a planned technology hub and university town near mainland China.

Northern Metropolis is where Hong Kong aims to attract R&D investments and global talent. By tapping neighboring Shenzhen’s manufacturing powerhouse, Hong Kong can build competence in emerging technologies like quantum computing, allowing the city to diversify its economy toward tech services.

The plan is also a social intervention. The rival financial center of Singapore was labeled a “nanny state” for its cradle-to-grave welfare policies. Hong Kong is now traveling in the same direction, actively using nudges — like liberal baby bonuses and concessional stamp duties for couples planning apartment purchases around childbirth — to confront the challenge posed by an aging population.

While those inducements don’t always work, where Hong Kong can catch up is housing. And that’s the other motivation behind the five-year plan. Northern Metropolis, covering a third of the city’s territory, is a plausible answer to its perennial apartment shortage — Hong Kong’s Achilles’ heel. The new economic hub, with 70,000 new dwellings planned over the next five years, is expected to help more families climb the homeownership ladder in one of the world’s most expensive real estate markets.

None of this, I suspect, would have pleased Cowperthwaite. His loathing of state intervention extended to refusing free primary schooling. Taiwan, whose tech prowess is now acknowledged globally, went in the opposite direction. Lee Kuan Yew, Singapore’s first prime minister,  spent a third of his early budgets on education.

As for Friedman, what the future Nobel laureate heard in 1963 was an affirmation of his ideology — he had published Capitalism and Freedom the year before. During the Asian financial crisis of 1998, he warned that the Hong Kong Monetary Authority’s stock-market intervention would undermine the credibility of its dollar peg. Well, the peg is still intact. And today, in an ultimate twist of state intervention, it is the US government holding a multi-billion-dollar stake in Intel Corp.

items.title: Fed's Hawkish Hike to Pressure Asian Currencies, Strategists Say
body: The US Federal Reserve’s hawkish hike is set to pressure Asian currencies, especially the yen ahead of the Bank of Japan’s monetary policy meeting on Friday, according to market strategists.

The yen could weaken toward its 200-day moving average of about 158 per dollar, while bond yields will be dictated by moves in their US peers, strategists said. Stocks, particularly those sensitive to interest-rate movements, are under pressure.
“Nerves are likely to linger across Asian markets given the newfound level of hawkishness from the Fed,” according to Tim Waterer, chief market analyst at KCM Trade.
Read: Fed Raises Rates to Curb Inflation, Drawing Rebuke From Trump

items.title: Australia migration cuts, NZ's world-beating sovereign wealth fund, Fed hikes
body: It’s well known that New Zealand is world class in many fields — rugby, wine, mountains and snow, just to name a few. One more thing to add to that list — relative to global peers at least — is running a sovereign wealth fund.

The New Zealand Super Fund returned 14.2% last financial year. As CEO Jo Townsend — an Aussie — told us, the strong result was partly powered by the rally on equity markets. That’s not the full story though, especially when you take into account an underweight exposure to tech stocks. A range of active strategies performed well outside shares: credit and arbitrage also did well, while real assets were more muted. Overall, the fund added NZ$9.3 billion ($5.4 billion), swelling the value of its investments to A$94.4 billion.

The catch? With the NZ Super Fund expecting to double its assets every 10 years — and no withdrawals slated for about three decades — Townsend says as it gets bigger, investing becomes a “more challenging” task.
- Amy Bainbridge, Melbourne reporter

Migration is in focus today, with Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke to explain how he plans to reduce migrant numbers in a speech at around 12:30 p.m. eastern time. The tighter rules will aim to cut the number of visa overstayers and make it harder for people on temporary visas such as students to bring family members to the country, according to the ABC and AFR.

Brookfield Asset Management agreed to buy Australian plumbing supplies company Reliance Worldwide Corp. The all-cash deal values the firm at around A$4.1 billion ($2.9 billion) and gives Brookfield exposure to the US construction and housing market. The Australian firm is best known for its Sharkbite push-to-connect plumbing fittings that eliminate the need for specialist tools.

Australia’s central bank should stand ready to hike interest rates as needed given inflation risks remain tilted to the upside, the International Monetary Fund said this morning, adding that the government could support disinflation by restraining fiscal spending.

New Zealand passed legislation enabling a free-trade agreement with India that was signed earlier this year, handing Prime Minister Christopher Luxon a win ahead of the November election. Australia is still in talks with India on updating the trade deal which began in 2022, with little public sign of progress on that.

Stocks in Asia were poised for losses, tracking a decline on Wall Street after the US central bank raised interest rates for the first time since 2023 and signaled further tightening to curb inflation. The dollar gained the most since June.The US Federal Reserve raised rates by a quarter percentage point and penciled in an additional hike later this year, with the move aimed at blunting inflation. That immediately attracted the public ire of President Donald Trump, who posted “LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!” on social media.

Bond traders are now pricing in three more rate hikes by the middle of next year, and the Bank of Japan is also expected to hike tomorrow. That trend may put even more pressure on the Reserve Bank of Australia to also raise rates. Governor Michelle Bullock will be speaking to a parliamentary committee on Friday in Canberra, with that to be closely watch for any hints how the board will decide when it meets the week after next.

JPMorgan Asset Management’s Bob Michele said his team has begun buying long-end US, Japanese, and Australian bonds, calling current prices “simply too cheap” and declaring that markets have reached “a point of maximum pain.”

The European Union continues to try and build up trade and economic ties outside the bloc, with President Ursula von der Leyen proposing to Canadian leader Mark Carney that his nation become the first “associate member” of the union. That title is more symbolic than anything but comes as the US and Canada are in a trade war and Europe is also looking for allies, after signing trade deals with India, Australia and others recently.

Saudi Arabia is seeking to return about half the capacity of its cross-country oil pipeline within days after the link was halted last week following drone attacks, a person familiar with the matter said. If that happens and the pipeline isn’t attacked again it could help lower global oil prices, which are rising again, pushing up petrol prices in Australia and elsewhere.

Concrete is probably the most ubiquitous product of human development, but a new documentary film The History of Concrete focuses on the everyday failures of concrete in people’s lives, rather than its global impact.

items.title: Hong Kong Follows Fed With First Rate Hike in Over Three Years
body: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority followed the US Federal Reserve in raising interest rates for the first time since 2023, a decision that could threaten a property recovery unfolding since last year.

The HKMA lifted its benchmark by 25 basis points to 4.25%, according to a statement on Thursday. The de facto central bank in the city moves in lockstep with the Fed to protect the local dollar’s peg to the greenback.
The focus now shifts to any moves the city’s biggest banks — including HSBC Holdings Plc and Standard Chartered Plc — will announce later in the day, including changes to their best lending rates.

In Hong Kong, the best lending rates are used as a base for banks to quote rates on mortgage loans, so they have an ability to encourage more credit and borrowing even as the benchmark tightens. The one-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate, a key mortgage reference rate, has climbed to 2.95% — the highest in almost three months — while staying far below its US equivalent.

Higher rates in the US are encouraging traders to keep buying the greenback against its Hong Kong counterpart, since investors can earn a profit from the differential. The Hong Kong dollar has been trading near the weakest level permitted under the city’s linked exchange rate system, which it last touched just over a year ago

While the city’s economy is on an upswing thanks to booming trade, higher borrowing costs risk becoming a drag on a property market that’s just emerged from a prolonged downturn, especially as buyers grow cautious over China’s efforts to curb mainland capital outflows.
Hong Kong home prices are expected to rebound the most in nearly a decade in 2026, driven by strong Chinese demand, limited supply and robust rental growth, according to Bloomberg Intelligence.

items.title: BOE Set to Hold While Warning on Inflation: Decision Guide
body: The Bank of England is expected to hold interest rates as it waits for more evidence that a fresh bout of inflation risks a damaging wage-price spiral.

Economists and investors expect the Monetary Policy Committee to leave the benchmark cost of borrowing at 3.75% on Thursday, where it’s been since December last year, as the economy is buffeted by events in the Middle East.

The majority of BOE rate-setters have so far argued that the current level of rates is doing enough to bear down on price pressures. However, that position is becoming harder to maintain, with oil and gas costs already above the “adverse” scenario set out by the central bank in late July and economists warning that inflation could hit 4% early next year.

Officials are therefore expected to set the stage for a hike in November, the first of several seen by financial markets. Alongside the rates decision, the BOE will also update its quantitative tightening asset-sale program for the year ahead.

The MPC is widely expected to vote 6-3 in favor of holding rates, the same as the last meeting in July. Three of 28 economists surveyed by Bloomberg believe the number of officials calling for an immediate rate increase will rise to four.

The dissenters have made their position clear. Huw Pill, the chief economist, and external members Megan Greene and Catherine Mann all fear inflation could set off a feedback loop as workers push for bigger wage increases and firms in turn raise prices to protect their margins. They want an insurance hike to stave off the risk.
Clare Lombardelli, deputy governor for monetary policy, is seen as the next most hawkish MPC member but she said at the July meeting that her vote to hold hadn’t been a close call.

The pressure to react to an inevitable price surge is mounting. The European Central Bank raised its deposit rate for a second time in three months to 2.5% last week and the US Federal Reserve on Wednesday lifted the federal funds rate to a range of 3.75% to 4%.

Markets are showing a slim but not negligible chance — around 12% — of a hike on Thursday, an outcome supported by economist DeAnne Julius. The former BOE policymaker told BBC radio “there’s a reasonable chance that the committee will decide to raise rates by 25 basis points” due to pressures from the Middle East and CPI rising above 3%.

Fears of resurgent inflation are likely to force the MPC to combine what is expected to be a cautious hold with hawkish words. “Risks are skewed towards tough hiking language, given soaring energy prices and market pricing,” said Robert Wood, chief UK economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics.
Governor Andrew Bailey signaled as much last week when he told lawmakers on Parliament’s Treasury Committee that inflation risks were on the upside as the conflict in the Middle East continues.

Market pricing, which suggests four rate rises to 4.75% by July next year, is doing some of the MPC’s work by tightening financial conditions. The UK labor market also remains subdued. The inflation outlook is nonetheless expected to deteriorate.

With oil well above $100 a barrel and gas prices sharply higher, household energy bills may jump 25% in January when the price cap resets, raising the prospect of inflation hitting double the 2% target, Bloomberg Economics has warned. Food prices hit by a summer drought and air fares are also expected to keep upward pressure on inflation.

“Rates may be restrictive, but the key policy question for the MPC will remain: are they restrictive enough?” said Deutsche Bank’s chief UK economist Sanjay Raja, who also sees inflation at close to 4% in December. “Risk management considerations have become stronger, and the likelihood of rate hikes have strengthened of late.”
The BOE’s forecasts are already out of date. Its July outlook, at which it updated all its key forecasts, was for 2.8% inflation in August. This week’s official reading was 3.1%.

The BOE is also likely to upgrade growth. In July, it thought second quarter growth would be 0.3%, below the subsequent 0.4% official reading. The momentum continued into July, with a month-on-month expansion of 0.4%. It means growth in the third quarter will likely far exceed the 0.1% the BOE forecast.
Read more: AI Helps UK Economy Unexpectedly Grow in Boost for Burnham
As the BOE does not publish a full set of three-year forecasts this month, the revisions to its outlook will be only for the immediate quarter ahead.

The BOE has been unwinding its £895 billion portfolio of government bonds since February 2022. So far it has shrunk the stock to £489 billion through a combination of active sales and letting maturing bonds run off the balance sheet.

The BOE’s stated intention is to sell the whole stock but it slowed the pace of reduction to £70 billion for the year to through September from an annual £100 billion previously. Alongside today’s rate decision, it will announce its quantitative tightening plans for the year starting October. It is widely expected to say the pace will be lowered again to £50 billion.

The MPC has three principles guiding the process: that interest rates remain the MPC’s main tool, that sales do not disrupt the functioning of markets, and that they are done in a gradual and predictable manner.

A run-off rate of £50 billion implies active sales – the more controversial part of the arrangement — will be maintained at around £20 billion. An internal BOE study recently concluded that QT has added 20-30 basis points to 10-year government borrowing costs.

Market participants surveyed by the BOE expect 15.6% of the active sales to be long-maturity bonds, totalling about £3 billion. The Telegraph newspaper reported this week that the BOE may halt long-dated sales altogether to avoid interfering with the government’s gilt issuance. The BOE, Treasury and Debt Management Office all declined to comment.

items.title: Asia Risks Unrest as El Niño, War Threaten Food Supplies, Consultancy Says
body: Severe weather disruptions will amplify food security risks in Asia, potentially triggering civil unrest and political instability in vulnerable countries such as India, Indonesia and the Philippines, according to consultancy Verisk Maplecroft.

The warning comes as the war in Iran has already disrupted fuel and fertilizer supplies, both of which are key agricultural inputs. Now, weather extremes linked to a powerful El Niño are further threatening crops across the region.

Indonesia, the world’s biggest palm oil producer, is suffering from a rash of hard-to-control wildfires that have disrupted harvests. The monsoon rains that top rice exporter India relies on are running 15% below normal, and Thailand’s sugar harvest is set to sink.
Read More: A Dozen Ingredients Show India’s Mounting Food Inflation Risk
The twin threats of war and weather are driving up food inflation — an established trigger for unrest, the risk consultancy said in a report released on Thursday.

Over half of countries that are at high- or very high-risk on Verisk Maplecroft’s Food Security Index also sit within the two highest categories of its predictive Civil Unrest Index. Those include India, as well as Bangladesh, the Philippines and Indonesia, where protests have already broken out in recent weeks.

“The data suggest if food price and availability pressures intensify, and governments are seen to respond ineffectively, unrest and political instability could emerge in these higher-risk markets,” the report said.

For conflict-stricken nations like Afghanistan and Myanmar, a food shock would raise the risk of a humanitarian catastrophe, it added. Thailand, highly reliant on imported energy and fertilizers, is also under growing pressure from debt-laden farmers ahead of the next planting season.

“The impacts are increasingly visible,” said Verisk Maplecroft. “In many key agriculture regions, planting and fertilization decisions were made during the peak of the disruption, meaning negative impacts may now be locked in even if the geopolitical situation improves in the coming months.”

Meanwhile, hedge funds see super El Niño as an opportunity. The head of ZAMS Asset Management, a former Balyasny Asset Management trader, said he’s expecting it to produce an “unusually alpha-rich environment,” while Moreton Capital Partners is targeting $500 million to bet on all the ways in which El Niño will upend food prices.

items.title: Al Gore Says Emerging Markets Are Leapfrogging US on Clean Tech
body: As the US doubles down on oil and gas, the rapid shift by emerging markets into alternative sources of energy is forcing a reset that will have profound consequences for global power dynamics, according to Al Gore.

A trend that was only nascent in some countries has now been turbocharged by the war in Iran, says Gore, who was vice president under Bill Clinton and is now the chairman of Generation Investment Management.

“We’ve seen incredible changes just in the months since this war in Iran started, with countries everywhere reevaluating where they stand and assessing how quickly they can move forward,” he said in an interview. A “real sea change” is underway in Thailand, Pakistan, and parts of Africa, Gore said, noting that Chinese clean-tech exports are helping drive the development.

In its sustainability trends report released on Thursday, Generation Investment Management said the dynamics described by Gore increase the likelihood that emerging nations will build their economic growth on clean electricity, and bypass the fossil-fuel-intensive phase that industrialized nations have relied on in the past.
“The greatest aspiration of the clean-energy movement seems increasingly plausible,” Generation said in the report.

India, the world’s most populous nation, is the “great testing ground of this ‘leapfrog’ idea,” according to the investment manager. The country’s growth has long been powered by coal. But solar adoption is now growing by more than 40% a year. Even before the Iran war, India was electrifying faster and using fewer fossil fuels per capita than China had done when it was at a comparable point in its industrialization.

The Iran war has now resulted in the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market, according to the International Energy Agency. Countries started making adjustments within weeks of hostilities breaking out on Feb 28. In March, Kenya stepped up purchases of Chinese solar technology by 207% compared to the month earlier, while Ethiopia and Nigeria bought 391% and 519% more respectively, according to a report by Ember.

In the first five months of the energy crisis triggered by the Iran war, clean power generation added since 2020 saved importing countries an estimated $36 billion in avoided coal, gas and oil imports, the Centre for Research on Energy and Clear Air estimated in August. The figure reflects $22 billion that would otherwise have been spent on gas, $10 billion on coal, and $5 billion on oil imports, it said.
“This is a second time in four years that fossil fuel prices have spiked and supplies have become quite uncertain,” Gore said. “This is a turning point.”
In the US, meanwhile, the Iran war’s impact on diesel prices and inflation is feeding discord among voters.

“There is now a change in the dialogue in the US inside the Republican party,” said Gore. “The impact on the economy and the impact on the environment” of attacking Iran “are now combined” in voters’ perceptions, he said.
Read More: Trump’s Economy Polling Slides as Iran War Saps His Superpower

items.title: Huawei Accelerates Launch of New AI Chip to Take On Nvidia
body: Huawei Technologies Co. is set to unveil new AI technology this week in defiance of US export control curbs, advancing its ambition to replace Nvidia Corp. in China and compete on the global stage.
Huawei’s rotating chairman Wang Tao will present its upcoming Ascend 960 AI chips, to be commercially available in 2027, at the company’s annual summit in Shanghai on Thursday.
Some critical details that analysts will watch out for include whether the new component will be powerful enough for training frontier AI models.

Huawei’s goal is to ensure its Ascend chips can operate every single AI model, in China and beyond, Chairman Guo Ping of the company’s supervisory board told new hires at an internal meeting earlier this month.

“We are closing the gap by innovating chip architectures,” Guo said. “Apple was not a leader in making processors at the beginning, but they delivered exceptional user experience through architecture redesigns and software optimization.”

Already, Huawei has been making inroads at home and beyond. DeepSeek is planning to deploy at least 160,000 Huawei Ascend 950DT chips at a data center it’s building in Inner Mongolia to operate its models. Huawei is also exploring foreign markets including Malaysia and Egypt, Bloomberg News has reported.

The Chinese telecom-to-smartphone firm is spearheading Beijing’s drive for self-sufficiency in critical technologies in the face of yearslong US restrictions aimed at crippling China’s chipmaking aspirations.
It is also leading a Beijing-backed campaign to export the Chinese technology stack abroad at a time when the world’s two superpowers are vying for geopolitical dominance everywhere.

Ascend 960 will succeed Huawei’s current Ascend 950 family of AI accelerators, of which the 950DT favored by DeepSeek is equipped with faster, higher-capacity memory for demanding AI inference workloads. Another upgraded iteration, Ascend 970, is already planned for 2028, the Shenzhen-based company previously announced when launching a three-year campaign to overtake Nvidia. Each new generation of chips will double the amount of computing power of its predecessor.

But Huawei’s AI chips are trailing Nvidia’s top-notch offerings. Frontier Chinese AI labs like DeepSeek are still largely relying on the US company’s chips for training their models, which they then operate using more domestic semiconductors, underscoring the challenge Beijing faces to wean itself completely off of western technology. At the same time, Nvidia’s most sophisticated silicon is still finding its way into China via smuggling, albeit in modest quantities.

A constraint in production capacity is also preventing Huawei from satisfying explosive demand for computing power in a market that Morgan Stanley estimates could reach 646 billion yuan ($96 billion) by 2030. Nvidia’s most advanced Blackwell processors are not directly available in China. Huawei recently raised pricing for the Ascend 950DT chip by 60%, citing tight component supply in communications with customers.
To overcome its disadvantages, Huawei has been trying to come up with innovative ways, including the recently announced LogicFolding technique, to improve its chip technology without the best gear.

Huawei has also introduced a so-called SuperPod structure that will soon allow as many as 100,000 Ascend chips to be linked in a cluster and enables faster data transmission via its UnifiedBus networking protocol. The company says its adaptations and networking can make up for shortcomings in single-chip performance relative to the likes of Nvidia.

“System-level competitiveness matters more than ever,” said Morgan Stanley analyst Charlie Chan in a recent research note. “The effective gap is narrowing through multi-die design, advanced packaging, rack-scale system architecture, optical networking, and software-hardware co-optimization,” Chen wrote.

Huawei is also making some progress on other fronts. Ascend 950 chips are the first Huawei AI accelerators powered by memory chips it designs in-house, though the company has provide little production details.

The Shenzhen electronics giant and other Chinese AI chipmakers have been cut off from the latest AI memory products from South Korea’s SK Hynix Inc. and Samsung Electronics Co. as well as US-based Micron Technology Inc. as part of US export controls.

items.title: IMF Urges RBA to Stay Hawkish Citing Inflation Upside Risks
body: Australia’s central bank should stand ready to hike interest rates as needed given inflation risks remain tilted to the upside, the International Monetary Fund said, adding that the government could support disinflation by tightening its fiscal stance.

“Returning inflation to target should be the near-term priority,” IMF staff said in the concluding statement of their 2026 Article IV mission released Thursday, referring to the Reserve Bank’s 2-3% band. “Monetary policy should remain focused on containing inflation risks.”

The IMF trimmed its forecast for economic growth this year to 1.9% from 2% predicted in April, and for next year to 1.6% from 1.7% as the RBA’s earlier rate hikes weigh on activity — including housing — and tighten financial conditions, with the Australian dollar one of the strongest G-10 currencies this year.

“Given persistent underlying inflation pressures and large uncertainty around whether financial conditions are sufficiently restrictive, the RBA should stand ready to hike rates as needed,” the fund said. “In addition, there is a risk that further large increases in global energy prices lead to stronger second-round effects and lift inflation expectations, warranting further tightening.”

The US and Iran exchanged strikes on oil tankers in the Persian Gulf earlier this month, driving up energy prices. Tensions flared again in the Strait of Hormuz over the weekend, while Saudi Arabia has come under pressure from the Tehran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen.

The IMF statement, which noted Australia started the year in a strong position, comes as the RBA is expected to deliver another rate hike as soon as this month. Policymakers boosted borrowing costs three times between February and May before holding at 4.35% at the last two meetings.

The IMF pointed out that government spending restraint would support the RBA’s disinflation goal and help rebuild fiscal buffers. At the same time, rising data center investment is already adding pressure on the construction sector and could lead to higher energy costs, the statement showed.
Listen and follow The Bloomberg Australia Podcast on Apple, Spotify, YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts.
Traders and economists will closely watch unemployment figures next week, which are the final major piece of economic data before the Sept. 28-29 policy meeting.
The IMF commended the government’s focus on productivity as welcome, though “a more ambitious reform strategy is needed,” it said.

“Further progress on smarter regulation, alongside addressing infrastructure bottlenecks and making the tax system more growth-friendly, would help boost productivity,” the fund said. “Success will require broader and sustained efforts across agencies and all levels of government to more systemically assess and minimize regulatory costs and distortions of new regulations.”

items.title: Salesforce Sees $63 Billion in Revenue in Fiscal Year 2030
body: Salesforce Inc. gave a long-term outlook for sales that exceeded analysts’ estimates, signaling to investors that the software company can boost revenue growth in the face of competition from artificial intelligence tools.

The company expects $63 billion in sales in the fiscal year ending in January 2030, Robin Washington, Salesforce chief operating and financial officer, said Wednesday during the company’s annual conference. The outlook includes revenue from Salesforce’s acquisition of Informatica, which was completed last November. Analysts, on average, estimated $61.4 billion, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.
The shares were little changed in extended trading after closing at $250.54 in New York. The stock has gained 67% since hitting a low on June 22, but remains down 5.4% for the year.

Salesforce, the leading maker of customer management software, is under pressure to prove it can thrive in an era of developing AI products. During its conference this week, Salesforce has touted a partnership with leading AI startup Anthropic PBC, which has helped ease investor concerns about direct competition from the firm.

Conversations with customers and partners at the conference were “notably more constructive than a year ago, with greater confidence in Salesforce’s AI product strategy and execution,” Tyler Radke, an analyst at Citigroup Inc., wrote in a note.

items.title: New Zealand Economy Beats Estimates, Boosting Rate-Hike Bets
body: New Zealand’s economic growth exceeded estimates in the three months through June, defying soaring fuel prices from the Middle East conflict that squeezed local households.

Money markets boosted bets on an October interest-rate hike after gross domestic product advanced 0.2% — double estimates — from the first quarter, when it rose an upwardly revised 0.9%, government data showed Thursday. From a year earlier, GDP expanded 2.6%, also beating forecasts, and growth for the 12 months through March was revised up.

The better-than-expected result and revisions suggest the economy started the second half of 2026 in stronger shape and with less spare capacity. The Reserve Bank, which projected a flat result last quarter, delivered back-to-back rate increases at its past two meetings, but hinted this month it was prepared to take a more gradual approach as it assessed how the economy was responding.
The economy “is in slightly better shape than the RBNZ had thought,” said Abhijit Surya, senior economist at Capital Economics in Singapore.

“We had thought that the RBNZ would wait until December before hiking again, given its cautious tone at its September meeting,” he said. “However, the modest upside surprise in the GDP data, along with the renewed surge in global energy prices in recent weeks, arguably bolsters the case for the Bank to press ahead with policy normalization in October.”

The Official Cash Rate currently stands at 2.75% and investors expect the benchmark will increase to at least 3% by the end of the year. The chance of an October move increased to 69% from 52% on Wednesday, swaps data show.

The modest expansion was driven by the export and tourism sectors, as well as a resurgence in construction, which offset a slowdown in household spending amid rising living costs. Broad global uncertainty over a potential resolution to the US-Iran war and the prospect of higher borrowing costs have been clouding New Zealand’s outlook.

Despite those hurdles, economists predict the recovery will gradually strengthen in the second half of the year. That may prove too little, too late for the ruling National Party, which is trailing in opinion polls as it campaigns for a November election under the mantle of superior economic management.
The government has projected a return to budget surplus by 2029, underpinned by 2.1% GDP growth this year and an average expansion of 3% a year thereafter.

The RBNZ forecasts 0.5% GDP growth in the third and fourth quarters of 2026. Early indicators support its assessment, with manufacturing continuing to expand in August and business confidence remaining positive.

items.title: OpenAI Reports New AI Safety Incidents, Sets Disclosure Plan
body: OpenAI shared several undisclosed incidents of its artificial intelligence models misbehaving, and unveiled a new framework for how it plans to track and disclose such occurrences going forward.

Some of the previously unreported instances of model misbehavior included OpenAI’s technologies concealing and fabricating information in order to return results, the company said in a blog post Wednesday. The ChatGPT maker has faced increased scrutiny since saying in July that some of its most advanced AI models had breached the systems of an external software company, Hugging Face.

In the report, OpenAI detailed various instances of its AI models misbehaving in order to achieve a task or succeed at an evaluation. Some examples included the models fabricating missing data, attempting to bypass network restrictions and AI agents sharing files with each other they were supposed to keep private.

OpenAI also outlined a case for employees to self-report similar incidents of so-called “misalignment,” which is when AI acts in ways that are not in line with human objectives, as well as a system to triage such self-reported occurrences.

“In the past, so as to better inform researchers, AI developers, policymakers, and the general public, we’ve sought to make our findings about misalignment public,” OpenAI wrote. “But without a systematic approach to reporting these findings, our disclosures have been ad hoc and less frequent than ideal.”
The company said the reports are only an initial set of disclosures, and not a comprehensive account of issues arising from its chatbots.

“We do not believe that the AI industry has solved alignment and monitoring to a sufficient degree to continue responsibly scaling at maximum speed for much longer,” the company wrote. “Decisions about how AI development should proceed in the months and years to come need to draw on evidence that people outside the companies building frontier models can examine for themselves.”

The Hugging Face incident was just one in a series of recent online hacks carried out by AI models made by OpenAI, Anthropic PBC and Meta Platforms Inc., causing widespread concern about the security risks posed by this increasingly powerful technology.

Anxiety about AI’s existential risks gained momentum last week, driven by the high-profile departure of Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon, who accused AI companies of “gambling with our lives” in a resignation post he shared on social media.

In the past several days, numerous AI company leaders, including Anthropic Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, have urged slowing the pace of the development of the technology to address its increasingly unpredictable risks — though they diverge on exactly how it should be handled.

On Saturday in a 3,800-word essay, Amodei called for government regulation and for the tech industry to support a broader AI slowdown. At a conference in San Francisco Tuesday, Altman and Nvidia Corp. CEO Jensen Huang both acknowledged concerns but argued AI companies would safely pace their technology on their own. And Meta Platforms Inc. Chief Executive Officer Mark Zuckerberg said Tuesday that AI labs should rely on independent evaluators and advisers to ensure that models are safe.
President Donald Trump vehemently rejected calls to slow AI’s development on Monday, dismissing fears about the tech’s risks as “a hoax” and rejecting the idea of new rules.

The AI boom has fueled a historic US stock market rally. Any pause or delay in progress on so-called frontier AI systems would be unwelcome among investors who are betting that the AI boom will drive hundreds of billions of dollars in capital expenditure.

items.title: Boehly, Walter Sell Chelsea Stakes to Clearlake After Rocky Era
body: Chelsea Football Club owner Clearlake Capital agreed to buy out chairman Todd Boehly and director Mark Walter, bringing an end to a turbulent period among the club’s owners.

The deal, announced late Wednesday, sets an enterprise value of about £5 billion ($6.7 billion), according to people familiar with the matter who asked not to be identified describing terms. Walter is selling as his businesses face scrutiny from US authorities. The transaction hands Clearlake control of the club.

Clearlake and Boehly led a consortium that bought Chelsea from Russian oligarch Roman Abramovich in 2022 but fell out over its direction in late 2024 following a period of heavy spending on players led by Boehly, a disagreement first reported by Bloomberg News. Talks over whether each side could buy the other out dragged on for years.

Now, the federal probe of Walter’s businesses has prompted him to reshape his holdings, stirring up deal talks on multiple fronts, including around his sports franchises. Last month, Walter agreed to sell the Los Angeles Lakers to Josh Kushner and Bob Iger for a record $12.5 billion. Walter’s TWG Global later said it wasn’t looking to sell more sports assets at “‘fire sale’ prices.”

The billionaire financier expected the Chelsea sale to amount to a premium on what he originally invested, a representative told Bloomberg last week as the agreement neared. He and Boehly may collect £950 million cash for their combined 25% stake, the Financial Times reported. The club’s broader enterprise value includes debt.

Chelsea’s on-pitch performance has experienced significant volatility since the London club’s 2022 takeover in a £2.5 billion deal. It slumped to 12th in the Premier League in the 2022/23 season before rallying to sixth a year later. Results improved in the 2024/25 campaign as the team finished fourth to secure UEFA Champions League qualification, alongside lifting the UEFA Conference League and FIFA Club World Cup trophies.
However, performance dipped again during the 2025/26 season, with Chelsea sliding to 10th position, missing out on European football, and ending the year without silverware.

The owners prioritized signing young talent on long-term contracts, outlaying more than £1.5 billion on nearly 50 players through July 2025. While the strategy generated high-value assets like star-player Cole Palmer, it led to squad bloat and frequent player turnover. Managerial changes also continued to impact stability.

The massive outlay on transfer fees created significant financial pressure for the club. Chelsea reported revenue of £490.9 million for the financial year ending June 30, 2025, the second-highest revenue in the club’s history, but alongside a pretax loss of £262.4 million, the largest ever recorded by a Premier League club.

By comparison, rival Liverpool FC reported revenue of £703 million in its latest public financial results, with pretax profit of £15.2 million. The club recently sold a stake to a group of investors including Jeff Bezos at an equity valuation of about $6 billion. Chelsea’s equity valuation of about $4.7 billion.

items.title: Fed's Warsh Heeds Own Advice With Record Short Press Conference
body: Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh has said he thinks policymakers should do a lot less talking. He followed his own advice on Wednesday when he held the shortest press conference on record for a Fed chair speaking after a regularly-scheduled policy meeting.

Warsh’s customary news conference following the Fed’s decision to raise interest rates for the first time in more than three years clocked in at right around 30 minutes. That was the shortest session since Fed chairs began holding regular press conferences in 2011.
The chairman stuck to his commitment not to foreshadow the Fed’s future actions, instead focusing on this week’s meeting and how Fed officials currently see the economy.

The Fed also changed the seating arrangement in the briefing room. While journalists from major newspapers and wire services used to populate the front row, the seating was switched to alphabetical order by outlet name. That meant Agence France-Presse got a spot in the front row. Reporters for the Wall Street Journal and Reuters were moved to the back of the room.

The future of the press conference, meanwhile, remains up in the air. One of five task forces created by Warsh will examine communications. It’s charged with reviewing how the Fed “conveys policy deliberations and decisions amid uncertainty,” an umbrella that could put the press conference, among other communications tools, on the chopping block.

The Fed chief has said he doesn’t want the central bank’s decisions to be front page news. At his first meeting as head of the Fed in June, he drastically shortened the post-meeting statement issued by policymakers.

He has also previously expressed skepticism about the benefits of news conferences, saying in June that the sessions are most useful when there is “something important to say.” In July he committed to continuing the regular press conferences — but only through the end of this year.

items.title: House Passes Bill Allowing New Tariffs on Russia Oil Buyers
body: Congress gave final approval to a bill to give President Donald Trump new powers to impose tariffs on countries that purchase Russian petroleum products, a setback for a coalition of business lobbyists concerned the legislation creates a legal underpinning for a broad new tariff regime against US trading partners.

The legislation, which the House passed Wednesday in a 262-159 vote, has been celebrated by Ukrainian officials eager for a tangible sign of US support in its fight against a Russian invasion. The war, now in its fifth year, is in a critical phase of escalation.
The measure now goes to Trump’s desk for his signature, after easily passing the Senate last month. The president plans to sign the bill in the coming days, a White House official said.

The top five purchasers of Russian petroleum products — a list that includes China, India and US allies like Turkey — could be hit with broad new tariffs, if Trump chooses to use the new powers. Democrats offered an amendment to clarify that the European Union would not be considered as one country under the bill, but the effort to preemptively limit the scope of the bill was rejected.

“This legislation strengthens economic sanctions against the Russian government, its financial institutions, and the foreign governments that aid Russian aggression against Ukraine by purchasing cheap Russian oil and gas and helping the Kremlin evade other sanctions,” House Speaker Mike Johnson said in a statement after the vote.
The bill appeared to stall in the House earlier this month after lobbyists from the US Chamber of Commerce, National Foreign Trade Council and other business groups opposed it.
Yet the White House ultimately urged House leaders to vote on it before leaving town for an extended break.

The legislation has caused divides in both parties, pitting Ukraine’s most ardent supporters against those more focused on tariff-spiked inflation in the run-up to a November midterm election focused heavily on voter dissatisfaction with the US economy. Ultimately, 58 Democrats voted for the measure, while seven Republicans opposed it.
House Foreign Affairs top Democrat Gregory Meeks of New York warned the bill will exacerbate an affordability crisis in the US by allowing more tariffs on US allies.
“We cannot grant the president more tariff authority that we know he will abuse,” Meeks said.
But Virginia Democrat Eugene Vindman, who was born in Kyiv, retorted that Russian President Vladimir Putin “will only back down when there are clear consequences for his aggression.”

Several vulnerable Republicans backed the new tariffs, taking a political gamble in an election where commodity prices and especially gasoline prices are front and center. Forcing China and India to buy oil from non-Russian suppliers could add further demand to a market where supply has been constrained due to the US war in Iran.

“Do not let the perfect be the enemy of the good,” Pennsylvania Republican Brian Fitzpatrick, an ardent supporter of Ukraine, said on the House floor, adding that the US has an obligation to support Ukrainians fighting on the front line. Fitzpatrick is facing a tough reelection fight due to concerns about inflation spurred on by Trump’s existing tariffs.

Ukraine President Volodomyr Zelenskyy is looking to secure a meeting with Trump on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly next week in New York, after a string of US official correspondence with Moscow has thrown into doubt whether the US will pressure Putin to end the war — or keep up efforts to constrain Ukraine’s attacks on Russian energy facilities that the US has blamed for a global surge in diesel prices.

Denys Sienik, Ukraine’s Chargé D’Affaires, Tuesday night at an independence day celebration in Washington, thanked pro-Ukraine lawmakers “for every vote you cast in support of Ukraine, in support of freedom.”

Whether the administration would actually use the new powers to boost pressure on Iran or Russia remains unclear. The White House negotiated broad waivers in the bill that give the president wide discretion not to impose penalties.

The bill allows the president to impose a blanket tariff of 500% on Russian goods imported to the US and an additional 100% tariff on the top five energy importers and countries that import Russian crude oil or natural gas, or that facilitate sanctions evasion. The new tariff authority expires after five years.

The bill would also extend the Iran Sanctions Act of 1996 through 2031, preventing a potential lapse in authority. That law imposes secondary economic sanctions on non-US companies doing business with Iran and was meant to expire this year.

items.title: Petrobras Expands African Oil Hunt With Ivory Coast Blocks
body: Brazil’s state-controlled oil company Petrobras SA signed production-sharing contracts for eight exploratory offshore blocks in Ivory Coast, its latest move to expand its footprint in Africa.

Chief Executive Officer Magda Chambriard had flagged the deal at an event on Wednesday, saying the ultra-deepwater blocks would help expand Petrobras’s exploration portfolio as the company seeks to replenish reserves ahead of an expected production peak around 2035.
“There is no future for an oil company without exploration,” she said during a lecture in Rio de Janeiro.

Petrobras will hold a 90% operating stake in the blocks, while PETROCI Holding, Ivory Coast’s state oil company, will keep the remaining 10%, according to a Thursday filing. The agreement will give Petrobras a stake in exploration areas with significant potential along Africa’s equatorial margin, the company said in the filing.

Latin America’s biggest oil producer has increasingly looked beyond Brazil’s prolific pre-salt fields for new exploration opportunities, targeting overseas areas where it can apply decades of expertise in deepwater drilling and production.

Petrobras will need to add about 9 billion barrels of oil equivalent to its reserves through 2050 to maintain current production levels as output from the pre-salt is expected to peak around the middle of the next decade, Chambriard said.
Read More: TotalEnergies Expands Energy Hunt in Africa Drilling Hotspot
In August Ghana’s Ministry of Energy and Green Transition approved Petrobras’s application to negotiate exploration contracts for four blocks.

Petrobras had already partnered with TotalEnergies SE to acquire a 42.5% stake in an offshore block in Namibia - where Chambriard said the acquisitions were “not enough” - and joined the Deep Western Orange Basin project in South Africa. It has also acquired minority stakes in three of Shell PLC’s blocks in Sao Tome and Principe.

items.title: Apple, OpenAI and Qualcomm Leaders to Attend Trump-Xi Dinner
body: Apple Inc. Executive Chairman Tim Cook and OpenAI Chief Executive Officer Sam Altman are poised to attend a White House state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping next week.

A person familiar with the matter said that Cook would be at the event, which US President Donald Trump is holding in Washington. OpenAI, maker of ChatGPT, confirmed that Altman was attending. The White House didn’t immediately comment.
The executives are expected to join other business leaders at the dinner, including Nvidia Corp. CEO Jensen Huang, Bloomberg News has reported.
Read More: Nvidia CEO Set to Attend Trump Dinner With Chinese President

The summit comes at a delicate moment for US-Chinese relations — and the artificial intelligence industry. Geopolitical tensions are simmering over the AI race, international trade and the Middle East. Trump said earlier this week that he maintains a “great relationship” with Xi.

AI leaders, meanwhile, are grappling with whether to slow development of the technology in the face of potential threats to humanity. OpenAI has disclosed a series of incidents by its AI agents, including a breach of startup Hugging Face.

Cook stepped down from the CEO job at Apple on Sept. 1. In the new role of executive chairman, he plans to remain involved with government relations, including dealings with the White House and China.
Read More: Apple’s Tim Cook Takes On Crucial New Role: Global Ambassador
CNBC previously reported that Altman was slated to attend the dinner.

items.title: Generac Shares Jump on $8 Billion Amazon Data Center Pact
body: Generac Holdings Inc. agreed to supply up to $8 billion worth of generators for Amazon.com Inc.’s data centers and issued a warrant for a stake in the company, according to a Wednesday securities filing. Generac shares jumped as much as 45% in after-market trading on the news.

The arrangement is the latest example of a tech giant striking a warrant-linked deal with a power equipment supplier to keep up with artificial intelligence-driven electricity demand. Oracle took a similar stake in fuel-cell maker Bloom Energy in April 2026.
Read More: Oracle Agrees to Buy Power From Bloom for AI Data Centers

Generac, a Wisconsin-based maker of backup power generators, disclosed it signed the long-term supply agreement with Amazon on Wednesday. Initial deliveries of backup generators to the Seattle-based tech company are expected to total $2.4 billion in 2027 and 2028.
The power company granted a warrant to an Amazon subsidiary to purchase as much as 2.6% of Generac common stock at an exercise price of $200.9266 a share. The warrant runs seven years, through 2033.

items.title: Stocks, Bonds Rise After Fed-Day Drop as Oil Falls: Markets Wrap
body: Treasuries pared losses as Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh’s resolve to tackle inflation calmed markets following the central bank’s first interest-rate increase since 2023. Oil extended its decline.

The yield on the rate-sensitive two-year US note fell two basis points to 4.72% after climbing to the highest since 2024 in the prior session. Yields on the benchmark 10-year and the 30-year bonds both dropped by three basis points. Asian bonds reversed earlier losses and tracked Treasuries higher.

Elsewhere, the Bloomberg Asia Dollar Index dropped 0.2%, while a gauge of the US currency held around a one-month high. The moves came after Warsh struck a hawkish tone, saying the rate increase “removed a dose of accommodation.”
Money markets priced in about a 50% chance of another Fed hike in October.

Elsewhere, gold, which typically loses its appeal as rates rise, held its losses from the previous session, trading around $4,280 an ounce. Crude oil extended its drop with global benchmark Brent falling over 1% to near $104.30 a barrel. President Donald Trump also said the Iran war will end soon.

Asian stocks swung between small gains and losses, while equity-index futures for the S&P 500 Index and the Nasdaq 100 Index climbed over 0.5%. Earlier, Wall Street traders drove stocks to the lowest since July on bets the Fed will keep raising rates to combat inflation.

“The Fed had no choice but to give the market a hike or risk a much bigger bond market selloff, which is shown in the 12-0 vote,” wrote Byron Anderson, head of fixed income at Laffer Tengler Investments. “The Fed is trying to calm the bond market rather than signaling a hiking cycle.”

The Federal Open Market Committee voted unanimously to lift the benchmark rate by a quarter percentage point to a range of 3.75% to 4%. The Fed’s so-called dot plot, which shows policymakers’ projections for the path of interest rates, indicated one more increase this year.

Investors are now weighing how quickly the Fed may tighten further as inflation pressures persist. Its projections point to another hike this year, putting upcoming economic data in focus ahead of the October meeting. Attention now turns to policy decisions in the UK on Thursday and Japan on Friday.

“The committee removed references to inflation being driven by supply shocks, suggesting policymakers are increasingly focused on broader and more persistent inflation pressures rather than viewing recent price increases as largely transitory or externally driven,” said Daniel Siluk, portfolio manager at Janus Henderson Investors.
In other corners of the market, oil retreated on signs that some recent Middle East supply disruptions are easing, with traders also adjusting positions after a blistering rally.

Brent fell as much as 5% on Wednesday as Saudi Arabia sought to restore about half the capacity of its East-West pipeline within days after drone strikes forced its closure last week. Also, President Trump said the Iran war will end “very soon.”

Warsh reinforced the inflation-fighting message he delivered at Jackson Hole last month. Speaking to reporters Wednesday, he said too many categories of goods and services were showing annualized price gains above 3% over six- and 12-month periods.
President Donald Trump said on social media after the decision that US interest rates should be at 1% or lower, though he stopped short of directly criticizing Warsh.

Wednesday’s move may mark the start of a broader tightening cycle, with both policymakers and traders anticipating at least one more increase this year. Attention is now shifting to the timing and pace of further moves.

“History is clear that once the Fed begins raising rates, they do it multiple times,” said Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer at Northlight Asset Management. “But the pattern is less clear about whether they will raise rates at consecutive meetings or leave rates unchanged” at some of them.

items.title: Oil Drops as Traders See Supply Outages Proving Short-Lived
body: Oil fell for a second day on signs that supply disruptions in the Middle East are set to ease, with a key pipeline being restored.

Brent dropped below $105 a barrel after losing 2.7% on Wednesday, while West Texas Intermediate was near $101. Saudi Arabia is seeking to return about half the capacity of its damaged East-West pipeline within days, and full operations in six weeks, a person familiar with the matter said.

“I wouldn’t call it an all-clear situation,” said Haris Khurshid, chief investment officer at Karobaar Capital LP. “The market is getting some capacity back, but it isn’t getting its margin for error back.”

Crude has rallied by about three-quarters this year, as the US-Iran war cut Middle East flows and the Russia-Ukraine conflict drags on. Surging oil and fuel costs have fanned global inflationary pressures, prompting the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates on Wednesday and signal more tightening.

The East-West pipeline — which carries oil across Saudi Arabia to its Red Sea coast — was damaged in attacks last week, boosting prices. The conduit has emerged as a vital workaround to shipments going via the Strait of Hormuz, which remains contested by Washington and Tehran.

Estimates vary for volumes going through Hormuz, which links the Persian Gulf to global markets. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright told Fox Business 18 million barrels of crude and products went through one day earlier this week, and the seven-day average was 11 million barrels a day. Meanwhile, Clarksons Research has put the daily figure at about 8 million barrels.

President Donald Trump is set to meet with Persian Gulf leaders next Tuesday in New York on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly to discuss the next steps in the conflict, Axios reported, citing people with knowledge of the plan.
The war will end “very soon,” Trump said at a campaign event in North Carolina. “We could have a deal any time we want,” he added.

Also in the US, Congress gave final approval to a bill to hand Trump new powers to impose tariffs on countries buying Russian petroleum products, potentially including China and India. The legislation, which goes to the president’s desk for his signature, has been celebrated by Ukrainian officials eager for signs of Washington’s support in its fight against Moscow’s invasion.

Kyiv has for months been targeting Russian refineries with waves of drone attacks. That has prompted Moscow to ban most exports of diesel to prioritize local supplies, and officials are considering extending the curb through October. US retail prices of the industrial fuel have advanced to a record.

items.title: Nuclear Power Services Firm Holtec Postpones Planned US IPO
body: Holtec Nuclear Corp., a supplier of specialty services to the nuclear power industry, postponed a planned US initial public offering which was expected to price Thursday.

The Camden, New Jersey-based firm cited market conditions and said it would continue to evaluate the timing of the offering in the future, according to an emailed statement confirming an earlier Bloomberg News report.
The company had been seeking to raise as much as $900 million in the IPO, offering 50 million shares for $15 to $18 each, according to earlier filings with the US Securities and Exchange Commission.

Holtec makes steel and concrete casks used to store nuclear waste, and is the main US company involved in decommissioning shuttered reactors including Indian Point north of New York City. It’s also developing its own reactor technology, with the aim of having its reactors in commission in the early 2030s. The company received funding from the US Department of Energy last year.

Nuclear energy has been seeing increased interest as artificial intelligence data centers look for ways to meet their growing power needs. But with small modular reactors still not commercially available in the US, some nuclear stocks have pulled back as investors await development progress.
Standard Nuclear Inc. went public in July in a downsized US IPO and closed 21% below its listing price on Wednesday. X-Energy Inc., which went public in April, has fallen 37% below its IPO price.

Holtec had net income of $205.6 million on revenue of $269.9 million for the six months ended June 30, compared with net income of $139.1 million on revenue of $286.6 million a year prior, according to its filings.
The offering was being led by JPMorgan Chase & Co., Guggenheim Securities, Goldman Sachs Group Inc., Citigroup Inc. and Bank of America Corp.
