items.title: Fed Raises Rates in Unanimous Vote: Evening Briefing Americas
body: In a unanimous vote, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates by a quarter percentage point and penciled in an additional hike later this year, steps aimed at containing rising inflation that’s been fueled in part by a global energy crisis triggered by the US-Israel war with Iran.

It was the central bank’s first rate increase since July 2023. In remarks to reporters, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh repeated that he was concerned about inflation, stepping away from sometimes contradictory signals he gave over the summer. He declined to answer questions about President Donald Trump, however, who appointed him amid a year-long White House campaign to get the Fed to lower interest rates.
Saudi Arabia is said to be seeking to return about half the capacity of its cross-country oil pipeline within days after the link was halted following drone attacks.

State-run Saudi Aramco is working to bypass a damaged section on the route that will allow it to resume part of the pipeline’s capacity and full capability in about six weeks. The 1,200-kilometer East-West line that stretches the breadth of the Arabian Peninsula was shut on Thursday after drone attacks launched by militias in Iraq. Saudi Arabia has also faced a series of strikes on energy and civilian infrastructure from the Yemen-based Houthi militants this month on its western Red Sea coast.
Microsoft artificial intelligence chief Mustafa Suleyman is warning that infusing tools like Anthropic’s Claude with humanlike characteristics increases the risks of such systems going rogue.

In an essay released on Wednesday, the longtime AI developer took aim at some of the language in the guiding documents behind Claude, Anthropic’s popular family of large language models. Claude’s constitution expresses ambiguity about whether the assistant is a moral entity, positing that the software may have “some functional version of emotions or feelings.”

To soften the blow from the US trade war, Canada may need to boost economic ties with other parts of the world. Prime Minister Mark Carney has made it clear he wants a closer relationship with the European Union.

But European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s offer to make Canada an “associate member” of the world’s most powerful trading bloc went further than many had expected. The relationship would be a new one — created to meet a unique moment — and the EU has yet to define its parameters. So what does it really mean?

The Clarity Act was supposed to deliver the next catalyst for a battered crypto market whose adherents were pinning their hopes on a rescue out of Washington. The breakthrough never materialized and the industry is now dealing with growing headwinds.

Bitcoin has sold off and crypto bellwethers including Coinbase Global and Circle Internet Group sank as well after the Senate failed to advance the bill on Tuesday. The hoped for pillar of support crumbled at a time when retail-investor interest has waned and higher interest rates and tighter liquidity have weighed on the market.

Foreign holdings of US Treasuries fell in July to the lowest level since October, led by declines in the stockpiles of France and Canada. Overseas holdings dropped by $50.4 billion from June, according to data published by the Treasury Department on Wednesday. The total now stands at $9.25 trillion.

Japan, the biggest foreign holder of Treasuries, saw a $12.8 billion drop in its holdings, to $1.1 trillion. The month of July included action by Japanese authorities to prop up the yen. More recent figures from Japan’s Finance Ministry indicated that Tokyo likely sold a portion of its holdings of foreign securities to help fund its yen intervention moves.

items.title: Le Pen Leaves Door Open to No-Confidence Vote Over 2027 Budget
body: Marine Le Pen, the French far-right leader and presidential candidate, kept open the possibility of censuring the government over the 2027 budget, while at the same time pledging not to take action that could damage the country’s strained finances.

“We will do nothing that could worsen France’s situation, particularly its budgetary situation,” Le Pen, who polls show is the leading candidate in next spring’s presidential vote, said in an interview with LCI TV that was broadcast on Wednesday night.

But Le Pen, the leader of the National Rally party in the National Assembly, ruled “nothing out,” including a no-confidence vote against the government of Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, given that she disagrees with many of his budget policies.

France’s economic outlook has deteriorated sharply in recent months as the Iran war led to a surge in energy prices, deadly heat waves curtailed agricultural production and political uncertainty weighed on investment.
Earlier: French Premier Survives Censure Votes Over 2035 Energy Roadmap

With the presidential election less than eight months away, opposition lawmakers have signaled they are unwilling to compromise with President Emmanuel Macron. But the government has also argued that it’s not in the interest of any presidential candidate to touch off another budget crisis that would hobble them if they win next May.

Le Pen reiterated pledges to lower the value added tax, cut government spending and French contributions to the European Union drastically, along with plans to limit immigration and financing for foreigners.

She added that, if elected, she would hold a referendum on a ban on wearing a Muslim veil in public places and seek to limit freedom of movement in the countries that make up the Schengen Area to citizens of European Union members.

items.title: Virginia's Data Center Alley Moves to Pause New Applications
body: A county in the heart of northern Virginia’s Data Center Alley advanced a measure that would pause the review of new data centers and substation applications for up to 12 months as a wave of similar such suspensions sweeps the country.
Loudoun County has the world’s largest concentration of data centers, with 233 facilities either built or under construction as of March, according to the county’s website.

Roughly 13 applications that have been submitted to the county but not yet gone through planning commission review could be impacted by the pause, Loudoun Board of Supervisors member Juli Briskman said.
Read More: Residents Are Surrounded in World’s Data Center Capital

The proposal, which was supported by seven of the nine board members, will be drafted into an official resolution to be voted on in an October meeting. The board would resume reviewing applications once they have finalized new zoning regulations in 2027.
Loudoun’s data center boom has generated 17,000 jobs and will help net a projected $1.3 billion in local tax revenue for the 2027 fiscal year, according to the county.

But rapid expansion has been met with opposition from residents, who argue development has negatively affected their quality of life and want the county to tighten regulations in order to better control growth. Among the worries, residents are complaining about noise, proximity to homes and the amount of electrical infrastructure that goes through their backyards.
It’s a tension that’s playing out across the country, as more than 300 moratoriums have been enacted locally according to a tracking website by Interconnected Capital LLC.
“They feel like they’re up to their eyeballs in issues with data centers,” Briskman said of how residents are feeling. “The community has been begging us to do this.”

items.title: US Tracking Cyber Threats Against Nearly 20 Ships Worldwide
body: US government agencies are tracking cyber threats against nearly 20 shipping vessels around the world, according to US officials familiar with the situation.

The Coast Guard has asked for advance notice if any of those ships plan to come into a US port, said the three people, who asked not to be identified because they aren’t authorized to speak publicly about the matter. The vessels’ specific destinations and manifests weren’t immediately known.

Several commercial vessels were targeted in potential cyberattacks in late August, one official at the federal Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency said, noting that hackers didn’t appear to have taken control of the targeted ships themselves. The Coast Guard is now tracking the vessels alongside FBI and Department of Homeland Security units, a Homeland Security official said.
Read More: US Coast Guard and FBI Conduct Cyberattack Probes on Tankers

Warnings about cyberattacks targeting the maritime sector have escalated in recent years with shipping vessels becoming increasingly dependent on digital systems for navigation, communications and other operations. Governments and security researchers have repeatedly cautioned that hackers are seeking to exploit those systems to disrupt supply chains. The cyber risks are plaguing a global shipping industry already under strain from wars and geopolitical rivalries.

The US Coast Guard said in a statement that it boarded two inbound foreign-flagged commercial vessels in the Gulf of Mexico to “ensure integrity of the vessel’s operational and information technology systems following indications that the networks of both vessels were compromised.” The first vessel was boarded on Aug. 21 to mitigate threats and the second on Aug. 24.

“Currently, there are no reports of operational disruptions, vessel instability, physical danger to crews, or environmental impacts,” the Coast Guard said, adding that it’s actively communicating with port operators, vessel owners and other stakeholders.

Antonio Cassidy, director of services at London-based maritime cybersecurity firm CyberOwl, said he hadn’t seen any indication of a broader hacking campaign targeting oil and gas tankers. But CyberOwl, which monitors cybersecurity on vessels, had observed a sharp increase in the number of incidents on ships in the first half of this year, Cassidy said.

In the case of more than half of the attempted intrusions that CyberOwl detected on the vessels it tracks, malware had been introduced to the vessels’ computers through storage devices, according to a company report. Most of the others came by way of an internet download or phishing.

In December, European investigators suspected Russian military hackers may have been behind a possible cyberattack on a vessel owned by MSC Mediterranean Shipping Co. The ferry, operated by MSC’s Grandi Navi Veloci unit, was immobilized in the southern French port of Sete as it prepared to sail to Algeria, Bloomberg reported at the time.

In March 2025, a hacker group calling itself Lab Dookhtegan claimed responsibility for cyberattacks that disrupted communications systems on more than 100 Iranian oil tankers, according to the cybersecurity firm Cydome.

Operational systems such as those inside ships are particularly vulnerable to cyberattacks because they contain old equipment that can’t easily be updated, said Maria Bartnes, cybersecurity research program director at Norwegian cybersecurity company DNV. They were created at a time when the prospect of a cyberattack was less likely, she said.
The intrusions, she said, were likely as much about creating insecurity and instability as they were intended to cause actual damage.
“That is part of the warfare,” she said, “making the enemy unsure about what is going on. For the state, for politicians, for the people on board the vessels — it can affect everyone.”

items.title: Fed Raises Interest Rates, Bucking Trump's Push for a Cut
body: Good morning. The Federal Reserve raises interest rates, bucking Trump. A Microsoft executive says human-like AI is a bad idea. And an AI-detection tool fights to gain our trust. Listen to the day’s top stories.

The Federal Reserve voted unanimously to raise rates by a quarter-point and penciled in an additional hike later this year, testing Chair Kevin Warsh’s relationship with Donald Trump, who has clamored for a cut. Traders are now fully pricing in three more hikes by the middle of next year. Two-year Treasury yields hit the highest since 2024, while the S&P 500 slipped.

Beijing is considering including BYD in a business delegation at Xi Jinping’s summit with Trump in Washington, according to people familiar. That would be a provocative move: The US has imposed 100% tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles and accused the carmaker of having links to the People’s Liberation Army. BYD denies supporting the Chinese military.

SK Hynix is exploring options to boost its global competitiveness after a report that it may work with Intel to make semiconductors in the US. Reuters had said the chipmaker may lease part of ‌Intel’s long-planned Ohio facility or form a venture with the company and major cloud computing firms. The South Korean firm said no decision has been made.

Buyout firm EQT is planning to spend $50 billion in India by 2030, including a significant investment in Gautam Adani’s data-center business. The bulk — around $30 billion — will go to data centers, with another $5 billion devoted to renewable energy to power them, the Stockholm-based firm’s chair said. EQT has invested $26 billion in India since 1998.

Saudi Arabia is looking to resume about half the capacity of a key oil pipeline within days after last week’s drone attacks, a person familiar with the matter said. The Middle East conflict and prospect of tighter US restrictions on Russian crude purchases are creating the most significant supply uncertainty in months for Indian state-owned refiners.

Microsoft’s artificial intelligence chief warned that infusing tools like Anthropic’s Claude with humanlike characteristics increases the risk of AI going rogue, and pushed back on the idea that it may become conscious.

Restricting imports of Chinese-made EVs but allowing unfettered trade in batteries may be congenial for Europe’s carmakers, but it’s no way to support manufacturing, writes David Fickling. The goal should be to build European battery champions without trying to exclude Asian companies whose expertise can help them along.

The makers of artificial-intelligence detection tool Pangram said it can identify AI-generated text with near-perfect accuracy. The harder task is persuading people to trust it.

items.title: Brazil Cuts Interest Rates to 13.75% Before Tight Presidential Election
body: Leia em português

Brazil’s central bank cut its interest rate by a quarter-point as inflation slows and the economy fades, just weeks before a tight presidential election that is fueling uncertainty over how much more policymakers can ease.

Board members led by Gabriel Galípolo lowered the benchmark Selic to 13.75% on Wednesday in a unanimous decision that was expected by all economists surveyed by Bloomberg. The reduction, which was the first on the eve of elections in 20 years, brought total easing since March to 125 basis points.

“The current scenario, marked by heightened uncertainty, deanchoring of expectations, and elevated risks surrounding the reference scenario, requires serenity and cautiousness in the conduct of monetary policy,” central bankers wrote in a statement accompanying the decision. “The Committee will continue to monitor developments in the scenario in order to keep monetary policy adequately restrictive to ensure convergence to the inflation target.”

Brazilians will head to the polls with surveys showing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in a virtual tie with right-wing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro. The tight race has investors focused on how the candidates would tackle rising public debt and spending. Any deterioration in perceptions of Brazil’s fiscal outlook could weaken the real and add to inflation pressures, making it harder for the central bank to keep cutting rates even as the economy softens.
Read More: Lula Must Fix Fiscal Woes If Reelected, Finance Chief Says

The decision came hours after the Federal Reserve raised its interest rates by a quarter-point and penciled in an additional hike later this year. Prospects of borrowing cost rises in the US have boosted the dollar against other currencies worldwide, posing another potential consumer price risk for Brazil.

“There are elements of uncertainty ahead, including the election and US interest rates,” said Leonardo Costa, an economist at ASA. “But the most likely scenario remains another rate cut at the next meeting” in November.

In the central bank statement, which was nearly identical to the communique published with the prior decision in August, policymakers said headline and underlying inflation have slowed, though they still remain above the 3% target.

Consumer prices rose 4.22% in August from a year earlier, below the 4.27% median estimate in a Bloomberg survey. The cost of living fell 0.32% from the previous month, the national statistics agency reported on Sept. 11.
Brazil’s central bank sees annual inflation at 3.2% in the first quarter of 2028, which is currently its relevant horizon for monetary policy.

There are mounting signs Brazil’s economy is cooling. The country created 58,568 formal jobs in July, the lowest monthly figure so far this year. Defaults on personal loans climbed that month to the highest level since 2009, weighing on consumption.
Overall economic activity fell 0.22% in July from the previous month, marking a second straight decline, the central bank reported earlier Wednesday.
“The set of indicators released since the last meeting shows a gradual moderation of economic activity, particularly in more cyclical sectors, albeit at a resilient level,” policymakers wrote.
The first round of Brazil’s presidential election is set for Oct. 4, with a runoff likely three weeks later.

Still, those votes are not the only source of uncertainty. The conflict in Iran remains unresolved, keeping oil prices volatile, while severe weather associated with El Niño poses risks to food costs.

“Global shocks have intensified,” said Caio Megale, chief economist at XP Inc. “And the domestic fiscal outlook is unclear - bear in mind that tonight’s was the last policy decision before the presidential elections.”

items.title: Canada's Carney to Reply After EU's Von der Leyen Proposes Associate Membership
body: Welcome back to Canada Daily, the newsletter on business, economics and politics from Vancouver to Montreal and beyond. If this was forwarded to you, sign up.
Canada and Europe have a status update: they are taking their relationship to the next level.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed that Canada become the first associate member of the European Union. Prime Minister Mark Carney will have the opportunity to respond when he addresses the European Parliament on Thursday.
Neither leader has spelled out exactly what the new label might mean for Canadians and Europeans. More labor mobility? Educational opportunities? Political cooperation? Maybe.
But what’s clear is that many Canadians — who feel their country’s relationship with the US has grown toxic — are ready to shake things up and try something new.

“I think Canadians have come to the conclusion that we need to look for other partners and other relationships given that ours with the United States has, for some, completely ruptured and may never go back to the way it was,” said Abacus Data CEO David Coletto.
A recent Abacus poll found 8 out of 10 Canadians support deeper integration, and about one half are in favor of full EU membership.
More than half of respondents said Canada has more in common with countries in the European Union than the US, and only 16% believe the opposite is true.
But Conservatives aren’t so hot on the idea of cozying up to the EU.

“Conservatives are clear: we support the decades-old free trade & NATO defense alliance with Europe. But no EU taxes, no EU laws, and no EU open-border immigration policies should be imposed on Canadians,” Conservative  Leader Pierre Poilievre said on social media.
Now, Canadians wait to learn whether this is just a flirtation — or the start of something serious.
Also in this newsletter: The Bank of Canada warns rate hikes may be on the horizon. New aluminum tariffs threaten to wipe out US sales. Record-high diesel prices come at the worst time.
The following was produced with the assistance of Bloomberg Automation.

Canada’s aluminum fabricators say their sales to the US will get wiped out as the Trump administration’s latest tariff measures make their products uncompetitive south of the border. Aluminum products are among the items the hit by new 50% levies. The latest move ends tariff exemptions for some goods made with the lightweight metal. “Our US business is dead,” one industry executive said.

The Bank of Canada warned of the risk it may need to hike interest rates, saying the longer gasoline prices remain elevated, the more likely those costs will affect other goods and services. Policymakers held the benchmark rate at 2.25% for a seventh consecutive time on Sept. 2 but made some hawkish comments. In a summary of deliberations for that decision, officials expanded on their worries: “If higher energy prices did spill over into other components of the CPI, members agreed that it could require a monetary policy response.”

Separating from Canada would cause significant economic damage to Alberta, and it would take years to recover, according to a study commissioned by the provincial government. The report, which comes a little more than a month before citizens vote on whether to hold a referendum on independence, said any secession process would dent gross domestic product by at least 2.2% in the first five years in a good scenario, or more than 10% in a poor one.

The Federal Reserve raised interest rates by a quarter percentage point and penciled in an additional hike later this year, steps aimed at containing inflation that will test Chairman Kevin Warsh’s relationship with President Donald Trump. The Federal Open Market Committee voted unanimously to increase the benchmark federal funds rate to a range of 3.75% to 4% on Wednesday. Yields on short-dated US Treasuries rose alongside the US dollar.

Venezuela is preparing to ship aluminum to the US under a deal with Mercuria Energy Group and Heeney Capital, diversifying beyond oil in a quickening revival of commercial ties following years of economic and diplomatic isolation. The modest aluminum cargo, the first bound for the US in years, is comprised of about 15,000 metric tons produced by state-owned Venalum.

Oil retreated on indications that some of the recent supply outages in the Middle East are beginning to resolve and traders adjust positions after a blistering rally over recent sessions. Brent slipped to settle near $106 a barrel, and West Texas Intermediate fell more than 3%, as Saudi Arabia seeks to return about half the capacity of its East-West pipeline within days after shutting the conduit last week because of drone strikes.
The S&P/TSX Composite Index fell 0.3%, dragged lower by energy and industrial stocks. Consumer stocks rose, led by Dollarama.

Record-high diesel prices are coming at the worst possible time for Iowa farmer Kinser Jensen. He’d held off buying diesel after the cost skyrocketed at the beginning of the Iran war, hoping prices would recede. But harvest is just weeks away, and with it the heavy fuel demands involved in bringing in the crop. Diesel is only getting more expensive. “At some point here, I’m just going to have to pull the trigger and buy the fuel,” said Jensen, who runs a 3,400-acre corn and soybean farm. The costs of diesel and home heating oil have surged faster than gasoline in recent months, particularly hammering states that are critical battlegrounds in November’s US midterm congressional elections.

items.title: Calpers CEO Notches $1 Milllion Bonus As Returns Beat Target
body: California Public Employees’ Retirement System voted Wednesday to give its chief executive officer a $1.1 million bonus and a salary bump, even as state workers fight for higher pay.

The board of the largest public pension fund in the US voted eight to two, with two abstentions, to boost CEO Marcie Frost’s bonus by 43% from last year. She will also earn the top salary allowed in the current fiscal year, with base pay increasing to $641,250, up from $601,398.
The pay bump comes after Calpers notched an annual return of 14.8%, beating the pension’s 6.8% annual target.

Calpers President Theresa Taylor said the pay increase was well-earned given that the pension system’s funding level has risen to 85%, up from 65% a decade ago, when Frost took over as the organization’s head.
“Marcie Frost is a CEO on top of her game and delivering excellent results for Calpers members,” Taylor said.

California is continuing a trend of providing top talent at its retirement funds’ pay packages that extend from six figures into seven figures. But the increase comes at a turbulent time for state government workers contributing to the $653 billion pension system. Governor Gavin Newsom has ordered state employees back to in-office work, reducing remote work for many, and a major union representing California government workers is considering a strike.
Read More: California’s 90,000-Worker Office Return Sets Up Union Clash

Two Calpers board members voted against the bonus, including a representative for state controller Malia Cohen, who cited concerns about the state’s budget outlook and the prospect of deficits in future years.

Retired Public Employees’ Association of California also opposed the payout, arguing the bonus is structured to provide a major payout for Calpers executives, meeting benchmarks the advocacy group contends are too low.
“Bonuses should reward exceptional performance, not merely doing the job you were hired to do,” Margaret Brown, the group’s president, said in a statement.

The bonus is apportioned based on the CEO’s salary and her performance, as well as the system’s performance, against various metrics approved by the board. Last year, the board voted to increase the range of the CEO’s bonus, allowing Frost to receive incentive-based pay that would total up to 150% of her salary for meeting expectations, up from 100%. They also raised the maximum bonus to 225% of salary, from 150%.

items.title: Exxon Is in Talks to Return to Venezuela as Deals Accelerate
body: ExxonMobil Holdings Corp. held talks this week with Venezuela’s government about re-entering the country as the Texas oil giant explores whether to follow US rivals back into the home of the world’s largest reserves.

Executives flew to Caracas Tuesday night for negotiations, aiming to secure access to several fields rich with heavy oil, according to people familiar with the matter. While talks have been ongoing for months, ExxonMobil is proceeding cautiously as executives consider investing in a country where it had its assets nationalized twice since the 1970s, said the people who asked not to be identified because the discussions are private.

The company is interested in retaking control of two giant fields it previously held in the Orinoco Belt — Petrovictoria and Petromonagas — before they were nationalized by former President Hugo Chávez in the mid-2000s, some of the people said. The company also wants to secure rights to two additional fields in the nearby Carabobo region, they said.

A return to Venezuela by ExxonMobil would mark a major step in US President Donald Trump’s effort to revive the nation’s oil sector since ousting former leader Nicolás Maduro. The supermajor would bring significant capital and expertise to rebuild battered infrastructure while signaling increased confidence in Venezuela’s investment climate.

There is no guarantee the talks will lead to a deal. Negotiations between ExxonMobil and Venezuela have been on and off for months, with progress stymied by long delays in communication, according to some people familiar with the matter.
An ExxonMobil spokesman declined to comment.

Trump administration is pushing hard for US companies to make deals with Venezuela to revive production. Continental Resources Inc., the privately-owned US producer controlled by billionaire Harold Hamm, announced an agreement Wednesday to enter Venezuela while Chevron Corp., Eni SpA and several others have announced their own deals in recent weeks.

ExxonMobil Chief Executive Officer Darren Woods called Venezuela currently “uninvestable” in January to the chagrin of Trump. Woods added, however, that the country had the potential to create the right investment conditions with help from Washington.
Significant challenges remain.

While Chevron remained in Venezuela after the nationalizations and during sanctions, ExxonMobil is not currently operating any oil fields in the country, meaning any new investment would require significant capital. There’s no guarantee Trump’s Venezuela policy will outlast his presidency. And there are substantial questions about the durability of the fiscal and regulatory reforms Venezuela has implemented to attract foreign oil companies.
“You can imagine to re-enter a third time would require some pretty significant changes,” Woods told US President Donald Trump at the White House meeting in January.
More recently, Woods said ExxonMobil’s expertise in Canadian heavy crude could provide a competitive advantage in Venezuela, where oil has a similar viscosity.
“The work on heavy oil, the technology developments we’ve been making, I think positions us uniquely in terms of low-cost production of the Venezuelan resources,” he said in May.
ExxonMobil already has the dominant position in neighboring Guyana, home to the fastest-growing oil fields in the world.

The deal Chevron signed with Venezuela earlier this month calls for the company to double its production there to more than 600,000 barrels a day by the early 2030s. It would require about $7 billion of investment, though the company plans to fund it from existing cash flow from its current Venezuela operations rather than investing fresh outside capital, Chief Executive Officer Mike Wirth said last week.

items.title: California's Gavin Newsom Does Something Right
body: This is Bloomberg Opinion Today, a screen-based recess for Bloomberg Opinion’s opinions. Sign up here.

“I have no experience in this process, so I’m going through it,” was California Governor Gavin Newsom’s answer when Jake Tapper asked him how a person would even decide to run for president. But you’d be forgiven for thinking he was talking about fly fishing — the activity the two bumbled through during a long-form CNN interview.

“Who the hell fly fishes in dress pants?!” one commenter wrote on YouTube. “This is the worst fly fishing cosplay I have ever seen. Jake is cracking the whip on every back cast and Newsom is laying his reel in the muck to untangle his line,” said another.

I’ve fly-fished exactly once — in a drift boat, not waders. Not only did I lose countless flies trying to mend upstream, I somehow broke the rod while trying to reel in a brown trout. So I have zero authority to opine on such matters. But with the help of Erika D. Smith, I can at least opine on Newsom’s political skills, which are sharper than his fishing.

During the interview, Newsom told Tapper he wouldn’t run for president in 2028 if former Vice President Kamala Harris mounted a third bid. Erika says the concession “blew more than a few minds” and sparked some questions. Does Newsom want an off-ramp? Or is this his way of forcing Harris to announce she doesn’t plan to run? Regardless, Erika called it a “shrewd political calculation.”

As she puts it, “Newsom essentially just did the entire Democratic Party a solid by trying to resolve a potential pileup of California candidates before it becomes a problem. Already, there’s a good chance another Californian, Representative Ro Khanna, will jump into the race. Add Newsom and Harris to the mix, and it would be political cannibalism.”

Why does it matter? Well, America is not California. A lot of people look at the state and don’t like what they see: maxed-out diesel prices, hazmat-grade homeless camps, corrupt infrastructure projects, struggling vegan eateries, severe weather events (water humps, anyone?) ... the list goes on. The knock-on effects of those problems are tough to ignore. Liam Denning says the state’s electric utilities are now virtually uninvestable thanks to the elongated wildfire season. Newsom attempted, but failed, to curb the utilities’ wildfire liability by blocking insurers from suing them.

Of course, few people are crying for utilities. “These are large corporations that have presided over huge increases in power bills,” Liam notes. But he says California needs a robust power grid to do business.

There is one thing Newsom’s state is making progress on: banning AI in schools. And so is its progressive coastal cousin out East. Abby McCloskey says Los Angeles and New York City — two of the country’s largest school systems — are barring access to AI for students this year. “This is exactly the kind of ‘common sense’ reform that Republicans could use to define themselves heading into the midterm election,” Abby argues.

Nia-Malika Henderson agrees, calling President Donald Trump’s recent AI cheerleading a “liability” for the party. But can Democrats take advantage? “Clear policy proposals would be great, but election years are where white papers go to die,” she writes. “Acting as AI skeptics and watchdogs is much more legible to the average voter.”

Abby also highlights the hypocrisy of the moment: “For all the emphasis Republicans have put on protecting children, students in Zohran Mamdani’s New York are going to be less screen-soaked than those in Greg Abbott’s Texas — where, per my sons’ experience in the public schools, there’s many a screen-based recess.”
If only they taught these kids how to fly-fish instead.

For years now, countless newspaper cartoons, magazine covers and comedy skits have ridiculed President Donald Trump’s efforts to pack the Supreme Court with sycophants he plucked from his YOU WILL AGREE WITH ME tree. But every now and then, the justices buck expectations: On Monday, four of the six conservatives helped block a Republican plan to make it harder to vote by mail.

“It’s noteworthy that the only two justices who voted to allow the mail-in-ballot scheme to go into place were appointed by previous GOP presidents,” Noah Feldman writes. “Given that the Court has been subject to coruscating criticism for voting rights decisions that (for now) help Republicans, it’s important to recognize that Trump’s own three Supreme Court appointees remain committed to defending the procedural integrity of elections from presidential meddling.”

That’s a relief. But also: The bar is sooo low! And Noah says there’s a caveat to the ruling. “We can’t assume that the Court will never make it easier for one party or the other to gain power,” he writes. So he encourages progressives to resist the urge to try to rig the system back in their favor: “Progressive court packing, if it were ever to come to pass, would inevitably give rise to conservative court packing. The Court would gradually become a legislative body rather than a judicial one.”

The 10-year Treasury yield hasn’t been this high since Glamorous by Fergie and Ludacris was on the radio, which obviously isn’t good. As Jonathan Levin writes, “These yields aren’t easy for many people, nor are they good politics for Republicans ahead of this year’s midterms. Younger and less wealthy households are struggling to buy their first homes, with affordability near the worst in decades.” But — and there is a but! — Jonathan says the round 5% figure that rocked Wall Street yesterday is “a perfectly normal feature of a humming, if uneven, economy.” For now, there’s little reason to be truly worried.

Europe is understandably upset to see its fast-fashion darlings Zara and H&M get upstaged by sleeker, faster and cheaper competitors in Asia. But is a fee framed under the guise of environmental do-gooderism really the way to fix the issue? Probably not. Juliana Liu calls France’s recent effort to set back the likes of Shein and Temu “neither effective nor intellectually honest.” Although France doesn’t outright name China or any companies, the rationale behind the cherry-picked fast-fashion law is clear: to curb Chinese imports. “If the goal is to protect homegrown industries and jobs, the authorities should say so — and create policies that address those challenges directly,” Juliana says.
The not-so-united states of birth control.
Mamdani’s bathrooms are not for scrolling.
A Chipotle collab you didn’t see coming.
RIP, Sunny.
The $60 bread loaf is here.
Cold martinis in London and NYC.

items.title: US Plan to Boost Biofuel Exports Targets Restrictions Abroad
body: The Trump administration, following up on its efforts to boost domestic biofuels production, is taking the next step to help the industry: targeting policies abroad that limit uptake of fuels made from US crops.

The US Department of Agriculture released a plan Wednesday to boost US exports of biofuels, a growing industry crucial for soaking up the country’s bumper corn and soybean harvest. Exports of ethanol and other US-made fuels like renewable diesel have surged with higher domestic production in recent years, but the plan signals that further growth depends too on changing policies abroad.
Read More: Biofuels Are Key to Avoiding Sharp Farmland Drop, S&P Says

The report features a “Biofuels Roadmap” that including seeking to “reduce and remove restrictions placed on crop-based biofuels.” It specifically calls out the European Union, which has climate policies that encourage petroleum alternatives but cap the role of fuels made from crops.
“ACTION: Continue preventing EU influence over policies adopted by US trading partners that place limits on biofuels and correcting their misinformation campaign,” the report says.

It also says the US will continue to engage United Nations agencies developing alternative fuel policies, including the International Maritime Organization, to ensure that “other countries, like Brazil, do not design rules that shut out American biofuels.”

Other ideas include encouraging trade partners like Mexico and India to import more US ethanol and addressing implementation challenges in countries that have set but struggled to meet blend mandates.

US ethanol exports hit record highs in 2025 and were trending higher over the first half of 2026, driven by its growing use globally as a gasoline blendstock, according to a separate USDA report released this week. Rising exports reflect the US having a president “willing to do what is necessary to reach these markets,” Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said at a Tuesday event hosted by biofuels group Growth Energy.

But the ethanol industry’s increased reliance on exports in part reflects struggles boosting domestic sales. Various proposals to remove restrictions on sales of gasoline with up to 15% ethanol — so called E15 blends — have faltered in Congress this year amid backlash from oil companies.

items.title: Trump Backs Warsh, Faults 'Hostile' Fed Board for Rate Hike
body: President Donald Trump said he still had confidence in Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh and criticized what he said was a “hostile” board even after the central bank unanimously defied his calls to lower borrowing costs.
“I do, I mean I’m relying on Kevin,” Trump told reporters about his hand-picked Fed chief, speaking Wednesday in North Carolina ahead of a campaign event.
His comments came hours after the Federal Open Market Committee voted to raise rates by a quarter percentage point, increasing the benchmark federal funds rate to a range of 3.75% to 4%.

Trump told reporters Wednesday that he had spoken to Warsh, though he did not say when that conversation took place. The president said he “didn’t try to convince him,” adding “you might as well vote with the board because it’s not going to matter.”
“I said do what you want,” Trump said. “It doesn’t matter because he doesn’t have the votes,” he continued. “No matter how good a job, he’s got a hostile board.”
Despite Trump’s remarks blaming what he sees as a “very political” board for the rise, the vote to increase rates was unanimous, with all twelve in favor of the move.

Trump’s comments suggest he is willing for now to give his hand-picked chairman leeway, even as he increases pressure on the central bank to lower borrowing costs. That creates a complicated dynamic for Warsh to navigate going forward, despite Trump asserting at his swearing-in ceremony he wants the chairman to be “totally independent.”
Read more: Fed Raises Rates as Warsh Bucks Trump to Contain Inflation
In a social media post earlier Wednesday, Trump said that US rates “should be 1%, or less” because “Our Country is BOOMING with new Investment” and has “the Best Credit in the World.”
“LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!” he posted.
Driving rates down to Trump’s desired level would require the central bank to make a significant reduction, a move that typically only accompanies a severe economic crisis.

Trump in his post continued to argue that interest rates have put the US at a competitive disadvantage to other world economies, tying it to the nation’s trade deficit by saying, “We are ‘carrying’ almost every country in the World, and that cannot go on any longer.”

In the past, the president has threatened to cut off trade with partners that have a trade surplus, unless the Fed lowered rates. It’s unclear how following through on that threat would lead to lower borrowing costs for Americans.

Wednesday’s rate hike, the first since 2023, came as policymakers lost confidence inflation would cool on its own. The Fed was expected to lift interest rates after recent data showed US consumer prices rising higher than expected in August. Higher energy prices from the US war with Iran — a conflict now in its seventh month — as well as Trump’s tariff policies have clouded the picture for the Fed’s inflation targets.

Officials in their post-meeting statement characterized inflation as elevated but also described the economy in positive terms, with strong productivity growth and capital investment as well as job gains that were keeping pace with the workforce.

Warsh in his press conference pointed to geopolitical risks as contributing to inflation. “There is no hiding from hot spots around the world, and our judgment about what is the most likely, or least likely, of the geopolitical situation has changed,” he said.

Warsh has vowed to protect the Fed’s independence even as he faced mounting pressure from a president frustrated by a soured midterm political climate for his Republican Party. Voters give Trump poor marks on the war in Iran and the economy, with high prices for healthcare, housing, energy and groceries a top issue for November’s election. Lower borrowing costs could help Trump and GOP lawmakers argue that an economic boost is on the way and help limit the electoral damage.

Trump dealt harshly with Warsh’s predecessor, former Chair Jerome Powell, regularly lambasting him for not moving more aggressively to reduce rates. He’s also pressured the central bank in other ways, including trying to fire Governor Lisa Cook, a move that has been blocked so far by the Supreme Court.

items.title: Midterms Pit Republican Cash Machine Against Democratic Fury
body: I’m Nancy Cook, Bloomberg’s senior national political correspondent, and each weekday I’ll be coming to you with inside-the-room reporting and insights that reveal what’s really happening in Washington — and how it impacts you. Email me with feedback and comments here.
The midterm elections are increasingly coming down to a contest of the Republicans’ massive financial advantage versus the enthusiasm and big turnout among Democratic-leaning voters.

Voters now trust Democrats more than Republicans on a laundry list of issues: to handle the economy, health care, immigration, the deficit, cost of living and foreign wars, according to a fresh New York Times/Siena poll that should give the GOP heartburn.

Fueled by anger over President Donald Trump’s return to — and expansion of — power, Democrats also showed up in droves to vote in primaries and special elections across the spring and summer — all while swing voters, like young men, Black men and Hispanics, began to fall away from Republicans.
These two data points show Democrats could do quite well in the upcoming midterm elections, which are only 48 days away.
Yet the chief stumbling block for Democrats, honestly, is money. Republicans just have so much of it.

The Republican National Committee raked in cash during the GOP midterm convention last week through photo-ops with the president, donor presentations and VIP backstage access while Trump’s main super PAC, MAGA Inc., has about $400 million on hand. Trump advisers have started to unleash the MAGA Inc. money and money from two other super PACs on House and Senate races. Those cash infusions in places like Texas could make a major difference

In the seven Senate races rated tossups by the Cook Political Report, super PACs and other outside spenders backing Republicans have spent $147 million in the first 15 days of September compared to $40 million for Democrats, according to Federal Election Commission filings — data compiled by Bloomberg’s money and politics guru Bill Allison.

And, it’s not just the financial advantage; the party has about three times as much money that they can spend on get out the vote efforts, advertising that’s both positive and negative and direct mail sent to voters homes.

Outside GOP-aligned organizations like the Faith and Freedom Coalition (made up of evangelical voters) and Turning Point USA (geared toward young people) are expected to help with on-the-ground efforts like voters registration and door knocking. The GOP infrastructure and cash flow nevertheless is strong and gives an edge in that lane.

But already we’re seeing the Republican vulnerabilities play out on the ground, with a Senate seat in Kansas now in play given negative coverage of the GOP candidate there. I know Republicans are worried about the Senate races in Ohio and North Carolina, which are competitive or trending toward the Democrats given my conversations on the sidelines of the GOP midterm convention. Vice President JD Vance is suddenly being dispatched on Friday to Iowa where Democrats aspire to pick up a Senate seat.
Many of these are red, or swingy states where Republicans did not expect to have to compete so aggressively. The map suddenly looks wackier than anyone expected.
That’s partly because the anger and frustration over the cost of living and the war in Iran is very real — and as Trump knows, anger can be a powerful motivator.

Voters who were furious about inflation and concerned President Joe Biden’s diminished state helped bring about Trump’s victory in 2024 as he won all seven battleground states — and discontent could easily fuel a big Democratic wave in November for the same economic reasons.
It’s just a question of which is more powerful in this election season: voters’ big feelings, or lots of cash.

The Federal Reserve raised interest rates by a quarter percentage point and penciled in an additional hike later this year, steps aimed at containing inflation that will test Chairman Kevin Warsh’s relationship with Trump.
The US House voted to refer the billionaire Leon Black to the Justice Department for contempt of Congress for refusing to cooperate with an investigation into sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Saudi Arabia is attempting to return about half the capacity of its cross-country oil pipeline within days after the link was disrupted in drone attacks last week, according to a person familiar with the matter.

Washington removed Venezuela from the group of countries it said had failed to meet drug-control obligations, and indicated that Colombia could follow next year if its new government makes progress against cocaine trafficking.

Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, has proposed making Canada the first associate member of the European Union, forging a novel transatlantic alliance as Trump tramples over the old one.

The US Department of Health and Human Services says it plans to begin a new research initiative related to autism, using AI and other technology to map how the condition develops and identify opportunities for early intervention.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced visa restrictions on South Africans who the State Department claims have engaged in government-sponsored discrimination against Afrikaners and other minority groups, escalating a diplomatic row between the two nations.

The US House didn’t vote on a bill to suspend the gas tax this week because “a big cross section of members” disagree on how best to address the high cost of fuel, Speaker Mike Johnson told Bloomberg Government.

House Republican leaders canceled the last votes of the week, allowing lawmakers to head home this evening for more than a month of recess before midterm elections that will decide control of both houses of Congress.

New York’s independent power producers are escalating a campaign against state-regulated utilities as both seek a greater share of the state’s clean energy market at a time when residents face soaring energy costs.
Today on Bloomberg Television’s Balance of Power early edition at 1 p.m., hosts Joe Mathieu and Kailey Leinz interviewed Stephen Moore a former senior economic adviser to Trump.
On the program at 5 p.m., they talk with Representatives Josh Gottheimer, a Democrat, and Mike Lawler, a Republican, who have teamed up on legislation intended to hinder rogue AI agents.

On the Big Take podcast, Bloomberg tech editor Sarah Frier joins Sarah Holder to break down the motivations behind the pleas by artificial intelligence company executives for a coordinated slowdown in development  — and how IPOs, inflation and the economy are all in play. Listen on iHeart, Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

Household debt is the reason behind a growing share of mortgage delinquencies, according to data from the Federal Housing Administration. The data shows that borrowers are likely facing a combination of too much debt and that they are struggling to keep up with high interest rates. A review of new delinquencies of more than 90 days by reason found that reduction of income is the main explanation of why people fall behind, but a record share reported that excessive obligations are forcing them into nonpayment. Interestingly, “No Contact” which refers to a situation in which the loan servicer has been unable to communicate with a delinquent borrower is up sharply this quarter. That reason rose from 8.3% a year ago to a record 13.2% in the third quarter of 2026. — Alex Tanzi

Trump will campaign in North Carolina for Michael Whatley, the state’s Republican Senate candidate, this evening.The US House will adjourn today for the election recess and will not return until after the midterms.
The United Nations General Assembly begins its 81st session on Monday in New York.

items.title: Foreign Holdings of US Treasuries Fell to Nine-Month Low in July
body: Foreign holdings of US Treasuries fell in July to the lowest level since October, led by declines in the stockpiles of France and Canada.
Overseas holdings dropped by $50.4 billion from June, according to data published by the Treasury Department on Wednesday. The total now stands at $9.25 trillion.

The foreign holdings data incorporate changes in valuation as well as net sales and purchases. The Bloomberg US Treasury index declined over 1% in July, amid investor angst about inflation risks exacerbated by the Iran war and continuing concerns over fiscal deficits.

Japan, the biggest foreign holder of Treasuries, saw a $12.8 billion drop in its holdings, to $1.1 trillion. The month of July included action by Japanese authorities to prop up the yen. More recent figures from Japan’s Finance Ministry indicated that Tokyo likely sold a portion of its holdings of foreign securities to help fund its yen intervention moves.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent suggested Tuesday that one reason why the US joined Japan in intervening to buy yen on July 31 might have been to help reduce the need for Tokyo to sell its American holdings.

“A stronger yen means that the Japanese government will not have to sell US assets to finance foreign currency intervention,” Bessent said at a House hearing Tuesday. He was answering a question on the benefit to the US of its help for Japan with the yen.

Mainland China, the third-largest holder of Treasuries, saw a $15.4 billion fall in July, Wednesday’s report showed. The total is now $618 billion. Belgium, whose holdings include Chinese custodial accounts according to market analysts, also saw its stockpile go down, to $470.7 billion.
The UK, the second-biggest holder, saw a $58.4 billion increase, to $998.3 billion.
France’s holdings tumbled $41.5 billion, to $348.4 billion, while Canada’s declined $33.3 billion, to $426.3 billion.

items.title: Drone Startup Zipline in Talks on About $1 Billion Raise at $20 Billion Valuation
body: Zipline is in talks to raise around $1 billion in a funding round that would value the drone delivery and logistics startup at roughly $20 billion, nearly tripling its previous valuation.

Venture capital firm Paradigm, which has previously invested in the startup, is in discussions to lead the fundraising effort, according to people familiar with the situation. Prior backer Tiger Global Management is also considering participation in the round, the people said, asking not to be identified because the information isn’t public.
The discussions are early and the figures may change, they said.

Zipline and Paradigm declined to comment. Tiger did not immediately respond to a request for comment.Founded in 2014, Zipline was valued at $7.6 billion earlier this year in a financing round aimed at helping the company expand its commercial deployment. The startup’s pitch is that it can get food orders to a consumer’s home in 30 minutes or less, maintaining the freshness of the delivery. It does this by deploying fulfillment software, inventory management, airspace tools and more. The company has delivery services that can work in both rural and urban areas.In August, Zipline announced a new partnership and investment from   Uber Technologies Inc. to help the ride-hailing company scale its food delivery services; the funding was at an undisclosed valuation. Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick recently unveiled his own work in the autonomous technology space, a robotics company called Atoms that is focused on food, mining and transportation.Top investors in Zipline include Valor Equity Partners and Sequoia Capital. The company’s website says that it has made nearly 3 million deliveries across over 140 million miles. Its customer include   Chipotle Mexican Grill Inc., Jimmy John’s and   Walmart Inc., according to its website.

items.title: Why Kevin Warsh Again Skipped the Fed's Dot Plot
body: For more than a decade, officials at the US Federal Reserve have shared their predictions on future interest rates via a small scatter chart published four times a year. Nineteen central bank policymakers can offer their projections, reflected anonymously on the dot plot.

In addition to providing rate forecasts, the chart serves as a source of clues to any disagreement among the policymakers. The Fed’s dot plot on Sept. 16 did capture a few differences in forecasts — but once again, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh declined to submit his own projection for the chart.

As was the case in Warsh’s first rate-setting meeting as Fed chairman in June, only 18 dotted forecasts for the rest of 2026 and for 2027 appeared on the September chart. Warsh, who has publicly criticized the dot plot and suggested that the Fed provide less guidance on where interest rates might be headed, has indicated that the future of the dot plot is under review by a newly formed Fed committee on communications.

The dot plot is a chart that shows estimates of where the federal funds rate, the short-term interest rate controlled by the Fed, should go in the coming years. As many as 19 interest rate policymakers — the seven governors on the Fed Board in Washington and the presidents of the 12 regional banks — can contribute to the dots. Each participant assigns a dot for what they view as the midpoint of the rate’s appropriate range at the end of each of the next three years and over the longer run. Investors focus on the median dot.
Read more: Fed Raises Rates as Warsh Bucks Trump to Contain Inflation

The dot plot was invented in late 2011, at a time when Fed officials were considering how to prepare markets for the shift they hoped to make away from the unprecedented level of support they had given the US economy after the financial crisis. The Fed chairman at the time, Ben Bernanke, and Janet Yellen, who served as Bernanke’s deputy before a four-year stint as chair, saw the dot plot as a way of giving markets a look into the Fed’s thinking beyond any immediate decision-making.
Read more: Warsh Caught Between Trump and Bond Market Bet on Rate Hikes

Statements by the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee focus mainly on current economic conditions and the immediate interest-rate target. They evolved over time, however, and have been used to deliver sometimes-forceful indications of the path ahead for rates.

When the dot plot shifts, it can send a powerful message to investors on whether the US central bank expects to raise or lower interest rates. It also creates a benchmark that can be used to highlight differences between the views of Fed officials and those in financial markets.

The dot plot carries no names, so there is no way to tell which rate projection was offered by whom just by looking at the chart. The anonymous nature of the dot plot is one reason it has critics as well as fans. But in June and again in September, Warsh acknowledged that he hadn’t submitted a forecast, leaving the chart with 18 dots instead of 19.

Maybe the biggest beef is that the projections aren’t an official consensus forecast. (Fed staff explored hammering out a consensus dot, but officials decided that it would be too hard to get agreement among so many officials with such disparate views.) Each individual member might base his or her forecast on a different economic model or set of assumptions, which means there is no consistency in how the dots are generated and no sense of the thinking behind them.

Further complicating matters, of the 12 regional Fed presidents, only five are voting members of the FOMC in any given year. That raises questions about how well the dots accurately reflect longer-term FOMC intentions.
Read more: What to Expect From Kevin Warsh at the Federal Reserve

Warsh has made his views clear. At the news conference after the Fed’s June 17 interest rate decision, Warsh said: “I did not submit a dot. For me, it’s not helpful in the conduct of policy. I suspect by year end, as I mentioned in my opening statements, there’ll be a review about communications broadly — press conferences, dots, meetings and the like, transcripts, minutes. This will be part of that.”

Other Fed leaders have had mixed feelings. In 2014, at her first FOMC press conference as chair, Yellen said people “should not look to the dot plot” as “the primary way in which the committee wants to or is speaking about policy to the public at large.” But in 2016, after Fed officials had trimmed their forecast for the number of rate increases that year to two from four, Yellen told reporters that the shift in dots “largely reflects a somewhat slower projected path for global growth” and a tightening in credit conditions.

Jerome Powell, who took over from Yellen as chair in February 2018, often played down the dot plot. But it also proved an aid on occasion, such as in June 2023, when Fed policymakers refrained from raising rates but the dot plot showed more increases to come later in the year — helping avoid any burst of investor exuberance over the probable end of the rate-raising cycle.

items.title: Tankmaker KNDS Considers Delaying Initial Public Offering
body: KNDS NV and its owners are considering pushing back its initial public offering, people familiar with the matter said, increasing the likelihood that one of Europe’s most-anticipated listings will be postponed beyond this year.

The Franco-German tankmaker has been holding discussions with the banks helping to co-ordinate its IPO plans, according to the people. The advisers pointed to the sluggish stock market performance of listed defense companies including Rheinmetall AG as a reason to wait, the people said.
The Wegmann family, which owns half of KNDS, will focus on selling as much as 40% of the shares to the German government in the coming weeks, the people said.
Deliberations are ongoing and decisions on the timing of a KNDS listing could change depending on market conditions, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing confidential information.
“KNDS and its shareholders will continue to monitor market conditions closely and stand ready to resume the IPO process,” the firm said in a statement.

KNDS announced plans in June to list on the Frankfurt and Paris stock exchanges. This followed a deal for the German government to buy a 40% stake from the group’s family owners as part of the IPO, resulting in a listed defense firm jointly owned by Germany and France.

But shortly after, KNDS put the plans on ice as it struggled to persuade investors to buy shares even at a reduced valuation of €12 billion ($13.8 billion). The firm cited volatility in the European defense sector for its decision.
Rheinmetall shares are down more than a third this year, while a basket of European defense stocks tracked by Goldman Sachs Group Inc. are trading effectively flat.

Bloomberg News reported in August that KNDS would restart investor meetings about a possible IPO. The fresh delay is a blow to Europe’s stock market, which has been struggling to attract new listings in a challenging environment where deals have been prone to delays.

items.title: Boeing Lays Out Challenging Months of Delays and Slow Output
body: Boeing Co. expects some testing on the upcoming 777X model to spill into 2027, even as the US planemaker reiterated that deliveries of the long-delayed model are on track to begin next year.
The company blamed the delays on the pending certification of a seal on the GE Aerospace turbine that powers the jet.

“That’s probably going to cause us a little bit of a challenge between now and the end of the year,” said Kelly Ortberg, Boeing’s chief executive officer, at a Morgan Stanley investor conference on Wednesday. “We may see some some of the testing spill into the next year. We’re still planning on 2027 deliveries.”
The 777X, which is now seven years late, is of major strategic and financial importance to Boeing in its duel with Airbus SE for a bigger slice of the lucrative long-haul market.

GE understands the root cause of a midseal durability issue on its GE9X engine, delivered the first units with upgraded midseals in August and is looking forward to entry into service in 2027, a company spokesperson said.
Shares of Boeing fell 3.7% and closed at $201.96 in regular trading, their largest drop since May. The stock has declined about 7% this year.

While Boeing reiterated its guidance of generating between $1 billion and $3 billion in free cash this year, Chief Financial Officer Jay Malave said it was “a little bit less likely” to exceed the mid-point of the range due to a slower pace of deliveries on the key 737 and 787 models.
The planemaker said production of the 737 Max was taking longer to stabilize at 47 a month, and that the in-house production of wings was an issue.

In May, Ortberg told investors that the Federal Aviation Administration had signed off on increasing output to 47 a month. The planemaker has longer term plans to increase that cadence to 63 a month over several years.

Ortberg also downplayed the prospect of a major order from China, tied to President Xi Jinping’s upcoming trip to the US, being firmed up in one fell swoop. The executive said that while the company expects there to be “an increment of orders going forward,” they will be announced by Chinese airlines at their own pace.

Ortberg said he expects certification on another long-delayed model “very soon.” Boeing has completed all the needed flight testing on the key 737 Max 10 variant and regulators are currently evaluating all the documentation, he said.

The long-delayed 737 Max 10 is the largest variant of Boeing’s best-selling jet family, and will take on Airbus’ top-selling A321neo jet. The model is key to generating cash and improving Boeing’s finances after a number of crises over the past near-decade.
Boeing is working on a turnaround after years of crises and quality lapses that triggered a leadership shakeup and tarnished its relationship with customers and US regulators.

items.title: Top Trump Aide Wiles Says She's Cancer Free After Treatment
body: President Donald Trump’s chief of staff, Susie Wiles, announced she is “cancer free” after undergoing treatment for breast cancer this year.
Wiles said Wednesday that she had a medical appointment at the Mayo Clinic this week including pathology testing that “came back clear.”
In a social media post, Wiles thanked her friends, family and doctors as well as Trump “for his unwavering support.”
“I am deeply grateful and will continue to work to advance his America First Agenda,” she posted.
Wiles announced in March she was diagnosed with early stage breast cancer, and said she planned to continue working through her treatment. Trump said at the time that her prognosis was “excellent.”

A longtime aide to Trump, Wiles became the first-ever female White House chief of staff upon his return to office. It’s a high-powered role leading the West Wing staff that is often referred to as the “second most powerful job in Washington.”
Earlier: Trump Says Wiles Has Cancer, Will Continue as Chief of Staff

The announcement comes at a pivotal moment for Trump and his fellow Republicans, who face a rocky path to maintain control of Congress in the November midterm elections. Trump has struggled to quell voter anxieties over the cost of living, which have been exacerbated by high energy prices stemming from the war in Iran.

items.title: House Holds Leon Black in Contempt in Epstein Subpoena Clash
body: The US House voted to hold billionaire Leon Black in contempt of Congress for failure to comply with two subpoenas issued in a committee’s investigation into sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The matter now goes to the Justice Department, which can decide whether to pursue charges against the co-founder of Apollo Global Management. If the DOJ brings a criminal case and Black is ultimately convicted, he could face a fine up to $100,000 and one to 12 months in prison for refusing to comply with the congressional subpoenas, one requiring him to testify under oath and the other to hand over documents.

A Justice Department spokesman said prosecutors take the contempt vote “seriously” and that Jeanine Pirro, the US Attorney for the District of Columbia “will review the referral of Mr. Black carefully.”
The House vote Wednesday came amid an escalating legal battle between Black and the House Oversight Committee, the panel investigating the late Epstein and his network.

“No one is above the law,” House Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer said in a statement. “We will continue to seek transparency for the American people and justice for survivors in our investigation of the federal government’s handling of the Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell criminal cases.”
Black’s attorneys, Susan Estrich and Aaron Cutler, called the vote “an outrageous action that ignores the facts and the truth about Mr. Black.”

Black walked out early from voluntary testimony in June regarding his relationship to Epstein. Black left the June interview after refusing to answer questions about nondisclosure agreements he made with women in Epstein’s orbit, the committee said.
The subpoenas demand he furnish the committee with the NDAs and return for testimony.
Read More: The Epstein Clause: How $500 Helped Build a Wall Around Secrets

Rather than show up for a deposition in early September, Black filed a federal lawsuit on the day his testimony was scheduled seeking to block the subpoenas. Black and his attorneys have repeatedly denied any wrongdoing by him and accused the committee of abusing its power.
Black’s attorneys have also asked the Office of Congressional Conduct to investigate Comer and accused the committee’s top Democrat, Robert Garcia, of making false statements about the billionaire.
“We intend to pursue our litigation challenging this action and will hold the Committee and Chairman Comer accountable in the courts,” Black’s lawyers said in the Wednesday statement.

When Black appeared before the committee in June, Black said in an opening statement to the panel that he never abused women and wasn’t blackmailed by Epstein, his longtime friend and adviser. He has acknowledged paying Epstein $158 million over the years, which he said was for estate and tax planning advice.

Epstein died in a New York jail cell in 2019 while awaiting trial on federal sex-trafficking charges. The House Oversight Committee has been investigating his networks, as well as potential lapses in federal law enforcement’s response.
Read More: Epstein’s Mysterious $158 Million ‘Work of Art’ for Leon Black

items.summary_zh: 美国众议院投票判定亿万富翁莱昂·布莱克藐视国会，因其未遵守爱泼斯坦调查传票，案件已移交司法部，若定罪最高面临10万美元罚款和12个月监禁。

items.title: Nagel Says Some Far-Right Policies Risk 'Total Economic Ruin'
body: Bundesbank President Joachim Nagel said proposals by some far-right parties in Europe would risk derailing their countries’ economies if they were enacted.

“What I hear from some of these right-wing parties — listening to some of their ideas — borders on total economic ruin,” Nagel said Wednesday in Paris. “That’s why I can only repeat once again: I’m very concerned with what’s happening there.”

While Nagel, whose also a member of the European Central Bank’s Governing Council, didn’t name any parties, he’s joined protests against the far right in Germany in the past and recently stepped up criticism of such groups in his homeland and in France.
Following a regional-election victory this month for the Alternative for Germany party, or AfD, Nagel said he was concerned by the development.

“What does this make with our country, with our society, the values we are sharing?” he said last week. “Some of these concepts are self-defeating in an economic sense. Is this helpful to attract foreign investors to come to this country? Definitely not. I think they will be reluctant. They will shy away from doing business here.”

items.title: Hawkish Warsh Lifts Dollar as Traders Bet on More Rate Increases
body: The dollar notched its best day in three months on prospects that the Federal Reserve will continue to raise interest rates after Chairman Kevin Warsh delivered a stern message on inflation.

Policymakers voted unanimously to boost the benchmark federal funds rate by a quarter point on Wednesday. The central bank’s first rate increase since 2023 lifted the Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index by 0.5% — its biggest jump since June 17, Warsh’s debut central bank meeting. Following the decision, Warsh reiterated at a press conference his concerns over elevated inflation, prompting traders to price in three Fed rate hikes through June of next year.

“Clearly the Warsh commentary was much more bluntly hawkish than investors expected,” said Nathan Thooft, a senior portfolio manager at Manulife Investment Management. “In the near-term, the combination of resilient US growth, sticky inflation and a Fed that is perceived as willing to keep policy restrictive does provide support for the dollar.”

Prior to the central bank’s decision, the dollar advanced in September alongside long-end US Treasury yields as inflation came in above expectations and oil prices rallied, fanning risks of runaway consumer prices across the globe. Warsh had prepared the market for the Wednesday rate increase by vowing to tame inflation in a speech at the Fed’s flagship symposium in Jackson Hole late last month.

“The September hike marks the formal transition from hawkish rhetoric to an active tightening cycle,” said Mark McCormick, BMO’s chief FX strategist. “The dollar rally has been developing in fits and starts all year, but the Fed’s shift from hawkish language to actual tightening gives it another leg.”

The greenback weighed down its major peers Wednesday, with the British pound falling as much as 0.7% ahead of the Bank of England’s policy meeting on Thursday, when officials are expected to keep rates unchanged. The yen lost as much as 0.9% to touch 156.42 per US dollar. Wells Fargo closed its trade recommendation for long yen against the dollar following the Fed decision.

Hedge funds, asset managers and other speculators have been cutting back on their upbeat dollar expectations in recent weeks. They trimmed their bullish dollar wagers to about $19.4 billion in the week ending Sept. 8, according to Commodity Futures Trading Commission data released Friday. That is a major shift from nearly $50 billion in those bets late July, which was the highest since 2014.

items.title: US Indictment Alleges Russian Global Assassination Network
body: Last year, a former military officer in the Russian intelligence services named Yuri Khrameev offered $25,000 to a US citizen to track and kill someone in Lithuania’s capital who was “telling lies about Russia,” according to US prosecutors.

The allegations were laid out as the Justice Department unsealed charges late Tuesday against five people working for Russia’s intelligence services to conduct attacks and slayings in Europe and the US. The defendants remain at large, the US Attorney’s office in the Southern District of New York said.

In a series of messages detailed in a US indictment, Khrameev — who was known as Colonel Yuri and allegedly tried to recruit people to kill Russian dissidents — explained that he also wanted to target infrastructure in NATO countries, including train stations, bus depots and warehouses stocking aid for Ukraine.

“I am interested in all the countries that are helping Ukraine,” Khrameev messaged the American, after he refused to carry out the killing. “Throw a bottle of gasoline at an electrical substation. Set fire to a warehouse of property or food. You’re looking for such objects yourself. You need to approach it creatively.”

“These defendants allegedly operated as part of a global assassination network that reached into the United States, attempting to recruit US citizens and foreigners to carry out killings at the behest of the Kremlin,” said Assistant US Attorney General for National Security John Eisenberg. “Actions like these represent a gross violation of our sovereignty and a threat to our national security.”

The federal indictment purports to offer a detailed look at Russia’s expanding campaign of so-called hybrid attacks against European nations that supply weapons and money to Ukraine. The new charges echo a series of cases across Europe this summer. In some instances, Russian security services attempted to recruit citizens or residents in other nations to damage infrastructure or target individuals in return for payment.
Read More: Russia’s Escalating Hybrid Attacks Put Europeans in a Bind

Earlier this month, Germany officially attributed the recent discovery of an explosive-laden drone at Leipzig-Halle airport to Russia, while Poland said in August that it thwarted an attempted assassination of a US citizen originally from Ukraine ordered by Russia.

Estonia also accused Moscow last month of being behind a fire at a defense firm. Two Ukrainian nationals, one recruited online by a Russian-speaking Telegram user, were convicted in the UK of conspiring to commit arson attacks on a car and property linked to then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer.

The new US charges outline what the Justice Department alleges is Moscow’s effort to kill Russian dissidents and threaten European and US security. This summer, Russian spies also allegedly recruited a Venezuelan citizen living in Brooklyn, New York, to surveil and kill a prominent Russian dissident believed to be living in Washington, according to the indictment. Two of them, including one nicknamed ‘Viking’ — a Cuban national living in Russia - told the recruit that they wanted them to make the dissident “disappear” in return for $40,000, which the recruit turned down, exposing their brazenness in wanting to also commit assassinations on US soil, the Justice Department said.

The new case may prove awkward for the administration. President Donald Trump has adopted a conciliatory approach toward Russian President Vladimir Putin, as he seeks to reignite peace talks between Russia and Ukraine.

ProPublica also reported earlier this week that a Russian oligarch, who has been personally sanctioned by Ukraine over his ties to Putin and accompanied the Russian president on a recent state visit to China, paid for a post-wedding celebration for Donald Trump Jr. earlier this year.
Read More: Trump Jr.’s Wife Says Russian Paid for Parties But Not Wedding

The Trump administration has not commented so far on whether it will take action against Russia if it proves the charges. Previous cases — for example the assassination attempt of former Russian intelligence officer Sergei Skripal and his daughter with a nerve-agent in the UK — have triggered US sanctions.
