items.title: Swedish Center-Left Projected to Win Election by Slim Margin
body: Sweden’s center-left opposition bloc is projected to win Sunday’s tight general election by one seat after days of limbo, effectively closing off — for now — the prospect of the far-right entering government.

According to broadcaster SVT, there was a 99.9% likelihood that the Social Democrat-led bloc secures a majority as late votes and overseas ballots are tallied to resolve the winner. It was effectively impossible for the ruling center-right parties to get the votes needed to catch up, the state-owned media said on Wednesday. About 30,000 ballots separated the camps.

With 99% of votes counted, former Prime Minister Magdalena Andersson was on track for 175 seats in parliament against 174 for the premier, Ulf Kristersson, and his allies. One seat was so tightly contested that the numbers flipped to 176 versus 173 intermittently.

The count was paused for two days after Sunday failed to produce a result, as election officials awaited the arrival of some advance votes, as well as the remaining ballots from Swedes residing abroad.
Read More: Swedish Voters in Limbo in Election Race Too Close to Call

Eking out the narrowest possible majority shows how the Social Democrats suffer from the fragmentation of the political landscape. Their 28% backing is the worst in more than a century and far from their mid-20th century heyday when the party regularly pulled in nearly half of the vote.

Still, the outcome supports a flickering revival of the center left across parts of Europe. UK Labour Prime Minister Andy Burnham is seeking to build on a recent bounce in opinion polls and Social Democrats already govern Denmark, Norway and Iceland. Center-left candidates will be tested again in Spain, France, Poland and in Sweden’s neighbor Finland over the coming year.

The result puts Andersson in pole position to pursue tricky coalition talks over the weeks ahead. It also deals a blow to Kristersson’s bid for reelection after his gamble backfired. He had promised to bring his far-right Sweden Democrat allies under leader Jimmie Åkesson into government for the first time.

By readily adopting a stronger position on crime, Andersson was able to outflank the right on its own turf. She also succeeded in drawing on her party’s history of strengthening public welfare to reassure Swedes feeling the pinch of weak growth and an uncertain job market.
In absolute numbers, the Sweden Democrats lost the most seats, totaling 10, while Andersson’s Social Democrats didn’t fare much better, giving up eight.
Andersson is likely to try and form a government made up of or supported by the Green Party, the Center Party and the Left Party in what appears a daunting challenge.
The Left Party has said it will not back a government it is not part of, while the Center Party has said it will not support a government that includes the Left Party.
Andersson insists it will be possible to persuade them to compromise on those pre-election red lines.

A key sticking point will be economic policy with the Left Party favoring higher taxes on income and business earnings to boost pensions and other welfare investments, positions which the Center Party firmly rejects.

Working with the Left hasn’t always been smooth sailing for Andersson. In May 2022 she put forward the paperwork for Sweden to join the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, a move that was robustly opposed by the Left.

Center leader Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist who has emerged as a kingmaker in the election, said the coming period will require “pragmatism and a willingness from several parties to find solutions across the old bloc divides.”
Read More: Sweden’s Small Pro-Business Party Emerges as Election Kingmaker
“The Center Party will be constructive in helping Sweden get a functioning government with policies rooted in the political center,” she said in written comments to SVT.
If Andersson fails to stitch together the support to be appointed prime minister, Kristersson will be next in line to try.

Under the Swedish system, a prime minister doesn’t need backing from a majority of lawmakers, but needs to ensure most members of parliament don’t actively oppose them. There can be four parliamentary votes on a new prime minister before a new election must be called.

items.title: Tether Gold Loans Swell With $1.5 Billion for US Bullion Dealer
body: Tether has emerged as a major bullion lender, providing about $1.5 billion in financing to a top US gold dealer after amassing one of the world’s largest private hoards of the precious metal.

The crypto giant accounted for the majority of the $1.7 billion of precious-metal leases outstanding at Gold.com Inc. by the end of June, according to the dealer’s annual report. Tether, which bought a stake in the platform earlier this year, was owed $1.45 billion in payables and advances from Gold.com at the end of the reported period.

Tether grabbed headlines in the gold market last year with a purchasing spree that made it one of the world’s largest buyers, surpassing almost every central bank. Its holdings stood at 146 tons in June, worth about $20 billion at current prices.
Much of the crypto firm’s firepower comes from USDT, the world’s largest dollar-pegged stablecoin, which Tether issues in exchange for dollars it can invest in assets like Treasuries and gold.
Read more: Tether Is Shaking Up the Gold Market With Massive Metal Hoard

Tether paid $150 million for a 13% stake in Gold.com earlier this year, and the two companies have also struck agreements to buy and sell precious metals from each other, as well as a deal for Tether to store metal in Gold.com’s Las Vegas facility. The dealer owns some of the largest bullion brands in the US, including A-Mark Precious Metals and JM Bullion.

“I think the sky is the limit as it relates to what we can do with Tether,” Gold.com chief executive Greg Roberts said on an earnings call this month. “We’re providing some opportunities for them that they aren’t able to take advantage of with other trading partners.”

The deal with Gold.com will help Tether in its efforts to put its vast bullion holdings to work and generate a return. The crypto firm met with several Swiss gold refiners earlier this year to discuss providing financing, people familiar with the talks said. Such lending, typically provided by large multinational banks, was under strain in the first quarter as record gold prices and volatility stretched banks’ credit exposure to refiners.
Gold.com and Tether didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

For buy-and-hold investors like central banks, gold mostly sits as a dead-weight on the balance sheet — yielding nothing and actually costing them money in storage costs. As a result, many are happy to lend out their bullion at low yields to banks, which in turn provide the metal to clients and counterparties.

Those cheap gold loans are the lifeblood of much of the physical bullion trade, allowing refiners, jewelers and others to finance the enormous value of gold they hold as inventory at any given time, without needing to borrow dollars or take exposure to swings in the price of the metal.

A $100 million gold-leasing facility agreed between Tether and Gold.com in February carried an annual rate of 1.75%, according to a term sheet filed with US securities regulators. That compared to a cost of about 6% on Gold.com’s bank credit facility at the time, although using leased gold instead of dollars can also mean forgoing potentially profitable derivatives hedges.
“It’s a great opportunity for us, it’s cheaper liquidity than our dollar facilities,” Roberts said on the earnings call. “We have found a very good opportunity that’s a win-win for both sides.”

items.title: UK May Have Trouble Following Closer EU-Canada Ties
body: The geographical distance between Canada and the EU is over 5,000 km but such are the profound shocks pummelling historic regional orders that the EU has proposed Canada become its first “associate member”.

Actually, shorelines suggest this isn’t geographical nonsense - Canada already shares a border with Denmark (via Greenland) and St John’s, Newfoundland is closer to Ireland than Vancouver (if these facts ever crop up in a pub quiz... you’re welcome).

But this relationship is about geopolitics, not geography. Mark Carney wants to reduce Canada’s dependence on the US, enabling him to better stand up to Donald Trump’s hectoring, and views closer ties with the EU as a way to do that. It is the next stage of the prime minister’s middle powers pitch from Davos.

The UK also sees itself as a middle power and so will, yet again, be paying close attention to Canada’s plays. But there are signs this afternoon that our government is feeling spurned. Our political editor says the gambit signals “Canada is well ahead of Britain in establishing better relations with the bloc on both trade and security.” In the search for substantial economic growth, returning to the EU is a lever many Labour politicians would love to pull. This Bloomberg analysis from June quantified the economic impact Brexit has had on the UK. But as Alex says:

Officials that spoke with Alex Wickham insisted, with so few details to go on, they weren’t bothered. It’s hard for Labour to really move back towards the EU with Reform waiting in the wings to cry betrayal of those who voted to leave. Still, if any EU-Canada deal is an advance on the UK’s current pact, it would be something for Prime Minister Burnham to attempt to piggybank on.

Meanwhile, this government needs fast fixes. The budget is less than six weeks away and we are in the critical two-week window in which the Office for Budget Responsibility takes its snapshot of borrowing costs and the like, off which it makes judgments on the government’s headroom. And what a badly timed two-week window it is.
Today inflation came in at over 3% - as Markets Today looks at lower down. And Georgia Hall writes about the failure of the UK’s strategy to prop up its long maturity debt by selling less.

But are things as dire as they first appear? Bloomberg Opinion’s Paul J Davies examined the perceived stampede of the super-rich from the UK off the back of the recent Bloomberg exclusive that billionaire Chris Rokos is off to Greece. Paul found that there are fewer Rokos-esque abrupt departures than first appears.
Here’s Paul:
Who would have thought that it would be the fact that the super-rich may not be leaving in droves that could cheer up this Labour government?
Want this in your inbox each weekday? You can sign up here.

Hi, I’m Morwenna from the MT blog. Today’s inflation data may have seemed relatively benign — or at least in-line — but a heating up driven by energy costs is not good news. That’s because in August wholesale energy prices only went up slightly, with oil ending the month just over $90 compared to below $85 at the end of July. It’s September that’s seen prices really rocket, with crude back up to almost $110 per barrel. Natural gas futures have also continued to rise. That means the broad impact of higher energy prices in August is only going to be augmented in September. And a new energy price cap coming in for households in October will push up bills from then as well.

That means the data is unlikely to bring the Bank of England much comfort. Coming after yesterday’s soggy labour market data, it only underlines the tricky balancing act needed to curb inflation without further throttling the economy.

A further cue may come from the Federal Reserve rate decision later today. There’s a lot of expectation that the central bank will raise interest rates, mainly because Governor Kevin Warsh has been teeing things up for an increase. Whether or not it proves to be the start of a hiking cycle rather than a gesture to save credibility, a hike from the Fed, after the ECB already did, could make things rather awkward for the BOE if it remains the odd one out for long.

items.title: AI Boom to Buoy Equities in Face of Rate Hikes: Everything Risk
body: Surging oil prices and 10-year Treasury yields risk slowing but not derailing the US economy. Global competition to keep pace in the AI boom is the ace in the hole for growth that interest-rate hikes can’t counteract.

Nominal GDP growth, the underlying pace of the US economy without adjusting for inflation, is actually accelerating from a trough in 2025. Outside of the pandemic-distorted numbers, growth is now near its strongest in the last few decades.

So I remain upbeat about both the US economy and US equities over the near term because the drivers of growth are so powerful that it would take an enormous demand shock to tip the country into a recession. In a May column I wrote about my view that higher Treasury yields and energy costs would derail the economy only if oil prices got to $150 a barrel or if we faced the twin threat of 5.5% long-term yields and $130 oil.
Since the US standard of crude oil is just over $100 a barrel and the 10-year Treasury is at roughly 5%, both a long way from levels I highlighted in May, I stand by that.
The real challenge for policymakers is how to slow the economy without sparking a recession when those spending the most money are locked in to low pandemic-era borrowing rates.

Two weeks ago, I wrote about US homeowners with 30-year mortgages fixed at ultralow levels and big companies similarly locked in to long-term fixed-rate financing. That means interest-rate policy basically gets meted out on a reduced cohort that isn’t benefiting from such low borrowing costs, such as small and medium-sized businesses, home buyers and auto purchasers. It’s cruel because that debt stress is disproportionately absorbed by lower-income households and mom-and-pop enterprises, those least able to deal with it.

As of mid-2022, the bottom half of US households was actually seeing higher income in real terms. However, Bloomberg Intelligence data shows that after the Federal Reserve kicked off an aggressive hiking cycle starting in 2022, holdings of cash-like instruments such as money-market funds for households in the lowest 20% in terms of income wound up falling relative to pre-pandemic.
That distress wasn’t enough to cause a recession given government deficits were growing and artificial intelligence investment was ramping up.

My suspicion is that recent comments from US AI leaders suggesting government regulation may be needed isn’t just about safety concerns. It’s also a backdoor way for them to slow their breakneck spending as they worry about being left behind in a potentially winner-take-all outcome. By my reckoning, regulation would effectively bar new entrants, allowing existing players to spend less.

But the latest headlines show Europe entering the AI race. And in China, companies including Alibaba and Tencent are boosting spending. Plus we have the lower-cost, lower-spend chatbot competitors DeepSeek and Kimi, which are a competitive threat no matter what happens with regulation. There’s probably little chance the spending cools, and it may even pick up.

My take on all this is it signals continued, inflationary economic growth, which is bad for bond investors. Look at the inflation-adjusted compensation investors demand for holding long-dated Treasuries. It’s certainly higher than what they wanted during the deflation-scare years after the dot-com crash and the Great Financial Crisis. But it has room to rise from around 2.6% today to 3% and beyond. Basically, as I see it, high yields are here to stay.

The comfort for bond investors is that the amount of current yield pickup means they’re unlikely to lose money if they buy at these levels. The catch, however, is that bond returns simply won’t be enough to cover future liabilities for pension funds and insurance companies. The traditional “60/40” balanced portfolio, more heavily weighted toward equities than bonds, is increasingly considered obsolete. Allocations are shifting more toward “90/10″ or “85/15” structures, driven not just by the outperformance of equity portfolios over the past decade, but also the need to hit return benchmarks. The move toward higher equity allocations argues for stocks doing well as long as nominal growth remains high.

Also, given market expectations for multiple Fed hikes by the end of 2027, I would argue that outcome would actually be stimulative and buoy stocks. A small, fast hiking cycle (say of 1 to 1.5 percentage points) in today’s rate-insensitive US economy could boost net interest income for banks and households, supporting equities further. Only when the impasse over shipping routes in the Middle East gets us to $130 a barrel will I start worrying.

items.title: Trump Lifts Venezuela Narco Status and Says Colombia May Follow
body: Lea en español

Washington removed Venezuela from the group of countries it says failed to meet drug-control obligations, and signaled that Colombia could follow next year if its new government makes progress against cocaine trafficking.
President Donald Trump cited Venezuela’s cooperation against drug cartels since US forces seized Nicolás Maduro in January, including the killing of Tren de Aragua leader Niño Guerrero.

“Given the positive steps taken under interim President Delcy Rodríguez, I have determined Venezuela should no longer be designated as having failed demonstrably to fulfill its drug control commitments,” Trump said in a statement sent to Congress Sept. 15.

Colombia will remain designated as having failed to meet its commitments for now. But Trump blamed former President Gustavo Petro for record cocaine production, while praising the new government that took office in August.
President Abelardo De la Espriella’s pledge to pursue an aggressive campaign against coca cultivation and cocaine production could get Colombia off the list next year, he said.

“I will consider lifting the country’s “failed demonstrably” status, which remains in place solely due to the incompetence and chaos produced by the previous far-left government in office throughout the bulk of the past year,” he said.

The decision underscores how Washington’s counternarcotics relationships in Latin America are being reshaped by victories for conservative leaders in several recent elections. Trump said he expects Venezuela to make further measurable progress in dismantling what he called narcoterrorist groups and in stopping drug trafficking through its territory to the US.
He also said Colombia is now poised to resume its role as Washington’s “foremost security partner in the hemisphere.”
Colombia’s ambassador to the US, María Consuelo Araújo, said the Andean nation will implement a strategy to eradicate illicit crops using all available legal methods.

“Our aim is to confront the entire drug-trafficking chain, from illicit crops, laboratories and chemical precursors to trafficking routes, criminal finances, command structures and international networks,” Araújo said in statement.

Colombia’s Constitutional Court has imposed strict conditions on any resumption of aerial glyphosate spraying because of potential health and environmental risks. De la Espriella’s administration has also moved toward testing alternative herbicides, though one planned pilot using glufosinate ammonium has faced a legal suspension.

items.title: Nigeria Seen Cutting Rates on Softer Prices, Stronger Naira
body: Nigeria’s central bank is expected to resume cutting interest rates at next week’s meeting, buoyed by slowing inflation and exchange-rate stability, according to Bank of America.

Annual inflation, which slowed to 15.4% in August and a stronger naira that is up 8% this year, have created “room for the Central Bank of Nigeria to begin cautiously easing monetary policy,” BofA Analyst Raghav Adlakha said in a report.

BofA expects the Central Bank of Nigeria to deliver a 100 basis point rate cut when Governor Olayemi Cardoso announces the decision on Sept. 22, followed by a similar reduction in November. That would bring the benchmark monetary policy rate to 24.5% by year-end, it said.
“Declining domestic yields, improved foreign exchange stability, and moderating inflation has created conditions that are supportive of monetary easing,” the analyst said.

Still, there is a risk of a reversal in portfolio inflows which could put pressure on the naira after the Federal Reserve raised US interest rates by a quarter percentage point on Wednesday, with a median projection for one more hike by year end. That could deter the Nigerian central bank from adopting such aggressive cuts, the report said.

So while BofA expects the easing cycle to begin in September, the CBN might prefer to opt for more gradual 50 basis point cuts, or delay further easing until global financial conditions become more supportive.

Bank of America is also predicting the naira to appreciate towards 1,300 against the dollar, supported by foreign exchange reserves above $50 billion. That’s in line with analysts at Citigroup who expect the currency to remain broadly within a 1,300 - 1,350 per dollar range. The naira was quoted around 1,330/dollar in afternoon trade in Lagos on Wednesday.

items.title: Kremlin Pushes to Keep Russia's Edge as Biggest Wheat Exporter
body: The Kremlin is pushing wheat exporters and growers to maintain Russia’s geopolitical advantage as the top shipper of the grain, despite disruptions to ports in the Black Sea region.

The agriculture ministry and Russia’s Grain Association, held meetings with the country’s biggest grain exporters in August and September, according to people familiar with the matter. At those meetings, officials and exporters were told they must find ways to maintain the country’s global lead, said the people, who asked not to be named because the talks were private.

The scale of the effort to boost wheat exports highlights the political significance of maintaining the advantage for Russian leader Vladimir Putin. Russia’s dominant position allows Moscow to not only earn revenues, but to use the flows to exert geopolitical pressure, reward allies, and punish adversaries.

The exit of the majority of big, western trading houses following Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine has allowed the Kremlin to further tighten its control over the industry. But despite Russian authorities seeking to reassure markets that the country will be able to maintain its usual export volumes, that may prove unrealistic.

“Russia is unlikely to maintain its usual wheat export volumes despite the measures being taken if Black Sea ports remain blocked,” said Yevgeny Karabanov, head of analytics at the Grain Union of Kazakhstan. “There is simply no way to replace that capacity.”

The recent escalation of hostilities in the Black Sea, with Russia and Ukraine attacking each other’s ports and shipping infrastructure, has shuttered grain exports from the key global breadbasket. Those ports accounted for some 70% of Russia’s wheat exports and the halt came just as the country harvested a bumper crop.

Russia has resorted to some unusual alternatives to get its grain to markets, including turning to its Far East, a route that’s historically been little used for grain shipments. Rail shipments from southern Russia to the Baltic ports of Ust-Luga and Vysotsk and to the Far East have also been subsidized. It’s also mulling scrapping export duties on wheat and other grains and plans a new grain terminal in Vladivostok.

A special task force has also been set up to coordinate exports in the absence of the traditional shipping routes. It’s tasked with working out, region by region, the best alternative routes based on geography and transport costs.
But these measures are either too nascent or too pricey to make up for the vast volumes typically shipped through the Black Sea and Azov Sea ports, the people said.

Efforts to redirect shipments to Baltic ports have also caused rail bottlenecks, Karabanov said, adding that the Black Sea shutdown was a “warning sign” for Russia’s preeminent position as a wheat exporter.
Despite bringing in significantly lower revenues than oil and gas, grain sales have allowed Moscow to build economic and diplomatic ties with food importing countries in the Middle East and Africa.

“Every fifth ton of wheat exported on the world market is of Russian origin,” Deputy Prime Minister Dmitry Patrushev said recently, highlighting the country as a “reliable and stable partner” for ensuring global food supplies.
The agriculture ministry and Russia’s Grain Association didn’t respond to a request for comment.

items.title: Ex-Balyasny Trader Bets El Niño Can Juice Hedge Fund Returns
body: A former Balyasny Asset Management trader who now runs a boutique hedge fund in London says he expects to be able to amplify returns by anticipating how an evolving super El Niño will affect markets.

The cyclical climate phenomenon associated with warming across the equatorial Pacific Ocean is already reshaping weather patterns across the globe. Zulfiqar Ali, founder and chief investment officer of energy commodities trading hedge fund ZAMS Asset Management, says that as El Niño gets “stronger and stronger,” his fund “is positioned to take advantage of dislocations as they happen, with a quick turnaround.”

More opportunities are likely to emerge toward the end of the year, when El Niño is expected to produce an “unusually alpha-rich environment,” he said. So far, the strategy helped ZAMS deliver its clients a 5.7% return in August and 13% year-to-date.

The 34-year-old Cambridge University mathematics graduate says he and his team of half a dozen traders, quants and weather strategists have been analyzing energy futures contracts and weather models to find price anomalies. ZAMS buys climate models from specialist weather-forecasting companies like MetDesk, and then tries to improve on them using in-house expertise.

It’s an idea that’s gaining traction. Bloomberg reported in June that Moreton Capital Partners is targeting $500 million to bet on all the ways in which El Niño will upend food prices. At Man Group, the world’s largest publicly traded hedge fund firm, the assessment is that the full range of contagion risks associated with El Niño has yet to be priced in.

“Our starting point is always a price forecast, which we combine with weather signals,” Ali, who left Balyasny two years ago to start ZAMS, said in an interview in his office in London’s Mayfair district.
About 80% of the money ZAMS makes comes from power futures, where Ali says “El Niño is a major factor” this year and into early 2027.

The fund, which oversees about $350 million in client money, tends to sit on about 25-30 positions at any given moment and holds these for an average of just eight days. Ali says his hedge fund’s approach allowed it to pre-empt the energy price implications of disruptions to nuclear power stations in France over the summer as temperatures soared and rivers dried up.

Ali acknowledges his El Niño strategy is high-risk, and that trades can quickly sour if his weather bets miss their mark. For example, earlier this year ZAMS had been shorting May contracts for French and German electricity. But then the wind stopped blowing, supply dried up and wholesale prices jumped, forcing ZAMS to register its worst month of the year, Ali said.

He says ZAMS had been following consensus expectations indicating that the transition from La Niña (a cooler Pacific Ocean) to El Niño (a warmer Pacific ocean) wouldn’t happen until the second half of the year. However, La Niña started transitioning into El Niño in May.
That “caught us off guard,” Ali said. The markets “moved 30% against us.”
Such experiences aren’t enough to prompt Ali to reconsider his broader strategy, though. That’s because he regards the El Niño cycle as a “dominant macro theme” that’s too big for his firm to ignore.

“These windows of opportunity are infrequent,” said Ali. “For allocators willing to look beyond conventional asset classes, there are few more compelling setups heading into year-end, and a strong reason to be invested before the start of winter.”

Ali says ZAMS’s strategy isn’t limited to the current El Niño cycle. He says the weather changes underway offer a glimpse “of what the future looks like because of global warming,” and investors should view this moment as a “call to arms.”
As the northern hemisphere moves into its colder months, Ali and his team at ZAMS are positioning for the fallout of El Niño to evolve.

“Winter is the season when these forces — climatic, geopolitical, and structural — are likely to converge most intensely,” he said. Combined, Ali says that promises to create a uniquely rich opportunity to beat the market “for managers with the analytical edge and risk discipline to navigate it.”

items.title: European Union Asks Canada to Join the Bloc as Associate Member
body: Ursula von der Leyen today proposed that Canada become the first associate member of the European Union. The European Commission president extended the invitation during her state of the union address in Strasbourg, a sign of closer ties between two economies hit by US tariffs.

It’s a tailor-made title that doesn’t exist in any EU treaties, and what it could mean in practice may become clearer tomorrow, when Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney makes his own speech to the European Parliament. Read our explainer of what it might look like here. The EU’s bid to expand its borders and reinvent itself after Britain’s infamous exit was shrugged off in London — though some are now calling on UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham to walk back his Labour party’s red lines on Europe in the next election. Until then, Britain may have to face up to a relationship with Brussels that’s largely on ice. — Caroline Alexander

Turkey’s stock market was hit by turmoil after an asset manger’s failure to meet redemption requests sparked wider concerns about liquidity stress. The Borsa Istanbul 100 Index fell 6% at one point, triggering a market-wide circuit breaker, and all but one stock dropped. The selloff came after an announcement by a fund called Pusula Portfoy yesterday that some of its investment and money market funds were unable to meet redemption requests. The fund suffered large outflows today.

Saudi Arabia is ramping up prompt sales of crude from outside the Strait of Hormuz following the shutdown of its East-West pipeline, which halted cross-country flows to its Red Sea coast. Saudi Aramco is said to have sold about 20 million barrels to Asian refiners that can be picked up from just outside Hormuz.

Saudi Arabia avoided the worst impacts of the US-Iran war until this month, when the Houthis in Yemen began near-daily attacks that may complicate the kingdom’s multi-trillion dollar plans to diversify its economy.

The US is said to be preparing to provide Israel with tens of thousands of the most destructive bombs in its arsenal. The package includes MK-84s and 20,000 BLU-117s, as well as I-2000 Penetrator warheads. It’s a fresh sign of President Donald Trump’s refusal to bow to pressure from some voters and lawmakers to scale back support for Israel over accusations that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s military committed atrocities in its campaign against Hamas in the Gaza Strip.

McLaren Automotive plans to open a new UK factory as it gears up for its first sport utility vehicle, a welcome boost for Prime Minister Andy Burnham days after Jaguar Land Rover announced job cuts. The company said it will create 1,000 new positions by 2032, investing £500 million ($674 million) in the additional assembly facility as well in its headquarters in Surrey, where it makes its sports cars, and a carbon-fiber manufacturing site in Sheffield. The location of the new factory is still being finalized.

Glencore has accused Radiant World and associated companies of sending falsified invoices to lenders — just as the the embattled group of traders filed a suit in Singapore seeking more than $2 billion in damages from Glencore. The claims mark an explosive end to a business relationship that for many years was extremely close. Bloomberg has reported that Glencore traded extensively with Radiant World, helping it secure financing and even acquiring warrants that gave it the option to take a minority stake in the smaller company.

items.title: Saudis Seek to Resume Half of Key Oil Pipeline Within Days
body: Saudi Arabia is seeking to return about half the capacity of its cross-country oil pipeline within days after the link was halted last week following drone attacks, a person familiar with the matter said.

State-run Saudi Aramco is working to bypass a damaged section on the route that will allow it to resume part of the pipeline’s capacity, the person said, asking not to be identified because the matter is private. The company is looking to return the conduit to its full capability in about six weeks, they said.
Aramco and the Saudi energy ministry didn’t respond to requests for comments.

The timelines for the East-West pipeline’s resumption and the volume of oil it can carry for export are being closely watched by traders after the link turned into a lifeline during the Iran war as Saudi Arabia used it to circumnavigate the severely disrupted Strait of Hormuz. Last week’s halt put millions of barrels a day of exports at risk at a time when markets are clamoring for supply, with crude above $107 in London.

Following the shutdown, Aramco has been ramping up oil sales from outside the Strait of Hormuz to partly make up for some of the lost volumes, Bloomberg reported earlier. It has sold about 20 million barrels to Asian refiners, including in China, this week that can be picked up in September and October, according to traders familiar with the matter.

But customers in Europe are facing delays, which has spurred a jump in regional crude prices. At least one refiner in the continent, Poland’s Orlen SA, has been buying millions of barrels of replacement cargoes from other sources following the Saudi disruption, traders familiar with the matter told Bloomberg.

The 1,200-kilometer East-West line that stretches the breadth of the Arabian Peninsula was shut on Thursday after drone attacks launched by militias in Iraq. Saudi Arabia has also faced a series of strikes on energy and civilian infrastructure from the Yemen-based Houthi militants this month on its western Red Sea coast. The Iran-backed group has threatened Saudi shipping in the Red Sea, helping drive oil prices in London to above $100 a barrel earlier this month.

The shutdown of the pipeline, however, was a major blow for the oil market. Saudi Arabia was using the 7 million barrel-a-day link at its full capacity earlier this year after traffic through the Strait of Hormuz came to a near standstill following Iranian attacks on ships. While the kingdom’s oil exports slumped to just about 3 million barrels a day in August, the lowest in at least nine years, shipments through Yanbu, where the East-West terminates, still made up a bulk of the sales.
Also read: Saudi Arabia Taps Key Pipeline the World Didn’t Know It Needed

The East-West link has been attacked previously during the war. A pumping station was targeted in April as part of a wave of attacks on production, refining and petrochemical facilities. The link had suffered only limited damage and flows had continued, people familiar with the matter said at the time. Supplies returned to normal levels within days.

items.title: Space-Tug Maker Impulse's Fundraising Round Tops $800 Million
body: Impulse Space Inc., a startup working on in-space transportation technology, announced that it has raised an additional $308 million in its latest funding round, taking the total amount raised in this most recent series to $808 million.

The new funds will go toward expanding Impulse’s team and help with continued development of the firm’s spacecraft products. The latest rounded included participation from Impulse’s existing investors, including 137 Ventures, Lux Capital, Valor Equity Partners and others.

“This shows you know how much our customers and our investors like what we’re doing,” Tom Mueller, founder and chief executive officer, said in an interview with Bloomberg Television. “We now see space combining with AI, so it’s just really energizing the industry.”

The funding is the latest in a series of big rounds by space companies in the wake of SpaceX’s initial public offering, the largest of all time. Stoke Space Technologies Inc. recently announced it had raised $1 billion, while the Exploration Company Gmbh closed a $450 million round.

Southern California-based Impulse is developing a series of spacecraft and engines that serve as “space tugs,” designed to help other vehicles travel to different orbits and destinations once they reach space. Its primary vehicles include Helios and Mira, which can host other customers’ payloads and boost spacecraft to higher orbits.
Mueller was one of the first employees at SpaceX and was instrumental in creating the Merlin engine used on the Falcon 9 rocket.
The company also appointed Adam Townsend as its first chief financial officer. Townsend previously worked at Vizio Holding Corp. as CFO and head of human resources.

items.title: United, American Say Fuel Cost Surge May Mean Capacity Cuts
body: United Airlines Holdings Inc. and American Airlines Group Inc. said they may need to cut more capacity in the fourth quarter, while Southwest Airlines Co. sees room to hike fares, as the aviation industry continues to contend with high fuel prices.

“If fuel prices remain as high as they are right now, I think that that’s going to require some adjustments in terms of our capacity planning as we take a look out into the future,” American Chief Executive Officer Robert Isom said at at a Morgan Stanley conference in California on Wednesday.

Speaking after Isom at the same event, United Chief Financial Officer Mike Leskinen said that if fuel remains high, the company will “make some adjustments into the first quarter and beyond into 2027.”
“We are not flying to maximize market share, we’re flying to maximize profitability and free cash generation, so we’ll make those adjustments,” Leskinen said.

Speaking later, Southwest Chief Financial Officer Tom Doxey said the airline sees “room to go” on fare increases, as the industry grapples with higher fuel costs amid the US-Iran war. Further capacity cuts are likely if fuel prices remain high, Doxey added.

Shares in American, United and Southwest all closed down fractionally in regular trading on Wednesday. United’s shares have declined about 5% this year, American is down 17%, and Southwest has fallen 5%.

American estimates fuel will add $1 billion in extra costs in the last three months of the year. At the same time, the airline is seeing benefits of its focus on premium products, with more revenue coming from the front of the aircraft. At this point, the company continues to feel “really good” about its guidance, he said.
Read More: Oil at $100 Ruins Hopes for Christmas Flights to Get Cheaper
United earlier this year forecast adjusted third-quarter earnings of $2.50 to $3.50 a share and sees about $6 billion in added fuel costs for 2026, which it plans to offset by the end of the year.

The Chicago-based airline, which has been able to stay nimble amid high costs alongside Delta Air Lines Inc. with its industry-leading premium strategy, moved quickly and aggressively on capacity. The carrier earlier this year announced a 5% reduction in scheduled flights for the second and third quarters, targeting weaker off-peak routes — midweek and overnight flights — and trimming operations at Chicago O’Hare.
“As you look into the fourth quarter, there’ll be some flights in December that we won’t fly, that we thought we were going to fly,” Leskinen said.

With the US-Iran war showing no signs of abating, analysts expect energy prices to remain elevated. US President Donald Trump has said the fighting would only end after the November midterm elections. Brent is up almost 70% this year, and refined products such as diesel have posted even steeper gains, reflecting supply risks from the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East.

The surging costs are significantly squeezing airline margins. New York-based JetBlue Airways Corp. last week cut its capacity outlook, expecting it to rise between 1.5% and 3.5% from a year earlier, down from its previous forecast for growth between 3% and 6%.

American Airlines has faced the most acute pressure among its major rivals, having cut guidance twice so far this year. In April, it guided to a full-year range of a $0.40 loss to $1.10 profit — down from its original $1.10–$2.70 profit target — after absorbing an estimated $4 billion in incremental fuel costs from the Iran war.

In July, it cut guidance again to a range of a $0.65 loss to $0.65 profit, as fuel expense surged over $2.2 billion or 83% year-over-year in the second quarter alone. American was able to offset only roughly 50% of that fuel headwind through higher fares.
Read More: American Airlines’ Shares Slump After Lowering Earnings Guidance

One penny of extra fuel cost equals about $10 million, Chief Financial Officer Devon May said at the conference, adding that the airline will guide to the fourth quarter when reporting earnings next month.

“That’s $1 billion dollar run up we’re seeing in the fourth quarter,” May said. “The great thing is we’re coming in with a stronger balance sheet or a less debt than we’ve had in more than a decade. The company is sitting on a lot of liquidity, so we feel really good about the positioning we have right now.”

items.title: Macklemore Ban at Ed Sheeran Shows Sparks Free Speech Debate
body: A fractious debate over free speech driven by pro-Palestine activism, the intervention of billionaires and anti-Israel sentiment is again raging across the US.

The epicenter of the flare-up isn’t Columbia University in New York City, where two years ago student-led protests against Israel spread to campuses nationwide and drew backlash from wealthy donors. Instead, this time the spark was lit across the Hudson River at the MetLife Stadium in New Jersey.
That’s where rapper Macklemore — an opening act for a concert earlier this month by superstar Ed Sheeran — declared “Free Palestine” and performed a protest track decrying Israel and Zionism.

The action prompted New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft to bar Macklemore from appearing during Sheeran’s upcoming concert at Gillette Stadium outside Boston. The rapper said that the billionaire pushed owners of other stadiums around the country to make Sheeran drop him from his tour altogether.

By Tuesday, all of Sheeran’s other opening acts — including Finneas, the brother and frequent collaborator of pop star Billie Eilish — had dropped out of the tour. So had Sheeran’s touring band. Lukas Graham, a Danish band that had been set to perform, said that “money doesn’t give you the right to own the conversation. Nobody’s bank balance should decide who gets to speak or which suffering we’re allowed to acknowledge.”

The protest track Macklemore performed, Hind’s Hall, encapsulates several themes that pervade progressive criticism of Israel: He calls the Jewish state’s actions in Gaza a genocide, frames its historical treatment of Palestinians as apartheid, condemns the conflation of anti-Zionism with antisemitism, criticizes lobbying groups like AIPAC and says “White supremacy is finally on blast.”

Some Jews agree with him — another theme Macklemore hits in his track. But for many others, belief in Zionism is central to their faith. They also say that Israel is being singled out unfairly, while the actions of Hamas are left unaddressed and sometimes even lauded.

“Too many lives have been lost and there has been too much suffering, but only sharing selective information and ignoring the actions of Hamas is not honest and only advances more divisiveness and hate,” Kraft, who is Jewish and has led efforts to combat antisemitism globally, said in a statement.

Kraft and others have argued criticism of Israel often mirrors a long history of antisemitism that predates the most recent conflict in Gaza. Macklemore has previously drawn fire for appearing at a concert wearing a costume that included a black wig, beard, and enlarged nose. He subsequently apologized, saying he realized the costume could “within a context of stereotyping, be ascribed to a Jewish caricature.”

Israel’s latest military action in Gaza was sparked by Hamas’ attack on the Jewish state on Oct. 7, 2023. Since then, American political and cultural discourse has been convulsed by ructions over US support for the country, rising antisemitism, and the free-speech rights of protesters. President Donald Trump’s war in Iran, in conjunction with Israel, has only inflamed the arguments. And the issue has been central to the rise of socialist candidates within the Democratic Party.
Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, the New York congresswoman seen as the left’s leading aspirant in the 2028 presidential election, criticized Kraft’s action against Macklemore.

“When you see what Robert Kraft did to line up all of the stadiums to censor speech in that one specific way, it’s become clear that this is not just about one music artist or two music artists, but this is about how just a handful of stadium owners and the elite can prevent an entire massive issue, in this case, the genocide in Gaza,” she said in a video posted by TMZ. Israel has rejected accusations of genocide.

Other critics have seized on NFL owners’ willingness to host Ye — formerly known as Kanye West — despite overtly antisemitic remarks. The rapper, who has apologized for the remarks and said he suffers from bipolar disorder, is scheduled to perform at AT&T Stadium, home of the Dallas Cowboys, in November. That stadium was among the venues that reportedly objected to Macklemore’s inclusion on Sheeran’s tour.

“Man who released a song called Heil Hitler and called himself a Nazi completely welcome to perform in a stadium,” wrote commentator Jemele Hill in a social media post. “Man who said Free Palestine is not.”
Macklemore on Wednesday said he planned to donate $1 million, the amount of his net earnings from Sheeran’s tour, to organizations supporting the Palestinian people and challenged Kraft to match it.

Shortly thereafter, Kraft released a statement saying that, before news of Macklemore’s challenge emerged, Sheeran called and asked the Patriots owner to match his own planned $2 million donation toward humanitarian aid in the region. Sheeran is planning to seek contributions from other venue owners, Kraft said.

Get-in prices for nearly all of Sheeran’s shows have decreased in recent days, according to prices from resale platforms compiled by aggregator site Ticket Data, including a 10% drop for this weekend’s show in Philadelphia. Tickets for his two shows at the Patriots’ stadium have fallen 5% and 10% over the last three days, to $126 and $113.
Sheeran, for his part, has said that dropping Macklemore from his tour was not his decision but that of the venues and concert promoter.

“After Macklemore’s performances at my New Jersey shows, venues on my upcoming tour dates communicated that they would pull the shows if he was still supporting,” Sheeran wrote on Instagram. “I was informed that this stance was based on how Macklemore conveyed part of his message during his performance, rather than on everything that was said.”
He said he sought to “build a bridge” and spoke with “activists on both sides” to try to find a resolution, but was unsuccessful.
“I am not complicit,” Sheeran added.

items.title: Venezuela enviará aluminio a EE.UU. con Mercuria y Heeney
body: Venezuela se prepara para enviar aluminio a EE.UU. mediante un acuerdo con Mercuria Energy Group Ltd. y Heeney Capital, en una señal de que la rápida reactivación de los lazos comerciales entre ambos países comienza a extenderse más allá del petróleo tras años de aislamiento económico y diplomático.

El cargamento, el primero de aluminio venezolano con destino a EE.UU. en años, comprende unas 15.000 toneladas métricas producidas por la empresa estatal Venalum y está previsto que salga de Venezuela el viernes, según personas con conocimiento del asunto, que pidieron no ser identificadas porque la información no es pública.
El envío podría ser anunciado por funcionarios estadounidenses esta misma semana durante la cumbre energética del G20 que se celebra en Houston, según algunas de las fuentes.
La Casa Blanca y el Departamento del Interior no respondieron a las solicitudes de comentarios.

La comercializadora Mercuria y Heeney, una firma privada de inversión minera con sede en Nueva York, negocian por separado con las autoridades venezolanas para operar la fundición de Venalum, según informó anteriormente Bloomberg.

Un acuerdo sobre Venalum reforzaría el interés de empresas estadounidenses y de otros países en el sector minero y metalúrgico de Venezuela, en momentos en que Washington busca asegurar el acceso a minerales críticos en un mercado dominado por China.

Construida en la década de 1970 por el conglomerado estatal de industrias básicas CVG y un consorcio japonés, la fundición de Venalum llegó a ser la más grande de Latinoamérica, con una capacidad anual de 430.000 toneladas. El complejo, situado a orillas del río Orinoco, se deterioró por años de falta de inversión y apagones crónicos, y actualmente opera a una fracción de su capacidad instalada.

El cargamento de 15.000 toneladas tendría un valor de casi US$50 millones a precios actuales y equivaldría a varias semanas de producción a los niveles operativos reducidos de Venalum. El envío tiene un peso simbólico, ya que se trata de un acuerdo que se anunciará en la cumbre del G20, aunque el volumen representa solo una pequeña fracción del consumo anual de aluminio de EE.UU.
Mercuria y Heeney no respondieron de inmediato a las solicitudes de comentarios.
Ni Venalum ni el Ministerio de Información de Venezuela respondieron a las solicitudes de comentarios.
Traducción editada por Malu Poveda.
Nota Original: Venezuela Plans to Ship Aluminum to US in Mercuria-Heeney Deal

items.title: United Nations Chief Calls for Coordinating Global AI Regulation
body: United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres said nations must coordinate global efforts to regulate artificial intelligence, echoing calls for closer monitoring of the technology after warnings from leaders of the world’s top AI firms.

“We cannot afford to ignore concerns that have been raised, especially by those on the frontlines of the development of AI,” Guterres told reporters on Wednesday. “I am aware of the geopolitical divides and the temptations they might generate. But the world cannot afford a race to the bottom on AI safety.”

His comments follow a prominent warning from Anthropic PBC leader Dario Amodei, which was endorsed by OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Elon Musk of SpaceXAI. Earlier this week, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney called for worldwide coordination on AI regulations with a new technology forum similar to the Financial Stability Board he once chaired in the wake of the global financial crisis.

Guterres’s warning that AI needs “genuine international cooperation and a coordinated global effort” also comes days before world leaders descend on New York for the UN General Assembly’s annual high-level week.

The UN chief, who launched an Independent International Scientific Panel on AI earlier this year, said he will discuss AI concerns with heads of state from around the globe and talk about guardrails in his remarks from the UN’s podium.
Read More: AI Bosses Clash With Trump on Their Calls to Slow AI Development
In the US, where AI investment and data center construction are fueling economic growth, Trump administration officials have shown little appetite for slowing down the technology’s growth.

President Donald Trump has criticized Amodei’s call for restraint and pushed back against the idea of AI guardrails, emphasizing this risks ceding the US lead on AI to geopolitical rival China. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has struck a similar tone, warning that “there is no day after tomorrow if China wins at this.”
Read More: Bessent Warns ‘Nothing Else Would Matter’ If China Wins AI Race

Guterres emphasized the importance of stronger safeguards and measures to manage the technology’s future dangers given its global reach. “AI does not stop at borders – and neither do its risks,” he said.

items.title: Novartis Experimental Drug for ALS Fails in Another Pipeline Hit
body: Novartis AG halted development of an experimental drug it hoped would treat amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or Lou Gehrig’s disease, the latest in a long history of failed efforts to find a cure for the deadly condition.

The mid-stage trial was discontinued after the medicine failed to show it worked better than a dummy drug in delaying disease progression. Novartis confirmed development was stopped in an emailed statement Wednesday.
ALS, which is also known as motor neuron disease, is a fast-progressing condition that leads to paralysis, trouble swallowing and difficulty breathing.
Novartis’s VHB937 is a monoclonal antibody which researchers hoped would work with the body’s immune system to protect brain cells from damage.
Read More: Novartis Needs Board Shakeup and M&A Revamp, Investor Says

The drugmaker has suffered a series of development failures in recent weeks, including a heart disease drug and one for a rare muscle-wasting condition. That has heaped pressure on Chief Executive Officer Vas Narasimhan and the board, as some of the drugmaker’s biggest products lose patent protection.

items.title: Harold Hamm's Continental Set to Announce Venezuela Oil Deal
body: Billionaire shale pioneer Harold Hamm’s Continental Resources Inc. is set to announce a deal to invest in Venezuela as the Trump administration pushes US companies to revive the nation’s oil sector, according to a person familiar with the matter.
The Oklahoma City-based company plans to make the announcement at the G20 energy ministers summit in Houston, according to the person who asked not to be identified because the deal isn’t public.
Continental declined to comment. Venezuela’s information ministry and the White House didn’t immediately respond.
Earlier Wednesday, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Fox Business Network that a “very well-known oil company, an American company” would announce an investment in Venezuela.
An agreement by Hamm, a significant donor to US President Donald Trump, would add to a slate of deal in recent weeks aimed at boosting Venezuela’s crude production.

Chevron Corp., GE Vernova Inc. and Eni SpA all recently announced agreements alongside Wright and acting Venezuelan President Delcy Rodríguez at a signing ceremony in Caracas. Other companies that signed deals include Geopark Limited and privately held Aspect Holdings.

Wright said the deals represent “tens of billions” worth of investments that marked a “transformation for Venezuela.” But some analysts have questioned their durability in the face of lingering concerns about contract sanctity in a nation with a history of nationalization.

Hamm, one of Trump’s most outspoken supporters in the oil industry, was among the first to use horizontal drilling to unleash crude from shale rocks, helping spark a surge in output that has made the US the largest producer in the world.

Restoring daily Venezuelan oil output to the 3 million-barrel-a-day mark not seen in roughly 15 years will require major injections of foreign cash, and it’s not yet clear if overseas drillers can make a go of it in the South American nation,
Dan Pickering, chief investment officer at Pickering Energy Partners, said at conference in Houston earlier this week.
Read more: Venezuela Oil Opening Is ‘Smoke and Mirrors,’ Pickering Says

The US government negotiated for a 35% stake in Venezuelan entrepreneur Alejandro Betancourt’s North American Blue Energy Partners, a privately held company granted 100-year deals in 17 Venezuelan oil fields. Betancourt is a contentious figure in Venezuela, but the Trump administration has defended its decision to partner with the investor.

Until now, smaller private companies have been leading the US charge to negotiate oil deals in Venezuela. Progress has been slow, and they don’t have the same financial power as Chevron for the large-scale drilling and production equipment needed to ramp up output.

items.title: Meloni to Abolish Italy Vehicle Ownership Tax to Woo Voters
body: Giorgia Meloni’s government introduced a sweeping vehicle ownership tax cut, as the Italian premier seeks to stem the impact of the energy crisis on consumers ahead of a general election next year.
“Today, the government is abolishing one of the taxes Italians hate the most,” Meloni said Wednesday ahead of a cabinet meeting that approved the cut.

Meloni has been under increasing pressure to address spiraling energy prices, with her government first rolling out a tax cut on fuel prices in March to boost consumption. The tax cut was again extended on Wednesday until Oct. 5.

The decision comes as Meloni’s coalition has been feeling pressure from the rise of the ultranationalist National Future party, helmed by former general Roberto Vannacci, who is advocating that Russian energy should be once again used to shield consumers from the cost of energy.
Still, Meloni was defiant. “I will govern for as long as the majority is solid,” she told reporters after the cabinet meeting.

It is unclear how the government will be able to fund the new tax cut, which costs about €2 billion ($2.3 billion), according to people familiar with the matter. Officials said the measure will affect about 70% of all cars and all motorcycles, for a total of about 14.5 million vehicles.

Bloomberg reported earlier Wednesday that Meloni could still manage to exit the European Union’s fiscal monitoring regime if its 2025 deficit is revised lower next week, a possibility which would afford her additional financial leeway.
Read More: Italy Still Able to Exit EU Deficit Monitoring, Dombrovskis Says

items.title: What Would Canada Having EU 'Associate Member' Status Mean for US Relations?
body: To soften the blow from its trade standoff with the US, Canada needs to boost economic ties with other parts of the world. Prime Minister Mark Carney has made it clear he wants a closer relationship with the European Union. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s offer to make Canada an “associate member” of the world’s most powerful trading bloc during her annual speech to the European Parliament on Sept. 16 went further than many had expected. Such a status could draw Canada deeper into Europe’s markets and strategic industries. But the relationship would be a new one, created bespoke to meet a unique moment, and the EU has yet to define what it means.

The idea is a partnership that falls short of full membership while still offering some of its benefits. Canada’s location makes it legally impossible to aim for full membership, which requires countries to belong to the European continent. Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein offer one possible model. As members of the European Economic Area (EEA), those countries need to follow the rules of the EU single market to trade with the bloc yet have no role in running its institutions or voice in making its laws. What they do get is the ability to sell goods and services and move capital into the EU without encountering many tariffs or other trade barriers.

The chair of the European Parliament’s trade committee, Bernd Lange, said an extended relationship with Canada could be similar to the EU-Swiss model, only with greater political engagement. “With Switzerland we have around 100 different agreements, quite close, but the Swiss are not integrated into the political decision-making process,” Lange said. He suggested that Canada could be given some say in EU decision making, without having full voting rights.

Both von der Leyen and Carney have identified manufacturing, technology, defense, energy and the Arctic as areas for deeper cooperation. Carney told Bloomberg in an interview that he hopes for movement in the areas of travel rights and education. Canada has already become the only non-EU country to participate in SAFE, the bloc’s €150 billion ($173 billion) defense-procurement loan program.

In terms of trade, it may be hard to deepen a relationship that’s already quite close. Trade between Canada and the EU is already governed by CETA, a wide-ranging trade deal sealed a decade ago that eliminated duties on almost all goods and gave the EU greater access to Canada’s services markets. Although CETA has provisionally entered into force, 10 EU countries have yet to ratify it — an indication, perhaps, of hesitation on the part of some EU countries about embracing further integration with Canada.

The idea of moving closer to the EU has broad backing in Canada. In an Abacus Data survey of Canadians conducted in early September, 80% supported closer cooperation with the EU on issues such as foreign policy, defense and economic opportunities, up six percentage points since February. Support for full EU membership was weaker, at 49%.

For some members of the EU, the idea of Canada joining, even as an associate member, may be difficult to swallow. Nine countries are officially in the queue to join the bloc, and any move that could be seen as granting Canada preferential treatment may encounter some resistance. Would-be member Ukraine has rejected the notion of a “membership light” for itself that was proposed by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

Nonetheless, the EU could do with a boost. Earlier this month, Iceland voted not to reopen accession talks with the EU, one reason being that it already enjoys significant access as an EEA member. Though Iceland is a small country of just 400,000 people, its rejection was something of a blow for Brussels.

The other big issue will be money. EU countries, which are in the midst of negotiations about the bloc’s next seven-year budget, are unlikely to take warmly to an associate member securing benefits of EU membership without paying in.

After US-Canada trade talks ended last month, President Donald Trump imposed 50% tariffs on $20 billion of Canadian goods, and Carney retaliated against roughly the same value of US products. Getting closer to the EU would help Carney pursue what his government describes as a sovereignty agenda aimed at reducing foreign dependencies. But Canada’s deep economic integration with the US, including interwoven cross-border supply chains, could force some difficult choices for Ottawa, including in areas where EU and US product safety and other standards diverge.

After the negotiations with Washington fell apart in August, Carney said one of the sticking points was that the US wanted a say in future trade deals that Canada might sign. That was an unacceptable constraint on Canada’s right to make its own decisions, he said. It’s also clear the Trump administration is interested in securing more of Canada’s vast natural resources, including oil and minerals, and it might not look favorably on any deal by Canada that guarantees Europe improved access to those raw materials.

Canada-EU trade has been growing and equaled C$134 billion ($96 billion) in goods last year, according to a research paper from Canada’s Library of Parliament. Services added another C$58 billion. That’s still a fraction of the country’s trade with the US, which was well over $800 billion last year.
As it would be a new kind of relationship, it’s not clear what the next steps would be to formalize Canada’s associate membership or whether it would come with similar obligations to full membership.

In the first instance, EU member states will need to take stock of von der Leyen’s suggestion. As head of the European Commission, the EU’s executive branch, she has the power of initiative. But EU proposals on enlargement must also be approved by the European Parliament and the council of the EU, representing member states. Full membership of the EU has to be unanimously accepted by all members. Leaders will have an incentive to make tangible progress when they meet for an EU-Canada summit in Montreal in October.

items.title: Zillow Loses Antitrust Battle Over Chicago Area Listing Feed
body: Zillow Group Inc. lost its bid to force Illinois’ largest provider of real estate listings to provide access to its data about homes for sale.

US District Judge John Tharp Jr. in Chicago dissolved a previous order that required Midwest Real Estate Data, the multiple listings service for the Chicagoland area, to temporarily maintain Zillow’s access to listings. Tharp ordered Zillow to engage in arbitration over its listings contract with MRED.

The ruling is a key win for Compass Inc., the largest US residential brokerage and a major source of listings to MRED. Zillow had sought to exclude Compass listings from its site, but MRED said that violated their terms of service and shut off all access for two days. Compass, which is seeking to build a private listings network, has been at odds with public portals like Zillow.
Tharp found that Zillow hadn’t offered enough evidence to sustain the allegation of an illegal group boycott between MRED and Compass it made in its May lawsuit.

“While the loss of access to listing feeds would undoubtedly harm Zillow, it will only experience such harm if it attempts to enforce its listing standards,” Tharp wrote in his opinion. “If Zillow doesn’t enforce its listing ban, it will not lose access to the listing feeds and it can avoid any harm.”
MRED said the decision reinforces the ability of listing services “to consistently enforce their rules and data licensing agreements.”

In a statement on its website, Zillow said it was disappointed in the decision, which it called “a step back for Chicago home buyers and sellers.” The company said it will continue with the case as it moves into arbitration.

Compass hailed the ruling as a win for consumers. “This decision affirms that choice belongs to the homeowner, and any effort to punish consumers for exercising that choice is anti‑competitive and harmful to consumers,” the company said in a statement.

Seattle-based Zillow previously won a court order that reinstated the Chicago-area listings after MRED cut off its data feed in May.  In his decision Thursday, Tharp declined to extend the order that MRED continue to provide listings to Zillow.

The Midwest may be the first of many regions where Zillow will have to fight for access to listings. In the last year, Compass has been working to establish partnerships with the nation’s largest MLSs, including those overseeing Tennessee, California, Delaware, Maryland, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Virginia, West Virginia and DC. These efforts could disrupt the US real estate portal industry, some of which like Zillow are third-party aggregators that rely on MLS data to source home listings.

In March 2025, The National Association of Realtors, a trade group representing more than 1.4 million agents, instituted new rules on listings that allow individual listing services to set the rules when sellers want to limit marketing of certain properties.

In response, Zillow created its own policy that it wouldn’t accept listings not available to the broader public, including those behind a login or registration wall or properties only visible to people working with the listing brokerage.

Compass filed an antitrust lawsuit challenging the policy last year. A federal judge in New York declined to block Zillow’s policy in February, saying Compass failed to show the home-listing site has a monopoly in the online home search market.
Compass subsequently dismissed its suit, and Zillow began enforcing its policy, except in Chicago.

MRED, the leading listing service in Illinois and counties surrounding Chicago, said in court filings that it informed Zillow that a ban on certain listings violates MRED’s own rules, which prohibit the filtering of listings based on the brokerage or agent.

Zillow alleged that MRED, which holds a monopoly on listings in the Chicago area, conspired with Compass, the largest broker in the area, to force Zillow to change its policies and block the home-listings site from competing in the market.
The case is Zillow v. Midwest Real Estate Data, 26-cv-5451, US District Court, Northern District of Illinois (Chicago).

items.title: Iran's Rare Win Over US Sets Up Clash at UN Nuclear Agency
body: Iran this week scored a diplomatic win at the UN’s atomic watchdog by securing a seat at the group’s organizing committee over US objections. That’s set to raise further hurdles for diplomacy on nuclear power.

Three days into its general conference, the United Nations’ International Atomic Energy Agency remains deadlocked over key issues like nuclear safety and security, following the tug-of-war between Washington and Iran. The clash between the nations, at war since late February, is emerging as a test for diplomats who are typically expected to reach a consensus on how the world should handle nuclear threats.

The IAEA’s meeting careened in an unexpected direction on Tuesday, when Tehran overcame US opposition with support from Persian Gulf neighbors — whose territory the Islamic Republic targeted with thousands of missiles and drones since the start of the war.

Middle Eastern nations had earlier appointed Iran to the conference’s organizing body, sparking objections from the US. Ambassador Preston Wells Griffith III called it “an affront” to the IAEA and its work.

“Electing Iran to the committee, just days after its non-compliance was referred to the United Nations Security Council, would be beyond shameful and an embarrassment to the credibility of this body,” Griffith said before demanding IAEA members vote to bar Iran from assuming its place on the committee.
Iran emerged victorious following additional debate and a secret ballot, with 44 countries backing the nomination against 35 that sided with the US’s position. Forty-two nations abstained.

Behrouz Kamalvandi, deputy head of the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran, chided Washington for what he described as a “childish type of behavior,” which included preventing the Islamic Republic’s top nuclear official from attending the meeting.
Read More: Iran Official Blocked From UN Nuclear Meeting at US’s Urging
“Nuclear science, technology, expertise and industry have taken deep roots in the country and cannot be eliminated through military actions or assassinations,” he said. “Iran will not surrender.”

The episode illustrates the widening political gulf at the heart of the IAEA, complicating efforts to fulfill its technical mandate. The watchdog’s inspectors haven’t been able to verify the state or location of Iran’s uranium stockpile since Israel and the US attacked it in June 2025. Earlier this month, a US-led initiative to refer Tehran to the UN Security Council was met with objections from China and Russia.
Read More: Iran Nuclear Impasse Deepens After US Wins UN Watchdog Vote
“This is a carryover from the mess created last year,” said Tariq Rauf, the IAEA’s former head of verification policy.

The acrimony which erupted at last year’s annual meeting stemmed from discord over the US and Israeli attacks, along with US President Donald Trump’s demands to eliminate IAEA references to diversity, equality and inclusion. The gathering ended in the early hours with no consensus achieved on any of the IAEA’s trademark activities related to nuclear safety or security.
“People were hoping this year would be on a more even keel,” Rauf said. “But it’s even worse.”

items.title: Heathrow's Expansion Is "Not Currently Compatible" With Net Zero
body: The UK is trying to strike a difficult balance between sticking to its legally binding climate targets and expanding infrastructure seen as essential to economic growth.

Today’s newsletter looks at the proposed expansion of Heathrow Airport and at why the Climate Change Committee advising the UK government says it is   incompatible with the country’s climate target  . Also, after a scorching “summer of truth,” the EU Commission’s president   unveiled measures and proposals   to shield the bloc against the worst impacts of heat.
Subscribe to   Bloomberg.com   for   unlimited access   to all our coverage.
By Jess Shankleman and Olivia Rudgard

Heathrow Airport embodies the difficulties of cutting emissions from flying just as authorities are looking to add a third runway that will allow the UK’s largest airport to meet increasing demand for air travel.

One option is to make airlines pay a government levy to cover the cost of cleaner fuels and carbon capture, the UK’s Climate Change Committee said today as it released a report on the issue. But the levy would significantly raise the price of plane tickets. What’s more, both sustainable aviation fuels and carbon capture face significant challenges and are largely unproven at commercial scale.

Adding a third runway to Britain’s largest airport “is not currently compatible with the UK’s net zero target,” Nigel Topping, chair of the CCC, said in a statement. “Government needs to ensure that the aviation industry takes responsibility for the emissions it creates.”

Air travel represents a growing share of global emissions and decarbonizing the sector is one of the most difficult challenges facing the energy transition. Airplanes are hard to electrify and lower-carbon alternatives to jet fuel, made from crops or waste, are expensive and insufficient to meet global demand.

That makes adding more flights and more emissions irreconcilable with climate goals, unless the industry is forced to invest heavily in engineered removals and lower-carbon fuels, driving up its costs and the cost of flying.

While the UK has succeeded in cutting emissions over the past 30 years, aviation emissions have continued to rise. Even without Heathrow’s expansion, emissions from aviation are forecast to continue growing between now and 2050.

The UK is already at risk of missing its goal of net zero emissions by 2050, in the absence of industry reform. Taken in isolation, expanding Heathrow would increase emissions by almost 7% by midcentury.

Under the CCC’s proposed Net Zero Aviation Pathway, the cost of a return ticket to New York would increase by about £400 ($539) by 2050 as airlines passed on costs to passengers, the CCC estimated — that’s about 6 pence to 9 pence per mile traveled. A round trip to Alicante, Spain, would increase by about £150. The full costs of decarbonization should be phased in gradually, starting “soon,” the CCC said.

Flight prices are likely to rise over that period if capacity remains constrained, the CCC said, but its proposal would ensure some of those higher costs pay for lowering emissions rather than boosting airline profits.

The CCC also urged the government to consider a frequent-flier tax, noting that public panels had strongly backed one and that almost 40% of international flights in 2024 were taken by people in the highest-income quintile.
By John Ainger and Laura Millan

Europe has just been through a “summer of truth” on climate change, said the European Commission’s President Ursula von der Leyen in her annual state of the European Union speech, which marks the start of the political year in the region.

Almost no part of the continent was spared, Von der Leyen said. The bloc’s economy and security largely depend on how it manages what she called “the tipping points of our times” — namely, climate change and artificial intelligence.

“We need to step up dramatically on preparedness,” she said. “We need better early warning systems and better health preparedness, we need urban adaptation and cooling and we need to support the most vulnerable.”

The EU will set up a “climate insurance alliance” to help cover losses as global warming increases the frequency and intensity of droughts, floods and wildfires, she said. Only a quarter of catastrophe losses are privately insured, with the rest of the coverage therefore needing to come from national budgets. A climate resilience framework, due next month, will map 100 of the most vulnerable regions in the bloc, she added.

Climber Alex Honnold is best known as the star of Free Solo, an Oscar-winning documentary that followed his rope-free ascent of the 3,000-foot (1,000-meter) face of Yosemite’s El Capitan. But he has also established the Honnold Foundation to bring solar power to those who most need it. This week on Zero, Bloomberg’s Akshat Rathi asks Honnold how he gets big things done and why helping communities get clean energy has become his other passion in life.
Listen now, and subscribe on Apple, Spotify or YouTube to get new episodes of Zero every Thursday.

South Africa’s Sasol, the world’s largest producer of fuel and chemicals from coal, has begun selling sustainable aviation fuel to a company that organizes luxury trips to Antarctica. The company hopes that tapping into a new market may help reduce its environmental footprint. The tour operator offers trips to Antarctica’s blue rivers, the channels of bright blue meltwater that run across the ice that’s disappearing faster because of climate change caused by humans burning fossil fuels in the first place.
