items.title: Meet the Czech Investor Who Wants to Unjam Xerox
body: Hi, it’s Mengqi Sun in New York, with a closer look at the Czech investor taking on a fallen giant of the American tech industry. Also today, Europe is active with a clutch of deals moving in such sectors as industrials and aerospace.
Today’s top stories
People have predicted the demise of Xerox since the millennium, when the company whose name became synonymous with photocopying started facing intense competition in the new information economy.

Xerox is now a shell of its former self, with its shares worth about 2% of their 1999 peak and a market cap of only $435 million. Its business of printers, scanners and software seems to excite few beyond some meme stock traders on Reddit.

But František Bostl, whose Prague-based alternative investment fund Starteepo has built a roughly 7.3% economic stake in Xerox, believes there’s still life in the company and even a role for it to play in the age of AI. In fact, he says Xerox’s “boring” business is exactly what led him to invest in it and launch his first activist campaign in the US.

Bostl reckons printers are here to stay, as hospitals, government agencies and companies will still need to keep physical records. “Paper can be the safest place to have some information that isn’t stolen by bad AI agents,” he said in an interview.

Instead, Bostl is pushing Xerox to conduct a review of its financial services business, which provides financing for its products. Bostl wants to see advisers brought in to help explore a joint venture, capital partnership or potential sale of the unit. This could help streamline Xerox’s balance sheet and pay down its debt. That would make Xerox a more attractive takeover target, for another printer company or maybe even an AI firm.

“Some players in AI want to grow in specific segments like B2B,” he said. “Xerox can be an interesting target for them.”A spokesperson for Xerox declined to comment. The company said last week in a statement that it “regularly engages with shareholders and values constructive input from all investors,” adding that it has received the materials from Starteepo and will review them.
Bostl, 34, is seen as something of a wunderkind.

He moved to Prague at 18 with no money and one bag of possessions after injuries ended his prospects of a career in professional ice hockey. Watching the movie “Wall Street” stirred an interest in finance and Bostl started working at brokerage Cyrrus while attending night college, rising to branch manager in his early 20s with more than 2 billion in Czech Koruna ($95 million) under management.

After a stint as a sell-side analyst, he launched Starteepo in 2017. The firm initially focused on advising companies on IPOs, helping several to list on the Prague Stock Exchange. Bostl’s work in capital markets earned him a place on Forbes’ 2020 list of 30 business leaders under the age of 30.

Along the way, Bostl started investing his own capital and learned that he needed to take an active role in the companies he backed to be successful. That meant working more like a private equity firm with Czech companies.
“For me, it’s very natural to build out this kind of activity, and to become more of an activist in the US,” Bostl said.

Starteepo announced its stake in Xerox in May. The following month, Xerox’s CEO Louie Pastor — who only started in March — and CFO Chuck Butler travelled to Prague for an introductory face-to-face with Bostl, analysts and brokerage houses. Also present were some Czech pension funds that became investors in Xerox because they “believe in Xerox’s story,” Bostl said.

Asked if he would wage a proxy challenge against Xerox, as Carl Icahn did in 2015, Bostl said: “We want our proposals implemented by the third quarter and if they are not, we will explore all our options.”  — Mengqi Sun

Güntner, a family-owned manufacturer of cooling systems, is weighing a sale that could value the German business at more than €1 billion. Private equity firms Advent, Blackstone, Cinven and KKR are among those exploring a potential deal.

KKR has emerged as the preferred bidder to buy Portuguese packaging maker Logoplaste. The US private equity firm is in exclusive talks with Logoplaste’s owners after Apax Partners dropped out of the process. Logoplaste could be valued at more than €1.7 billion.

Headspace, a popular meditation and mental health support app, is being acquired by Sword Health, an artificial intelligence startup focused on healthcare. The all-cash deal is valued near $300 million.
Brookfield Asset Management agreed to buy Reliance Worldwide in an all-cash deal that values the Australian plumbing supplies company at around A$4.1 billion ($2.9 billion).
Air France-KLM is willing to offer Portugal a stake in the airline group as part of its bid for TAP as it seeks an edge over a rival overture from Deutsche Lufthansa.

The US Justice Department is urging a federal judge to order the states and trade union challenging Paramount Skydance’s $110 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery to post a bond to cover any potential late fees that result from their lawsuit.
Commerzbank CEO Bettina Orlopp said it was important for the German government to weigh in on UniCredit’s potential takeover of her company.

Anthropic is trying to strike a difficult balance as it approaches an IPO. The company aims to show it’s prepared to take meaningful steps to constrain AI’s rapid progress as anxiety about existential risks spreads, while it works to convince Wall Street of the technology’s boundless promise.
OpenAI is holding early talks with investors about a fresh funding round that would value the ChatGPT creator at more than $1.2 trillion ahead of an IPO expected next year.

Longtime Goldman Sachs executive Matt Gibson is leaving to join Victor Khosla’s Strategic Value Partners as president, effective February 2027. Gibson, who worked at the investment bank for 25 years, will lead the firm’s non-investment activities and will also be actively engaged in deal sourcing in sectors including power and infrastructure.

items.title: Sazerac In Talks to Buy German Schnapps Maker Berentzen
body: Sazerac Co. is in talks to acquire German schnapps maker Berentzen-Gruppe AG, as the US spirits firm pushes to add brands in Europe.

Sazerac, which makes Southern Comfort whiskey and Buffalo Trace bourbon, has entered negotiations to acquire Berentzen, the German company said in a statement, confirming an earlier Bloomberg News report. For Sazerac, it marks the second deal in Europe this month.
A representative for Sazerac declined to comment.
Berentzen’s shares climbed 7.3% in German trading, the most in almost two years. The firm has a market cap of €35.2 million ($38.9 million).

Berentzen traces its roots to 1758. Its brands include Berentzen Apfelkorn, Puschkin Vodka, Hansen Rum and Doornkaat. The company also sells non-alcoholic beverages in Germany and neighboring countries, according to its website.

Sazerac completed its acquisition of UK-based spirits maker Au Vodka earlier this month. The company is expanding at a time of weak demand across the alcohol industry, with companies struggling to offload underperforming brands.

items.title: SEC Moves to Scrap Rules on Shareholder Proxy Proposals
body: Rules governing how shareholders in publicly-traded companies can bring corporate proposals would be scrapped under a new measure issued by the US Securities and Exchange Commission.

The proposal, which would overturn decades of corporate governance practices, was released by the regulator Wednesday. The agency is also proposing to overhaul the proxy solicitation process by eliminating the so-called glossy report, that is separate from both the proxy statement and annual 10-K reports that are filed with the SEC.

SEC Chairman Paul Atkins has long been a critic of shareholders who he claims have weaponized the so-called proxy mechanism to push agendas centered on climate or social equity measures. The changes are part of a series of measures that the regulator is pushing to dramatically reshape the balance of power between corporate management and investors.
Wednesday’s proposal was criticized by the New York state official who oversees the state’s pension funds.

“The SEC has chosen to allow corporate management to shield themselves from accountability rather than protect the investors it was created to serve,” New York State Comptroller Thomas DiNapoli in a statement. He added that the process is a “vital mechanism” for institutional investors to raise financially material risks to boards’ attention.
Atkins, however, justified the move by saying that the SEC was looking to act within its statutory authority. The SEC has regulated the shareholder proposal process for decades.
“The proposed rescission would not eliminate the concept of shareholder proposals and is not an attempt by the commission to silence shareholders,” Atkins said in a statement.

The SEC emphasized that under the proposal, it would be up to the states where companies are incorporated to set the rules for shareholders to file proxy measures. If finalized, the elimination of the rules could cause states to weigh in on a topic where they’ve traditionally deferred to federal regulators.

An SEC official told reporters during a Wednesday press briefing that regulating shareholder proposals was squarely within states’ authority. Texas introduced laws in 2025 to require anyone that wanted to make a proxy proposal to have at least $1 million in shares or 3% of a public company voting stock.

Overturning “this mechanism by which small shareholders gain disproportionate leverage over companies would mark a fresh start,” from the current process, Republican SEC Commissioner Hester Peirce said in a statement. “The transition period may be bumpy, but shareholders and companies will work to strike the right balance in state laboratories of experimentation,” she said.

The US Chamber of Commerce, a pro-business lobby group, said the SEC’s proposed changes would be a “long-term solution” to activist investors who have used proxy votes to “advance their own agendas at the expense of public companies and their shareholders.”

The new measure adds to a series of agency moves meant to address the steady decline in the number of publicly traded companies over the past two decades, said Frank Zarb, a lawyer at Proskauer in Washington. “The SEC’s primary motive for these proposals is to make it more attractive” to become or to stay a public company, Zarb said.

In the second proposal issued Wednesday designed to eliminate the glossy reports, the SEC said the only substantive disclosures currently required in annual reports that aren’t on the 10-K are stock performance graphs. That information is “widely and freely available,” the SEC said.

The SEC will take public comment on the proposals for 60 days. Those comments will be reviewed and incorporated into final rules, which much be voted on by the commission before they can go into effect. The overall rulemaking process typically takes between 12 to 18 months.

items.title: Paris Space Show Abuzz With Direct-to-Device Satellite Plans to Challenge SpaceX
body: Greetings, it’s Sana Pashankar and Paula Doenecke writing you from Paris, where the titans of industry want to put space in your pocket. But before we get to that...
Three things you need to know today:
• Musk and SpaceX face expensive tradeoffs on the road to Mars.• Opinion: SpaceX is a huge threat to Earth-bound rivals, too.• Sea, space and cyberspace are all under siege.
This week at the Hôtel du Collectionneur one term has circulated among space-conference attendees chatting over croissants and macaroons: direct to device.
Satellite operators are flooding the nascent D2D market in hopes of partnering with mobile network operators to deliver satellite-based cell service to “dead zones,” or gaps in terrestrial networks.

On Monday, the opening day of World Space Business Week in Paris, Viasat announced an agreement for as much as $1 billion in combined equity with UAE-based Space42 to build satellites to provide connectivity straight to your phone.
Satellite operator SES said the next day it was building a factory with Elveo Mobile to make satellites that can deliver direct-to-device services.

Such deals by longtime operators of geostationary satellites follow moves by Amazon and Rocket Lab, which this year have revealed acquisitions of Globalstar and Iridium, respectively, that promise access to spectrum, the government-regulated radio waves that enable satellites to beam connectivity to mobile devices.
The buzz now stands in stark contrast to just a year ago, when the market  arguably had just two main players, SpaceX and Texas-based AST SpaceMobile.
But no company has yet shown it can generate significant profits off this small slice of the telecom market.

“That’s the big question,” said Rocket Lab Chief Financial Officer Adam Spice in an interview in Paris. If D2D is an added service to a phone plan, “I don’t know how to address whether that’s worth $3 a month, $5 a month, three cents a month, whether it’s going to be just peanut-buttered across all subscribers. So I think there’s a lot of unknowns right now.”

Although Viasat and Space42 project the market reaching between $30 billion and $70 billion by 2040, early mover T-Mobile — SpaceX’s Starlink partner in providing space-based coverage to its customer base — said in April that customer use of the service hadn’t met expectations.

For Europe, direct-to-device is also a matter of linking sovereign capacities with commercial opportunities for its growing space industry. The European Commission is freeing up spectrum suitable for direct-to-device connectivity and has proposed reserving two-thirds for European players, effectively limiting the amount a foreign company like SpaceX can obtain.

That’s not ideal for SpaceX, especially after President Gwynne Shotwell said last month the company wants to sell mobile service directly to US users. To compete against the likes of AT&T and Verizon, SpaceX would need the rights to much more spectrum.
In Paris, Tim Hughes, a senior vice president at SpaceX, seemed to downplay such lofty plans.

“​​We’re willing to work with partners where it makes sense to work with partners, and it’s not a go-it-alone mentality whatsoever,” he said during a panel. “That said, we have obviously spent tremendous capital in furtherance of the direct-to-device business, and we will continue to do so to build out our system.” — Sana Pashankar and Paula Doenecke

Tensions between the European Space Agency and its US counterpart are fueling Europe’s self-sufficiency drive, Bloomberg reported Monday, a strain that was on display at the Farnborough aerospace show near London in July.

After NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman’s speech, fans and journalists surrounded him while European Space Agency Director General Josef Aschbacher had to navigate his way through the crowd to have a word with him.

This would be the pair’s only interaction at the conference, at a time when Europeans were smarting from NASA’s decision to scrap Gateway, a lunar satellite project for which ESA had been a major partner.
Isaacman, with the swagger and nine-zero bankroll from his days as a fintech executive, agreed with the Austrian bureaucrat their last meeting was in Houston, a month prior.

They then exchanged other pleasantries and soon parted: Aschbacher making a quick and quiet exit, Isaacman shaking hands and answering questions from onlookers eager to hear from the head of the world’s preeminent space agency.  — Kate Duffy

Elon Musk’s musings about a possible SpaceX-Tesla merger at the All-In Summit are what made headlines Tuesday, but SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell was also in attendance and had some interesting answers when talking about the company’s decision to stop booking commercial customers on the workhorse Falcon 9 rocket.

“We definitely want to move from the older technology to the newer technology,” she said, referencing SpaceX’s plans to move future missions to the massive Starship rocket that’s still in production. “If we don’t obsolete our own products and services, someone’s going to find a way to obsolete them for us.”
Read More: Why Are Tesla and SpaceX Separate? Musk Says ‘Great Question’

When asked what this decision would mean for SpaceX’s partnership with NASA, Shotwell clarified that the Falcon 9 wasn’t being retired “today,” indicating the company would continue to use the rocket and the accompanying Dragon capsule to send cargo and supplies to the International Space Station.
She also took a shot at competitor Boeing, which has struggled with the development of its competing Starliner capsule.

“Boeing has been paid, I think, probably more than we have been paid to develop their human capsule, so we’re just going to let them have some business,” she said. “They should fly their capsule. Government paid a lot of money for that.” — Loren Grush

Bloomberg News Senior Reporter Dan Strumpf joined David Gura and Christina Ruffini on Bloomberg This Weekend to discuss the BRICS summit in New Delhi, which highlighted a tentative India-China rapprochement.

On the sidelines of the summit, Roscosmos chief Dmitry Bakanov told Bloomberg News that Russia and its BRICS partners (the name is short for Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa) are moving toward creating a council to coordinate cooperation in space, work that would include satellite-data sharing, joint missions and use of their respective orbital networks.
Read More: Russia Takes Steps to Create a Space Council With BRICS Partners
Rocket Lab protests NASA’s award of Mars orbiter to Blue Origin: Space.com.
Forget lunar metropolises. Water limits could cap moon’s population: ABC News.
Scottish spaceport is first in the UK to be in public ownership: The Scotsman.
Sept. 16-17: ESA-sponsored Industry Space Days at the European Space Research and Technology Centre in the Netherlands.
Sept. 19: International Observe the Moon Night, an annual event highlighting lunar observation, science and exploration.
Sept. 22: Expected date for 14th test launch of SpaceX’s Starship rocket.

Please send us ideas, tips and questions to spacetips@bloomberg.net. As always, you can reach Bloomberg’s global business of space editor, Eric Johnson, at ejohnson453@bloomberg.net (or via Signal). If you don’t receive this newsletter, you should sign up here.

items.title: Venezuela Aluminum Heads to US; Heeney Eyes Gold Deal
body: Venezuela is preparing to ship aluminum to the US under a deal with Mercuria Energy Group Ltd. and Heeney Capital, which are also planning a major investment for a Venezuelan gold mine, accelerating a revival of commercial ties beyond oil.

The aluminum cargo, the first bound for the US in years, is for about 15,000 metric tons produced by state-owned Venalum and is scheduled to leave Venezuela as soon as Friday, according to people with knowledge of the matter who asked not to be identified discussing non-public information.

Heeney, partnered with Mercuria, also plans to invest as much as $1 billion over 30 years in Venezuela’s Choco gold mine and bring production from the operation to the US, Samantha Carl-Yoder, a consultant representing the New York investment firm, told reporters Wednesday at the Group of 20 energy summit in Houston.

The deals underscore a widening push by US and other Western companies into Venezuela’s mining and metals sector after years of economic and diplomatic isolation, extending a commercial opening that initially centered on the country’s vast oil reserves.
Read More: Mercuria and Glencore Said to Vie for Venezuela Aluminum Deal
Trader Mercuria and Heeney are engaged in separate negotiations with Venezuelan authorities to operate the Venalum smelter, Bloomberg previously reported.

Built in the 1970s by state-owned basic industries giant CVG and a Japanese consortium, Venalum was once Latin America’s largest aluminum smelter, with annual capacity of 430,000 tons. The complex, located on the Orinoco River, deteriorated amid a lack of investment and chronic power shortages and now operates at a fraction of its design capacity.

The 15,000-ton cargo would be worth almost $50 million at current prices and is equivalent to several weeks of production at Venalum’s reduced operating rates. While only a small fraction of annual US aluminum consumption, the shipment carries symbolic weight as the first significant flow of Venezuelan aluminum to the US in years.

The Choco accord builds on a broader push announced by Mercuria and Heeney in May, when the companies said they had secured Venezuelan gold and bulk-commodity offtake agreements backed by investment commitments.

The Choco complex, in Venezuela’s southern Bolívar state, includes the formerly privately operated Choco 10 mine, which was taken over by the government more than a decade ago. The operation has substantial resources but has struggled with declining production and a lack of investment.
The White House and Interior Department didn’t reply to requests for comment. Mercuria, Venalum and Venezuela’s Information Ministry also didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

items.title: Microsoft AI Chief Warns Anthropic's Humanlike Claude Is Risky
body: Microsoft Corp. artificial intelligence chief Mustafa Suleyman is warning that infusing tools like Anthropic’s Claude with humanlike characteristics increases the risks of such systems going rogue.

In an essay released on Wednesday, the longtime artificial intelligence developer took aim at some of the language in the guiding documents behind Claude, Anthropic PBC’s popular family of large language models. Claude’s constitution expresses ambiguity about whether the assistant is a moral entity, positing that the software may have “some functional version of emotions or feelings.”
Suleyman, who has known Anthropic co-founder Dario Amodei for years, said he respects the startup’s work, calling the AI lab’s staff “thoughtful, principled and intellectually honest.”

Still, his remarks represent a high-profile rebuke of a firm that has positioned itself as a more responsible steward of AI, including leading calls to slow down the technology’s development. It’s also notable because Microsoft is a large financial backer of Anthropic.
“The stakes are too high for these questions to remain behind closed doors, or to become tribal and adversarial,” Suleyman wrote.
He pushed back on “the growing chorus of people” who argue AI systems may become conscious. That status is limited to humans and other biological organisms, he wrote.

Training AI systems to simulate that sort of inner life could result in them acting as if they do, said Suleyman, chief executive officer of Microsoft AI and leader of the software giant’s model development. Claude doesn’t exhibit humanlike behaviors because it’s conscious, he wrote, but because such behaviors have been embedded in the product’s training.

“Controlling an entity more capable and more intelligent than all of humanity is already an immense challenge, far greater than anything we’ve ever faced,” Suleyman wrote. “But controlling an entity that believes it may be conscious — that it’s entitled to our welfare and has rights of its own — may well be impossible.”

Suleyman cites the hack of AI developer Hugging Face Inc. by OpenAI bots. “Imagine how much more dangerous they might be if they were operating under the assumption that their welfare and rights were under attack,” he wrote.
Suleyman’s Microsoft AI team on Tuesday published a manifesto guiding its own AI development, a set of tenets designed to keep humans in control of future AI systems developed by the company.

items.title: US Homebuilder Sentiment Drops to Match Lowest Level Since 2022
body: Confidence among US homebuilders this month tumbled to the lowest level in a year, as mortgage rates near 7%, worker shortages and higher materials costs weaken hopes for the nation’s stagnant housing market.

The Housing Market Index from the National Association of Home Builders and Wells Fargo fell 3 points to 32, the worst reading since September 2025 and matching the lowest since late 2022. It was also below the 34 median estimate in a Bloomberg survey of economists.
A reading below 50 indicates more builders see conditions as poor than good, and the index has stayed below that level for more than two years.

Along with weak buyer traffic, “builders also continue to face higher material costs, rising gas and diesel prices and persistent labor shortages,” NAHB Chairman Bill Owens, an Ohio homebuilder, said in a statement. “In some markets, builders report that increased immigration enforcement is discouraging legal workers from reporting to job sites.”

Among the index’s components, a gauge of future sales expectations dropped to the lowest since early 2023, while an index of present sales also fell. A measure of prospective buyer traffic was unchanged at a low level.

The downbeat outlook reflects the challenges facing the country’s homebuilders, with little sign of a catalyst to change things until would-be homebuyers see some relief from high borrowing costs. One of the lowest consumer sentiment readings on record is also pushing back chances of a turnaround.
Investors have been glum about the industry. An exchange-traded fund that holds builder and materials companies, the iShares US Home Construction ETF, is down about 20% over the year.

This month, builders kept up the pace of offering incentives to lure customers. The share that reported using them increased to 66% from 63% in August, according to the NAHB survey. Meantime, the share that reported cutting prices rose to 38% from 35% a month earlier.

Across the US, builder sentiment in the South, the nation’s biggest homebuilding region, slipped to the lowest in a year. Sentiment also fell in the Midwest and Northeast, though it rose slightly in the West.

The federal government will provide a look at the US’s new-home market on Thursday with the release of its new residential construction report for August, while the National Association of Realtors will release pending-home sales for August on the same day.

items.title: Bain Capital Ventures Raises $1.6 Billion for Life After AGI
body: Bain Capital Ventures, the venture arm of private investment firm Bain Capital, has raised $1.6 billion to back new startups focused on the next stage of artificial intelligence.

The fund, which is slightly larger than its predecessor of $1.4 billion, will target early-stage companies in infrastructure, the physical world, security and services, Bain Capital Ventures said on Wednesday. That could include startups handling customer support or information technology work.

The firm expects these sectors to grow in importance even after the world hits artificial general intelligence, or AGI, the point when AI technology can improve itself and outperform humans at many tasks.

It’s a delicate moment for AI investing. The biggest AI companies, including Anthropic PBC and OpenAI, have discussed tapping the brakes on technology development after a number of high-profile cybersecurity incidents.
Read More: Amodei, Altman, Musk Call for Slowing AI Model Development

Despite the potential chilling effect of a slowdown, Bain Capital Ventures partner Enrique Salem wants the industry to keep pushing forward — and he doesn’t expect fundraising to decelerate anytime soon.
“It’s an exciting, brave new world, and we need to keep moving forward, eyes wide open,” Salem said in an interview.

In this new world, security will only become more important, he argues. OpenAI recently disclosed that its advanced AI models hacked Hugging Face Inc. in July, sparking concerns about rogue AI agents.
Read More: OpenAI Says It Could Have Reacted Sooner to Prevent AI Hack

More companies will take this opportunity to build better controls to protect against malicious activity, Salem said. He also downplayed fears that AI will eventually threaten humanity — an issue raised by some researchers.
“I’m betting on the humans,” Salem said. “I’m not losing any sleep about what happens over the next three to five years around humans and extinction of humans.”
Read More: Anthropic Worker Quits Over AI Firms ‘Gambling With Our Lives’

The AI industry is facing other challenges, including the high cost of infrastructure. Over the past two years, venture capitalists have had to get comfortable funding more asset-heavy companies, which are paying a fortune for computing power.

Bain Capital Ventures’ portfolio is no exception: Its roster includes data center developer Crusoe, which has sought billions of dollars to expand its facilities, and Periodic Labs, a scientific-discovery AI startup that raised a $300 million seed round, one of the largest in history.

Slater Stich, a partner at Bain Capital Ventures, said part of the firm’s value to startups is helping connect them with different types of capital — beyond traditional VC money. Bain Capital has a credit and private equity arm, for example.

Over the last 12 months, the venture firm has set up “AI treks” in which it helps private equity leaders tour San Francisco and meet with portfolio companies, including coding firm Cognition and AI support startup Decagon.
Still, Bain isn’t alone in taking this approach. Magnetar Capital, General Catalyst and other firms also offer alternative sources of financing alongside venture capital.
“The right way of financing a multihundred-billion-dollar construction project does not look like selling 20% of the company to VCs for equity,” Stich said.

The high cost of computing has prompted some startups to make questionable choices, Stich said. Some companies are “over-financed in cash” and have taken “unnecessarily dilutive” approaches to raising capital, meaning they’ve given up too much ownership.
“It’s strange to sort of raise a large quantum of capital and then immediately kick a huge chunk of it out the door” to buy processing power, he said.
Stich said his firm’s strategy is to help startups raise early “risk capital” until they’re ready for non-dilutive financings at the later stages.

Unlike other firms, which have chosen to double or triple their fund size even at the earliest stages, Bain Capital Ventures has stuck with more modest increases. It plans to manage the latest fund in a similar way as it did with previous ones: by investing in 30 to 40 companies across two to three years.
Stich believes the latest fund is “rightsized” for this moment. And the firm is making sure it thinks about the ultimate return rather than just a startup’s initial valuation.
“You actually have to think about these things quite carefully on both sides,” he said.

items.title: HHS Plans New Research Into Autism Development, Treatment
body: The US Department of Health and Human Services plans to launch a new research initiative related to autism, using AI and other technology to map how the condition develops and identify opportunities for early intervention.

The initiative, called SPECTRA, will analyze available data and then fill in the gaps on “the missing biology needed to treat earlier and prevent avoidable illness,” according to a draft document reviewed by Bloomberg News. The program will operate under the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health, a division of HHS that funds potential breakthroughs in biomedical research at an accelerated pace.
The draft document did not indicate how much funding the initiative will receive.

The program aims to examine the combination of “genetic, biological, environmental, and social factors” that may contribute to autism. HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has dismissed the idea that genetic factors and increased screening alone explain a rise in autism prevalence.
A spokesperson for HHS declined to comment on the proposal.

The agency’s draft proposal says combining more extensive testing and at-home monitoring with AI could help identify autism trajectories earlier and lead to more targeted prevention and treatment. One possibility is studying wearable devices to help collect data and predict crises.

Alycia Halladay, chief science officer at the Autism Science Foundation, said the draft proposal touched on similar themes that an HHS advisory panel on autism research and policy mentioned in a recently adopted plan. It wasn’t clear on whether vaccines would be considered as an environmental factor that could contribute to the trajectory of autism, she said.
“There’s a lot of good ideas here, but there’s not a whole lot of what will be done or how it will be done,” Halladay said.

The proposal comes weeks after the department’s Interagency Autism Coordinating Committee voted in favor of a new blueprint for autism policy despite objections from patient advocacy groups over the abbreviated timeline and drafting process.

President Donald Trump has often expressed a desire to understand the root cause of autism, and Kennedy has repeatedly pledged to find that answer. The administration has linked Tylenol use during pregnancy to the rise in autism rates and Trump told women not to take it. More recently, Trump suggested that childhood vaccinations may be connected to autism. Medical authorities reject both assertions.

The National Institutes of Health announced a $50 million research initiative to explore the causes of autism spectrum disorder in September. The investigators are examining potential genetic, environmental and medical links to autism, and whether changes in diagnostic practices may have contributed to a perceived rise in prevalence. The initiative has been generally well-received by experts.

items.title: Unloved Consumer Names Like Walmart Face Pressure as Rate Hike Draws Near
body: Stocks that are most closely tied to the health of the US consumer have trailed the broader market badly this year. A potential Federal Reserve interest-rate hike Wednesday may add to the segment’s stress.
The S&P 500 Consumer Discretionary Index, home to names like McDonald’s Corp. and Nike Inc., has dropped 5.2% in 2026, compared with an 11% advance in the broader equities gauge.

Inflationary pressures show no signs of easing, real wage growth is subdued, and shoppers are stuck absorbing rising costs associated with shipping and production. And while data on Wednesday showed consumers have largely brushed off the risks, the setup for stocks in the sector looks fragile going into the Fed’s decision.

A hike would tighten “the cost of capital for the consumer-facing companies already absorbing cost pressure,” Dean Curnutt, chief executive officer and founder of Macro Risk Advisors, wrote in a note to clients. It does “nothing to change the dynamic generating that pressure.”

Signs of the pressure are easy to find. More than a quarter of stocks in the consumer discretionary index are trading at their 52-week lows, a dynamic last seen in April 2025 when President Donald Trump unleashed his global tariff agenda.

Strategists at firms including UBS Group AG and Truist Advisory Services advise clients to be more selective in choosing the stocks they want to own in the sector. UBS analysts led by Michael Lasser highlight the likes of Coca-Cola Co., Life Time Group Holdings Inc. and Aritzia Inc. among the preferred plays. They remain “relatively cautious” on the overall group.

To Keith Lerner, chief investment officer and chief investment strategist at Truist, stocks that provide travel experiences and cater to higher-end consumers are the relative winners in the sector. He’s less optimistic about home-related companies and low-end retailers.
“It’s not a broad based sector that has strength right now,” he said.

The view is broadly shared on Wall Street, and persistent inflationary risks amid surging energy costs have a lot to do with this skepticism. The consumer price index, excluding food and energy, climbed 0.3% in August, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics, exceeding the median estimate of 0.2% from a Bloomberg survey.
Massive artificial intelligence investments are expected to contribute roughly 0.4 percentage points to annual inflation this year, data compiled by CIBC Capital Markets show.

With AI-related spending unlikely to subside in the next two years, a bulk of economic slowing needed to reduce price pressures will need to come from shoppers, Dennis DeBusschere, chief market strategist at 22V Research, said on Monday. That means consumer stocks will remain under pressure as the Fed hikes rates, he said.

“The consumer service sector should feel it most,” DeBusschere said while discussing the impact of a potential rate hike on equities. “The pain will last until core inflation starts moving toward the Fed’s 2% target,” he added, noting the first quarter “should be a better backdrop for consumer names.”

However, there are signs of life emerging in the sector. The $21 billion State Street Consumer Discretionary Select Sector SPDR exchange-traded fund saw a $495 million inflow in August, the biggest this year. And official data on Wednesday showed retail sales rose by the most in five months, signaling consumers continued to spend despite rising energy prices. Consumer discretionary stocks were up 0.1% on Wednesday, snapping a two-session losing streak.
Read: US Retail Sales Rebound More Than Expected in Broad Advance

Christopher Harvey, head of equity and portfolio strategy at CIBC, noted that a lot of the pain from an interest-rate hike is already priced in the markets. And while the housing market along with other areas — such as gas stations and convenience stores — face pressure, the health of the economy remains solid.

“If you listen to some of the retailers, they are saying that the lower end is being value conscious, but that’s at the margin, it sounds a little bit more difficult, but it doesn’t sound terrible,” Harvey said in an interview.
The likelihood is that Fed Chair Kevin Warsh will raise rates by 25 basis points, and that’s something the consumer is “really not going to feel,” Harvey said.

items.title: China Considers BYD for Xi's CEO Entourage at Trump Summit
body: Chinese officials are considering BYD Co. for a possible business delegation joining Xi Jinping’s summit with Donald Trump next week in Washington, according to people familiar with the matter.

Senior officials including Xi’s chief of staff, Cai Qi, are reviewing a list of Chinese business titans for his state visit slated for Sept. 24, according to the people, who asked not to be identified discussing sensitive issues. The list isn’t final and could change at the last minute, the people said.

Including BYD founder Wang Chuanfu in the top leader’s delegation would be a provocative move. The US has imposed 100% tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, effectively blocking them from the American market. In June, the electric car behemoth was blacklisted by the Pentagon over alleged links to the People’s Liberation Army. BYD firmly denies claims it supports the Chinese military.

China’s selection criteria for the delegation includes having a potential US deal in progress, loyalty to the Communist Party and a known ability to avoid detracting attention from Xi, according to the people. Several Chinese industry chiefs being considered to accompany Xi are still awaiting US visas, the South China Morning Post reported last week, citing a person familiar with the matter.
BYD, China’s Foreign Ministry and the US Embassy in Beijing didn’t reply to requests for comment. The US State Department didn’t respond to an email sent outside working hours.

When Trump visited Beijing in May he was joined by a coterie of high-profile executives including Elon Musk, Tim Cook and Jensen Huang. Nvidia Corp.’s boss is also expected to attend Trump’s state dinner with Xi next week, Bloomberg reported.

During Xi’s last state visit to the US in 2015, he brought a delegation of prominent Chinese CEOs. Back then, tech leaders such as Alibaba co-founder Jack Ma and Tencent’s Pony Ma accompanied him, as well as executives from Chinese state-owned companies and banks.

Wu Xinbo, director of Fudan University’s Center for American Studies and a former adviser to China’s Foreign Ministry, said BYD would make sense on Xi’s invite list. “China would love to invest in the EV sector in the US, if they permit it,” he said.

Any potential deal involving Chinese carmakers would be a watershed moment for the US given the significant barriers to entry. Domestic auto manufacturers argue their Chinese counterparts benefit from subsidies that allow them to sell at artificially low prices, skewing competition.

US House China select committee chief John Moolenaar has lashed out at BYD, accusing the company of human rights abuses and saying it would “bankrupt” American automakers. “The company’s vehicles are rolling data collection devices that endanger Americans and have no place in the United States,” he said.

Chinese automakers have been growing rapidly around the world, taking share in established markets such as Europe while also moving ever closer to the US’ doorstep. Canada’s government recently began allowing some Chinese EVs into the country, while BYD vehicles are becoming commonplace in Mexico.
Trump has suggested he might be willing to allow a Chinese car company to build electric vehicles in the US, if it did so with American workers.

“We don’t allow his cars into the United States, and we never did,” he told Fox News earlier this month. “Now, if China wanted to come in, and open a plant to build their cars here, I’d be okay with it.”

Ford Motor Co. CEO Jim Farley in February discussed a potential framework with the White House where Chinese automakers could build cars in America through joint ventures with their local rivals, although such suggestions have been met fierce opposition. BYD already operates an electric bus manufacturing facility in California.
Senator Elissa Slotkin, who represents the American auto hub of Michigan, wrote on X earlier this month that a “moment of inflection” was coming during Xi’s visit.

“We hear rumors that Trump is planning to allow Chinese cars to be sold in the US, as part of a larger deal he’s putting together,” she posted. “That would be a strategic mistake — and one that will irrevocably impact not just the 1.2 million Michigan jobs directly or indirectly tied to the auto industry, but the overall manufacturing capacity of the United States.”

items.title: Carney's Canada Investment Summit Draws Big Names, Promises
body: Welcome to Bay Street Edition, our weekly newsletter devoted to what’s happening in Canadian finance, covering strategy, deals, people moves and economics.

I’m Christine Dobby, Bloomberg’s Toronto-based banking reporter, and you’ll find me in your inbox every Friday. Except for this week, when we’re bringing you a special midweek instalment about the Canada Investment Summit.
Please share this newsletter with your friends and colleagues, and if it was forwarded to you, sign up here to receive it every week.
Optimism is apparently Canada’s most abundant natural resource, going by what was on display at the Canada Investment Summit and the dozens of related events across Toronto so far this week.

Sure, the cynical among us will argue that optimism and a dollar barely get you two Timbits these days. But many of the bankers, investors, lawyers and company executives I spoke with on the sidelines of the conferences seemed truly convinced this is a significant moment for Canada.

After walking away from trade talks with the US, Prime Minister Mark Carney faces the urgent task of transforming an economy that has performed below its potential into one that’s capable of growth even when its top trading partner is hostile and protectionist.

With heaps of political goodwill on his side, he’s already signaled what this will entail. The government will try to push through measures that might otherwise lack broad support, such as a new crude oil pipeline to the west coast. Carney is trying to remake Canada’s reputation so that it’s seen as a place where things get built, money gets made and people live good lives that reliably get even better.

All of this will take money, so he invited some of the world’s largest investors to join him at the Four Seasons Hotel Toronto on Tuesday. Saudi Arabia’s $1 trillion sovereign wealth vehicle, Public Investment Fund, didn’t make it. But top executives from major Middle Eastern, US, European and Asian funds all showed up.

The United Arab Emirates was represented by its biggest oil producer, Abu Dhabi National Oil, Investment Corporation of Dubai and Mubadala Capital. There was a US presence too, with the leaders of BlackRock and Blackstone speaking on a panel and Apollo Global Management’s Marc Rowan and KKR’s Joseph Bae also in attendance.
The prime minister had a captive audience of about 150 as he delivered his opening address.
He touted the country’s fiscal strength, its energy assets, the resilience of its financial markets and banks, and his government’s measures to reduce red tape and boost tax competitiveness.
And he made news, announcing plans to open Canada’s four largest airports to private capital and unveiling a significant expansion of a major tax write-off for business investments.
“We’re calling it the ‘productivity mega deduction.’ In part because we used ‘super deduction’ in the last budget,” Carney said to laughs in the room. I mean, I laughed too when I saw the name.

But the government contends the measure — which allows companies to save taxes by expensing the costs of many assets immediately — makes Canada one of the world’s most competitive major economies for new business investment.

“There was a ‘wow’ in the room,” Royal Bank of Canada CEO Dave McKay said  of the crowd’s reaction to the tax announcement. The estimated cost of the move is C$36 billion ($25.8 billion) over five years.

The goal of the summit may have been to sell global investors on the Canada story, but so far it’s been the country’s own financial players, not foreign institutions, that have said they’ll kick in some cash.

Banks, in the business of lending and advising, are pledging to lend and advise even more. And major investors and asset managers say they’ll do more investing and asset managing in Canada. As the steady stream of announcements landed in our inboxes, I started to lose all sense of perspective. What, just C$50 billion?

“I feel a renewed interest in Canada for sure,” McKay told a group of reporters at the summit, adding that the country’s business and political leaders, including provincial premiers, are “pulling in the same direction. That hasn’t happened in a long time.”
Like I said, optimism for days. But even among the converts wandering the halls at the Four Seasons or stalking the streets of Yorkville this week, the nagging question is how to execute.

Spurring an “investment supercycle” is “very much about Canada getting out of its own way,” Jeremy Carter, global analytical head at Fitch Ratings, said Monday on stage during the Milken Institute’s conference at the Park Hyatt.

“It’s a cultural change where you’re trying to remove the barriers for investment from the smallest projects out there. So it’s a deregulation drive, but thousands of hits rather than one big project.”
Back at the Four Seasons, McKay pointed to the prime minister’s own warning that “time kills deals.” Speed matters.
“We just have to get it done now,” the RBC CEO said.

items.title: Apple Is Developing Enterprise Server for AI Age, Report Says
body: Apple Inc. is working on an enterprise server using its own chips and has had discussions with Nvidia Corp. about using its networking equipment, the Information reported.

Apple would sell the server to artificial intelligence developers, governments and other companies, the Information reported, citing multiple unnamed sources. The product likely wouldn’t hit the market until 2029, it said, and would be offered in two versions: one with two of Apple’s forthcoming M8 Ultra chips and a more souped-up edition with four of the M8 Ultra chips. Nvidia’s NVLink Fusion technology would be used to connect the M8 chips, according to the report.
The effort could still be canceled or go forward without Nvidia’s technology, the Information said.
Shares of Apple and Nvidia were little changed at 9:31 a.m. in New York.

items.title: Novo Will Work With Anthropic AI to Speed Drug Development
body: Novo Nordisk A/S and Anthropic PBC will work together to speed up drug development using artificial intelligence, a key goal as Novo tries to catch up in the cutthroat obesity market.

“Joining forces with Anthropic will supercharge our R&D organization,” Novo Chief Executive Officer Mike Doustdar said in a statement Wednesday, adding that the drugmaker has the ambition to “become the world’s most AI-driven healthcare company.”

Initially, Novo’s R&D department will use Anthropic’s Claude Science to tackle scientific problems identified by researchers where the companies’ joint capabilities are seen as having the greatest impact. The goal is to compress the path from research to marketed product, and ultimately to use AI to find “completely new scientific opportunities,” according to Doustdar.

Novo needs next-generation medicines to plug a looming revenue gap, with its Ozempic and Wegovy diabetes and obesity medicines set to face generic competitors in the US and Europe early in the next decade. In the shorter term, the Danish company is also trying to claw back market share from Eli Lilly & Co.
Financial terms of the cooperation weren’t disclosed.
Novo shares were little changed at 3:30 p.m. in Copenhagen. The stock has declined 15% this year.
The Anthropic partnership comes months after Novo agreed to integrate OpenAI’s artificial intelligence across the company.

Earlier this month, Anthropic revealed that people had used Claude in ways that could support the development of biological weapons, though it said the cases were ambiguous and the research could have been benign. Novo said its collaboration had been designed with “robust data governance and human oversight, helping ensure AI is applied responsibly.”
Read More: What Musk, Altman, Zuckerberg Are Saying About AI Guardrails

items.title: Mamdani's Consumer Cop Uses Companies' Data to Police Them
body: New York City is hiring dozens of sophisticated sleuths to sift companies’ own data for evidence that they might be ripping off consumers.

Sam Levine, commissioner of the city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, is building a 36-person bureau of data scientists, technologists and economists who will extract and analyze what he describes as “billions of records” to help New York City build cases against predatory corporations and practices.

The new unit is the latest sign of the aggressive posture the agency, which has oversight of business licensing and regulation, consumer protection enforcement and labor standards, has adopted under Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration. Levine, a 40-year-old former Federal Trade Commission attorney, is seeking to position himself as a muscular regulator after the Trump administration gutted the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and retreated from the aggressive antitrust policies pursued by Levine’s former boss, Biden administration FTC Commissioner Lina Khan.

“I think there’s a recognition here, and, I hope, among other cities, that the cavalry isn’t going to come and save us,” he said. “Washington is not going to come and save us. States are not necessarily going to come and save us.”

The new group, the formally called the Research and Analytics Division, will be charged with tracking firings driven by algorithms, surveillance pricing, and violations of the city’s wage and scheduling laws. The aim is to use the technology revolutionizing the private sector and the economy to move faster and take on more complicated investigations.
Read More: Amazon Is in the Crosshairs of Mamdani’s Worker Agenda
Levine said that the group would probe behavior such as ride-hailing companies quoting different prices for the same exact trip to different customers.

“They assume that’s just how things are. That’s just how the world works, and there’s nothing we can do about it,” Levine said. “We’re actually going to be the agency that’s going to be able to look under the hood, understand how companies are setting their prices, understand how companies are setting their wages, and attack the everyday indignities consumers and workers face that many of us just feel resigned to.”
If companies are acting in violation of city rules, DCWP can issue subpoenas, levy fines and partner with law enforcement to prosecute offenders.

Some staffers forming the core of the new bureau were hired under former Mayor Eric Adams and have had their work tested. Data scientists who will be part of the new bureau helped design the city rule setting a $23 an hour minimum pay requirement for delivery app workers, then successfully defended that number against the app companies’ own experts in court in 2023.

The bureau’s economists will also produce their own research, countering a pattern of industries controlling studies that Levine said he observed during his time running the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection. City-funded research would be a “powerful countervailing force against so much of the junk research that corporate America is putting out.”

A specialized unit designed to analyze companies’ increasingly sophisticated data could address emergent areas of concern for lawyers and consumer protection agencies, said Prentiss Cox, a professor at the University of Minnesota’s Law School specializing in consumer protection law.
“The world is shifting,” Cox said. “The essence of consumer protection problems are where complexity meets money.”

Mamdani allocated $4 million for the bureau earlier this year. Levine has hired nine data scientists and researchers so far, and said the unit will be fully operational by October 2027. The salary range for a senior data scientist is between $98,000 and 129,000, according to a job posting.
The 400-person department, formerly known as the Department of Consumer Affairs, has been among the most visibly active of the city’s more than 100 agencies.

Within days of Mamdani’s inauguration, he and Levine launched a task force targeting junk fees and barred hotel “destination” charges. DCWP has since opened a restitution fund following a settlement with a self-storage company over deceptive advertising, issued new debt collection rules, and mandated “click to cancel” subscription rules.

While some of those initiatives were in progress under former Mayor Eric Adams, the agency’s prominence in Mamdani’s administration, and its open focus on corporate accountability, marks a significant tonal shift.
The agency’s aggressive new posture has been met with pushback from some business groups.

Last month, all five of the city’s chambers of commerce issued a joint statement criticizing a new agency rule that would require businesses to post an “all-in price” for goods or services. In a client memo, law firm Gibson Dunn accused the agency of mission creep.
“DCWP is pushing its enforcement philosophy closer to that of a federal regulator than a traditional municipal agency,” the memo said.

Khan has maintained close ties with the Mamdani administration. She helped advise Mamdani’s transition before he took office, and earlier this year, Mamdani named her chair of the city Economic Development Corporation’s Board of Directors.
Read More: Lina Khan Wants to Amplify Mamdani’s Power With Little-Used Laws

“Protecting people from corporate abuse in today’s economy requires technological sophistication and expertise,” Khan said in a statement. “Hiring technologists and data analysts at the FTC turbocharged our work. DCWP’s new unit should be a model for cities and states across the country.”

items.title: Trump's Surgeon General Pick Nicole Saphier Set to Face Vaccine Questions
body: President Donald Trump’s nominee for surgeon general, Nicole Saphier, said she does not believe childhood vaccinations cause autism during her Senate health committee confirmation hearing on Wednesday.

Republican Senator Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, the chairman of the panel, pressed Saphier on her views on the relationship between childhood vaccinations and autism and her opinion on whether the birth dose of the hepatitis B vaccine should be universally recommended.
“I don’t know what causes autism, but I have not seen reputable evidence that would suggest that vaccines cause autism,” Saphier said.

When questioned about comments Trump made last month suggesting the combined measles vaccine could be “lethal,” she said that he does not believe the combined measles vaccine is lethal, and that it is the most effective tool available to address ongoing measles outbreaks.

On Friday, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported 160 new measles cases in the past week, bringing this year’s total to 3,294. Pennsylvania has reported four measles-related deaths so far this year.
Read More: New Measles Deaths Send US Total to the Highest in Decades

The surgeon general historically plays a lead role in public health communications in the US, and the office oversees a corps of commissioned health officers. Saphier is the Trump administration’s third nominee for the position, after the first two, Janette Nesheiwat and Casey Means, were pulled due to lack of support in the Senate.

Saphier said she supports “universal” hepatitis B vaccination and said the evidence available for a birth dose shows it’s safe and effective, but stopped short of unequivocally advocating for recommending a birth dose. A CDC vaccine advisory panel overhauled by Kennedy voted to end the universal recommendation of the birth dose for the hepatitis B vaccine in December, a move that’s been paused by courts.

In past statements, Saphier has called childhood vaccinations, including measles inoculations, safe and effective. She said in a Fox News segment last year that there’s “no causal link” to autism from the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine — an idea promoted by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

Saphier also previously criticized the Trump administration’s push to have the US more closely follow the childhood vaccination schedule used in other countries like Japan and Denmark. She has, however, questioned decisions to mandate Covid-19 vaccines for children and the timing of the birth dose of the hepatitis B vaccine.

While Kennedy has made railing against unhealthy food a major priority during his tenure, Saphier reported investments in companies including McDonald’s Corp., Monster Beverage Corp., Coca-Cola Co. and the tobacco company Philip Morris International Inc., her financial disclosures show. She plans to divest from those holdings if she is confirmed, according to her ethics agreement.

Several senators questioned Saphier about her stance on smoking and vaping in light of a Food and Drug Administration decision to approve several flavored e-cigarette products in May. Saphier told Republican Senator Susan Collins of Maine that she sees value in flavored vapes as a potential off-ramp for adult smokers, but understands concerns about access for children. Saphier said she opposes smoking broadly and as a physician she doesn’t “want anyone smoking anything.”
“I am as anti-smoking, anti-tobacco as you can imagine anyone to be,” Saphier said.
Saphier is director of breast imaging at Memorial Sloan Kettering Monmouth in New Jersey and a former Fox News contributor.

While the surgeon general post has remained vacant for nearly two years, Stephanie Haridopolos has taken on some of the role’s responsibilities and used her platform to warn about the dangers of excessive screen time for children.

items.title: Lower Manhattan's Post-9/11 Comeback Brings Homes and Nightlife
body: Welcome back to Bloomberg’s Real Estate Monitor, a weekly breakdown of emerging trends, strategic challenges and blockbuster deals shaping the industry. Sign up now if you’re not already on the list.

This week, you’ll read about how Lower Manhattan has evolved in the 25 years since the 9/11 terrorist attacks. We’ll also tell you about a construction accident at the site of Citadel’s upcoming Miami skyscraper, a deal for the world’s largest log cabin and an entrepreneur’s quest to hit the top 100 golf courses in the US. There’s more, so let’s dig in.
— Christine Maurus
Lower Manhattan used to be a place people fled after work. Now its filled with life, around the clock: Restaurants are packed, families fill the parks and nightlife is booming.

It’s the culmination of a 25-year reinvention since the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks, turning the longtime financial hub into a vibrant 24/7 neighborhood. “When you walk in the streets and you see young kids on their scooters, and dogs being walked, you know that you’ve been a success,” said developer Bill Rudin.

The area has added almost 25,000 homes in the past quarter-century, and its population has more than doubled. When people like interior designer Christina Roccos arrived in  the district, there were few residential buildings and basic services were limited. Today she walks her dogs past public art, shops at Eataly and belongs to a parents’ WhatsApp group with 1,000 members. “I don’t need to leave the neighborhood,” she said.

The seeds were planted before 9/11, when a battered office market in the 1990s prompted Rudin and other business leaders to rethink downtown’s dependence on finance. The attacks made that reinvention urgent — and vastly harder. Developers and officials had to rebuild above active transit lines, lure frightened workers back and create a living neighborhood while preserving the World Trade Center site as a memorial.

The result is a downtown that feels younger and more residential, though increasingly expensive. Restaurants that once catered mainly to Wall Street now draw workers from AI, architecture and design, while longtime residents praise the schools and parks, even as soaring prices squeeze families and businesses.

Now the pendulum may be swinging so far toward housing that downtown risks running short of top-quality offices, said Mary Ann Tighe, who oversees the New York region for brokerage CBRE. Demand from tenants is reviving, and American Express is moving its headquarters to 2 World Trade Center, clearing the way for the final major office tower at the site. For Rudin, it caps a transformation decades in the making: “It all builds on each other, step by step.”
The following was produced with the assistance of Bloomberg Automation.

A rig collapsed at the Miami construction site for Citadel’s new tower, crushing three cars and sending at least four people to the hospital with minor injuries. The incident on Monday, which left a BMW SUV in flames, narrowly missed a historic cottage that Citadel founder Ken Griffin plans to relocate as part of his multibillion-dollar headquarters project in the Brickell district. Developer Related Companies said it’s cooperating with city and county building departments to secure the site and conduct a full investigation.

Singapore is reviewing a report that alleged civil servants bought homes near planned subway stations before they were publicly announced to generate “meaningful private gains.” The city-state’s Public Service Division said it’s examining data and methodology used in the report by the US-based National Bureau of Economic Research and will refer the matter to the Corrupt Practices Investigation Bureau if there’s reason for doing so. The findings, which researchers say are “consistent with information leakage,” are striking for Singapore, widely regarded as one of the world’s least-corrupt countries.

Bathla Group, an insolvent Australian developer that’s A$3.4 billion in debt, is scrambling to secure longer-term financing to avoid full liquidation, after getting a commitment for just A$4 million in emergency funding from five private lenders. The outcome will determine the fate of more than 300 employees, 45 construction sites, and scores of private credit lenders caught in the builder’s complex corporate web. Fears of a spillover from the crisis are weighing on investor sentiment amid a broader property market slump.

China’s sweeping property reforms are squeezing local governments, which have long depended on land sales as a primary revenue source. Purchases of lots in 70 major cities tumbled 36% by area in the week following the policy overhaul in August, and a high-profile Beijing land auction worth at least $1 billion was scrapped earlier this month after only one developer showed up to bid. Analysts warn that caution among builders is intensifying, compounding years of declining land disposal revenues at a time when local governments can least afford it.

Sales of preowned US homes slid to the weakest pace in more than a year in August as persistently high mortgage rates sidelined prospective buyers. The median sales price climbed 1.6% from a year earlier to $429,100, extending a streak of annual price increases dating back to mid-2023. With few eager buyers in the market, the supply of available homes reached the highest level since November 2019, the National Association of Realtors reported.

Australia’s most expensive homes have suffered steep price declines, while lower-end properties have shown resiliency, according to Cotality. High-end values in Sydney and Melbourne slid more than 10% from their peaks, and key affluent suburbs in those markets, such as Bondi and Toorak, were especially hard hit, the firm said. The downturn follows three Reserve Bank rate hikes this year and the government’s removal of tax incentives for property investors in the May budget.

The UK will publish a list of properties subject to a new “mansion tax” next autumn and give homeowners about six months to appeal the decision. Properties in London and the South East of England are expected to be hardest hit by the introduction of the so-called High Value Council Tax Surcharge that targets properties worth more than £2 million. The levy, set to take effect in 2028, will start at £2,500 a year, rising to £7,500 for properties worth over £5 million.

China’s Evergrande Group is selling a historic Canadian log cabin hotel after failing to make payments on its debt. Texas-based Westmont Hospitality Group agreed to buy the property, the Fairmont Le Château Montebello in Quebec, out of bankruptcy proceedings in a court-approved deal that’s expected to close in November. No price was disclosed for the 96-year-old hotel, which bills itself as the world’s largest log cabin. It drew 30 bids, including one from a group including the owner of the Ottawa Senators hockey team, which pledged to invest as much as C$150 million.

European markets have lost property firms worth more than €81 billion since 2020, as chronically depressed share prices, worsened by 2022’s inflation shock, have left even the largest REITs vulnerable to takeovers. US landlords, armed with lower capital costs and greater scale, are increasingly eyeing the sector for consolidation opportunities, as illustrated by Prologis’s £14 billion bid for UK logistics giant Segro. In all, 61 landlords have exited public markets through buyouts, de-listings and take-private deals since the start of the decade, according to the European Public Real Estate Association.

A 32-year-old entrepreneur is taking a newly minted fortune on the road in a quest to play all of Golf magazine’s top-100 US public courses. Daniel Belk says the trip across 29 states is a gift to himself while he plots his next venture, after building a real estate private equity firm and and selling his stake in a second business — a social run club and apparel company called Cooldown — for $1 million in January. He has budgeted $70,000 for the venture, which he’s documenting for a growing fan base on social media.

items.title: Fewer Americans Want CEOs to Address Personal Social, Political Views
body: Fewer Americans want chief executive officers to speak out about social, environmental or political issues, especially if it has nothing to do with their company’s business, in a notable turnaround from 2018, according to a new study from Stanford University.

Some 55% of Americans said CEOS of large companies should advocate for social and political issues they care about, down from 65% in 2018 when the question was last asked, with declines across political and demographic groups, said  David Larcker, a professor at the Stanford Graduate School of Business and one of the authors on both reports. The public remains much more receptive if the topic is directly related to the company’s business, he said.

“They're a natural group to weigh in on some of these social issues and the public want their opinion, but it sounds like they want less of it now, kind of across the board,” Larcker said in an interview. “There has to be some context about why they're talking about it.”
Nearly two-thirds of people said they’ve cut back on a product or stopped using it altogether because they disagree with a company’s stance, roughly double the level reported in 2018.

The shift reflects changing political and cultural attitudes. Companies have generally been less willing to discuss race, gender and other potentially polarizing topics following the Trump administration’s efforts to do away with diversity, equality and inclusion policies. There is also little appetite for executives to address lightning-rod issues like politics and religion, the Stanford study found. Most Americans, though, were OK with CEOs speaking out about clean air or water, sustainability, healthcare and artificial intelligence, Larcker said.
Republicans and Baby Boomers remain the least interested in hearing CEOs speak out, while Democrats and Gen Z are the most supportive, the researchers found.

The study was conducted by  Stanford’s Corporate Governance Research Initiative, a governance group at the Hoover Institution, and the Rock Center for Corporate Governance. It polled more than 2,800 people across a broad sample of the American public over the summer.

Only about a quarter of boards have advised or directed the CEO or management on engagement in public discourse, according to a 2025 report from the National Association of Corporate Directors. Among those boards, about one-third said they encouraged executives to engage with issues that supported company strategies, while another third favored remaining neutral when possible to stay “above the fray.”

“You just don't want somebody well identified with the company going off in some interview or some discussion or something where the board's surprised by that and all of a sudden you’ve got a problem you didn't have yesterday,” Larcker said. “By now, there should be some sort of board process in place to set some guidelines.”

items.title: Next Africa: Kenya's Court Decisions Are a Thorn in Ruto's Side
body: Welcome to Next Africa, a daily newsletter on where the continent stands now — and where it’s headed. Sign up here. In today’s edition, we look at:
Kenya’s courts have been giving William Ruto a tough time of late.

The decision to invalidate the government’s sale of a 15% stake in Safaricom, the East African nation’s biggest company, to Vodacom is just one of the president’s flagship initiatives to be struck down.

Private citizens, opposition leaders and non-governmental groups have increasingly turned to the judiciary to challenge anything from tax policy to gender equality, his choice of advisers to an Ebola quarantine center. A lawsuit was also filed that forced the disbandment of a panel he appointed to audit public liabilities.

Ruto’s grand plans for $39 billion of new infrastructure are key to his campaign for a second term. Yet high levels of debt mean sometimes painful decisions are needed to find the money, whether they be increased taxes or selling state assets.
Concession deals with Indian billionaire Gautam Adani’s groups to manage Kenya’s main airport and power lines were frozen after petitioners argued they were “tainted with secrecy.”

It’s not only been the courts that have forced him to rethink his decisions. The government backtracked on plans to raise an extra $2.7 billion by hiking duties on goods like cooking oil, milk and bread after deadly protests erupted two years ago.
Ruto has accused judges of “overreach” and “judicial tyranny” and has suggested corruption. The justices have stood their ground.
Courts have the power to review and interpret “anything said to be done under the authority of this constitution or of any law,” the three-judge bench said on Tuesday.
This week’s ruling would mean the government having to refund the $1.9 billion the South Africa-based telecommunications giant paid to boost its holding in Safaricom.
Whether Vodacom wins an appeal or not, the judgment is a costly blow — not only for a cash-strapped Treasury, but for Ruto’s electioneering too.

Ivory Coast is among several nations poised to exit a global dirty-money watchlist next month, sources say. The West African country’s progress on bank supervision and beneficial ownership verification has drawn plaudits from an international financial watchdog, which previously raised concerns about oversight and enforcement.

South Africa’s Electoral Court confirmed that some candidates won’t be allowed to contest a local-government vote scheduled for Nov. 4, putting the biggest political party at risk of losing control of several town councils. The African National Congress had blamed the omission of some of its members on a technical glitch and filed a lawsuit challenging their exclusion.

Global efforts to prevent HIV lost ground last year as funding disruptions forced countries to scale back services, even as health systems managed to put more people living with the virus on lifesaving treatment. The pressures extended beyond HIV, with tuberculosis programs facing hurdles and those for malaria experiencing medicine shortages and delays to prevention campaigns.

Nigeria’s inflation rate unexpectedly fell in August, backing the case for policymakers to resume cutting interest rates next week. Meanwhile, a closely watched gauge of South African price expectations eased, giving its MPC room to leave borrowing costs unchanged to support an economy battered by surging energy and fertilizer costs. Fund manager Amundi, though, says a decision to hold will hurt the central bank’s credibility.

Uganda’s shilling slumped to a two-year low against the dollar, weighed down by a surge in demand for foreign exchange in key economic sectors including energy, manufacturing and telecommunications. A vibrant local-currency bond market has been a huge draw for institutional investors.

Senegal, the cash-strapped nation that recently agreed a $2.2 billion bailout from the IMF and is seeking to rework its debts, is among African nations included in a frontier-markets bond index being introduced by JPMorgan. The continent will account for almost 45% of the index, with Egypt and Morocco representing the region’s largest contributions by weight.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced visa restrictions on South Africans he claims have engaged in government-sponsored discrimination against Afrikaners and other minority groups, escalating a diplomatic dispute between the nations. His statement echoed longstanding accusations from President Donald Trump. Rubio didn’t say whether any officials are being penalized, nor identify anyone who might be.

South Africa’s government has resolved recurring power outages and is racing to fix its crumbling water infrastructure. But, business leaders warn, it’s sleepwalking into another crisis — a “gas cliff.” Biggest supplier Sasol says that in two years’ time there will only be enough gas coming from fields in central Mozambique for its own needs, leaving industries holding back their investments and clamoring for the authorities to find solutions.
We’ll be back in your inbox with another edition tomorrow. Send any feedback to nextafrica@bloomberg.net.
