items.title: Von der Leyen Touts Associate EU Member Status for Canada as Carney Looks On
body: Welcome to the Brussels Edition. I’m Suzanne Lynch, Bloomberg’s Brussels bureau chief, bringing you the latest from the EU each weekday. Make sure you’re signed up.

It may not have quite the razzmatazz associated with the US president’s State of the Union speech in Congress, but this morning’s annual address by European Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen to the European Parliament made quite the splash.
Despite leaks in the run-up, von der Leyen had a few surprises up her sleeve. Chief among them, her announcement that Canada should become an associate member of the European Union.
Addressing Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who was seated close by, she proposed “opening the door” to Canada becoming the EU’s first associate member.

The idea is a bold one. For decades, the idea of semi-EU membership has surfaced in different guises. Some countries already have tailored relationships with the EU. Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein are members of the European Economic Area, effectively giving them access to the single market.

Switzerland, which is not in the EEA or EU, has its own bilateral relationship with the bloc, which gives it rights and responsibilities. A decade after Brexit, the UK is still working out its relationship with Brussels, complicated by the status of Northern Ireland.

One easy win would be to include Canada in the European Political Community, an annual gathering of European leaders — including non-EU countries like the UK, Turkey and Azerbaijan — devised by French President Emmanuel Macron.

The big question following today’s speech is how von der Leyen’s call will land in national capitals. The EU’s enlargement debate was complex to begin with. Nine countries are technically in the queue to join the bloc, with negotiations on membership for Ukraine and Moldova accelerating.

In fact, von der Leyen isn’t the first to propose “associate membership” this year. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz floated the idea of associate membership for Ukraine in May, an idea that worries the Ukrainian government amid concerns that it could be saddled with a “two-tier” membership.

Carney’s own speech to the European Parliament tomorrow could shed more light on how the notion of associate membership might work in practice, with both sides already signaling an interest in further cooperating in defense, tech and critical raw materials.
Canada may be poised to make its debut in the European Song Contest next year, but securing associate membership in the bloc is likely to be an infinitely more complicated process.

Luis Garicano, executive director of the recently-formed Rhine Group, told Bloomberg TV that Europe has lost the race for frontier AI models. However, the region can still do the implementation side of the technology, he told Stephen Carroll in an interview. The new group, co-chaired by former ECB President Mario Draghi, wants to tackle Europe’s competitiveness challenges, and build on the landmark report published two years ago.

Poland’s revved-up stocks have further to run as new investors pour cash into eastern Europe’s biggest equity market, according to UniCredit. Foreign funds are increasing allocations for Polish stocks, with some entering the market for the first time, Mateusz Kacprzak, head of corporate and investment banking at UniCredit in Poland, said in an interview. The WIG20 stock gauge has advanced 28% this year, outpacing a 20% jump in emerging-market equities. The price of the benchmark Warsaw index has tripled in less than four years, flipping the narrative around stock investing in Poland, where returns lagged peers for nearly two decades.

Europe’s rally has become more concentrated this year, amplifying risks just as investors turn less optimistic about its economic outlook. An underperformance against US stocks has deepened over the past month, despite Europe’s stronger economic surprises and worries about artificial intelligence spending by American tech giants. While oil above $100 increases the likelihood of interest-rate hikes in both regions, pricey crude is a bigger problem for import-dependent Europe.

items.title: UPI's New Fee Tests the Economics of India's Payments Boom
body: Welcome to India Edition, Bloomberg’s daily dive into what’s moving the worlds of business, markets and politics in this dynamic, fast-paced economy. I’m Menaka Doshi. If you didn’t receive this directly in your inbox, you can subscribe here, and share feedback with us here.
Today, I look at the differing viewpoints on the UPI fee to be levied from Oct. 15, and my colleague Sudhi Ranjan Sen unpacks India’s gains at the recent BRICS Summit and the way forward.

It’s a fee, it’s a tax, it’s a fintech savior, it’s a trade maneuver. Those have been the myriad reactions to the new merchant fee being levied on UPI — India’s most popular digital payments system, which processed 24.51 billion transactions worth 29.9 trillion rupees ($312 billion) in August alone.

Starting Oct. 15, UPI payments to merchants above 2,000 rupees will attract a Merchant Discount Rate, or MDR, of 0.40%, capped at 300 rupees per transaction. Capital-market transactions will attract a much lower 0.02%, also capped at 300 rupees. Railways, telecom, insurance and fuel payments above 2,000 rupees will carry a flat 5-rupee fee.

Person-to-person transfers and recurring payments (such as utility bills) will remain free. So will qualifying UPI payments to small merchants receiving up to 100,000 rupees a month. The MDR will be borne by merchants and can’t be passed on as a separate UPI surcharge to customers. The revenue will be shared within the payments ecosystem.

The government and the National Payments Corporation of India, which built UPI under the Reserve Bank of India’s oversight, say the fee will help fund continued investment in technology, security and the expansion of digital payments. They also point out that UPI remains considerably cheaper than cards. Standard credit card MDRs typically range from 1.5% to 2.5%, while debit card MDRs can go up to 0.90%, NPCI said in a statement. UPI, launched a decade ago, is now the world’s largest real-time payments system by transaction volume.

The fintech community has welcomed a new source of revenue for payment companies that helped popularize UPI but had no obvious way to monetize it. “The introduction of MDR on UPI would materially change the narrative around fintechs,” Amrish Rau, CEO of payments company Pine Labs, said in a post on X.

Critics call it a tax on merchants, who they say will find covert ways to pass the cost on to customers, potentially slowing UPI’s spread. “Any MDR on UPI - will kill the one thing in India which is working like clock work,” Ashneer Grover, co-founder and former managing director of BharatPe, posted on X.

Then there’s the trade angle. Despite Indian government denials, some trade experts and opposition politicians have said the fee is in response to criticism from the Trump administration that a free UPI works as a trade barrier and has skewed the playing field for American payment majors like Visa and Mastercard.

Worse still, the “biggest beneficiaries” will be Walmart-owned PhonePe and Google Pay, which together process more than 80% of UPI transactions while gaining access to valuable spending data, trade expert Ajay Srivastava said in emailed comments.

There are practical grievances too. Nithin Kamath, founder and CEO of online broker Zerodha, objects to brokers paying a fee simply to receive clients’ money — even before any investment is made. Brokers can’t force customers to trade or pass the UPI fee on to them, leaving them bearing costs on transactions that may generate no revenue, he said in a social media post.

All that notwithstanding, the fee marks a new era for UPI, the homegrown payments network that put India on the global payments map. The question now is whether UPI can make money without losing the price advantage that made it ubiquitous.
US bond traders have piled into bearish positions ahead of the Federal Reserve meeting, betting that the Treasury selloff will continue...
...and their counterparts in India fear the RBI’s push to drain excess cash will spark an extended bond slump as inflation picks up.
Long-suffering Paytm investors may finally have something to cheer about: the stock is nearing its IPO price for the first time since listing.
New Zealand’s parliament passed legislation enabling a free-trade agreement with India.
Don’t Miss

Want more? Sign up for Markets Daily India, a subscriber-only newsletter featuring key insights before the trading day starts. Keep track of the twists and turns — and the global fallout — of the war with Iran here.
Hello, I’m Sudhi, Bloomberg’s Senior Government Reporter in New Delhi.
India’s BRICS summit didn’t deliver a dramatic breakthrough, though that may not be the best way to judge its success.

For New Delhi, getting an increasingly diverse grouping to agree on a joint declaration covering West Asia, terrorism, trade and reform of global institutions was an achievement in itself. BRICS has usually moved forward through small areas of agreement rather than sweeping deals, and this summit followed that pattern.

Oliver Stuenkel, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, argued in Foreign Policy in March that BRICS was never designed to operate as a geopolitical alliance or produce unified positions on every security crisis. Its members cooperate where interests overlap, while leaving room to disagree elsewhere. Nor are such divisions unique to BRICS: NATO and the Group of Seven have also struggled to maintain common positions on geopolitical questions.
New Delhi pushed for reforms at the IMF and World Bank, tapping into a broader concern among emerging economies that they still have too little say in global economic decisions.

Rather than calling for a breakup of existing institutions, the declaration pushed to give developing countries a greater voice within them. It called for a more representative UN and Security Council and stronger support for a rules-based trading system centered on the WTO.

Artificial intelligence offered another contrast. The declaration backed wider access to AI, while stressing safety, security and the need to manage risks. Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump has dismissed fears of AI causing irreversible harm to humanity as a “HOAX.”
Prime Minister Narendra Modi summed up the broader argument more directly, saying the Global South should move from “rule-takers” to “rule-shapers.”

That may be BRICS’s real value. At a time when the UN and other multilateral institutions are struggling to forge collective responses to wars, trade disputes and other global crises, it gives a disparate group of countries a place to work together where their interests converge.

But those gains need to be kept in perspective. Washington remains deeply suspicious of moves that it thinks are aimed at weakening the dollar or turning BRICS into an anti-US bloc. Donald Trump has previously threatened steep tariffs on BRICS countries over efforts to find alternatives to the dollar and, separately, on countries aligning with what he called the group’s “anti-American policies.” India has tried to steer a different course, presenting BRICS as non-Western rather than anti-Western.

China’s rotating presidency in 2027 will offer a chance to build on New Delhi’s incremental gains. Beijing, by far the grouping’s largest economy, will have considerable influence over where BRICS goes next. India, meanwhile, will be watching how that agenda develops, given its interest in keeping the grouping broad-based rather than allowing it to tilt too strongly toward any one country or an overtly anti-Western position.

Trade, greater use of local currencies and cross-border payments remain unfinished business from New Delhi, where members agreed to keep working on them while allowing for different national priorities. If the focus stays on making trade easier, there may be plenty of common ground.

Save the date: Bloomberg New Economy Forum - New Delhi: This October, the Bloomberg New Economy Forum convenes its global community of business and public-sector leaders under the guiding theme, “A World in Play: Defining the New Levers of Power.” This year’s Forum, held Oct. 13-15 in New Delhi, will examine the shifting geopolitical landscape and explore the risks and opportunities reshaping the global economy. Visit BloombergNewEconomy.com/India to learn more.
Thanks for reading India Edition. —Menaka

items.title: NHL Record Scorer Ovechkin Backs Putin's Party in Election Video
body: Russian hockey superstar Alexander Ovechkin, captain of the National Hockey League’s Washington Capitals, appeared in an election campaign video for President Vladimir Putin’s ruling party, reviving controversy over his support for the Kremlin leader who’s waging war in Ukraine.

Ovechkin, the NHL’s all-time leading goal scorer, stands behind Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov and Margarita Simonyan, editor-in-chief of state-funded broadcaster RT, who are both sanctioned over the war, as part of a group supporting the United Russia party in this week’s parliamentary elections.

“When people deal with us honestly, we can always come to an agreement. When they lie to us and break their word, they have only themselves to blame,” Lavrov is seen saying on the video. “Don’t expect mercy. We will stand together as one, just as we are today.”
Lavrov’s words carried an implicit reference to Russia’s war in Ukraine, which is now deep in its fifth year and shows no sign of ending, with US-brokered peace talks largely stalled.

Russia is holding parliamentary elections Sept. 18 to Sept. 20, the first national vote since Putin ordered the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Lavrov is one of the top candidates on United Russia’s election list.

The Kremlin is seeking a decisive victory for United Russia that it can present as evidence of public support for Putin and the war, even as ordinary Russians increasingly feel the economic and social consequences of the conflict.
Read: What’s at Stake for Putin in Russian Wartime Election: Explainer
Ovechkin has publicly supported the Russian president before. He joined the so-called “Putin Team” ahead of the 2018 presidential election.

Putin, a hockey enthusiast who has played in exhibition games, called Ovechkin the previous year to congratulate him on his wedding and give the newlyweds a dinner set, according to an interview Ovechkin gave to Russian media.

In April 2025, when Ovechkin broke the NHL’s all time scoring record, both Putin and US President Donald Trump praised the player for the achievement. “Great hockey player, a great gentleman,” Trump said at the time.

Many other Russian athletes, including those who’ve never publicly supported the Kremlin, were barred from international competitions in 2022 over the war. Some are now gradually returning to international sports, often competing under a neutral status rather than representing Russia.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov on Wednesday declined to comment on Ovechkin’s appearance in the video.
Ovechkin was asked to participate in the video while he was in Russia this summer, a Washington Capitals spokesman said on Tuesday, according to the AP.

items.title: Broad Rise in US Retail Sales Highlights Resilient Consumer
body: US retail sales rose by the most in five months in a broad advance, showing consumers continued to spend despite rising gasoline prices.

The value of retail purchases increased 1.2% in August after a revised 0.5% decline in July, according to Census Bureau data released Wednesday. The median estimate in a Bloomberg survey of economists called for a 0.8% advance. The figures are not adjusted for inflation.
Consumer spending has been resilient this year, helping power overall economic growth. While the boost from tax refunds has faded, low unemployment and stock market gains are supporting households.

Twelve of 13 retail categories in the report posted increases, including gasoline stations and online retailers. Back-to-school shopping likely supported outlays at general merchandise stores as well as spending on clothing, electronics, sporting goods and other hobbies.

“This consumer has time and time again surprised us with their resilience,” said Shannon Grein, an economist at Wells Fargo & Co. Still, “I don’t think the consumer has enough support behind them to keep at this pace. This is a very strong retail sales print, so I’d expect them to pull back.”

So-called control-group sales — which feed into the government’s calculation of goods spending for gross domestic product — increased 1.4%, the most in nearly two years. The measure excludes food services, auto dealers, building materials stores and gas stations.

Sales at nonstore retailers, primarily online shopping, climbed 2.6% in August — the most since February 2025 — after falling the prior month. Amazon.com Inc. moved its Prime Day sales event to June this year from July the year before, a shift that likely distorted data and dragged down July’s headline retail sales numbers.

The value of gasoline station sales rose 3.1%. The nationwide average price of a gallon of gas held above $4 a gallon through August, according to American Automobile Association data. Prices have since climbed above $4.30 this month as wars in the Middle East and Ukraine limit fuel supplies.
Read More: Midterm Battlegrounds Hit by Diesel, Heating Oil Price Spikes

The retail data showed sales at motor vehicles and parts dealers rose 0.6%. Industry data earlier this month showed auto sales climbed in August to the strongest pace since April 2025. Excluding autos and gasoline, sales also rose 1.2%.
Receipts at restaurants and bars, the only service-sector category in the retail report, climbed a robust 1.2%. Sales declined at building materials stores.
US retailers are looking for ways to appeal to choosier consumers. Walmart Inc. last month said it lowered prices on thousands of items, in part with proceeds from tariff refunds.

The latest consumer snapshot comes as the Federal Reserve considers raising interest rates in an effort to tamp down inflation, which has held above the central bank’s target for more than five years. Futures show that investors expect a quarter-point rate hike when the Fed’s interest-rate setting committee concludes a two-day meeting later on Wednesday.
Last week, a Bureau of Labor Statistics report showed that overall consumer prices were up 3.4% from a year earlier, climbing a full percentage point since the Iran war sent energy prices higher.

Still, many Americans have been squeezed as pay gains fail to keep up with rising prices. Compared with a year earlier, inflation-adjusted average hourly earnings fell for the fifth consecutive month in August.
Separate data out Wednesday showed US import prices increased in August by more than forecast. Compared with a year earlier, the costs of imports rose 7% — the most in four years.

“It is hard to imagine that the degree of strength seen in August retail sales can be sustained through the fall, but I expect the consumer to weather this storm,” Stephen Stanley, chief US economist at Santander US Capital Markets LLC, said in a note.

items.title: Russian Oil Uncertainty Hangs Over India's Largest Buyers
body: Indian state-owned refiners are facing the most significant supply uncertainty in months, according to people with direct knowledge of the trade, as the impact of a drawn-out conflict in the Middle East is compounded by the prospect of tighter US restrictions on Russian purchases.

Oil supplies through the Strait of Hormuz have been disrupted since the end of February, but Saudi Arabia was last week forced to close a crucial workaround — the East-West pipeline — after drone attacks, impacting more than 400,000 barrels a day of flows to India alone.

Those disruptions are expected to be temporary, with Saudi Arabia currently working to bypass a damaged section in order to return about half the capacity within days, Bloomberg reported earlier. Russian crude, however, is already commanding a premium, the people said, and could become even tougher to handle after the US Congress gave its approval on Wednesday to a sweeping US sanctions bill that paves the way for punitive tariffs on countries dealing with Moscow’s oil industry.

State oil refiners’ September and October requirements are secured, but the processors are facing tougher decisions when it comes to November and beyond, the people said, asking not to be named as discussions are not public.
Read More: House Passes Bill Allowing New Tariffs on Russia Oil Buyers

India has relied heavily on discounted Russian oil and relatively secure term Middle Eastern supplies to contain import costs through the past months. A twin squeeze — especially if President Donald Trump signals he will use the new tariff powers — leaves refiners competing for barrels from further afield. That will crimp margins at refiners unwilling to cut run rates and already selling gasoline, diesel and cooking gas below cost.

India is currently Russia’s top buyer of seaborne crude, but its refiners have already been leaning on the US, Brazil, Canada, Venezuela and Africa for additional and more varied supplies. That diversification will continue, but at a price, the people said.

The timing of the crunch, months into a Middle East energy crisis, is particularly difficult. India’s crude inventories fell to 93.5 million barrels in the week beginning Sept. 14, the lowest since May, according to Kpler. That’s enough to cover the equivalent of about 20 days of imports.

At the same time, a new 180,000-barrel-a-day refinery in Rajasthan is ramping up and Indian Oil Corp. is expanding existing plants, adding over 340,000 barrels a day capacity by December, increasing the country’s need for crude.

items.title: Ed Yardeni Cuts S&P 500 View to 7,900 on Downturn Risks
body: Ed Yardeni, one of the biggest stock bulls on Wall Street, is slashing his year-end forecast for the S&P 500 Index a month after raising it, citing increasing risks of a downturn in the next three to six months.

The president and chief investment strategist of Yardeni Research Inc. cut his target to 7,900 from 8,400, which was the highest estimate on the Street as of last month. The new target implies a 4.1% increase from where the equity gauge closed on Tuesday. It also falls in the middle of pack, based on a Bloomberg survey of more than 20 strategists.

“Given the recent backup in bond yields, we are lowering our estimate for the forward P/E of the S&P 500 at year-end from 19.8 to 18.6, which lowers our year-end target from 8,400 to 7,900,” Yardeni wrote in a note to clients.
The veteran strategist had upgraded his S&P 500 target to 8,400 from 8,250 in August, a level that topped his own Street-high target for the gauge amid “fabulous” earnings momentum.
Earlier: Yardeni Raises S&P 500 View to 8,400 on ‘Fabulous Earnings’

Yardeni is the second strategist this week to lower his view for the S&P 500 as analysts grow increasingly skeptical heading into the end of a midterm election year. The downward forecast revisions are the first among major Wall Street strategists since March, during the throes of uncertainty caused by the war in Iran.

Wells Fargo & Co.’s Ohsung Kwon cut his target to 7,700 from 7,950 this week, saying a decade-long earnings growth cycle will eventually slow down while technology-sector risks are mounting. Kwon had raised his target in June, when the US and Iran were preparing to sign an interim peace deal that he said would alleviate macroeconomic concerns.

There have been others, however, who boosted their outlooks this week, including Bank of America Corp.’s Savita Subramanian and Tallbacken Capital Advisors’ Michael Purves, whose 8,500 target is now a Street high.
Yardeni still expects that “the economy will grow without a recession through the end of the decade.” The analyst said his target for the end of this decade remains at 10,000.
He added that the previous year-end forecast of 8,400 has now become a mid-2027 target for the S&P 500. His 2027 earnings-per-share target of $425 is unchanged.

All eyes are on the Federal Reserve as they vote on whether to raise interest rates on Wednesday, an outcome most traders anticipate as Chairman Kevin Warsh vows to get inflation under control. Yardeni wrote in a previous note that “for stocks, the stagflationary mix of higher inflation and slower growth would be particularly troublesome.”

items.title: UK MPs Urge Action on AI, Citing Parallels With Financial Crisis
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham is facing calls from senior Labour MPs and some of his own government officials to provide greater clarity on the UK’s artificial intelligence policy, after a muted response to dire warnings about the risk of a catastrophic event.

The limited understanding of the technology’s capabilities among the people developing it has parallels with the global financial crisis, according to Chi Onwurah, a Labour MP who’s chair of Parliament’s Science and Technology Committee.
“It’s a black box,” Onwurah told Bloomberg in an interview. “The last time experts didn’t understand what they made, it was the mortgage-backed securities that caused the financial crisis.”
In balancing the risks of AI with its commercial and economic opportunities, Burnham is grappling with a policy problem no major country has managed to resolve.

The UK wants to be a leading player on cutting-edge technology, and is seeing early signs that AI is behind a recent lift to an otherwise flat-lining economy. At the same time, it is increasingly concerned about the cybersecurity and economic risks shared by the likes of Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman. Meanwhile, the new prime minister is attuned to the skepticism of Labour MPs and British voters, many of whom are instinctively worried about the threats AI poses, including to jobs.
That dilemma left UK ministers with little to say this week in response to the warnings — a vacuum that’s being filled by voices calling for government to do more.

The UK’s AI minister had expected to respond to an urgent question in Parliament on Tuesday, according to people familiar with the matter, but the speaker didn’t pick the topic, opting instead for a debate about granting protected status to English whisky.

UK government officials involved in AI policy warned that the new Burnham administration did not appear to be prioritizing it, especially in light of the recent concerns emanating from Silicon Valley, which they said they shared.

There is a lack of interest and knowledge about frontier technologies among Downing Street’s ministers and political advisers, one of the people said, while another said they wanted government ministers to outline a strategy in the face of rising risks.

Onwurah said the government should use the infrastructure it already has in place to regulate the technology, for example by restricting companies that don’t cooperate with the UK’s AI Security Institute, or AISI. “We need to take action,” she argued. “If you say you can’t do anything, that’s what gives the public fear and anxiety. What’s the point in government if it can’t do anything about an existential threat?”

She suggested companies could be prevented from selling enterprise software in the UK if they refused to submit their frontier models to the country’s AISI. Anthropic at first withheld its latest Mythos model from the AISI, in a move that highlights the vulnerability of the institute, which is seen as one of Britain’s best assets but is reliant on the cooperation of American and Chinese companies.

“We know the UK will not be able to deliver a security regime on its own,” Liam Byrne, chair of Parliament’s Business and Trade Committee, told Bloomberg. Still, he echoed Onwurah on the dismal precedents of government inaction: “We know that historically self-regulation does not work, and leads to some sort of crisis that requires taxpayer money to sort out.”

Burnham controversially abolished the UK government’s science and technology department when he became premier, folding it into other departments, although he also elevated the status of the AI minister so that he now attends cabinet, in a signal of the area’s increased importance.
That minister, Kanishka Narayan, wrote an article for the Times newspaper on Tuesday in which he suggested the government could strengthen its regulation of AI, without offering further details.

“Nothing is off the table,” he wrote, arguing the UK is “is starting from a position of strength” due to its AISI, but that testing new models will not be enough. The country “will need to harden our defenses” with a “generational uplift in our cyber defences” and “protecting critical infrastructure,” Narayan wrote.

The minister acknowledged that people are becoming “increasingly concerned” about the tech, with almost half of Britons believing it a realistic prospect that AI could end all human life, according to an YouGov poll published last week. The article marked a shift in language for a minister who had previously said he was not especially worried about a catastrophe.

A government AI taskforce is reporting to Cabinet Secretary Antonia Romeo, who is seen as becoming more personally involved in a wide remit of policies across government departments. Louise Haigh, Burnham’s de facto deputy, used a speech on Tuesday to insisted the government would “heed the warnings of those who are at the forefront of developing this technology,” though again offered no details on how.
In an unusual development, King Charles III is convening a summit on Thursday to discuss international cooperation on AI, alongside company executives and representatives from the Vatican.

By contrast, US President Donald Trump has described the notion that AI could wipe out humanity as a “hoax” and declined to legislate or waive anti-collusion laws to allow large AI companies to cooperate on slowing development.
Several British tech firms have urged their own government to be temperate in regulating the industry, pointing to an opportunity to provide less stringent rules than the European Union.

The UK already has a “complicated web of rules governing AI,” said Alexandru Voica, head of policy at London-based AI company Synthesia. “We should spend more time making those rules work, and less time reacting in real time to fears about theoretical risks or news reports from the Silicon Valley AI doomer bubble.” The EU passed its AI legislation in 2024, setting different requirements according to categories of risk.

Still, the election manifesto on which Labour was elected in 2024 promised that it would “ensure the safe development and use of AI models by introducing binding regulation on the handful of companies developing the most powerful AI models.”
Victoria Collins, the Liberal Democrat technology spokesperson, in a post on X: “More than two years on, we are still waiting.”
“People said you couldn’t and shouldn’t regulate the internet and social media 20 years ago,” Onwurah said. “This is the same thing.”

items.title: Carlos Ghosn, French Politician on Trial Over $1 Million Fee
body: Carlos Ghosn, the former Nissan Motor Co. chief executive officer, is on trial in Paris for alleged corruption linked to €900,000 ($1 million) in payments to French politician Rachida Dati.

While the car tycoon — holed up in Lebanon after an audacious escape from Japan in 2019 — won’t set foot in the courthouse, Dati appeared Wednesday to face the accusations. She received the money more than a decade ago, at a time when she was a member of the European Parliament and also a lawyer.

Despite a failure by the prosecutor to properly notify Ghosn of the trial dates, the Paris criminal court decided to dismiss a request he made to postpone the trial. The 72-year-old will be judged in absentia.

Over the next few days, the court will focus on what services Dati was actually paid for by Renault-Nissan BV, the Amsterdam-based entity set up to coordinate an alliance between the French and Japanese manufacturers — and whether Ghosn was entitled to use the money for them. At the heart of the case is whether Dati provided any genuine advisory work or was monetizing her political influence.

The pair, who both deny wrongdoing, risk a 10-year jail term over the allegations. The European Union’s assembly tightened its rules around the time of the payments. Although EU lawmakers weren’t prohibited from earning consultancy fees for outside work, the new rules explicitly barred them from accepting payments in exchange for influencing parliamentary decisions.

The trial comes as Dati’s political career is flagging after she lost the race to become the new Paris mayor in March. The 60-year-old was previously French culture minister in various governments of President Emmanuel Macron.

“Dati’s defense will demonstrate that she worked exclusively as a lawyer for RNBV and that the unfounded allegations of influence-peddling at the European Parliament are an artificial construct by the prosecution,” her lawyers Olivier Baratelli, Olivier Pardo and Antoine Beauquier said before the start of the trial.
The court hearings were scheduled to end on Sept. 28, with a ruling expected months later.

A strategic alliance between Renault SA and Nissan was forged in 1999, ushering in the the Ghosn era — who was at one point simultaneously CEO of both companies prior to his downfall. He was arrested in Tokyo in 2018 on charges of financial misdeeds and then freed on bail.

Ghosn’s subsequent 2019 escape from Tokyo shifted his legal troubles to France. By then, Renault had already finalized an audit of expenses that he’d decided. Some of these were referred to French criminal authorities, leading to this trial and another investigation into spending on events and travel.

As part of this case, a Renault shareholder also filed a complaint highlighting that Dati was in a position to vote on parliamentary decisions that could impact the carmaker when she received the €900,000 payments. The shareholder further said that no evidence of Dati’s work had been found as part of the Renault audits.

Before the trial started, a lawyer for Ghosn said in an email that his client hadn’t received the indictment ordering a trial, and was notified about the court hearing dates too late. Jean Tannous said that required pushing back the trial in order to let Ghosn properly assess the allegations against him and defend himself.

“Mr. Ghosn isn’t trying to avoid the trial,” the lawyer said. “He has expressly informed the court that he is willing to take part in the trial by any legally permissible means, including by videoconference from Beirut, since he is currently subject to a court order prohibiting him from leaving Lebanese territory.”

items.title: Why Gavin Newsom Is Willing to Wait for Kamala Harris
body: California Governor Gavin Newsom blew more than a few minds this week when he said that he wouldn’t mount a highly anticipated bid for president in 2028 if his longtime frenemy, former Vice President Kamala Harris, decides that she wants to run too.
“If she runs, you will not?” CNN’s Jake Tapper asked Newsom as the two fly-fished in Montana.

“Of course not,” Newsom said — so matter-of-factly that Tapper could only gape for a moment. “Why would I? I wouldn’t do that to her. I wouldn’t do that to you. I wouldn’t waste everyone’s time. Who needs that?”

The remarkable exchange has understandably prompted all sorts of speculation from political observers. Some say it’s proof that Newsom knows Harris is running and he wanted a graceful off-ramp. Others say it reveals that she isn’t running and this was Newsom’s way of forcing her to make an announcement.
Whatever Newsom knows (or doesn’t) about Harris, his interview with Tapper is a shrewd political calculation that could help his standing with both voters and the Democratic Party.

In many ways, Newsom’s show of public deference to Harris is entirely in keeping with their longstanding political and personal relationship. A spokesman for the termed-out governor told the New York Times that he and Harris have been “friends long enough that they wouldn’t play cat-and-mouse games on something this important.”
Yet their rivalry is legendary in California politics.

It was 22 years ago that both Democrats were sworn into office on the same day in San Francisco. Newsom became mayor and Harris became district attorney. Since then, their careers have followed parallel trajectories. Newsom ran for lieutenant governor, while Harris ran for California attorney general. Newsom ran for governor, while Harris ran for the US Senate and then became vice president.

That Newsom and Harris have managed to avoid running for the same office at the same time has, so far, averted what would surely be an ugly, internecine political war that would force the advisers, donors and political allies that they’ve long shared to pick sides.
Newsom alluded to this during his interview with Tapper. “I know her base of supporters. I know her friends,” he said. “The Zen diagram is just pure crossover. I wouldn’t do that to people.”

Indeed, the presidency has long represented a seemingly inevitable collision course for the two Democrats. Harris has run — and lost — twice, while Newsom has spent the past few years raising his profile, touring swing states and building an apparatus for a national campaign.
Both have said they will decide whether they are running sometime after the midterms in November. In that way, what Newsom told Tapper should be seen as a series of chess-like political moves.

First, whether or not the governor knows what Harris has planned, his decision to publicly put the ball in her court puts additional pressure on her to make a decision. Harris is now leading most polls of early presidential contenders, followed by Newsom. What she decides matters.

Harris was in a similar position last year, as the gubernatorial race in California was heating up. She hemmed and hawed for months before finally announcing that she’d decided not to run, essentially freezing the field in the meantime and setting up a primary so chaotic that Democrats feared a Republican might capitalize on it and win.
That would be a nightmare at a national level. The sooner Harris makes a decision about a third bid for president, the better for everyone, including Newsom.

Second, if Harris doesn’t run and Newsom does, he will have made a gentlemanly show of deferring to the nation’s first Black vice president — right before he needs to win over Black voters in South Carolina.

The state is first in line on the Democratic Party’s presidential primary calendar, and South Carolina Representative (and kingmaker) Jim Clyburn has praised the governor, telling reporters, “I feel good about his chances.” Being seen as disrespecting Harris by getting “in the way of her ambition” — as Newsom once told CNN he has “never” done — would surely undermine that goodwill.

And third, Newsom essentially just did the entire Democratic Party a solid by trying to resolve a potential pileup of California candidates before it becomes a problem. Already, there’s a good chance another Californian, Representative Ro Khanna, will jump into the race. Add Newsom and Harris to the mix, and it would be political cannibalism.

Newsom also alluded to this during his interview with Tapper. “Electorally, it’s a gift from God for everybody else,” Newsom said. “They can enjoy the hell out of it. Mutually assured destruction. It services no greater good.”

Newsom has long dismissed the narrative about his frenemy rivalry with Harris. “We’ve been sort of on this track, but it was always adjacent,” he said in 2024, after Harris became the Democratic nominee for president. “The tension was a sort of manifestation of punditry.”
Sometimes, though, the pundits are right.

items.title: Knicks Star Jalen Brunson Launches Brand Advisory Firm With Family
body: New York Knicks All-Star Jalen Brunson and his family are launching Thirty Third Management Group, a brand advisory firm that will manage his off-court business and represent other clients across pro sports, business and philanthropy.

“It’s my experience in this field with Jalen as an NBA player that there are many tentacles to what they want to do in their outreach,” said Sandra Brunson, Jalen’s mother, in an interview. The expanded role of an athlete’s persona beyond the court is increasing the “need for this specialized one-on-one attention.”

Sandra, who has managed her son’s business activities for eight years, will be the president of Thirty Third. Outside of her son, the company’s foundational clients will be Brunson’s wife, Ali Marks, who has a physical therapy business and Brunson’s charitable foundation. Erica Brunson, Jalen’s sister, will serve as the firm’s director of client services.
The firm will take on as many clients as it can manage and are already in the process of bringing a few on board, according to Sandra Brunson. Women’s professional sports will be a priority.

The company’s name comes from the Dallas Mavericks selecting Brunson in the second round of the 2018 NBA Draft with the 33rd pick. Players drafted that late rarely have careers like Brunson, who last season led the Knicks to their first NBA title in 53 years and won NBA Finals MVP. No money was raised in the formation of the firm, but Sandra Brunson didn’t rule that out in the future.
“Thirty Third gives us the chance to take ownership of my off-court business, to build something that reflects who we are, and to do it together,” Jalen Brunson said in a press release.

items.title: Ardagh Barred by Court From Selling Metals Packaging Unit
body: Ardagh Holdings SA, one of the largest makers of glass bottles and metal cans in Europe, has been blocked from selling its metal-packaging business, potentially complicating the new owners’ efforts to monetize one of the group’s most valuable assets.

A district court in Luxembourg recently issued an order prohibiting the company from proceeding with a sale of all or part of its interests in Ardagh Metal Packaging SA, Ardagh said in a statement Wednesday. The order followed an application by certain minority holders of senior secured notes issued by ARD Finance SA, a former parent of Ardagh Group.

Last year, creditors including Arini Capital Management Ltd. and Canyon Capital Advisors LLC took control of Ardagh from Irish billionaire Paul Coulson after a lengthy debt restructuring aimed at tackling more than $7.9 billion of liabilities and pushing out near-term maturities. Ardagh Metal Packaging was a key prize in that battle.

A group of PIK holders challenged the restructuring in Luxembourg, alleging the company unlawfully stripped away their collateral. They lost in first instance and appealed the decision. They also litigated the share pledge appropriation that was part of the restructuring plan and the case is still pending.
Ardagh Holdings said in Wednesday’s statement about the sale of the metal-packaging business that is “vigorously challenging the order and has made an application for it to be withdrawn.”

items.title: India's New Fee On UPI Payments Faces Pushback From Brokers, Retailers
body: Indian retailers and stockbrokers are worried that a new fee on payments through the state-backed digital network could increase costs, squeezing margins.

From Oct. 15, businesses will have to pay a merchant discount rate of as much as 0.4% on transactions above 2,000 rupees ($21) on the Unified Payments Interface. The levy will be capped at 300 rupees for transfers of 75,000 rupees or more.

The new fee — rolling out during the festival season — will apply to most UPI business payments by value. Spends above 2,000 rupees accounted for 67% of the money consumers paid to merchants on the network in August, despite making up just 4% of the volume, data from the operator National Payments Corporation of India showed.

It is a worry as many items and bill amounts can be more than 2,000 rupees during the festival season, said Kumar Rajagopalan, chief executive officer of the Retailers Association of India. “This could mean that some retailers start asking for cash instead of digital payments.”

From malls and mom-and-pop stores to roadside tea stalls, UPI transactions are ubiquitous, helping turn the country into the world’s biggest real-time payments market by volume. Soaring usage over the past decade prompted banks and payments firms to seek a fee to recoup some of the technology costs.
Read More: Modi Courts Diaspora to Expand Ubiquitous Payment System Abroad

A lower MDR of 0.02% — capped at 300 rupees — will be levied on payments above 2,000 rupees to securities firms. Brokers are concerned that they will end up paying the fee on money transferred by clients but not used for trading or investment.

“If we can’t pass the UPI charge on to the customer, there is essentially no limit to the cost a customer can impose on a broker without generating any revenue,” Nithin Kamath, chief executive at Zerodha Broking Ltd., India’s second-largest broker by active clients, said in a post on X.

Merchants have been reluctant to take on even modest costs. A LocalCircles survey of 32,796 businesses across 242 districts published earlier this month found 41% were unwilling to bear any fee on UPI payments above 2,000 rupees, while just 17% would accept a charge of 0.3% or higher.

The decision to levy the fee on UPI payments is also facing pushback. A public interest litigation has been filed in the country’s top court challenging the move, while a lobby of gasoline dealers has sought an exemption from the MDR.

While larger businesses are likely to absorb this with little friction, for those operating on tight margins, “even a small percentage can change how they think about accepting digital payments,” said Kunal Jhunjhunwala, founder of Mumbai-based Airpay Payment Services.

Small merchants receiving as much as 100,000 rupees a month on UPI will remain exempt, according to the statement Tuesday. The Finance Ministry advised businesses to absorb the levy and not pass it on to users.
“If there is any increase in costs, retailers and merchants will find a way to pass it on to consumers,” Rajagopalan said.

items.title: SK Hynix Says Exploring Options After Report of Intel Tie-Up
body: SK Hynix Inc. said that it’s exploring options to boost its global competitiveness after a report that it may team up with Intel Corp. to make semiconductors in the US.

The South Korean memory chipmaker issued the statement after Reuters reported the company may potentially lease part of ‌Intel’s long-planned chipmaking facility in Ohio or form a venture with Intel and major cloud computing firms.
The memory chipmaker says it hadn’t made a decision about a deal with Intel.

“We would like to clarify that nothing has been finalized regarding cooperation with any specific companies mentioned in the article or memory chip production in the United States,” the company said in its statement. “SK Hynix is exploring various options to strengthen its global competitiveness, but no specific plans or arrangements have been finalized at this time.”
Intel shares rose as much as 6.4%, while SK Hynix’s US traded stock gained as much as 3.3%.
US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has urged SK Hynix and other Asian chipmakers expand memory chip production in the US to help address a global shortage.
Intel declined to comment on the Reuters report, but said it’s committed to its Ohio investments.

items.title: Pete Hegseth's Main Character Energy Draws Bipartisan Critics
body: I’m Jonathan Tamari, senior Washington reporter for Bloomberg Government, and each weekday I’ll be coming to you with inside-the-room reporting and insights that reveal what’s really happening in Washington—and how it impacts you. Email me with feedback and comments here. If this newsletter was forwarded to you sign up here.
Today: Pete Hegseth’s unflattering spotlight, the EU and Canada deepen their alliance, and AI’s unlikely new billionaires.
Even in an administration stacked with main character energy, Pete Hegseth stands out.

But the attention swirling around the Defense secretary is increasingly negative as the former Fox News star runs into bipartisan frustration with the Iran war, his brawling style, and purges of Pentagon leadership.

While the military is traditionally one of the most apolitical and respected arms of the government, Hegseth is likely to be a top target for Democrats should they take over one or both chambers of Congress next year.
Some lawmakers aren’t waiting that long.

Outgoing Representative Thomas Massie, a Republican who has clashed with the Trump administration (and whom Hegseth personally campaigned against), brought articles of impeachment against the secretary Tuesday, calling him a threat to the “integrity of the armed forces” and the Constitution.

The move could force an awkward vote for Republicans in the coming days, making them take a stand on one of the leading faces of an unpopular war. (Just last night the House voted for a second time to stop the war, with seven Republicans joining Democrats.)
But Hegseth’s approach — a break from the “stentorian” and largely non-partisan style of past secretaries, Schake said — is taking a toll.
Just 32% of voters approve of his job performance, while 57% disapprove, according to a Quinnipiac University poll released last week.

The price of his most significant undertaking — the Iran war — was on display Tuesday. The non-partisan Congressional Budget Office said the conflict has cost $38 billion and will increase inflation about 0.5 percentage points by early next year.
It also found that the fighting has depleted stockpiles of munitions that could take five years or longer to rebuild.
The secretary’s fractious relationships (including locking Democrats out of some briefings) have complicated the Pentagon’s massive funding request and potential nominations to fill key vacancies.
Hegseth, though, still appears to have support from the person who matters most — Donald Trump — and embodies many of the traits the president admires. Swaggering. Combative. Looks good on TV.
Hegseth’s delight in using force and crusade against what he sees as an over-emphasis on diversity fits with the broader ethos of the administration, and has pleased many Republicans.

Banks said the big personnel changes allow Hegseth to install people aligned with his vision, and praised the defense chief for keeping the military “focused on fighting and winning wars,” not the agendas of the Biden era.
Hegseth’s controversies, however, have piled up, including:

The latest attention grabber: for a major speech this month, Hegseth wants an audience of service members who meet waist-to-height requirements and “impeccable” grooming standards, The Wall Street Journal reported.
His purge decimating the ranks of top military leaders has drawn some of the most substantive critiques, raising fears the military is facing a talent drain.
Even some Republicans are frustrated.
When I asked GOP Senator Mike Rounds about Hegseth’s standing, the Armed Services Committee member told me “it’s up to the president,” while urging the secretary to deal more openly with Democrats.
The chilly view from some Republicans could leave Hegseth with fewer defenders if Democrats take power and launch into him with investigations and hearings.
Trump’s top warrior is going to be in for a fight.
The EU is inviting Canada to join as its first associate member. They can compare notes on their break ups with the US and UK.
The US and China are discussing cutting some tariffs ahead of a Trump-Xi summit next week, increasing hope for extending their trade truce.

Iran’s drone attacks have set off “probably the greatest spending spree in Gulf defense history” in response, with more than $5 billion in contracts that could reshape the region’s security landscape.
Three people were killed and one injured when a TV news helicopter crashed in Los Angeles.
Record-high diesel prices are coming at a bad time for many Americans — and Republicans campaigning in critical Senate battlegrounds.
The risks to tech stocks are growing as midterm election campaigns increasingly focus on AI fears.
“It’s like gold bars raining from the sky.” The AI boom is even making billionaires out of business people who make obscure hardware or products.
Senior Trump administration officials met with Anthropic’s top Washington executive Tuesday to discuss AI safety risks.
Mark Zuckerberg said AI builders should rely on independent evaluators to ensure that models are safe, sidestepping calls for a broader slowdown.
Meta’s AI push is leaning on Dina Powell McCormick as its fixer and bridge to the world outside of Silicon Valley.
K Street lobbying firms disclosed nearly $112 million in revenue from a range of clients with a stake in AI policies in the first half of the year, a Bloomberg Government analysis found.
Adding to complications around the AI debate: Whatever the US does, slowing down China will be difficult.
The US is preparing to sell Israel thousands of bombs that are among the military’s most destructive, the largest single transfer of such weapons in years.

Saudi Arabia is ramping up sales of crude from outside the Strait of Hormuz following the shutdown of its East-West pipeline. And recent Houthi strikes have created a crisis for the kingdom and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.
The Senate Agriculture Committee is likely to advance the massive farm bill today, but Democrats remain unwilling to support it without changes to cost shifts for SNAP.
The Senate voted to advance a bill to create federal standards for student athletes entering “name, image, and likeness” deals and set eligibility rules.
Kalshi’s latest offer allowing users to place sports-style bets on clinical trials and pending drug approvals is amplifying concerns.
An outspoken Argentinian governor is bringing back a currency that can only be spent inside his province, defying President Javier Milei.
Rio de Janeiro’s staggering crime and corruption has taken on heavy symbolic weight in Brazil’s presidential race.
Nov. 3 will likely be a referendum on the Trump administration and the governing Republican trifecta, BGOV’s Greg Giroux and Brandon Lee write.

Affordability, political corruption, and AI are top of mind for voters as they head to the polls. Off-cycle redistricting has changed some congressional borders this year, with a net benefit to the GOP-friendly maps.

Democrats need a net gain of three seats across dozens of competitive races to flip control of the House — and the Senate remains a toss-up where a net loss of four seats would cost Republicans their majority.
Read more in the new BGOV OnPoint: Look Ahead to the 2026 Midterm Elections, which highlights the balance of power in each chamber, House and Senate races to watch, and key dates.
Trump rallies for Senate candidate Michael Whatley in North Carolina.
The Fed is expected to hike interest rates this afternoon.
Hong Kong leader John Lee outlines five-year plan for the Asian financial hub.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi meets his Chinese counterpart.

items.title: KKR Is Said to Be Preferred Bidder for Portugal's Logoplaste
body: KKR & Co. has emerged as the preferred bidder to buy Portuguese packaging maker Logoplaste, according to people familiar with the matter.

The US private equity firm is in exclusive talks with Logoplaste’s owners after Apax Partners LLP dropped out of the process, said the people, who asked not to be identified because the discussions are private. A deal could be reached in the coming weeks, they said.
Deliberations are ongoing and there is no certainty that the talks will result in a transaction.

A takeover of Logoplaste could become one of the biggest deals in Portugal this year and would happen amid strong private equity interest in assets in the country. Other businesses attracting bidders include water utility Indaqua, which earlier this year received offers valuing it at about €1.3 billion ($1.5 billion).

Ontario Teachers’ Pension Plan Board, which owns 60% of Logoplaste, has been working with advisers on a sale of the business. Bloomberg News previously reported that KKR and Apax had submitted binding offers for Logoplaste, which could be valued at more than €1.7 billion.
Representatives for KKR, Apax, Logoplaste and OTPP declined to comment.

Logoplaste Chairman Filipe de Botton, a member of the founding family, and board member Alexandre Relvas own the remaining 40% of the company and have the option to remain as shareholders, the people said.

Logoplaste generates about €1 billion in annual revenue and pioneered a “wall-to-wall” manufacturing model that places production facilities at customer sites. Founded in 1976, the company operates more than 60 plants across 16 countries and supplies customers including Kraft Heinz Co., Diageo Plc and L’Oréal SA.
The business was valued at about €1.4 billion, including debt, when OTPP acquired its majority stake from Carlyle Group in 2021.

items.title: Mamdani's AI Ban in New York Schools Is Worth Copying
body: It used to be conservatives who wanted to tread carefully with new things. These days, it’s progressives sounding the alarm on artificial intelligence. And I’m not just talking about the risk of human extinction.
Two of the country’s largest school systems have dramatically restricted AI access for students this year. They also happen to be bastions of coastal progressivism. Conservative parents, take note.

For the 2026–2027 school year, New York City’s Department of Education passed sweeping rules forbidding students from using AI until high school. Learning apps with AI features will be removed from student devices. Companion chatbots will be banned in all grades.

And not only that. Screens of any type will be banned in New York City public schools until third grade. Goodbye to school-issued tablets starting in pre-K and kindergarten, a practice that’s become widespread in the last five years. Hello to limits on screen time, including a 45-minute cap for middle schoolers.
The West Coast has taken it a step further. The Los Angeles public school system passed a districtwide moratorium on AI for all grade levels that applies to all school-issued devices.

This is exactly the kind of “common sense” reform that Republicans could use to define themselves heading into the midterm election. Since the Covid pandemic, Republicans have enjoyed an upper hand on education issues. There were the demonstrably harmful and lingering effects of extended school closures, promulgated largely by progressive districts. There were Biden’s efforts to block charter schools, despite their proven successes at boosting student achievement. And there were culture-war arguments that made Democrats appear more concerned about pronouns than whether kids could read.

But for all the emphasis Republicans have put on protecting children, students in Zohran Mamdani’s New York are going to be less screen-soaked than those in Greg Abbott’s Texas — where, per my sons’ experience in the public schools, there’s many a screen-based recess.

The Dallas Independent School District — one of the largest in Texas — has AI guidance for families that reads: “See how AI is enhancing your child’s learning,” and “Sit with your child while they use AI. Treat it like reading a book together.”

Keeping AI out of public schools isn’t going to do anything to slow development of the technology. Nor does it have anything to do with what happens at home; data from Common Sense Media and elsewhere suggest that AI use among teens is already ubiquitous. That’s a problem for another day.

What progressives in New York and LA are saying is that when it comes to educating our nation’s children and teaching them how to think, we are going to do it the old-fashioned way. That’s a message that more conservative districts ought to get behind.

Because the recent experiments we’ve been running in public education aren’t working. The newly released Program for International Assessment (PISA) found that 15-year-old US students’ reading scores have fallen near their lowest level in 25 years, with a 14-point drop in the last three years alone — as is the case across much of the developed world. (The report also says that half of students use AI for education.)
Our domestic tests, such as the Nation’s Report Card, show similar lost ground. Less than half of American students are reading or doing math at grade level.

To be sure, AI and screens are only two of many factors that may have pushed down student scores over the last decade. Others include absenteeism, which rose during Covid and has persisted since; scrapping traditional teaching approaches such as phonics and multiplication tables; and lots of testing with little accountability for underperforming schools, teachers and students. That’s a wide-ranging group of possibilities.

So perhaps AI presents a convenient scapegoat for challenges that are much more difficult for schools to solve. Nevertheless, we should solve what we can. The last thing American students need amid already-sagging scores and declining skills is AI slop in the classroom.

Americans’ satisfaction with the quality of K-12 education in the US has fallen to 32%, a new low in Gallup’s 27-year survey. It’s down 11 percentage points over the past two years. Democrats, Republicans and independents are almost equally disappointed.

Revealingly, schools received the highest marks on preparing students to adapt to new technologies. In contrast, only 4% of Americans believe that schools are preparing students to critically think and solve problems. This is backwards.

A generation of children is no longer learning at school like they need to. There are a lot of reasons for this. But allowing AI to supplant the basics of reading, writing and arithmetic  should not be added to the list.
Conservatives of all people should know it — and demand their school districts follow the examples set by New York and Los Angeles. On this issue, anyway.

items.title: AI-Fueled Profit Growth Set to Flow Through Every S&P 500 Sector
body: The next earnings season is set to be robust across the board, as the benefits of artificial intelligence spending start to flow across the economy.

Every single sector in the S&P 500 is expected to deliver earnings growth for the third quarter, the first time since 2021, when corporate America emerged from the pandemic slump, Bloomberg Intelligence data shows.

“Things have started to broaden out — even last quarter, we have seen pretty sizable beats from non-AI companies as well,” Ohsung Kwon, chief equity strategist at Wells Fargo, said in an interview. “We are starting to see broader strength in earnings.”

Industrial firms that make products like vacuum pumps, cooling systems and specialty paint coatings have seen revenue surge as data center construction continues to stoke demand for their products. Consumer firms are getting a boost from the AI buildout, which is creating jobs and demand for housing, while rising stock portfolios are encouraging people to splurge on shopping, travel and dining out.

“The overwhelming theme, which has been driving the broadening as well, has to do with the scale of AI-related capital spending,” said Venu Krishna, head of US equity strategy at Barclays. “That dollar amount is so high that what the hyperscalers are spending in terms of AI capex is effectively the revenue for a whole bunch of other industries, whether it’s storage, whether it’s hardware, whether it’s parts of industrials, parts of energy, parts of utilities.”

The big winners of the last few quarters — Big Tech and oil — are still expected to stand out with earnings growth far ahead of other sectors at 62% and 111%, respectively. The rest of the benchmark is also seen expanding as a wider range of companies benefit from growing AI use.

“When rates go up, one of the first casualties is construction jobs, but we haven’t seen that because the data center growth has been so dramatic that most of the labor has been reallocated,” Krishna said.

Aramark boosted its outlook for the second time this year after signing new deals with data center operators to provide catering, cleaning and transportation services at their campuses, which are expected to bring in between $400 million and $500 million in additional revenue over the next two years.

Consumer firms are also starting to capitalize on the implementation of AI in their own operations. Investments in AI-powered shopping tools, customer service and distribution can make baby clothes company Carter’s Inc. more efficient and help drive margin expansion, according to BI’s Mary Ross Gilbert.

The healthcare benchmark is set to return to earnings growth this quarter, while banks should deliver double-digit growth. Companies in these sectors are among the most willing to quantify AI-related gains, including cost reduction or improved productivity, according to research led by Barclays’ Krishna.

Financial services firms are also set to profit from potential blockbuster initial public offerings of AI firms, and regional banks should benefit as more wealth flows through communities that are home to data centers, Kwon said.
Though sectors like consumer staples, real estate and industrials are set for solid growth over the next few quarters, some tougher spots remain.

Among financials, the insurance industry is poised for an earnings decline in the third quarter as pricing weakens and loss costs rise. The media and advertising sector, part of communication services, is held back by tighter marketing budgets and customers turning to AI to make their own campaigns.

The AI spending boom brings some risk being tethered so closely to one sector, Kwon said, adding that he turned more cautious on equities a few weeks ago because of concerns about continued AI-related capital expenditures.
Potential challenges include rising interest rates and growing pressure on credit markets, according to Krishna.

Growing public backlash in some communities where data centers are being built, as well as recent calls from top AI leaders to potentially slow development of powerful frontier models over safety concerns, could add more uncertainty.

“Data center moratoriums, especially heading into the midterms, I think that’s a big risk as well, especially on sentiment,” Kwon said, adding that any delays in data center construction would be a downside for AI and tech stocks. “The AI trade is really a bottleneck trade right now, and any delays would alleviate that bottleneck at least a little bit.”

items.title: Temporary Protected Status for Immigrants Needs Reform Not an End
body: Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has temporarily deprived Democrats of a potent midterm rallying cry and averted a crisis for El Salvador’s president, one of President Donald Trump’s top fanboys, by tacitly agreeing to continue shielding 170,000 El Salvadorans from deportation — a protection that was set to expire on Sept. 9. DHS now says that a decision “will be made at the appropriate time,” in effect suspending the immigrants and their families in a fearful limbo.

The administration may yet seek to deport the Salvadorans. After all, the second Trump administration has already stripped more than one million immigrants from 13 countries of such protection, often willy-nilly and in seeming contravention of the conditions set by Congress when it created a program for Temporary Protected Status (TPS) some three decades ago. Under its terms, the US grants temporary permission to live and work in the US to those unauthorized immigrants whom the US judges are unable to return to a designated country because of conflict or environmental disaster.

But even if the administration doesn’t strip Salvadorans’ protections, Mullin’s nondecision last week perfectly captures the moral and intellectual bankruptcy of its crusade against TPS. The move also highlights the urgent need for Congress to strengthen the program it created and stop ceding its powers to shape immigration policy through legislation.

A look back at TPS’ origins in the landmark Immigration Act of 1990 helps to explain why. Prior to the act’s passage, no laws on the books provided blanket protection from deportation to citizens of crisis-ridden countries in the US illegally. Instead, the executive branch relied on an ad hoc mechanism called “executive voluntary departure” (EVD). At the recommendation of the secretary of state, the attorney general could exercise a form of prosecutorial discretion and not pursue a given country’s citizens for removal. From 1960 to 1990, the US granted that status at various times to 16 countries, including Poland, Iran and Uganda.

Compared with the case-by-case handling of individual refugees and asylum applicants from all over the world, EVD was downright loosey-goosey. A 1988 congressional report argued that the criteria under which protection was granted were subjective and opaque. The Immigration and Naturalization Service couldn’t track the number and whereabouts of EVD’s beneficiaries, much less screen them. The program operated pretty much at the discretion of the executive branch.

That discretion could yield some uneven outcomes. Indeed, the refusal of the Reagan administration to grant EVD to Salvadorans spurred Congress’ creation of TPS. Fleeing conflicts in El Salvador, Guatemala and Nicaragua during the 1980s, hundreds of thousands of Central Americans had come to the US seeking refuge. But the White House thought that granting Salvadorans sanctuary, either as individual asylum seekers or temporarily as an EVD group, would discredit its efforts to support El Salvador’s repressive right-wing regime. So it brushed them off as would-be economic migrants.

Some high-profile carnage tipped the balance, not least the murder of six Jesuit priests in San Salvador in November 1989. When the 1990 Immigration Act subsequently made its way through Congress, it included an amendment authorizing the attorney general to designate a country’s nationals for “Temporary Protected Status” because of either an ongoing armed conflict, environmental disaster or extraordinary and temporary conditions preventing the safe return of their nationals. El Salvador was singled out for protection, for a period of 18 months.The legislators who championed TPS stressed the “T” for “temporary.” The attorney general (and subsequently, DHS secretary) could extend a country’s TPS if it continued to meet the conditions for designation. But the program made no provisions for a path to permanent residence, nor did it confer the ability to sponsor relatives and reunite families. Congress reinforced that message by stipulating that any future legislation to create a TPS pathway to permanent residence must pass the Senate by a three-fifths majority.

And yet despite these good intentions to ensure that the status was indeed temporary, the program spiraled down what was often the path of least political resistance. Several TPS designations, for instance, have been extended more than a dozen times. But even as these increasingly long-term TPS recipients settled down, got married, built businesses and knit together communities, their fate in the US continued to depend on periodic review.  Moreover, their inability to confer legal status on overseas family members, in turn, opened a new channel for unauthorized immigration that fattened the cartels. Under a well-meaning but feckless Biden administration reeling from a border surge, the number of TPS beneficiaries tripled, from around 410,000 to nearly 1.3 million.

The Trump administration’s response has been to blow up the program, to the cheers of the MAGA faithful. As Tricia McLaughlin, an assistant secretary at the Department of Homeland Security, crowed a year ago, when yet another TPS designation was yanked, “This is what restoring sanity to America’s immigration system looks like.” Is it sane to send Afghans, Burmese, Haitians, South Sudanese, Syrians and Yemenis back to countries whose levels of violence, persecution and instability have prompted the State Department to issue do-not-travel warnings to Americans? The surreal reasoning behind some of these terminations is right out of Orwell or Kafka. It certainly doesn’t comport with Congress’ intention to create a transparent, consistent and accountable framework for granting temporary protection from deportation.

DHS’ cold feet about ending El Salvador’s TPS designation last week are the ultimate tell that the US is back in the bad old days of putting political considerations above facts on the ground and humanitarian need. After all, El Salvador is one of the few countries where conditions have markedly improved since its citizens received a new grant of TPS in 2001, following earthquakes that killed thousands and displaced almost one-fifth of its population.

But booting out El Salvadorans who have been here for more than two decades would trigger heart-rending headlines that the White House doesn’t want before the midterms. There are, for instance, 150,000 US citizen children with a parent who is a Salvadoran TPS recipient. Trump is already underwater in public opinion polls for his handling of immigration. He doesn’t need more bad press on this front. And he also doesn’t want to hammer his Salvadoran buddy President Nayib Bukele, whose country is housing several hundred US deportees in a new mega-prison for $6 million, has crypto business ties with Trump’s secretary of commerce and relies heavily on remittances from Salvadorans working in the US.

Yet there is a salutary lesson for the US and its Congress in what happened to El Salvador’s first TPS designation, the one that legislators inserted directly into the statute. Roughly 187,000 Salvadorans registered for TPS after it was instituted in January 1991. When it expired 18 months later, President George HW Bush granted them “deferred enforced departure” — another executive branch workaround — for a year, which President Bill Clinton (reminder: a Democrat) then terminated in 1994. Eventually, many of the Salvadorans were able to qualify for permanent residence under the bipartisan Nicaraguan Adjustment and Central American Relief Act.

In other words, the system worked: TPS was not extended, a short-term executive branch protection kicked in, and Congress passed a law that delivered many of the Salvadorans from limbo. You may or may not agree with the outcome, but all the players were coloring inside the lines.The same thing could have happened to the Salvadorans granted TPS in 2001. In a better world, the House of Representatives would have taken up and passed the Senate’s 2014 bipartisan “Gang of Eight” immigration reform bill, which included provisions that would have potentially allowed Salvadorans and other TPS holders to apply for permanent residence. The US will always need statutory, temporary protection for individuals who might not qualify as refugees. TPS needs to be fixed, with tighter constraints on extensions and certifications, not junked. Instead of allowing a mad king to flout the spirit if not the letter of one of its more sensible legislative initiatives, Congress must do its job and grasp the nettle of immigration reform.

items.title: Air France-KLM Said to Offer Shares in TAP as Part of Its Bid
body: Air France-KLM is willing to offer Portugal a stake in the airline group as part of its bid for TAP SA, according to a person familiar with the matter, as it seeks an edge over a rival overture from Deutsche Lufthansa AG.

The group has told the Portuguese government that it would be open to the state taking shares in Air France-KLM as part of a transaction, said the person, who asked not to be identified discussing private negotiations. Such an arrangement would allow Portugal to gain some influence within a major European carrier group that’s also expected to take control of Scandinavia’s SAS AB by year end.

Air France-KLM and Lufthansa are both vying for a stake in the asset, and the two sides have emphasized that their bids are about more than just price. Air France-KLM has pointed to its efforts to protect the TAP brand, maintain Lisbon as a hub and potentially expanding the group’s activities in Portugal.
At the same time, Air France-KLM will only pursue a deal that fits within its risk profile and is financially viable, the person said. An official for the carrier group declined to comment.

Portuguese Business newspaper Jornal Economico reported last week that Air France-KLM had included in its offer the possibility of the Portuguese government receiving shares in the group. The rival bid by Lufthansa doesn’t include such a component, it said.
Lufthansa said in a statement that its goal remains “to establish a long-term partnership with TAP and Portugal” and that it would not comment on further details at this point.

Portugal’s government has entered an additional round of negotiations with Lufthansa and Air France-KLM over the sale of a minority stake in TAP as it seeks improved offers from both airline groups. TAP is attractive because of its extensive network linking Europe with Brazil, Latin America and Africa.

A decision is expected to take place in the coming weeks, according to the government, which has said both offers are close overall in their value. Portugal plans to sell as much as 49.9% of TAP, including 44.9% to a strategic investor and as much as 5% to employees.
Even before a decision has been reached, the Franco-Dutch carrier group is expanding in Portugal

Air France-KLM will increase capacity in Portugal by 12% in available seat kilometers this winter, it said Tuesday. Air France, KLM and budget subsidiary Transavia will operate 24 routes and as many as 238 weekly services, connecting five airports in Portugal with destinations in France, the Netherlands and Belgium.
