items.title: Armani Taps ex-Versace Designer to Head Emporio, Accessories
body: Giorgio Armani SpA named Dario Vitale creative director of Emporio Armani and Giorgio Armani accessories, bringing fresh talent to the Italian fashion house following the death of its founder a year ago.
Vitale, whose appointment takes effect immediately, is the first designer outside the Armani family to hold the role, the company said in a statement Wednesday.

Thw group offers fashion lines ranging from the more mass-market Armani Exchange to exclusive and red-carpet gowns from Giorgio Armani Privé. Armani’s niece Silvana oversees womenswear design while group Chairman Leo Dell’Orco is head of menswear.
Vitale was briefly artistic director of Versace last year, but left after Prada SpA bought the label, known for its exuberant style. Prior to Versace, Vitale was at Miu Miu, another Prada brand.

Bloomberg News reported in June that Armani was in the process of hiring a new designer for Emporio Armani. The line offers black dresses for €840 ($969) and formal men’s suits for €1,250, putting it among the more affordable brands in luxury fashion.

Handbags haven’t traditionally been a significant revenue generator for Armani, but naming Vitale as head of accessories may signal a desire to boost that offering. Handbags tend to carry high profit margins, making them a key category for luxury groups.

Armani’s death occurred during a downturn for personal luxury goods, with his namesake company posting organic sales that fell 2.8% last year at constant exchange rates. His heirs have added industry veterans to the board and elevated Giuseppe Marsocci to chief executive officer.

In his will, Giorgio Armani directed his heirs to find a strategic partner 12 to 18 months after his death. He named eyewear firm EssilorLuxottica SpA, beauty conglomerate L’Oreal SA and leather goods giant LVMH Moët Hennessy Louis Vuitton SE — or a company of similar standing — as preferred bidders for an initial 15% stake, which could rise to nearly 70% within five years. As an alternative, the company could also be listed on a public stock market.

items.title: LNG Buyers Turn to US as Hormuz Crisis Forces Supply Rethink
body: Welcome to our guide to the commodities driving the global economy. Today, Asia Energy Team Leader Stephen Stapczynski looks at how the gas industry plans to fill a widening supply gap.
One word — diversification — was on the lips of most executives at the world’s biggest natural gas conference in Bangkok this week.
That’s the industry’s euphemism for cutting exposure to the Middle East.

After all, more than six months into the US-Iran war, there’s still no sign of liquefied natural gas flowing again through the Strait of Hormuz. A fifth of global supply remains effectively trapped inside the Persian Gulf.

Publicly, speakers at the Gastech event stressed that Qatar and the United Arab Emirates will continue to be important suppliers to the world. On the sidelines, however, another thought was whispered: What if LNG traffic through Hormuz never fully returns to normal?
Buyers and traders can no longer afford to wait, and their search for alternative supplies has put the US — already the world’s biggest exporter — front and center in the conversation.
With America set to roughly double LNG capacity by 2030, those countries most exposed to the Middle East disruption like Pakistan and Bangladesh are exploring how to secure some of this supply.
Companies in Thailand are doing the same, while Japan’s Inpex Corp. is considering investing in an export project in the US.
For buyers, American LNG offers a hedge. Cargoes can be shipped to Asia or Europe depending where they’re needed more, or where prices are higher.

The economics are also attractive. Long-term contracts linked to Henry Hub, the US benchmark, are delivering LNG to Asia at roughly $8 per million British thermal units today. The current spot price is close to $30.
But there’s a catch.

Rising construction costs, supply-chain bottlenecks and competition for fuel needed to power data centers are making US Gulf Coast export plants more expensive, a trend that’s being reflected in the price of new contracts. That matters to cash-strapped economies.
If the US and other suppliers like Canada and South America don’t seize this opportunity, buyers may simply opt to burn more coal or accelerate their shift toward renewables.
And if that happens, diversification takes on a wider meaning — not just a shift away from the Middle East, but from LNG itself.
—Stephen Stapczynski, Bloomberg News
China’s gasoline and diesel inventories are plunging as refiners grapple with a tightening domestic market, raising the chance the government may move to limit fuel exports again.
Oil dropped as a rally driven by supply disruptions left gains looking overdone and a US industry report pointed to a rise in stockpiles.

Saudi Arabia is ramping up prompt spot sales of crude from outside the Strait of Hormuz following the shutdown of the kingdom’s East-West pipeline, which halted cross-country flows to its Red Sea coast.
The US is investigating potential cyberattacks on oil and gas tankers, as concerns grow around the threat to maritime safety posed by hackers interfering with vessels’ electronic systems.

Prospects for an extension to the US-China trade truce are solidifying as the two sides discuss slashing tariffs on goods, including American energy and agricultural products, ahead of next week’s summit between presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping.

Glencore accused Radiant World and associated companies of sending falsified invoices to lenders, cutting ties just as the iron ore trader filed a suit in Singapore against the Swiss-based commodities group, seeking $2 billion in damages.

Gas turbine makers are concentrating their expansion on the biggest machines, betting that utilities and data centers will need scale and efficiency in generating electricity. Four-fifths of the industry’s additional manufacturing capacity by 2030 will go for heavy-frame turbines that are typically rated over 100 megawatts, according to analysis by BloombergNEF.

Bloomberg Green returns to New York on Sept. 23 during Climate Week, convening industry leaders, policymakers and climate innovators to explore what’s next in the transition to a more resilient and future-ready world.

items.title: AI's Existential Fears Meet Wall Street Financing FOMO in Europe
body: JPMorgan Chase & Co. and Goldman Sachs Group Inc. are among banks lining up to finance billions of dollars in European AI debt as the region races to close the gap with the US.

The Wall Street underwriters are vying for a leading role in financing Europe’s push to reduce its reliance on overseas technology. Both have assembled specialist teams to pitch deals to data-center operators and investors.
“There hasn’t been a great deal of issuance here but there has been intense investor focus,” said Noah Roth, JPMorgan’s London-based head of EMEA leveraged finance. “There’s a lot of FOMO.”

Investors may not have to miss out much longer. Anywhere from $5 billion to $10 billion of data-center bonds could reach European markets by the end of the year, with a much bigger wave expected in 2027, according to Goldman Sachs estimates.

By contrast, the US has already seen more than $350 billion in AI-related issuance so far this year, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. AI executives there are warning of catastrophic risks from their most advanced models and states including Texas and New York are restricting new data centers.
Read More: Are We Losing Control of AI? What’s Driving Fears: Explainer

Europe, meanwhile, is worried about not building fast enough. European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde has warned that relying on US technology risks giving Europe’s trading partners enormous leverage.

“Regardless of whether or not we have a European champion in AI, Europe will need to have data centers, for European security and for data sovereignty,” said Giacomo Reali, a leveraged finance partner at Linklaters.
Closing the gap won’t come cheap. Europe may need about $3 trillion through 2035 to fund cloud infrastructure, data centers and other critical technologies, according to Bloomberg Intelligence.

Until now, banks, project finance and securitizations were enough for Europe’s smaller-scale projects. The next generation will require deeper pools of capital. Among them: Start Campus, a planned 1.2-gigawatt facility in Portugal.

Projects of that size will pave the way for a bigger role for both investment-grade and high-yield debt markets. AI-related debt represents about 5% of European high-yield issuance, versus 19% in the US, according to Dealogic and Goldman Sachs research.

Each new 100 to 200 megawatt center in Europe could translate to “$1 billion, $2 billion debt deals at a minimum,” Miriam Wheeler, global head of leveraged finance at Goldman Sachs, said on the sidelines of her bank’s leveraged finance conference in London. She estimates Europe’s role in the global AI build-out could rise to as much as 25% from 10%.
“We think if you start seeing more of that mega capex come to Europe, then you’ll start to see it financed in the 144A market, investment-grade and non-investment grade,” she said.

The first European high-yield data-center deals are likely to borrow heavily from the US playbook. Cahill Gordon & Reindel partner Ariel Goldman expects issuers to take the “cleanest, easiest path” to establish a track record before more customized structures.

Before that can happen, a large amount of lender education will be needed to bring investors up to speed with the risks of committing to projects that have yet to be built. Data centers’ heavy consumption of electricity and water is drawing greater scrutiny from lenders with ESG mandates. Even if investors don’t want to be left behind in the AI wave, they aren’t prepared to finance every project.

The sole data center bonds priced in Europe’s junk bond market, from CoreWeave Inc., have been trading below their face value since news emerged that key client Meta Platforms Inc. was developing a competing cloud-infrastructure business.
“The threshold and diligence we need to do is quite high,” said Sid Chhabra, head of securitized credit, CLO management and euro high yield at RBC BlueBay.

European investors spent much of the summer doing their homework. In July, some made the hour-long trip from London to Slough to tour data centers owned by Equinix Inc. It was an unusual amount of effort for a £280 million ($377 million) bond deal.

The turnout said something about the scarcity of AI-related debt in Europe. Equinix’s asset-backed securities offering is tiny compared with the trillions of dollars needed to finance the global build-out of artificial intelligence infrastructure.
But for the daytrippers to Slough, the data-center deal was an early opportunity to get in on the AI boom. Orders for Equinix’s bonds ended up totalling over £510 million.

“We will see companies in the sector ultimately needing to raise billions from the market,” said Ben Thompson, head of EMEA leveraged finance capital markets at JPMorgan. “We will see how big that number can be.”

items.title: Venture Investors Find Liquidity Fix Outside IPO Market
body: Welcome to Going Private, I’m Sinead Cruise and this is Bloomberg’s twice-weekly newsletter about private markets and the forces moving capital away from the public eye. Today, we look at Earvin “Magic” Johnson’s links to under-pressure mogul Mark Walter, the latent dangers in money market funds  and a possible shakeup in the way private equity is financed in the future. But first, we look at one firm helping venture capitalists cope with feast-or-famine money markets. If you’re not already on our list, sign up here. Have feedback? Email us at goingprivate@bloomberg.net
In private equity, access to liquidity is a matter of life or death. In venture capital, it might be the difference between life and no life at all.

Elon Musk aside, entrepreneurs are increasingly turning to secondary markets to exit investments. Some owners and their angel investors struggle to navigate this terrain even though it offers a chance to back some of the world’s most promising firms before everyone else knows they exist.

Basil Moftah and Leena Khalil, managing partners at UAE-based VC secondaries firm Key Capital, are among those seeking to connect capital providers with founder-owned firms, so the latter can skip unpredictable public debt or equity offerings.
Home to a vast number of privately-owned companies ranging from tiny to titan, the Middle East is the ideal incubator for a multitrillion dollar global VC secondaries market, according to Moftah.
“There’s a neglected set of shareholders who would like to be able to take money off the table for whatever reason they may have,” he told Going Private.

VC ownership registers are often highly fragmented, comprising shareholders with positions too small to appeal to institutional investors or buyout firms who rarely show appetite for stakes without influence or control. This can rob owners of the chance to monetize incremental value as a startup grows.
According to the PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor, US startups raised more than $400 billion in the first half of 2026, surpassing every previous full-year investment total on record.
But the majority of that capital is flowing to AI companies and financings of $100 million or more, leaving some smaller businesses sitting on fresh ideas they can’t yet afford to develop.

“What excites us is being part of what will become a very meaningful asset class over time but this will only happen if the angels and experts also find a way to liquidity. If they can’t, they’re going to stop fueling innovation,” Moftah said.

Khalil, who co-founded e-commerce platform Mumzworld.com prior to joining Key Capital, said company owners with global profile were increasingly reaching out to Key in search of liquidity for themselves or their staff.

Some of those entrepreneurs have had hopes of lucrative IPOs dashed by volatility. Others want alternative ways to access capital locked into fledgling firms and to stay in control to capture maximum possible upside at a later date.

The average sum sought is $2 million-$3 million but could be as large as $30 million and as small as $500,000 — the sum one single mom in the Middle East raised to help with her daughter’s wedding expenses. Any discounts agreed are kept confidential to protect the company’s value and other investors.
“This is what people tend to look for, meaningful enough to be life changing, but not necessarily giving up all the holding they have,” Khalil said.

Moftah says a personal approach is vital to help unlisted companies reach new owners who understand and respect the founders’ vision. The firm is hosting its fourth Key Trek event in London from Sept. 30, bringing founders from dozens of private tech firms together with investors who want exposure to the region.
Participants include real estate platform PRYPCO, AI infrastructure firm ThinkAI, health-tech BioSapien and digital banking firm Hala.

“It’s like a matchmaking service, if you like,” Moftah said. “It takes us quite a while to get to know the companies and the founders, but once we have that relationship, we’re then their support mechanism in liquidity management.”

It’s no secret that regulators are sizing up the $1.8 trillion private credit sector on their mission to safeguard financial stability. What’s less clear is whether the $9 trillion money market funds industry might actually pose a bigger threat.

A paper by prominent academics Matteo Aquilina, Peter Cincinelli and Giovanni Urga suggests watchdogs should pay greater attention to the hazards presented by ‘prime’ MMFs, particularly those that grow rapidly during stock market bull runs.MMFs have been a critical part of the non-bank financial system for decades and play a major role in providing short-term financing to governments, while so-called ‘prime’ structures offer funding to banks and companies.

After analyzing data on 3,568 US dollar-denominated products between 2004 and 2022, the authors said quickfire inflows indicated a race for yield among investors who could end up withdrawing assets as rapidly as they had invested.

Such a scenario could leave MMFs potentially unable to roll over purchases of commercial paper or certificates of deposit and, in extreme cases, force fire sales of other holdings to meet redemption demand, according to the paper.“This could lead to a significant reduction in activity in short-term funding markets, with knock-on effects on the ability of banks and corporations to finance their operations,” the authors said, calling on policymakers to incorporate MMFs more explicitly into systemic-risk monitoring frameworks.

“It is particularly striking that ‘bigger’ does not necessarily mean ‘riskier’“,  according to the study, which found larger MMFs were generally associated with lower systemic risk in normal market conditions.
“However, this changes during equity-market booms: suddenly, rapid fund growth is associated with higher systemic risk,” the authors said.
Private credit firms are already working to improve the industry’s public image after an unprecedented exodus from semi-liquid funds in the first half of 2026.

Most managers have rolled out gating mechanisms to manage any outsized redemptions without needing to dump quality assets or compromise the interests of investors staying put. MMFs have few such tools to fall back on.

Some 46 direct lending market participants are contributing data to a pioneering deep-dive into the industry by the Bank of England. Results due next year are widely expected to shape future supervision of the sector.“Our analysis suggests that regulators and other policymakers need to look beyond banks and broad macroeconomic indicators when assessing systemic risk,” said Urga, director of the Centre for Econometric Analysis at the University of London’s Bayes Business School.“Understanding these dynamics is essential for designing a resilient financial system.”
Regulators scrutinizing the business affairs of billionaire mogul Mark Walter are leaving no stone unturned, with ties to sporting legends like Earvin “Magic” Johnson now under the microscope.
The attention centers on Amistad Financial Group, which last year took over EquiTrust Life Insurance, the insurer Johnson bought from Walter’s Guggenheim Partners in 2015.

Amistad is being probed over its potential role as an intermediary for loans between Walter-linked companies, including Delaware Life Insurance Co. and Clear Spring Life and Annuity Co., people briefed on the matter told my colleagues Tom Maloney, Weihua Li and Vivien Ngo.

The two firms lent at least $2 billion to companies that fall under Amistad’s corporate umbrella by the end of 2025, according to a Bloomberg review of filings. Some of those loans were reclassified as affiliated from unaffiliated by Walter’s insurers this year.
Investigators are trying to discern if Amistad may have been used to mask the transfer of money from Walter’s insurers to his other investments.

Separately, insurers owned by Amistad, including Equitrust, lent at least $4 billion to three of the other intermediaries whose arrangements with Walter are under investigation. The insurers have asset management agreements with Guggenheim.

While affiliated investments aren’t forbidden for insurers, there are questions over how some of Walter’s businesses disclosed their transactions. Walter-controlled insurers have already said more than $20 billion of financing should have been — but initially weren’t — described as affiliated transactions.
When insurers lend money to a related party, there’s a higher bar to get those loans rated as investment grade compared to loans to non-affiliated entities.

“There is no victim here. No one has been harmed, and no one has claimed they were harmed,” Walter’s investment group, TWG, said in a statement last month. TWG spokespeople didn’t respond to a request for fresh comment.

A Guggenheim spokesperson said customer allocations were based on numerous considerations, including investment objectives and risk parameters, and not on the identity or ownership of clients. Potential conflicts were subject to additional controls, including disclosure and consent when required.
Representatives for Amistad, EquiTrust and Johnson didn’t respond to requests for comment.

Walter has started to unwind some of the loans to affiliated companies. Last month, he also agreed to sell his stake in the Los Angeles Lakers for $12.5 billion to former Walt Disney Co. CEO Bob Iger and investor Josh Kushner.
Fitch analysts recently cut the outlook on EquiTrust to negative, and wrote that Amistad could require the insurer to pay material dividends to its new parent company in order to service its debt.

Co-investments and directs are likely to become the largest two sources of capital in the private equity industry within five years, usurping blind-pool funds increasingly falling out of investor favor, data from Houlihan Lokey shows.

Around two-fifths of 56 respondents to the firm’s maiden LP Compass survey said they expect co-investments to outgrow traditional primary funds, compared with just 20% who expect the latter to retain its top ranking.

Co-investors typically invest in identifiable assets alongside a sponsor via a separate vehicle, while a direct investor invests directly onto the balance sheet of identifiable assets — outside a fund structure or the co-investment vehicles associated with them.

“The growing investor enthusiasm for investing in identifiable assets of all kinds, either in the primary or secondary market, explains one of the survey’s more striking findings, namely that the vast majority of investors are open to paying annual fees and carry for co-investment,” according to

Matt Swain, managing director and global co-head of equity capital solutions at Houlihan Lokey said the enthusiasm for investing in identifiable assets, in the primary or secondary market, signals that the vast majority of investors are now open to paying annual fees and carry for co-investment.“This was not the case five, or even three years ago,” he said.
Almost four-fifths of investors expect co-investment and direct volumes to hit a record in 2026, following an estimated $215 billion of combined activity in 2025.

Some 59% expect directs to deliver the highest returns of any major form of PE investment, while 38% expect co-investments to lead the pack. No investors expect the best returns to come from secondary investing or primary fund investment — though the strategies are still seen as crucial to diversification and lowering risk in PE.

“The notion that co-investments and directs offer even better alignment of economic interest than more traditional forms of PE stems from the fact that on average co-investment and directs concentrate a greater portion of everyone’s capital in single assets – putting more at risk for everyone,” Swain said.

Golub Capital managing director and head of structured products Alan George is joining Silver Point Capital to become its head of credit financing and leverage solutions. George, who worked at Golub for nearly 18 years, will help develop Silver Point’s financing and debt capital markets capabilities, the company said in a statement.
Thank you for reading Going Private, Bloomberg’s twice-weekly newsletter on private markets. Contact us for feedback and tips at goingprivate@bloomberg.net.

items.title: EU Floats Canada Becoming the Bloc's First Associate Member
body: Good morning. The European Union courts Canada. America’s diesel crunch couldn’t have come at a worse time. And AI is minting the most unexpected billionaires. Listen to the day’s top stories.
— Marc Perrier and Harry Black

The European Union floated Canada becoming its first associate member. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen offered the invitation during her state of the union address with Canada’s Mark Carney in attendance, saying the group needs to “re-imagine” its partnerships. The Canadian prime minister warned earlier this year that the “rules-based international order” was effectively dead and has repeatedly pushed for so-called middle powers to band together.

OpenAI is eyeing a funding round at a valuation of more than $1.2 trillion, giving it room to potentially delay its IPO and keep shopping for acquisitions, a person familiar said. And as the AI safety debate rages, Meta Chief Executive Officer Mark Zuckerberg said labs should rely on independent evaluators and advisers to ensure that models are safe. Senior US officials are said to have met with Anthropic to discuss risks. And check out this story on how Donald Trump has few good options to curb China’s rise as an AI superpower.

Stocks and bonds are finding relief after days of selling as traders wait for the Federal Reserve’s interest-rate decision today and updated projections before placing bets on where markets will head next. A dip in oil prices helped steady sentiment. See the latest market themes right here.

Saudi Arabia is ramping up prompt spot sales of crude from outside the Strait of Hormuz after the shutdown of its East-West pipeline halted flows to the Red Sea coast. Separately, the US is preparing to provide Israel thousands of bombs among the most destructive in its arsenal, the largest single transfer of such weapons in years.

Three people were killed and one injured when a TV news helicopter crashed between two commercial buildings in the Chatsworth neighborhood of Los Angeles, according to officials. The helicopter was providing coverage for KNBC and Telemundo 52.

America’s diesel crunch couldn’t have come at a worse time. Higher prices are squeezing voters that backed Trump in 2024, especially farmers in states like Iowa and Kansas as they gear up for harvest.
Trump’s naval blockade of Iran is costing the Pentagon roughly $32.5 million a day. It’s also testing the limits of America’s military might around the world.Big Take Podcast

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh may try to soften today’s expected interest-rate hike with a dovish message, John Authers writes. That may ease pressure from Trump, but risks pushing Treasury yields even higher if investors expect less tightening to curb inflation.More Opinions

Forget chips and data centers. The road to AI billions also runs through drawer slides. The boom is minting fortunes in some of manufacturing’s least glamorous corners, from server rail kits to micro drill bits.

items.title: After Talking the Talk on Inflation, Fed's Warsh May Be Made to Walk
body: I’m Chris Anstey, a senior economics editor in Boston. Today we’re looking at the Fed’s looming rate decision. Send us feedback and tips to ecodaily@bloomberg.net. And if you aren’t yet signed up to receive this newsletter, you can do so here.
Following his first policy meeting as Fed chief, Kevin Warsh said in June, “We’ve got some work to do on the price-stability front” after inflation had run way over the 2% target for years.
After his second, in July, he referenced “impatience” among the public in getting inflation down, and declared, “where necessary and appropriate, we will not hesitate to act.”
In August, at the Jackson Hole conference, he said “we have work to do” unless there’s confidence prices are moving to 2% “clearly and at sufficient speed.”

There’s little doubt in Fed watchers’ minds that Warsh has been talking the talk on fighting inflation. His longtime colleague, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, was among those saying he had come out “tough” on that score. But as this newsletter noted in July, the question was whether he’d really walk the talk.

On Wednesday, Warsh faces the millennia-old “boy who cried wolf” issue from Aesop’s fables. If he doesn’t vote to hike interest rates, the Fed-watching community is unlikely to believe his inflation rhetoric going forward. His credibility risks being shot.
That’s after Friday’s consumer price index report, the last before this week’s meeting, was difficult to be interpreted as showing inflation was “clearly” and speedily moving to 2%.

Ironically, had Warsh been less tough-talking before that report, it might not otherwise have been viewed as a decisive blow for a rate increase. Some of those who switched their call after the release appeared to do so reluctantly.

Goldman Sachs was among those changing to a quarter-point rate-rise forecast on Friday. The CPI report “has not changed our fundamental inflation view,” economist David Mericle wrote in explanation. “We do not see a strong economic case for raising.”

The Goldman team is among those flagging that inflation currently is being kept high by one-time factors. Energy costs have surged due to the Iran war, for example. But policymakers likely will move nonetheless because they will want to avoid the market reaction that would likely follow from remaining on hold when the market is pricing a nearly 90% chance of a hike.”

In other words, a failure to deliver on Wednesday would risk investors concluding that Warsh’s price-stability cries are hollow. The risk is they’d then price in faster inflation for longer, sending yields — and mortgage rates — even higher. But on the fundamentals, Anna Wong at Bloomberg Economics is among those viewing a move as risking a mistake.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s 3% US economic growth target, which underpins his goal to stabilize the federal debt trajectory, could come close to doing just that, according to Wells Fargo analysis. But there are some provisos, economists Tom Porcelli and Michael Pugliese wrote in a note Tuesday.

Stabilizing debt-to-GDP over the next decade would require both 3% to 3.5% in gross domestic product increases per year and “no major changes” to taxation and spending policies, the duo wrote. The US hasn’t sustained that sort of trend growth rate since before the financial crisis that began in 2007. But, “on the face of it, let’s simply call this possible.”

What makes things more challenging is the aging US population means labor force increases won’t be helping as much as they used to. That means “it would take the fastest labor productivity on record to achieve this outcome” for growth. As for Washington forgoing major tax and spending policy changes for a decade? The duo didn’t immediately weigh in. US budget experts have been skeptical, as Bloomberg reported Tuesday.

items.title: Nvidia's Jensen Huang Touts Himself as an AI VC Role Model
body: Welcome to Tech In Depth, our daily newsletter about the business of tech from Bloomberg’s journalists around the world. Today, Ian King reports on Jensen Huang’s undimmed enthusiasm for all things artificial intelligence.
AI safety: OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind are working together to address the risks of new AI models. The companies want to fend off new safety regulations.
Meta’s chips: The social media company plans to deploy its in-house AI chip in data centers by the first half of 2027. The aim is to help cut its massive AI costs.

Amazon’s data loss: Amazon said it can’t recover some information stored in data centers in the Persian Gulf damaged during the US-Iran war. The facilities includes those in Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates.

Radical Ventures, a Toronto-based venture fund focused on AI companies, announced a late-stage growth fund with more than $1 billion — the largest-ever venture fund in Canada. Radical Ventures will use the fund to try to create “trillion-dollar companies,” said co-founder and Managing Partner Jordan Jacobs.

A week before he took a phone call from the president on stage Monday, Jensen Huang delivered another of his signature tongue-in-cheek yet some how deeply serious lectures to another room full of very influential people.

At the Goldman Sachs Communacopia conference in San Francisco, Nvidia’s founder and chief executive officer didn’t even address the first question about the growth of artificial intelligence before he started his routine.
“I just think we should just take a pause and acknowledge that I was right,” he said, eliciting his usual chorus of polite laughter from the audience. “Take a pause. Take your time.”

Then, as he usually does, Huang went on to treat questions — from, in this case, Goldman analyst Jim Schneider — as little more than speed bumps or opportunities to pause for a breath as he set about delivering the latest version of his thesis on why the AI market is only just getting going. What should be one of the most demanding and knowledgeable crowds in the capitalist system were reduced to the status of a benign and friendly audience.

To be fair to attendees and Huang, he’s very much put numbers where his mouth and money are. Part of this most recent pitch was to emphasize his confidence in the astounding 70% growth Nvidia expects to deliver next year. This is already a $5 trillion company, keep in mind — and he promised Nvidia will work hard to get more supply and try to even exceed that.

When it next reports earnings, Nvidia will deliver its first quarter of more than $100 billion in revenue, according to Wall Street forecasts. It’s not only breaking three figures of billions in a three-month period for the first time, it’s got there very quickly. In the April quarter of 2024, it had just $7.2 billion in sales.

My colleague Lynn Doan on Tuesday set out nicely how, even with frontier AI labs Anthropic and OpenAI expressing misgivings about the runaway pace of artificial intelligence advances, the frenzied demand for AI hardware and chips of the sort that Nvidia sells will remain more than robust.
Read More: Are We Losing Control of AI? What’s Driving New Fears

Something else that Huang brought up about Nvidia’s activities stood out to me. It’s not the usual rhetoric you might hear from a businessman simply selling his wares, despite the familiarity of his delivery. Huang characterized himself as an investor who should be followed.
“People are starting to recognize that wherever I invest, it’s not a bad place to invest because I’m an informed investor,” he said. “I’m not taking any risks.”

The reference was to the tens of billions of dollars he’s invested and tens more he’s promised as part of Nvidia’s drive to speed up the adoption of AI across the economy. The company addressed the concern that this is getting out of hand and increasing the risk of AI being a bubble during its most recent earnings call. It gave a breakdown of commitments over the next few years that can be totaled up to more than $500 billion in their various forms.

That’s one company planning or spending more than half a trillion dollars. No one is worried that Nvidia isn’t good for that amount, if current trends persist. The company delivered more than $50 billion in net income in its most recent quarter. Huang himself said he’s only providing a small amount of what’s required and what he’ll get in return more than makes up for it.

By providing financial backing for a wide range of AI data center operators, he’s simply greasing the wheels of broader uptake of the technology, the CEO argues. He doesn’t do that unless he’s sure that those he’s helping out have customers lined up to use what’s being deployed.

That’s already led to seemingly smart investments. Nvidia owns about $50 billion in stock of publicly traded companies, including SpaceX and Intel, most of which now represent substantial gains over what was paid for the stakes. But Nvidia the investor is doing far more than keep an eye on publicly traded companies it has an interest in.

Nvidia’s venture capital arm lists 96 holdings in its portfolio and the company is is using a variety of financial techniques to boost a myriad more. It’s providing loan guarantees, assuming leases, giving massive purchase commitments to boost supply and investing in other component makers to ensure their technology is readily available and doesn’t become a roadblock.

It’s also making acquisitions. In the last three weeks, Nvidia invested $3.5 billion into Taiwan’s MediaTek and paid about $13 billion for French startup Hugging Face, adding an even more global dimension to its holdings.

All this is being done by a company that was until very recently a niche provider of semiconductors mainly focused on components for gamer PCs. Now, as Huang says, Nvidia is in the computer infrastructure business with multiple products ranging all the way from chips to massive networked computer systems, software and services. It also has a portfolio that’s more diverse, complicated and valuable than those of most investors and fund managers at the Goldman Sachs conference Huang was addressing.

The ability of Huang and his team to manage that risk, alongside their day job of running the world’s most valuable company in a highly technical and competitive industry, has massive consequences for the whole AI surge. In typical fashion, Huang made light of it.
“We put a little bit of money in and a lot of money comes back. Is that finance talk?” he said. “I’m not taking any risks.”
The day’s most read story in tech and entertainment:

The debate about the risks of artificial intelligence development raged from Silicon Valley to Washington Tuesday after a researcher at Google DeepMind became the latest staffer to voice fears about the direction of the technology. “I earnestly believe that AI has the potential to kill us all,” Bilal Chughtai wrote in a post on social media.

items.title: Trump Officials Target Harvard, Stanford, Yale in Effort to Stop DEI Practices
body: The Trump administration is revitalizing its moribund college pressure campaign with an aggressive turn toward rooting out campus diversity programs.

Pivoting away from the antisemitism probes that yielded massive cash settlements early in President Donald Trump’s term, the Justice Department has launched a sweeping new effort against more than 100 elite universities. The goal is to root out race-based admission and hiring practices, reduce foreign influence on campus, and permanently rewire how federal funding flows to top schools. Officials hope the push will reinvigorate an initiative that became mired in lawsuits and political setbacks despite early concessions from some universities.

Premier medical schools are squarely in the crosshairs. Their low acceptance rates and heavy reliance on federal research dollars make them highly vulnerable targets. But the DOJ is also revving up new investigations into international donors, looking to both reduce the proportion of global students studying at US colleges and other nations’ ability to shape research and curriculum.

The offensive is already roiling campuses, paralyzing critical research and leaving visiting students in legal limbo. Recent DOJ probes include race-based admissions at Yale University’s medical school and Chinese student scholarships at Harvard University, with Stanford University potentially next. The agency has also recently branched into top-ranked law schools at Duke University and the University of California Berkeley.
Administration officials argue the brute-force approach is the only way to bring defiant campuses to heel.

“It’s a hostage situation,” said Harmeet Dhillon, the Justice Department’s civil rights chief, in an interview with Bloomberg. “Faculty are like petulant children. They view it as a jihad to protect their turf.”
Still, it’s not clear the administration chose this new battlefield as much as retreated to it.

After notching several high-profile deals with top colleges like Columbia University and Northwestern University, the White House’s war on higher ed seemed to reach a stalemate last fall. Talks with Harvard University and the University of California stalled after the administration lost a series of court battles. Other attempts to goad institutions into broad policy changes, like offering priority treatment for research funding, fell flat.

In came Dhillon, with a far more combative strategy and a wider range of targets. She had helped guide the settlement talks over alleged antisemitism, but after taking the reins from White House policy advisors late last year she turned her agency’s focus from litigating a handful of campus protests to enacting a far-reaching enforcement campaign for her stringent vision of school civil rights law.
“There's only a subset of institutions that have the anti-Semitism problem,” she said. “Almost every institution of higher learning in the United States has the DEI problem.”

Schools seen as protecting racial diversity initiatives in defiance of the Supreme Court’s 2023 affirmative action ban drew immediate attention. So too did those with low acceptance rates and a high proportion of international students.
“American students are being shut out of opportunities that are being given to foreign students who can pay more money,” Dhillon said. “That’s certainly the case at Harvard and Columbia.”

Federal agencies are laying the groundwork to radically alter their relationship with universities. The administration is overhauling standard practices around research funding, financial aid, and student visas, threatening to reroute money away from elite traditional breadwinners toward schools that demonstrate willingness, or eagerness, to comply with their demands. The federal government is one of the primary sources of funding for universities, providing $121 billion in student aid and $65 billion in research grants across the sector in fiscal year 2024.

In some cases, Dhillon’s brash approach has generated controversy and questions about its efficacy. Some officials in the administration blame her, in part, for the dissolution last fall of a nearly final settlement deal with Harvard, according to a person familiar with the matter who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

But the Justice Department appears less eager to declare one-off political victories, even against Harvard. The government is still engaging in settlement talks, but officials say they’re not as amenable to splashy payouts that would allow universities to continue operating in a similar manner. Instead, they’re pursuing agreements that enshrine lasting changes to school policies and rewriting the rules around coveted research grants.

The administration is also tearing up the system undergirding all federal support for higher ed, unveiling a broad new plan that would require university accreditors to remove standards asking colleges to “provide any preferences on the basis of race.” Under the new rules, the accreditors would also examine intellectual diversity among faculty and consider students’ post-graduate earnings, which critics have said could disfavor liberal arts colleges in particular.

Ken Marcus, who led the Education Department’s civil rights office during Trump’s first term, described the new enforcement strategy as “the approach of an administration that sees the problems on campuses not as isolated managerial issues, but as part of a more systemic problem.”

Dhillon, in sometimes polarizing language, said the effort has made college leaders more pliant as they scramble to head off public showdowns that threaten billions of dollars in federal funding. More than a dozen have met with her in person, she said, many traveling to her office in Washington, D.C., to entreat the administration to ease off.

“I have universities come to me proactively and say, ‘don’t sue us, here’s our homework, here’s our lawyer, we’re happy to give you whatever you want,’” she said. “They’re opening their books. They’re opening their kimonos.”
Sometimes that’s enough to appease administration officials; Dhillon said most campus investigations are resolved quickly and privately.

Others escalate, like at the College of William & Mary, where last month the DOJ launched a probe into several scholarship programs; or at Yale University, where the agency’s finding of admissions discrimination forced campus leaders into talks that sparked backlash from students and faculty.
The consequences for refusing to comply, or at least engage, could be devastating. Even the wealthiest universities are already feeling the pinch.

The Massachusetts Institute of Technology reported a 20% drop in federal research funding this year; Harvard’s is reportedly down 18%. Johns Hopkins University, historically the top federal grant recipient, has seen a 45% plunge.

Dhillon said some of that money may flow toward public universities more willing to abide by the government’s demands. She said a few, like Arizona State University and the University of North Carolina, had reached out to assure her they were dismantling DEI programs. Federal research funding at UNC’s Chapel Hill campus dipped just 2.5% in 2026 from 2025.
“Those institutions raised their hand and said, hey, if Harvard doesn’t want to cooperate, we’ll be more than happy to take their funding and their researchers,” she said.
The point, Dhillon said, is to make colleges tread lightly.
“I view it as kind of like speeding tickets,” she said. “If no one is ever checking people’s speed, then there will be more speeding.”
The impact of the recent broadside is already being felt across campuses, from the Ivies to small liberal arts schools and public research powerhouses.

Fear of a DOJ probe is prompting some schools to do away with scholarships intended for minority groups or eliminate campus support services for identity-based student communities. And as Dhillon threatens to ramp up the agency’s investigations into foreign influence, colleges are cutting ties with  international donors and research partners; the University of North Carolina ended its relationship with Fudan University in China last month “out of an abundance of caution.”

If the Trump administration succeeds in establishing political prerequisites for future federal research funding, it could result in a tectonic shift in the business of higher education, destabilizing universities that serve as economic engines and sending struggling colleges off a financial cliff. Further research cuts could also undermine initiatives to improve public health, mitigate the effects of climate change or boost US economic innovation.

Critics — including former Justice Department officials — say the crackdown on diversity efforts comes at the expense of genuine civil rights protections. They worry students have lost their primary means of redress for harassment and discrimination in the classroom, a role the agency has played since the Supreme Court’s 1954 integration order in Brown v. Board of Education.

Shaheena Simons, who led the agency’s education section until she resigned last April, said her former team “stopped investigating and talking about discrimination against Black students and students of color.” Instead, she said, the order came from on high to prioritize President Trump’s executive orders, like those declaring war on DEI or promising retribution for antisemitic student protests.
“That’s a real departure, even from the first Trump administration,” she said.

Even as the government’s crackdown is reshaping some campuses, other universities are resisting. Harvard has refused some of the administration’s more onerous demands, buoyed by legal victories and a more than $55 billion endowment, the largest of any US college.

Last August, a settlement with Harvard appeared imminent, which would have required the university to invest half a billion dollars in workforce training. Not long after Dhillon took on a more leading role, the deal fell apart acrimoniously. Since then Harvard has won multiple court cases, including one pushing back on the accusations of antisemitism that served as the catalyst for the entire conflict; the administration has since appealed that decision.
Some in the administration blame her aggressive, uncompromising approach for the impasse, according to a person familiar with the talks.

Dhillon faulted constituencies within Harvard for stymying her agency’s efforts, particularly faculty and lawyers, who “have a perverse incentive sometimes when they're in litigation not to want to settle a case.”

Despite setbacks, she said talks have continued and “there is a willingness to move on.” But she said the administration would only settle on its own terms — and the White House had plenty more leverage to use.

“The idea that they’re going to ultimately win a war of attrition, where they get to continue to be funded by the federal government to the tune of billions of dollars without consequence, is actually silly,” she said. “At some point, their runway is going to run out.”

Dhillon’s multi-front war on universities has also strained the federal civil rights bureaucracy. Her division’s staff of seasoned attorneys dwindled from roughly 400 to just over 100 within months of her confirmation. And critics say she has largely eschewed her division’s traditional role as a backstop against discrimination toward minorities in favor of action against diversity programs.

“The administration publicly shut down some desegregation cases,” said Laura Tayloe, a former DOJ lawyer focusing on education who resigned last summer. “The switch to admissions cases was a double shift.”

Tayloe said that by the time she left the education opportunities section, the 45-person team had dwindled to less than five employees. Most left voluntarily, an exodus that some former staffers say was driven by Dhillon’s agenda.
Ejaz Baluch, a lawyer who formerly worked in the DOJ’s employment discrimination section, doesn’t think the agency’s methods will hold up should colleges refuse to settle and counter-sue instead.
“It’s almost offensive how rudimentary their current approach is,” he said.

Dhillon described the departures as a natural result of her shakeup, but acknowledged the shortage had been a challenge. She’s undertaken mass hiring in a bid to reinforce the ranks, swearing in more than 100 attorneys in July alone. Still, there are more challenges on the horizon, with the Justice Department preparing to take on the duties of the civil rights office at the Education Department, which Trump has promised to dismantle.

The Justice Department says that even with limited resources, the push has yielded results. During the investigation into Duke’s law school, Dhillon said her staff found admissions officers were using essay responses as a “workaround” to boost diversity and tracking applicants’ identities in spreadsheets.
A spokesperson for Duke said the school was “committed to complying with the law and will continue to do so in a manner that is consistent with our academic mission.”

If defending these policies was what Dhillon called a “jihad” for some faculty, dismantling them has also been a lifelong crusade for her. A product of elite higher education herself, Dhillon has been a passionate opponent of affirmative action since her days as an undergraduate at Dartmouth College.
“The kids who were getting admitted under these programs were kids from Park Avenue, who are definitely more privileged than me, an immigrant from the Deep South,” she said.
“Now,” she continued, “it's going to be different.”

items.title: US and China trade truce and tariffs
body: The US and China are eyeing tariff cuts on goods including American energy and agricultural products ahead of the leaders’ summit next week.

The moves are expected to be carried out under an earlier plan for reciprocal tariff reductions on roughly $30 billion in trade, with most-favored-nation rates applied to some items from China. Next week’s meetings are also likely to result in an agreement to cut duties on Chinese inputs for manufacturers, Bloomberg News is reporting Wednesday.
Fill Story: US-China Discuss Cutting Some Tariffs as Leaders Prepare to Meet

That all lines up with comments earlier this month from US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, who told Fox News this month that he expected to see “announcements on agriculture and non-tariff barriers related to agriculture” during Xi Jinping’s visit.
To negotiate a the framework for any agreement for the two leaders to announce, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he’s planning to meet this weekend with his Chinese counterpart, He Lifeng.

Extending the nearly year-old trade truce between the world’s largest economies would remove a potential headwind for a world economy already facing several. Companies, consumers and governments are grappling with wars in Iran and Ukraine, elevated oil prices and rekindling inflation concerns that are pushing up global borrowing costs.
Read More: US 10-Year Yield Rises to Highest Since 2007 as Fed Looms
The World Trade Organization, holding a public symposium this week in Geneva, has called this the most consequential juncture for international commerce in the past 80 years.
Oil and AI
But expectations for President Donald Trump’s talks with Xi in Washington remain tempered by China’s relations with Iran and Russia, as well as competition in artificial intelligence.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who took a phone call from Trump during a public appearance earlier this week, is slated to attend Trump’s state dinner with Chinese leader Xi Jinping, Bloomberg reported this week.

While Trump and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei agree on the need to prevent China from catching the US in AI development, doing that remains difficult in practice. Plus, fears of AI’s superhuman potential prompted senior Trump administration officials to meet Tuesday with Anthropic’s top Washington executive to discuss the safety risks.

Meanwhile, the cost of shipping US crude to Asia has surged to a fresh record as buyers are desperate to secure energy shipments amid escalating disruptions to supplies in the Middle East. China’s gasoline and diesel inventories are plunging, raising the chance the government may move to limit fuel exports again.
More on US-China Ties:
—Brendan Murray in London

In this Talking Transports podcast, Amazon Supply Chain Services Head Peter Larsen discusses how ASCS is expanding across ocean and air freight, trucking, intermodal, fulfillment and parcel. Larsen says parcel is “cooking with gas,” while international markets offer significant growth potential. Listen to this episode also on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

Made in Japan | Japan’s export growth slowed a tad in August while remaining at an elevated pace, with shipments of semiconductors and chip manufacturing equipment surging. The value of exports rose 19.3% from a year earlier, as imports gained 28%. By destination, shipments to the US increased 25%, while those to China advanced 21% and European exports gained 11%.

items.title: US Mortgage Rates Rise to 6.97%, Highest In More Than a Year
body: US mortgage rates last week climbed to the highest level in more than a year, marking the latest setback for an already sluggish housing market.

The contract rate on a 30-year mortgage rose 12 basis points to 6.97% in the week ended Sept. 11, according to Mortgage Bankers Association data released Wednesday. That was the highest since May 2025.

Rates had dipped to their lowest level since 2022 in February, just before the start of the Iran war. Since then, they’ve moved significantly higher, in part because rising energy prices are stoking inflation concerns.

Escalating borrowing costs have tamped down demand for loans. The MBA purchase index, a measure of loan applications, edged down 0.8% from the prior week. The group’s refinance index fell 8.8% to its lowest level since May 2025.
On Wednesday, the Federal Reserve is expected to raise interest rates for the first time since 2023 in an effort to tamp down inflation.

The Fed’s decision won’t directly impact mortgage rates but could reverberate across bond markets. Mortgage rates closely track the 10-year US Treasury yield, which climbed this week to the highest level in almost two decades.

The MBA survey, which has been conducted weekly since 1990, uses responses from mortgage bankers, commercial banks and thrifts. The data cover more than 75% of all retail residential mortgage applications in the US.

items.title: Nobel Laureate Michael Kremer Picked as World Bank Top Economist
body: The World Bank Group said that Nobel laureate Michael Kremer will serve as its new chief economist starting Oct. 1, heading research for the institution, according to a statement Wednesday.

Kremer, who holds a Ph.D from Harvard University, was awarded the 2019 Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences jointly with Abhijit Banerjee and Esther Duflo “for their experimental approach to alleviating global poverty,” and his current research focuses on topics such as education, healthcare and access to clean water.

“Michael has spent his career not just identifying what works in development, but proving it at scale, and that is exactly the kind of thinking we need,” World Bank President Ajay Banga said in an emailed statement.

Kremer, a University of Chicago professor and director of its Development Innovation Lab, will succeed Indermit Gill. He was also a professor at Harvard, and a research associate with the National Bureau of Economic Research.

“The challenges ahead are enormous, including creating jobs at scale, unlocking the private capital needed to fund development, and ensuring people have the health, education, and other services they need to thrive,” Kremer said.

Under Banga, the World Bank has been promoting job creation and seeking out partners in the private sector, at a time when bilateral lending and grants to developing nation and grants have dropped. Ending “extreme poverty” is one of the bank’s top goals, and it provided more than $118 billion of financing across loans, grants and guarantees in fiscal 2025.
The International Monetary Fund, another key Washington-based lender, recently named former Bank of England policymaker Silvana Tenreyro as its chief economist.

items.title: California's Electric Utilities Are Becoming Uninvestable
body: Climate change has lengthened California’s wildfire season by several months. The state’s wildfire politics season, meanwhile, has become perpetual. Sacramento just botched another opportunity to bring it to an orderly close, making a chaotic outcome for the state’s power grid and how the costs of wildfire damage are spread more likely.

California’s utilities are held liable for wildfires caused by grid-equipment regardless of negligence, due to the state’s especially strict interpretation of the legal concept of “inverse condemnation.”  This allows victims there, or their insurance providers, to sue the utilities to recover costs and damages, which then flow to either shareholders through a loss of profits or ratepayers via higher bills.

The constitutional quirk flew under the radar until about a decade ago, since regulators routinely allowed utilities to recover relatively small wildfire-related costs through bills. It snowballed into a crisis as the extent, and costs, of California’s wildfires exploded, eventually leading to PG&E’s bankruptcy in 2019 in the face of enormous claims and penalties.

California hurriedly created a Wildfire Fund in response, essentially an insurance pool to reassure financiers that the state’s utilities were still investable and creditworthy (PG&E reemerged from chapter 11 in 2020). Then just one set of wildfires, in Los Angeles in early 2025, showed that the fund wasn’t big enough.

Governor Gavin Newsom led an effort this summer to essentially curb the utilities’ open-ended wildfire liability, in large part by blocking insurers from suing utilities to recoup their payouts to victims, a process called subrogation. Insurance companies were understandably nonplussed and pushed back, successfully. State Senate Bill 492 had much of Newsom’s agenda stripped out — and then even that amended version didn’t get voted on. On news of the amendments, shares of two big Californian utilities, PG&E Corp. and Edison International,PG&E is the parent of regulated utility Pacific Gas and Electric Co., while Edison is the parent of Southern California Edison. A third investor-owned utility holding company, Sempra, owns San Diego Gas and Electric, but its more diversified portfolio shields it from California-related risk to a greater degree.plunged.

It is not easy to argue, as Newsom did, that the utilities need a break. These are large corporations that have presided over huge increases in power bills; California’s residential tariffs are now almost double the national average. Plus, these companies are linked to some of the worst disasters in recent memory. In 2020, PG&E pleaded guilty to 84 counts of involuntary manslaughter arising from the Camp Fire of 2018.

Yet California needs investment in its power grid: To meet growth, to achieve ambitious climate goals and to attract business. While some may cheer the drop in utilities’ share prices as karma, it isn’t just investors who pay.

The whole point of regulated utilities is that their low risk and high dividends attract long-term shareholders at a low cost of capital to fund the grid. When that balance is disrupted, households must foot more of the bill or needed investments languish. That’s the direction California is headed in when PG&E and Edison are rollercoasters. The current set-up means an investor could see their stock wiped out by a wildfire, whether it resulted from corner-cutting by the utility — where a loss would be justified — or just a high wind launching a dry branch into a power line.

Unless utilities are released from “the obligation to act like insurers with uncapped liability,” it is hard to see a solution, says  Michael Wara, Director of the Climate and Energy Policy Program at the Stanford Woods Institute for the Environment and co-author of  a recent study on the topic. Besides the impact on capital costs, Wara points out the regressive nature of funneling wildfire liabilities through bills, since people living in, say, California’s Central Valley have little choice but to run their power-hungry air conditioners full blast, effectively subsidizing homes in higher-risk areas. It also acts as a tax on electricity, blunting efforts to address climate change.

But California’s insurance market has not weathered the wildfires well, either. State regulation of insurance premiums under Proposition 103 effectively prevents them rising to levels commensurate with risk, pushing major providers to either pause or otherwise restrict new policies there. The number of homeowners resorting to the state-run FAIR program has surged. Closing off subrogation would likely cause more insurers to curb business there.

Controls on the price of insurance have also encouraged construction in fire-prone areas without incentivizing home-hardening. On balance, an insurance premium provides a more useful signal to managing that risk than inflated charges buried in the cost of electricity.

Transitioning more of the burden toward insurance premiums would involve a shock for homeowners that the state would need to manage with temporary support, Lauren Teixeira, senior analyst at the Breakthrough Institute, argues in a recent report. She also argues for a state catastrophe reinsurance fund to underpin the insurance industry and even modifying the interpretation of inverse condemnation to protect utilities when they aren’t at fault.

Rex Frazier, president of the Personal Insurance Federation of California, is no fan of shifting liabilities to the industry he represents. But he acknowledges that the state needs investable utilities and suggests that draws on the state Wildfire Fund be capped at a certain level, beyond which they are funded by a temporary increase in the sales tax.

Good luck with all that, one might respond. But such suggestions, different as they are, reflect the same goal of trying to make electricity affordable in California, while tying incentives around wildfires more closely to homeowners’ decisions. They also recognize that the ballooning impacts of climate change are a statewide threat, not just localized misfortunes.

The message from those yo-yoing share prices is that unlike California’s residents, insurance providers, power companies and politicians, the investors and creditors funding the grid can easily walk away.

items.title: AI Slowdown Calls Collide With Stock Market's AI Bets
body: Welcome to Bloomberg’s AI Today newsletter. Every weekday we’ll break down artificial intelligence’s threats and opportunities for businesses, workers, finance and economies. Sign up now if you’re not already on the list.

Not so fast.Speed is at the heart of this week’s convulsions about AI, in which industry leaders endorsed the idea of slowing down development to prevent catastrophic dangers to humanity. Following unauthorized hacks by models and whistleblower warnings, it’s become clear that the rapid pace of artificial intelligence has sometimes outstripped our ability to control it.

For finance and investing executives, it has the makings of a particularly pointed balancing act. On Tuesday, ANZ Group Holdings CEO Nuno Matos warned that AI could be destabilizing to society and declined to rule out large-scale job cuts at the bank as it integrates AI. “It’s creating risks at a much higher pace than what their own builders and developers were thinking,” he said.

That sharpening sense of the risks is solidifying as the benefits from the technology become more tangible across the industry. The same day Matos took the stage in Sydney, Blackstone’s chief financial officer Michael Chae said the money that Blackstone put into AI will begin to show up in earnings as strong performance generates growth in fees.

That makes widespread support for a marked slowdown seem far-fetched for now. And calls for a slowdown will do nothing to stop big tech companies from raising and spending more, say fixed-income specialists at AllianceBernstein. They added that hyperscalers’ fundraising plans operate on 10-year-plus tenors. So, they argue, these plans won’t be disrupted by short-term headlines calling for slower AI development.

On today’s Big Take podcast, Sarah Holder and Bloomberg tech editor Sarah Frier break down the motivations behind AI leaders’ calls to slow the development of so-called frontier models. Listen wherever you get your podcasts.
The following was produced with the assistance of Bloomberg Automation.

The US faces significant challenges in preventing China from becoming an AI superpower, with Anthropic’s Dario Amodei urging policymakers to restrict advanced chip sales, crack down on smuggling, and prevent unauthorized AI distillation by authoritarian countries. While President Trump has maintained some export controls, his administration has been open to selling China certain Nvidia chips and has avoided more aggressive measures such as sanctions or entity-list designations against Chinese companies engaged in AI distillation.

OpenAI is collaborating with rivals Anthropic and Google DeepMind on AI safety measures, with the effort having been underway for several weeks, according to OpenAI’s global policy chief Chris Lehane. Lehane stated that no antitrust waiver is needed for the three companies to coordinate on safety. Meanwhile, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg said artificial intelligence labs should rely on independent evaluators and advisers to ensure that models are safe.

TSMC Co-Chief Operating Officer Y.J. Mii compared AI to a “three-year-old superman,” describing it as powerful but lacking the judgment to distinguish right from wrong. Mii said the chipmaker takes a cautious approach to AI, particularly regarding sensitive research and development data, citing risks of leaks if employees mishandle the technology.

OpenAI is in early talks with investors about a new funding round that would value the company at more than $1.2 trillion, ahead of a planned IPO that CEO Sam Altman has confirmed will not occur this year. The additional capital could push the IPO back by one or two quarters and support further mergers and acquisitions, following recent acquisitions including Jony Ive’s AI device startup io and developer tools startup Astral. If completed, the round would surpass rival Anthropic’s $965 billion valuation set during its May fundraise.

Carlyle Group’s head of global research and investment strategy Jason Thomas has warned that AI project financing echoes the pre-crisis mortgage model of 2005–2007, where lenders relied on sponsor credit quality rather than evaluating underlying project risk. Thomas cautioned that as liabilities escalate and revenue outcomes for AI data centers become more uncertain, the financial system could face similar vulnerabilities.

Wells Fargo strategist Ohsung Kwon has cut his S&P 500 year-end target to 7,700 from 7,950, citing mounting risks in the technology sector as AI investment concerns grow. Kwon downgraded tech to equal-weight from overweight, warning that active data center moratoriums rose 175% nationally over the past three months and that a likely Democratic election sweep could bring increased AI regulation. A clash between the Trump administration and AI leaders, including Anthropic and OpenAI, is further fueling uncertainty.

FTSE Russell, the index arm of the London Stock Exchange Group, is fielding growing client inquiries over whether AI-driven emissions from hyperscalers will trigger automatic cuts to sustainable index weightings, as some $330 billion in passive investments track its sustainable indexes. The index provider says it is evaluating technology companies’ AI-related sustainability risks on a case-by-case basis and will increasingly adjust weightings accordingly, reflecting broader investor anxiety that reducing Big Tech exposure could come at a significant financial cost.

AllianceBernstein fixed-income specialists argue that calls to slow AI development won’t derail hyperscaler fundraising or capital spending, noting that financing plans operate on 10-year-plus tenors and won’t be disrupted by short-term headlines. The firm still expects top AI hyperscalers to increase capital expenditures in the near term, forecasting more than $1 trillion in spending next year, though AB warns that AI-led growth will eventually slow and create a drag on overall US economic expansion.

Japanese manufacturer Minebea Mitsumi is pausing M&A activity to capitalize on surging AI hardware demand as the company shifts focus to scaling output of ball bearings, motors, and actuators for data centers and humanoid robots. The Nintendo supplier is fielding ballooning orders for components used in AI server fans and humanoid joints, while Nvidia’s next-generation Vera Rubin platform is expected to drive demand for an even broader range of Minebea Mitsumi parts, including stepping motors originally designed to feed paper in fax machines that can now regulate liquid flow in AI server cooling systems.

A US Census Bureau study found that new graduates in AI-exposed majors saw a 5-percentage-point drop in employment and a 13% earnings decline following ChatGPT’s November 2022 debut — a hit the authors compare in magnitude to graduating into a large recession. Computer science and software-related fields dominated the most-affected group, with many graduates forced into lower-paying roles in retail and restaurants, raising concerns that AI displacement could shape career trajectories for years.

Meta Platforms plans to deploy its new in-house AI chip (code-named Arke) in data centers during the first half of next year, with a follow-on chip called Astrid set to enter data centers by end of 2027. The chips, developed in partnership with Broadcom on design and TSMC on manufacturing, are intended to reduce Meta’s reliance on Nvidia processors while delivering improved performance per watt and per dollar.

The upcoming Sept. 24 White House summit between President Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping represents a missed opportunity to establish US-China cooperation on AI safety, writes columnist Dave Lee. Trump dismissed calls for AI regulation on Truth Social, calling them a “SICK conspiracy” benefiting China and claiming the only necessary guardrail is a “strong and smart president.” The author contends that meaningful AI risk mitigation requires global-scale cooperation, and Trump’s posturing undermines the potential for productive dialogue.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called for AI companies to “pace the frontier” of cutting-edge research, drawing public agreement from OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Elon Musk. However, writes columnist Parmy Olson, a genuine slowdown in AI development is unlikely, as Anthropic is pressing ahead with a Nasdaq IPO that could value the company at $2 trillion. Amodei’s language suggests managing the pace of AI development rather than halting it, even as the company’s own researchers warned of existential risks.

Large language models may be inadvertently reducing political polarization by delivering more uniform information to users, reversing a trend driven by media fragmentation since the 1990s. Political polarization intensified as broadcasting gave way to a fragmented media landscape, allowing audiences to self-select into ideologically distinct information bubbles. While AI’s homogenizing effect on information consumption could narrow political divides, the outcome remains uncertain.

items.title: UK Workers Hide AI Use From Their Bosses, Deloitte Survey Finds
body: Almost one in ten UK workers have used an AI tool that their employer has banned or would disapprove of, according to a survey by Deloitte that highlights the growing tension between employees and their bosses over using the technology.

The survey found that 63% of workers have used AI tools at work, suggesting that many are keen to use AI to improve their work or speed up mundane tasks. The same proportion of the 25,000 respondents worried their manager may think AI can do their job.
The results suggest workers are eager to embrace AI, but feel their employers are constraining access or may use adoption as a pretext to cut jobs or suppress pay.

Workers are thinking “this could increase my profitability or this could diminish my worth” at the same time, said Paul Lee, who ran the survey. He says this contributes to a “stigma” around AI in the workplace.

The figures reinforce evidence that unauthorized AI use is widespread at work. Data security firm Cyberhaven, which tracks data movements across hundreds of companies, found that a third of employees accessed AI through personal accounts, and almost 40% of AI interactions involved sensitive data. A report from Microsoft in October put the unauthorized AI figure at 71%.

Last week the UK National Cyber Security Centre warned about the hidden risks of “shadow AI”, where employees use AI outside an organization’s approved systems, including the exposure of sensitive information, and losing track of decision-making. David Chismon of the NCSC said it’s “widespread,” adding: “IT security teams should not assume they are seeing the full picture.”

“Organizations can’t hope to block connections to all possible AI tools, so they need to develop a positive cyber security culture with open dialogue about the tools staff might wish to use and to set clear guardrails around what secure use of AI looks like,” Chismon said.

Using unauthorized IT tools pre-dates AI, according to James Longster, a partner specializing in technology at law firm Travers Smith, who likened the current trend to people with USB sticks and personal cloud storage.

“The problem for companies is that when you’re using an unauthorized AI system, that’s nearly always going to be the kind of commercially consumer version of that AI, which will ingest the data and use it for training,” Longster said. “An employee might be uploading the crown jewels into a commercially available AI.”
Ailie Murray, a partner specializing in employment at Travers Smith, said businesses are increasingly concerned about unauthorized AI use but it’s “early days.”

Gloucestershire Police has dismissed a member of staff for using AI against the force’s rules, and circumventing blocked sites by using personal accounts. Separately, the Independent Office for Police Conduct is investigating an officer for alleged gross misconduct over their AI use. The cases were first reported by the Financial Times.

Another case is being heard in an employment tribunal where an employer said it dismissed an employee for his reliance on AI-generated writing, but they argue they were dismissed for raising concerns about the company’s handling of data.

“One of the issues is that employers don’t necessarily have the evidence if employees are using, for example, their own personal ChatGPT on their mobiles,” Murray said. She added there’s also a gray area over whether they’re using that to bolster their own general knowledge or to complete work tasks.

A more immediate concern is that employees are taking AI tools into their own hands because employers aren’t keeping pace. Most respondents in the Deloitte survey said their company leaders have a poor or non-existent understanding of AI, while half of AI users said they received no formal guidance or training.

That echoes an earlier report by Accenture, which found that while employees have adopted AI quickly for minor tasks, company-level change is moving more slowly, with businesses yet to change their systems and workflows around the tech.

There’s nascent evidence that AI is lifting Britain out of its economic slump, with the Office for National Statistics citing AI as a major driver of the country’s annualized growth rate tracking at 2.4%. But to unlock the full benefits of AI at work, companies may need to catch up with their employees.
