items.title: Illycaffe CEO Wants to Make US Its 'Second Domestic Market'
body: Illycaffe SpA wants to turn the US into a “second domestic market,” its chief executive officer said, after the Italian coffee roaster invested in expansion there over the past several years.
“The US is currently worth 20% of our revenues,” CEO Cristina Scocchia said in an interview. “We want to take this contribution to 30%.”

The company has been investing in the US, China and Europe, absorbing some of the cost as coffee prices have surged over the past five years. The strategy, including marketing and communication spending, has worked as demand has increased, Scocchia said in a Bloomberg TV interview.
While coffee consumption is rising in China, “the potential of the moment is not as big as the potential we see in Western Europe, and even more so in the US,” she said.
Scocchia, who joined Illycaffe in 2022, has discussed taking the company public for several years. An IPO remains a “strategic opportunity,” but the economic environment isn’t right, she said.
“We will keep on focusing all of our efforts on growing the business,” she said. “When market conditions really improve, we will evaluate the options, including the IPO.”

In the first half of the year, Illycaffe reported consolidated revenue of €373 million ($430 million), a 19% increase at constant exchange rates. Volumes rose across all key markets, including Italy and North America. In terms of country revenue, the US is already second to Italy.
Illycaffe was founded in 1933 in Trieste by Francesco Illy. In 1935, he created a coffee maker dubbed “Illetta,” considered the blueprint for modern espresso machines.
The privately held company is still controlled by the Illy family, with backing from minority shareholder Rhône Capital. The private equity firm has held about a 20% stake since late 2020.
Scocchia previously served as CEO of L’Oréal Italy and of makeup company Kiko.

items.title: Warsh Under Pressure to Perform With Bond Markets Forcing His Hand
body: In a sign of how quickly the inflationary picture has worsened, attention is shifting from whether the Federal Reserve will raise borrowing costs at its Wednesday meeting to how many hikes will follow.

Wall Street is pricing in a more than 90% chance that the central bank will deliver its first rate increase since 2023 — a level of conviction that has proven right for decades — and priced in another hike by the end of the year.

Pressure will be on Chairman Kevin Warsh to provide guidance on the Fed’s future path during the post-meeting press conference. His failure to offer a clear explanation for the decision to hold rates at July’s meeting sparked a jump in long-term bond yields and a wave of criticism from traders and economists.

Warsh faces a difficult choice between appeasing bond investors looking for more aggressive tightening and keeping President Donald Trump happy. As recently as Sunday, Trump repeated his argument that the US should have the lowest borrowing costs in the world. That’s even as a Treasury selloff drove yields to the highest since 2007.

The Bank of England is also looking down the barrel of rising inflation before its meeting Thursday. UK drivers now face the most expensive diesel and petrol costs since 2022, helping drive inflation to a five-month high in August. While the bank is expected to keep rates unchanged, traders are pricing in four hikes over the next 12 months. Yields on 30-year bonds are the highest since 1998.
It wasn’t that long ago central banks were on an easing path. Now the only question is, how high will they go.
Credit limit: China’s central bank governor signaled a long period of massive credit growth has come to an end.

Days after official data showed loan expansion weakened far more than expected in August, People’s Bank of China Governor Pan Gongsheng said in an article published in the Communist Party’s policy magazine Qiushi that the slowdown in overall financing helps keep the debt levels in the economy stable.

In an unusually lengthy analysis, he cited several reasons for the moderation, including the rise of high-tech sectors that rely less on debt compared with property developers. China’s credit engine once powered industries and markets all over the world.
Aligning paths: Hong Kong’s leader John Lee set out plans to almost double the city’s spending on innovation in coming years as his government seeks to build new growth engines.

The innovation target was announced as Lee unveiled Hong Kong’s first five-year development plan, aimed at aligning the former British colony’s economic policies more closely with those of mainland China. The city will target an increase in spending on innovation to around 3% of GDP after 2030, up from 1.63% in 2024.

Boom scrolling: ByteDance’s Zhang Yiming has become Asia’s richest person for the first time, marking a comeback for the TikTok developer as fortunes linked to AI surge above the billionaires of traditional industry.

Zhang, 43, is worth more than $105 billion after riding out a regulatory tug of war that nearly shut down the social media app in the US. He has eclipsed the wealth of Indian tycoon Gautam Adani, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. His gain marks an eightfold rise in his wealth from the $13 billion recorded in March 2019, when Bloomberg first started tracking his wealth.

Strike a deal: SK Hynix has reached an agreement with its union to pay out half of all profit-sharing bonuses in cash, resolving a dispute that threatened to disrupt production at the world’s second-biggest memory chipmaker.

About 57% of the labor group approved a revised wage and collective bargaining agreement, SK Hynix said. In the latest pact, 50% of profit-sharing bonuses will be paid out in cash and half in company shares, replacing a previously proposed 40-60 cash-stock split.

Clean break: Monaco is among several nations poised to exit a global financial watchdog’s dirty money watchlist next month, marking a change in fortune for the city-state that’s home to the world’s highest concentration of millionaires and billionaires.

The French Riviera principality was placed on the Financial Action Task Force’s “gray list” in June 2024, bringing with it heightened scrutiny over shortcomings in its efforts to tackle illegal money flows. However, officials from the Paris-based monitor have since found significant progress, according to people familiar with the matter.

items.title: Mideast Crude Prices Surge as Traders Scour Market for Barrels
body: The price of Middle Eastern crude loading outside the Persian Gulf rose to the highest since March on growing concerns that supply shortages may be returning to the critical levels seen in the early days of the conflict.

As traders scrambled for replacement barrels following attacks last week that halted a key Saudi pipeline, Oman crude futures advanced to $132.09 a barrel. Their premium to international benchmark Brent jumped to almost $24, also the highest since March.

Demand is high for crude from Oman because the country lies beyond the Strait of Hormuz. Abu Dhabi’s Murban grade, another key benchmark that’s delivered by pipeline to outside the Persian Gulf, is trading near $124 a barrel, a level last seen in the early days of the US-Iran conflict.

While some oil cargoes are still able to transit the strait, the risk of strikes on vessels has been rising. Attacks on shipping in the Red Sea and the Saudi pipeline — the main conduit for the kingdom’s exports since the conflict began — have taken millions more barrels out of the market.

The rising competition between buyers for alternative supplies is pushing crude prices higher, adding to concerns about inflation that have contributed to soaring bond yields and bets on an interest rate hike from the US Federal Reserve.

Saudi Arabia has been forced to close the East-West pipeline — the primary conduit that helped the country keep oil flowing to world markets after the closure of Hormuz — after multiple drone attacks along its route last week. Millions of barrels a day were moving through the pipeline at a time when markets are clamoring for supply.

“The stop of flows through the East-West pipeline — even if it is only temporary — puts the pressure back on the transits through the Strait of Hormuz again,” said Florence Schmit, a senior energy strategist at Rabobank. “That in itself creates a new round of uncertainty given the latest wave of attacks on ships trying to pass through.”

The Mideast benchmarks are showing that stress in the market, despite signs the Saudis are trying to raise supplies through Hormuz. It’s unclear how much those efforts will be able to offset the loss of the pipeline.

items.title: Bond Traders Are Convinced the Fed Will Hike Interest Rates
body: Bond traders are pricing in a Fed interest-rate increase today with a level of conviction that has proven right for decades.

Interest-rate swaps tied to Fed meeting dates show traders see about a 94% chance that Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh and his colleagues will lift the benchmark policy rate by a quarter point from the current 3.5%-3.75% range.
Whenever expectations of a hike have been that high, the Fed has invariably delivered one, according to Bloomberg-compiled data going back to 2008.
“The market is not prepared for a hold or dovish hike,” said Caesar Maasry at investment manager Lunate.
The stakes are high after US bond yields surged to the highest since 2007, with surging oil prices fueling inflation concerns.

What’s the risk if the Fed surprises markets with a hold? Traders say that would drive long-term yields even higher and fuel anxiety that the Fed doesn’t have a grip on inflation. Meanwhile, short-term yields, which closely track Fed policy, would be depressed.
Still, some traders are guarding against a surprise. Demand has surged for options that would pay off if the Fed unexpectedly holds. —Ye Xie and Anya Andrianova, with Edward Bolingbroke
The UK’s strategy to prop up its long-maturity bonds by selling less in the wake of the Liz Truss-era crash is failing to pay off.

Instead, borrowing costs have climbed further since that meltdown in 2022, taking 30-year yields to the highest since 1998. They’re now only a whisker away from 6%, despite the UK shifting sales away from long maturities.

“Unfortunately some of it is muscle memory,” said Fred Repton at Neuberger, when asked about the hangover from the Truss era. “It’s starting to look a little bit precarious frankly, the level of yields and the cost of refinancing that is now continuing to increase.” —Georgia Hall

items.title: Mytheresa Owner Sales Rise as Wealthy Splurge on Luxury Site
body: LuxExperience, owner of the e-commerce site Mytheresa, posted a rise in sales as the multibrand platform’s strategy of catering to the ultra wealthy helped it navigate a tough environment for high-end fashion. Shares soared.

Net sales at LuxExperience B.V. rose 7.6% excluding currency changes in its fiscal fourth quarter, the company said in a statement Wednesday. The growth was led by Mytheresa, its profit engine. LuxExperience said its adjusted EBITDA margin is set to rise between 2% and 3% in the current year from the 2.1% in the three months ended June.
Shares jumped as much as 26% in New York, pulling the stock out of the red for the year and giving LuxExperience a market capitalization of about $1.25 billion.

“We are bucking the trend, we are in sync with where the growth is and we are profiting from the polarization in luxury demand,” LuxExperience Chief Executive Officer Michael Kliger told Bloomberg News in an interview Wednesday. “Because we don’t have a network of stores, we can adjust our marketing efforts to where the growth is, allowing us to be nimble.”

Growth at the platform has come as luxury companies from LVMH Moët Hennessy Louis Vuitton SE to Hermès International SCA and Kering SA have seen their share prices tumble as demand weakened in key markets like China. The US has been a bright spot for the sector, a market where Mytheresa experienced 39% growth last quarter, Kliger said.

LuxExperience was created through the combination of Mytheresa, which offers a highly curated assortment of the latest luxury ready-to-wear, accessories, shoes and jewelry, and Richemont’s Net-a-Porter, Mr Porter and Yoox’s websites, the latter being a discount platform for off-season collections.

The merger of the platforms was completed in April last year with Switzerland’s Richemont SA now owning about 36% of the capital of New York-listed LuxExperience with MYT Holding LLC holding around 48%.

Founded as a boutique in Munich in 1987 before launching its website version two decades ago, Mytheresa now ships high-end women’s and menswear as well as children’s clothes to more than 130 countries. Its website offers labels including Gucci and Bottega Veneta, both part of Kering as well as Dries Van Noten, which belongs to the Spanish beauty group Puig Brands SA.

Mytheresa’s average basket stands at around €875 ($1,010), while the platform’s 100,000 most important customers shop every 28 days with even higher average baskets, Kliger said, adding that LuxExperience continued to see strong momentum in the current quarter. The Row, Richemont’s Alaïa, Kering’s Yves Saint Laurent and Phoebe Philo are particularly popular with Mytheresa customers currently, Kliger added.
The market for multibrand fashion e-commerce platforms has been challenging in recent years following the pandemic boom and the collapse of Farfetch, which ended up selling to Coupang Inc.

Unlike other platforms, “our strategy was always to focus on the big spenders and never chase the aspirational one-time luxury buyers,” Kliger said. Mytheresa organizes brand events for its very important customers in exclusive locations such as Lake Como or Porto Cervo.

items.title: Walmart and Insurer Scan Health to Sell Medicare Advantage Plan
body: Walmart Inc. and nonprofit insurer Scan Health Plan are partnering to sell Medicare Advantage plans to seniors, betting that they can use the big-box retailer’s data to push down the cost of healthcare.

Prices for medical care have risen steeply in recent years, making it more difficult for health insurers to profit by selling Medicare Advantage plans, which are a private version of Medicare. Insurers have been pulling back and closing some plans, forcing millions of people to find other coverage. Scan hopes their plan may help fill some of that gap.

“Partnering with Walmart, in particular around its low prices, can help solve some of the challenges that our patients face around accessing the things that they need to be able to live a healthy life,” said Zachary Myers, Scan’s national general manager.

Walmart already collects data on some shoppers’ spending habits as part of a program that recommends healthier choices. Scan hopes these nudges from the retailer will encourage enrollees in the co-branded Medicare Advantage plan to behave in ways that will lower overall healthcare costs, Myers said.
Walmart didn’t say how many customers have opted in to having their shopping data collected.

The Medicare Advantage plan will be available in two states, Myers said, declining to specify which ones. He also didn’t say how many people are expected to enroll or share more specifics about the plan, which is still pending regulatory clearance, or disclose financial details of the partnership. Walmart also declined to offer details on the plan.
If approved, the plan will be sold in the upcoming annual enrollment period, which starts Oct. 15. Coverage would begin Jan. 1.

This is the second co-branded Medicare Advantage plan with a retailer that Scan has announced in recent months. Scan is also selling a Medicare Advantage plan with Costco Wholesale Corp. A Scan spokesperson said the Costco and Walmart plans have different benefits and will be offered in different states.

items.title: Brazil Central Bank to Cut Interest Rate to 13.75%
body: Brazil’s central bank is widely expected to cut its interest rate by a quarter-point in the final policy decision before a cutthroat presidential election. What happens to borrowing costs after that vote is anyone’s guess.

Policymakers led by Gabriel Galípolo will lower the benchmark Selic to 13.75% on Wednesday, according to all analysts surveyed by Bloomberg. The decision, which will be announced after 6:30 p.m. in Brasilia together with a statement, would bring total easing since March to 1.25 percentage points.

Central bankers are meeting less than a month before voters cast their ballots, with polls showing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in dead heat with Senator Flávio Bolsonaro. The election is adding another layer of uncertainty to the policy outlook, with shifts in investors’ expectations for Brazil’s fiscal trajectory likely to reverberate through local markets. Changes in those perceptions could move the currency and feed into inflation expectations, which remain above the 3% target.

“The central bank won’t react directly to the outcome of the election, but it will react to how markets respond to it,” said Alberto Ramos, chief Latin America economist at Goldman Sachs & Co. LLC. “If we see a sharp selloff in the real, that would raise the probability that the central bank pauses its easing cycle.”

The election is far from the only source of uncertainty. Brazil central bankers will announce their decision hours after the Federal Reserve sets its own rates, with expectations for a hike priced in futures markets. The conflict in Iran remains unresolved, keeping oil prices volatile, while severe weather stemming from El Niño poses risks to food costs.

That complexity leaves policymakers with limited visibility beyond this week’s decision. Central bankers have avoided signaling their next moves, preferring instead to maintain flexibility and to make decisions on a meeting-by-meeting basis as the outlook evolves. They have also stressed that monetary policy needs to remain tight because inflation expectations are still above their goal.

In recent months, Lula has rolled out billions of dollars in stimulus to support demand, complicating policymaker efforts to tame inflation. Those measures have also intensified investor concerns over how his administration would manage public finances and contain government debt if he wins a new term.

Those worries could affect monetary policy through the exchange rate, making the vote particularly important for the real, which is trading near the stronger end of its recent range, said Brendan McKenna, a strategist at Societe Generale.

“Markets see a greater chance of fiscal consolidation under a Bolsonaro administration, while a Lula victory without a clear adjustment plan could trigger a selloff,” McKenna said. A weaker currency fans inflation by making imports more expensive.

After September, the bar for easing gets higher, McKenna sad. He expects policymakers to hold rates through the end of 2026 as the election and its aftermath inject greater volatility into Brazilian markets.

Some Brazil-watchers, like XP Inc. Chief Economist Caio Megale, say the easing cycle has more room to run regardless of the political tensions. He expects two additional quarter-point cuts by the end of 2026, which would lower the Selic to 13.25%.
“If the central bank cut rates in a less favorable environment, there’s no reason to stop now,” he said.

Better-than-expected inflation readings and a weakening economy are providing needed relief for policymakers. On Wednesday, the central bank’s economic activity index, a proxy for gross domestic product fell 0.22% in July from the month prior, slightly worse than -0.2% median estimate from analysts in a Bloomberg survey. From a year ago, activity gained 1.14%.
Brazil created 58,568 formal jobs in July, the lowest monthly figure so far this year, while personal loan default rates jumped to the highest level since 2009.

And while consumer price expectations remain above 3% target, they have not deteriorated further since the last rate decision in August. Economists surveyed by the central bank see inflation at 3.8% in 2028.
“The scenario is moving in the direction the central bank anticipated,” said Leonardo Costa, an economist at ASA.

Diogo Guillen, Itau’s chief economist and a former central bank director, is more cautious. His base case is for policymakers to pause the easing cycle at 13.75%, given the high degree of uncertainty and lingering inflation risks.

But he also sees another possible path: continuing to cut rates in quarter-point steps. That scenario would become more likely if both the exchange rate and inflation forecasts remain around current levels, he wrote in a note.
“The central bank will likely stick to data-dependent language because it wouldn’t make sense to box itself into a corner,” said David Beker, chief Brazil economist at Bank of America Corp.

items.title: Almost £20,000 Wiped Off London Properties, Official Data Show
body: London house prices tumbled at their fastest annual pace in two and a half years, with almost £20,000 ($26,940) wiped off the average valuations in the capital since the peak.

Average prices were down 3.3% in the 12 months through July, the sharpest fall since January 2024, the Office for National Statistics said on Wednesday. Values have fallen in eight of the past 12 months, declining a seasonally adjusted 0.5% in July alone.

The capital’s market continued to massively underperform the rest of the country. London and the south west of England were the only regions see year-on-year price falls. Nationally prices were up 1.4% to an average £273,000.
While London remained the most expensive part of the country, the average house price has dropped £19,000 since the peak in mid-2025 at £550,000.
The capital’s housing market has been hit hard by rising mortgage rates with its buyers disproportionately affected given the amounts borrowed are the largest in the country.

The pressure from borrowing costs is unlikely to let up after traders ramped up bets on the Bank of England hiking interest rates four times over the next 12 months. Moneyfacts data show that the average two-year mortgage rate has climbed to 5.77%, the highest since May. The five-year rate has hit 5.83%, levels not seen since November 2023.

It adds to a slew of factors weighing on London prices in recent years, including a clampdown on landlords and rising taxes. The upper part of the market may also be impacted by the surcharge on properties worth more than £2 million from 2028.

The most expensive areas of London recorded the sharpest price declines over the past year, with homes in Westminster dropping almost 21% and Kensington & Chelsea losing 14%. The ONS figures are derived from actual transactions recorded with the Land Registry.
Robert Wood, chief UK economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, warned national house price growth is likely to slow further over the coming months.

“The typical 2-year fixed-rate 75% LTV mortgage rate will rise to around 5% by the end of the year, if market rate expectations hold at current levels, which, along with higher energy prices, will hit housing demand,” he said.
The ONS also said private rents climbed 3.8% in the year through August to an average of £1,400 per month — the fastest increase this year. In London they rose slightly slower at 3.5%.

items.title: Fed Decision, Inflation, War and AI Feed Into Bond Market's 'Toxic Stew'
body: The market for US Treasury bonds is one of the largest in the world, with as much as $1.2 trillion traded daily. It’s so big, it’s a powerful mirror of the US economy, reflecting risks near and far: inflation, wars, budget deficits, demographic cliffs. Judging from a recent pronounced spike in the yields on some of the most widely tracked US Treasuries, some of those worries are mounting: The 30-year recently hit a two-decade high while the interest rate on the 10-year — the benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and some types of commercial credit — has climbed by more than half a percentage point since May. The upward creep hasn’t sat well with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has committed billions of dollars to bond buybacks in an attempt to drive down rates, an effort many economists and financiers have criticized and one which, at least so far, hasn’t really worked.

The US economy’s vital signs are strong: Unemployment is historically low and the specter of recession has receded, thanks in large part to a  massive spending boom on artificial intelligence. So what’s unsettling the bond market? It’s a mix of things, according to economist Martha Gimbel, executive director of the Budget Lab at Yale University: “They’re all kind of swirling around each other, creating a toxic stew.”

One major ingredient in that unappetizing dish is the federal debt, which in mid-August officially surpassed $40 trillion. What’s especially worrying to that endangered species called the fiscal hawk is that over the past two decades, the US debt pile has been growing at a more rapid clip than the overall economy. Since 2006, gross federal debt has increased almost fivefold, while gross domestic product expanded by less than 2.5 times. “Debt is compounding faster than the economy that has to service it,” wrote Torsten Slok, chief economist at asset manager Apollo Global Management Inc., in a newsletter, going from below 40% of GDP to roughly 100% over that period.

The fault lies with the politicians in Washington (and here both parties are to blame), who have built up a tolerance for ever larger budget deficits. “I am comfortable having deficits in poor economic times or crises,” says Tara Sinclair, head of the economics department at George Washington University. “But we can’t just keep building debt upon debt upon debt upon debt forever.”

President Donald Trump has argued that the US has the capacity to grow its way out of its debt problem. “The way you take care of debt is with growth, and we have tremendous growth. We’ve never had growth like we have right now,” he said in August.

The general view among economists is that politicians shouldn’t be peddling magical cures when the reality is that, sooner or later, Americans will be made to swallow a bitter brew. The US could just print a bunch of money and use that to pay its debts. But the side effects would be painful. The value of the dollar would drop against other currencies, igniting inflation. And it would be anathema to investors. Who wants to buy a 10-year bond from a country where the price of a latte is doubling every month?

There’s a second option: slashing spending to narrow the deficit. That might entail cuts to entitlement programs like Social Security and Medicare and other government services. But as we know from the UK and Greece, a large dose of austerity could deeply damage Americans’ quality of life, slow the economy and hamper the government’s ability to function. It’s also likely to precipitate the ouster of whichever party administered the shock therapy.

At moments when politicians can’t (or won’t) make the tough calls, there is one institution whose job it is to be the grown-up in the room: That’s the Federal Reserve. Jacking up interest rates, hammering the housing market, slowing the economy and doing whatever grisly task is required to bring inflation under control — it’s all in the job description. It’s for this reason that members of the Fed aren’t popularly elected and can’t be easily removed by politicians.

Except right now the Fed’s ability to be the economy’s designated downer is under question. Trump has made it clear he wants the central bank to lower interest rates to juice the economy (which would have the side benefit of lowering US debt-servicing costs), and he has all but ordered  Kevin Warsh, who was sworn in as chairman in May, to comply. Once known as a hawk who favored an aggressive approach to controlling inflation, Warsh got in touch with his dovish side to secure Trump’s nomination. Markets have spent the past few months trying to divine which way he will tilt.

Warsh has made that task more difficult by dialing back the decades-long tradition of transparency and open communication established by his predecessors. “Markets don’t like that,” says Sebastian Mallaby, author of The Man Who Knew: The Life and Times of Alan Greenspan. “They would rather be told what’s going to happen. They would rather have their hands held by the central bank.” Former chairs  Jerome Powell,  Janet Yellen and  Ben Bernanke did a lot of hand-holding in the form of “forward guidance,” telegraphing interest-rate moves in advance to tamp down financial volatility. Warsh’s pledge to take a page from the Greenspan playbook and be more tight-lipped about Fed policy is one of the reasons yields on 10- and 30-year Treasuries have risen. Says Mallaby: “Long-term interest rates go up to compensate investors for the extra risk” that they will be surprised by a Fed move.

Warsh has criticized the Fed for moving too slowly to raise interest rates in the aftermath of the Covid-19 pandemic, allowing inflation to become entrenched. With the war in Iran pushing up fuel prices, he faces his own quandary: Hike now or take a chance that inflation drifts farther away from the central bank’s 2% target.

Yale’s Gimbel says the world’s current fixation on Warsh “is an important reminder of how important the Federal Reserve is in all of this.” Warsh’s words (or lack thereof) move the US bond market, which moves the global bond market. “If you assume the Fed isn’t going to be as reliable, or as effective, as it's been in the past, that’s something you have to start thinking about incorporating into the price of the bond.”

Free-spending politicians and circumspect central bankers aren’t the only ones affecting markets. For ages, US Treasuries have been viewed as best in class among all types of debt — despite trade wars, debt-ceiling battles and other political games of chicken — because the world assumes there’s virtually zero chance a country that can print its own money will resort to defaulting on debt. “ There hasn’t really been other places to go that are the same level of safeness and convenience,” Gimbel says. “What are you going to do, put your money in France?”

But these days, US treasury bonds have a different kind of competition. In the past five years, Alphabet, Amazon.com, Meta Platforms, Microsoft and Oracle, the five biggest spenders on new data centers in the US, have collectively added some $412 billion to their debt obligations, according to Bloomberg calculations. Several of these companies have country-size balance sheets and sterling credit ratings. The upshot is that investors have lots of good choices for supersafe places to put their money, so it stands to reason that Uncle Sam might have to offer a higher return to beat out other bond issuers.

So will US Treasury yields stay higher for longer — driving up the cost of government borrowing along with mortgages and other types of credit — or will they start drifting back down if Warsh proves to be more hawk than dove or if there’s compelling evidence AI can help the economy grow out of its debt problem? The answer is hard to pin down, but GWU’s Sinclair, at least, isn’t worried about investors at home and abroad suddenly losing their appetite for US bonds. “Our central role both in global trade and in the global financial system means everybody in the world is invested in the US not having some kind of major financial crisis. Everybody’s going to try and prevent that.” In other words, the US bond market is now so big and so important to the global economy, it’s become too big to fail. Read next: Are Robots Ruining the Treasury Market?

items.title: Trump's AI Cheerleading Is Becoming a Republican Liability
body: President Donald Trump just doesn’t get AI.
He doesn’t get that Americans are worried about a jobless AI future.

And he doesn’t get that some industry leaders are fearful of super-smart, uncontrollable AI agents posing an existential threat. For Trump and his GOP allies, this is a politically perilous and unsustainable failure to read the room. It will increasingly shape this fall’s elections and campaigns to come. Trump’s tone-deaf, billionaire-buddy approach has given Democrats a chance to cast themselves as the responsive and responsible leaders on AI.

But their work must start now. Clear policy proposals would be great, but election years are where white papers go to die. Acting as AI skeptics and watchdogs is much more legible to the average voter.

On Wednesday, Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders is convening a private, bipartisan meeting with AI industry leaders on the dangers of the technology. He is also set to introduce a bill calling for a pause on the development and deployment of superintelligence until a federal agency is created to monitor such an advance and weigh the dangers to the public. Democrats should make this central to their pitch to voters.

Trump, who has for years been able to shape people’s thinking by sheer repetition, is trying mightily to do the same with AI and data centers, which he believes have gotten a bad rap and simply need a better public relations campaign. He is cynically moving to discredit the AI industry leaders who have called for a slowdown, suggesting that they are doing China’s bidding.

“The robots will not be taking over. The AI will not be taking over the rest of the world. The whole thing is a hoax. Now with that, we have to be a little bit careful. We have to… you know… we have to do things, and we have to do them prudently,” Trump said on a clubby call with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during an industry summit. “If we’re gonna lead, and I have an expression, it’s ‘Whoever wins AI, wins.’ That’s how big it is. It’s a bigger than the internet.”

Trump’s AI boosterism makes sense from his perspective. He has said AI is the “oil of the next 20, 25 years,” bringing to mind the great wealth generated by oil barons. The industry, which Trump has called a “golden goose,” is also powering stock market gains and job growth related to data center construction.

But like his efforts to brand affordability “a hoax” and recast his ballroom as “vital for National Security and Military Operations,” his attempts to change Americans’ minds on AI have opened up a chasm between him and voters.

Americans simply don’t share Trump’s unbridled optimism about AI’s future. An NBC News Decision Desk Poll found that 70% of Americans are more worried about AI than excited about it and some two-thirds say AI comes with high risks for society. Similar shares of Americans are opposed to data centers, including 57% of Republicans. Job loss is the main concern, particularly among younger voters.

Voters also have little faith in Trump’s management of AI. A University of Massachusetts Amherst poll found that 57% of respondents think that Trump has handled AI poorly. Although Trump claimed his administration has “tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies,” he has taken steps to deregulate the AI industry. He terminated former President Joe Biden’s 2023 executive order on safer and more trustworthy usage of the technology, issued an executive order that bars states from regulating it and has used the Department of Justice to target states that try to mandate AI safeguards.

On Thursday at a private fundraiser with Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, former President Barack Obama said that if Democrats win, the party should “put together a framework for a very public conversation,” according to a transcript obtained by the New York Times.

“I would be thinking about the economic impacts in very concrete ways and understanding what does it mean if there’s going to be job displacement,” Obama said. “If it turns out that you’ve got a lot more people who can’t find full-time work because they’ve been rendered redundant, how are we going to respond?”
That’s the very question on the minds of many Americans.

“President Trump said, ‘Whoever wins AI, wins.’ I would say, that’s close, but really, it’s ‘Whoever wins, AI wins.’ It doesn’t matter who builds AI, if the AI does not stay on a leash,” said Nate Soares, co-author of If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies; Why Superhuman AI Would Kill Us in a CNN interview. “And what has got a lot of these researchers worried over the past couple of months is that there have been real instances of AIs breaking out of containment, doing things that they were not instructed to do, showing evidence of goals that the humans did not try to put into the AIs. And a lot of people haven’t noticed that yet.”
Well, Americans are starting to notice. And the party that seizes on their understandable populist dread will win.

items.title: Midterm Elections: Rising US Diesel, Heating Oil Prices Hit Voters in Key States
body: Record-high  diesel prices are coming at the worst possible time for Iowa farmer Kinser Jensen.

He’d held off buying diesel after the cost skyrocketed at the beginning of the Iran war, hoping prices would recede. But harvest is just weeks away, and with it the   heavy fuel demands involved in bringing in the crop. Diesel is only getting more expensive.

“I’m not exactly sure what we’re going to do,” said Jensen, 32, who runs a 3,400-acre corn and soybean farm with his 62 year-old father in northeastern Iowa. “At some point here, I’m just going to have to pull the trigger and buy the fuel.”
Jensen, a 2024  Donald Trump supporter who gravitates toward Republicans, said the high diesel prices are causing him to question how farmer-friendly the Trump administration really has been.

The costs of diesel and home heating oil have surged faster than gasoline in recent months, particularly hammering states that are   critical battlegrounds in November’s midterm congressional elections — just as mail-in ballots arrive.

In Alaska, many remote communities rely on diesel generators for electricity. The climate is harsh,  freight moves over long distances and per-capita usage of diesel and home heating oil is more than four times the national average. In Midwest states like Iowa, Kansas and Nebraska, farm equipment runs on diesel. In Maine and New Hampshire, large numbers of homeowners depend on heating oil to get through cold winters.

Grain Belt farmers are engaged in an energy-intensive race against time and weather, involving heavy combines that crawl across fields cutting, pulling, threshing and cleaning crops; tractors to tow grain carts alongside; and trucks to deliver the harvest to silos and grain elevators. Many homeowners right now are filling heating oil tanks for the first time since spring.

In rural Windsor, Maine, 75-year-old retiree Steve Hoad said he is confronting a choice between putting off repairs to his farmhouse or dipping into his savings because heating oil is costing him an additional $230 a month, based on the increase in prices since the Iran war started.
“It is a significant burden that I have to think about how I will bear,” Hoad said. “There aren’t a lot of options.”

Average retail US diesel prices crossed $6 a gallon for the first time ever last week and kept climbing to $6.27 on Monday, according to the American Automobile Association. As of Monday, they had jumped almost 70% since the US launched the Iran war in February.
Diesel and heating oil prices are tied closely because the two are nearly indistinguishable and produced through almost identical refining processes.

The Iran war has especially hit those fuels because the world relies on Middle Eastern crude oil to feed refineries that produce diesel and gasoline. The Middle East is also a critical exporter of diesel itself, but flows of refined products through the Strait of Hormuz remain sharply curtailed. Taken together with a ban on diesel exports from Russia — the world's second-largest exporter in normal times — global diesel supplies have tightened sharply.
The average retail heating oil price in Maine was $5.39 a gallon as of Sept. 8, more than 40% higher than before the start of the Iran war in February, according to state data.

Maine consumes more heating oil per capita than any other US state because half of all households rely on it as their primary heat source, according to the Maine Department of Energy Resources. New Hampshire, which also has a competitive Senate race, isn’t far behind.

Fuel costs often figure prominently in voters’ perceptions of presidential performance, said Kevin Book, managing director at Clearview Energy Partners, an independent research firm based in Washington.

The financial burden from the current price spike is hardest on lower-income and fixed-income households “that have to pay up this extraordinary premium in cash to heat their homes for the winter,” he added.

“These are the marginal votes that can decide close elections in swing states,” Book said. “High prices might be a reason you stay home” if you’re a Republican, or be motivated to vote if you’re a Democrat.
Democrats are harnessing that discontent.

At a US Senate debate over the weekend on Alaska’s Kodiak Island, home to about 12,000 people and 450 locally owned vessels, Democratic candidate Mary Peltola cited the impact of diesel costs on the fishing industry, which drives nearly the entire local economy and is a key private-sector employer in the state. Diesel not only propels fishing boats but powers their hydraulics and refrigeration.
“Diesel is getting more and more expensive for our fishermen,” Peltola said. “We need someone in DC fighting to lower our costs, not to jack up our costs.”

Former Ohio Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown, who’s challenging Republican Senator Jon Husted in a competitive race, has aired an ad featuring a farmer criticizing Husted’s votes supporting the Iran war and tariffs, citing higher diesel and fertilizer costs.
“At a certain point, it’s not just politics anymore,” the farmer says in the ad. “When you start taking money out of my pocket, it becomes personal.”
Read more:   Democrats See Wider Path to Take Senate as Trump Backlash Grows

The Trump administration blames the record diesel prices on Ukrainian attacks that decimated Russia’s diesel exports, as well as the reduction in US refining capacity under previous Democratic presidents.

Trump said in a social media post on Monday that both Ukraine and Russia have agreed not to attack any energy targets. Ukrainian officials later said they were caught unaware by the announcement and no deal had yet been reached.

But diesel prices would not be at record levels if not for the conflict in the Middle East, said Jason Miller, a supply chain professor at Michigan State University. And after predicting for months that the Iran war would end quickly, Trump has now conceded that the conflict won’t end until after the midterms, leaving oil and gasoline prices elevated through the election.

Margins for making diesel fuel from crude oil were at record highs of near  $115 a barrel as of Tuesday, indicating a severe shortage. The US Energy Information Administration predicted the country's distillate fuel stockpiles — which include diesel and heating oil — would dip below the 100 million barrel mark by the end of September, for the first time since 2003. Meanwhile, stockpiles of the fuels are just above their lowest levels on record on the East Coast.

items.title: Headspace Meditation App Being Acquired by AI Startup Sword for $300 Million
body: Headspace, a popular meditation and mental health support app, is being acquired by Sword Health, an artificial intelligence startup focused on healthcare.

The Headspace acquisition, announced Wednesday, is expected to close by the beginning of the fourth quarter of 2026, the companies said in an interview. The all-cash deal is valued near $300 million, according to a person with knowledge of the matter, who declined to be identified discussing private details of the transaction.

Sword said the deal will lead to an improved Headspace app with more personalization and the ability to more proactively take action on user needs. The acquisition “reinforces” its work in the mental health space and allows it to “meaningfully expand” and improve its platform,” Sword Chief Executive Officer Virgilio Bento said in an interview.
“The stronger we are at delivering access to high-quality mental health, the greater our impact will be on cardiometabolic conditions, women’s health, and physical care,” Bento said.

Headspace, which was founded in 2010, made a name for itself with guided meditations, expert-led courses on topics such as anxiety and sleep-focused audio content known as Sleepcasts. The app has been downloaded more than 100 million times across 200 countries, while over 20,000 businesses offer Headspace to their employees, the companies said.

For its part, Sword allows clinicians to remotely monitor patients during care sessions such as physical therapy via a smartphone camera. The phone can track movement and progress via AI to provide feedback. It also uses AI to be able to predict, prevent and treat pain. Earlier this year, Sword acquired rival Kaia Health, a digital platform to help members manage back and joint pain from home, for $285 million.

Sword, which was valued at $4 billion after its last funding round in June 2025, could file to go public as early as 2028, according to Bento. Sword will likely raise more funding later this year, he added.

items.title: Meta CEO Zuckerberg Leans on Powell McCormick to Clear Path for AI Push
body: At a Meta Platforms Inc. board retreat last December, Chief Executive Officer Mark Zuckerberg asked Dina Powell McCormick to take a walk with him around his sprawling Kauai compound, known as Koolau Ranch.

Zuckerberg told Powell McCormick, a former Trump administration official and Goldman Sachs Group Inc. executive who’d joined the board eight months prior, that the $1.7 trillion company was banking its future on artificial intelligence. To do that, Meta would need to raise a tremendous amount of outside capital. And Zuckerberg would need a right-hand adviser with the robust connections and political capital required to smooth the way with both financial institutions and governments.

“It became clear to me that she could play a bigger role in Meta’s next chapter,” Zuckerberg recalls. He asked her to trade the board seat for a key internal role. Zuckerberg told her it would be the most important job she’d ever have.

A well-connected power player in both Washington and on Wall Street, Powell McCormick has built relationships with a shocking breadth of people including former US Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice, BlackRock Inc. CEO Larry Fink and pop star Katy Perry, and has had plenty of big jobs. But about a week after Zuckerberg’s pitch, she resigned from the board. In January, she became president, vice chairman and co-leader of Meta Compute, its effort to build and monetize the infrastructure fueling the AI revolution.

Nine months in, Powell McCormick’s remit extends far beyond helping to hash out deals for Meta Compute. Interviews with more than a dozen Meta insiders, outside executives and government officials and Powell McCormick herself show she’s an executive trusted by Zuckerberg and his top deputies to tackle the company’s thorniest problems – including countering the backlash to AI and weighing in on major legal and reputational fights, like Meta’s recent settlement of up to $18 billion with state attorneys general over children’s safety on Instagram and Facebook.

Powell McCormick has appeared for Meta at Davos, traveled with President Donald Trump and an entourage of Silicon Valley’s most famous to China and met with King Charles III, freeing Zuckerberg to spend his time in Menlo Park with the engineers and researchers rushing to build Meta’s next generation of models. While Zuckerberg, 42, is the cerebral engineering leader obsessed with improving Meta’s products for the AI race, Powell McCormick, 53, has her pulse on the world outside of Silicon Valley, and can be Meta’s bridge to opportunities and fixer of challenges.

“She is a close, trusted advisor of the whole senior leadership team, but especially of Mark,” said CJ Mahoney, Meta’s chief legal officer. “She’s generally the last person who’s consulted on really important decisions.”

Those decisions are only going to become more high stakes for the company as it makes its biggest technological and capital bet to date. Meta is expecting to spend more than $600 billion on its AI buildout before the end of the decade, and that’s not including the many billions more it’s leveraging from Wall Street.

At the same time, the public has perhaps more reason to be skeptical of Meta and its ambitions than ever, as existential fears about AI and the data centers needed to support it threaten to dominate public conversation. Over the last week alone, intensifying concerns inside some of the top AI companies have pushed the chiefs of OpenAI, Anthropic PBC and SpaceXAI to call for a swift slowdown of its development. Zuckerberg waited to chime in publicly until after other leaders had spoken, and said Meta was already focusing on building safe AI. But the CEO, with more than two decades of high-profile clashes with governments on privacy and safety, doesn’t have a history of winning over public trust easily. That’ll be up to Powell McCormick.

Born in Cairo and raised in Texas, Powell McCormick seemed a fitting pick for Meta’s board when Trump returned to the White House for a second term. The company was seeking to make inroads with the administration and her Washington ties were plentiful. Joel Kaplan, the new chief of global affairs, knew her well from the George W. Bush administration, where she eventually served under Rice. Powell McCormick later became a Goldman Sachs partner, with a talent for working with sovereign clients, and served as a deputy national security adviser in Trump’s first administration. Her husband, former Bridgewater Associates CEO Dave McCormick, became a US senator from Pennsylvania in 2025.

“Frankly, they haven’t had enough conservatives in the tech world,” said Arkansas Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders, who worked with Powell McCormick during Trump’s first administration. “Dina is the right person to be in that role.”

That was one benefit – but Zuckerberg saw a bigger value-add: Powell McCormick had relationships with some of the world’s biggest sources of capital that could help finance Meta’s infrastructure boom.

On a day-to-day basis, she’s helping do the crucial work of laying out Meta’s entire approach to AI infrastructure. It’s not just a question of how much computing power Meta can secure, but how to acquire it at the right cost to the company, and from whom. Powell McCormick co-leads the team that must solve for those issues.

She, along with head of infrastructure Santosh Janardhan and Daniel Gross, who is responsible for mapping out the company’s future compute needs, meet weekly to plan as far as decades into the future with inputs, including the pricing and longevity of chips, that are continually in flux. Beneath Gross sits a trading-desk-like team that monitors component prices, supply shortages and other factors.

“Compute is a very scarce asset,” said Powell McCormick, speaking in an interview on Monday from the company’s headquarters in Menlo Park. Dressed in jeans and a white button-up — a far departure from her prior Washington uniform of suits and coordinated sets — she blended in seamlessly at the tech company.

“It’s an asset we can use, obviously, and an asset we can monetize,” she added, nodding at reporting, first broken by Bloomberg News, about the company’s efforts to potentially stand up a cloud infrastructure business.

Meta has been at the center of two of the biggest benchmark deals in the intensely lucrative and competitive chips and data center space: one in rural Louisiana, where Meta is building one of the largest data centers on the planet, and the other, more recently, in El Paso, Texas.

Powell McCormick, an energetic conversationalist who remembers people’s children’s names and is willing to make introductions, already has turned to her Rolodex to help clinch deals and explore new financing structures for these ambitions. Earlier this spring, she took her Meta Compute co-heads on a Wall Street tour to meet with executives of BlackRock, Blackstone Inc., Brookfield and others. Out of these conversations ultimately emerged discussions for potential financing partners for the El Paso project.

Leveraging her 25-year-relationship with Larry Fink, who said he values the new kind of “connectivity” that Powell McCormick is bringing to the company, Meta and BlackRock reached a deal to build the $14 billion data center together. Powell McCormick, Fink, Meta Chief Financial Officer Susan Li, and BlackRock CFO Martin Small brought their teams together for more than a dozen calls, which ultimately led the financial firm to raise more than $12 billion in debt to fund the facility. BlackRock will hold an 80% interest in the joint venture, while Meta will retain the remaining 20%.

Beyond McCormick’s business relationships in New York’s power circles, she used her sprawling network, political connections and public policy muscle to jockey for buy-in across Texas, getting everyone from high-ranking state officials to small local utilities on board.

Meta used a similar joint-venture structure with partner Blue Owl Capital Inc. to help finance its Louisiana data center, dubbed Hyperion. The setup gives the tech giant control of operations while keeping debt off its balance sheet. Powell McCormick called it a “great model” first set up by CFO Li – and a success she looked to replicate.

Some following Meta’s strategy are not convinced that it will land with the broader public. Sarah Kreps, director of the Tech Policy Institute at Cornell University, said there’s a striking disparity between the might and deep pockets of the tech and banking giants, and the amount they’re reinvesting in the community where they’re planting their AI flag.

“I’m struck by the perception of this arrangement being one of Big Tech and Big Finance coming in with a sophisticated cost and risk sharing, and hand waving toward the local bargain question of who pays for electricity, water, infrastructure, and incentives,” Kreps said, noting the $14 billion venture will dedicate a $500,000 grant to El Paso public schools. It “just looks like a scale mismatch that exacerbates the perception problems that the community programs are meant to fix.”

Kreps’ skepticism gets at a bigger problem: Across the US, Americans are increasingly concerned about AI and the data centers needed to support them, an anxiety that is becoming a defining, bipartisan issue for voters in the looming midterm elections.

About 61% of US adults oppose the construction of new data centers in their area, according to a survey conducted this summer by the Annenberg Public Policy Center at the University of Pennsylvania – and a Reuters/Ipsos survey conducted this spring found that feeling largely transcends party lines. Nearly 40% of American adults see data centers as “mostly bad” for the environment and home energy costs, according to Pew Research Center data from earlier this year, while it found in 2025 that half of Americans are more concerned than excited about AI permeating daily life.
“We are facing incredible headwinds at the federal level, the state level, the local level,” said Lindsay Elin, Meta’s vice president of external affairs, who now leads the community engagement team.

Beyond her job as a dealmaker, Powell McCormick plays an important role in protecting “the investments that we’re making and to ensure that we can continue to build these data centers that we need,” Elin said. Meta’s new president has set up brainstorming sessions focused specially on how to change public sentiment toward data centers, which led to the new company tagline, “The future is for everyone,” and a $1 billion fund to invest in the communities where Meta builds them, Elin said.

Meta, with Powell McCormick’s help, is seeking to give “our allies cover to continue to support data center builds,” Elin said. Should constituents offer more support, she said, city councils wouldn’t feel the need to pass moratoriums.

Meta executives said they see Powell McCormick as an effective communicator – and one who can at times be better at communicating outside of Silicon Valley with the broader public than Zuckerberg. He would prefer to be at Meta digging into its most technical product problems, rather than schmoozing and dealing with public backlash, people familiar with the matter said.

Zuckerberg, ever since hiring Sheryl Sandberg to be his chief operating officer in 2008, has leaned on an executive in a communicator role to do the political part of Meta’s work. As a high-profile woman in Meta’s top ranks, Powell McCormick faces the comparison to Sandberg often. While they both had backgrounds in finance and politics and a flair for mentoring – a subject that Powell McCormick has written a book about – Sandberg was more of an operator, taking a promising startup and developing it into a serious global advertising juggernaut. Powell McCormick is taking an industry titan and smoothing out its rough edges, and facilitating deals, one conversation at a time.
Meta’s partners have become used to working with – and traveling with Trump alongside – Powell McCormick.

“She understands what it takes to build — not just the massive infrastructure financing behind AI factories, but the relationships and the vision,” said Jensen Huang, president and CEO of Nvidia, who spent an hour and a half with Powell McCormick talking about how to strengthen the companies relationship when she assumed the new role.

She has been the driving force behind new company-backed programs aimed at training and securing jobs for skilled trade workers and pouring resources into communities where Meta is expanding its footprint.

By some counts, she has been successful. One of the country’s top electricity providers and Meta’s closest energy partners, NextEra Energy Inc., announced Wednesday it will hire 1,000 people out of Meta’s America’s Workforce Academy – an initiative stood up by Powell McCormick – placing trained technicians like electrical workers, pipe fitters and welders on power generation projects across the US, some involving Meta’s own data centers. Meta is investing $115 million in the academy in its first year, starting in Louisiana, Ohio, Indiana and Texas.

Meta is also looking to bring more locals inside the company. Justin Osofsky, the company’s chief partnerships officer, said he and Powell McCormick are working together to hire people directly in the communities where it’s building data centers. “It’s really important that you have people on the ground that understand the culture, the relationships, and how best you can partner within a state,” he said.

Still, some see the goodwill programs and local hiring as too little too late — inadequate to the task of changing public perception of Meta and the AI industry more broadly. Worries about the long-term impacts of the technology are near boiling over, and data center backlash is poised to become a major issue in the November midterms.

“It’s increasingly difficult to separate sentiment around Meta’s AI strategy from sentiment around the broader AI industry, which continues to show volatility amid questions about the scale, returns on AI investment, and growing concerns about the technology itself,” said Jacob Bourne, a technology analyst at Emarketer focused on AI and emerging technologies.

“I wouldn’t say Meta’s efforts have been ineffective,” he added of the workforce programs, grants and other local investments. “But I haven’t seen evidence that they’ve meaningfully moved broader public sentiment around AI or data centers, where concerns increasingly extend beyond jobs and economic benefits.”
There are also larger questions from investors about the return on investment of Meta’s aggressive AI spending, and how the company will monetize compute.

“Her job is to build out the infrastructure, [Zuckerberg’s] is to figure out how to monetize it all,” said John Belton, a portfolio manager at the investment management firm Gabelli Funds. “Investors are more for focused on that second part.”

Though Meta is still working to win the trust of the communities it’s planting in, as well as its own investors, Powell McCormick has undoubtedly already won the backing of the company’s most senior leadership. She is involved in problems big and small, leading some insiders to question where her job begins and ends.

Others suggest that’s the wrong question altogether: Mahoney, Meta’s top lawyer, likened her current role to that of Brad Smith, the vice chair and president of Microsoft Corp., or even a position more akin to her role on Trump’s National Security Council. She’s a connector, both externally, and internally, bringing together different parts of the company, getting competing power centers to work together and escalating the right problems to Zuckerberg to make sure the company is moving at speed.

That mix of skills is working for Zuckerberg: “She has accomplished an incredible amount in a short time since she joined and we launched Meta Compute,” he said. “I’m learning a lot from her and she’s exactly the kind of leader we need for our next chapter.”

Powell McCormick feels the weight of the moment – and is watching it play out in Menlo Park, in Texas, in Washington, in Louisiana. She believes Zuckerberg’s original pitch to be true: “It will be one of the most important things I’ve ever done,” she said.

As the interview continues, the communications executive seated beside Powell McCormick in Menlo Park receives a message – the Meta president is due at Zuckerberg’s home for dinner with a small group of senior leadership, known, fittingly, as “small group.” As Powell McCormick opines on the importance of baking safety into AI systems, and earning the trust of its users, another ping.
Then a man walks out into the courtyard with a yellow Post-It. Not so discreetly, it communicates that Powell McCormick is needed – and now.

She’s already spent four hours that day in the company of Zuckerberg and his closest advisers, discussing the company’s AI ambitions and Meta’s annual conference, known as Connect, which will take place next week – the latest flurry of events that has her ping-ponging from coast to coast on a weekly basis.
But her presence is wanted again.

items.title: Dirty Politics Dominate in Brazil's Presidential Election
body: Welcome to Balance of Power, bringing you the latest in global politics. If you haven’t yet, sign up     here  .
Rio de Janeiro has drawn countless visitors on the fame of its golden coastline and intoxicating samba.
Its   dirty politics are just as legendary — and helped propel Brazil’s premier conservative political family onto the national stage.

Now, Flávio Bolsonaro is attempting to carry his family’s Rio-rooted brand of politics to Brazil’s top job. In his bid to unseat President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, he’s leaning on a message forged in a city consumed by crime, corruption and broken promises to voters.
It   might just be enough to win.
Polls show Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, neck and neck with Lula going into the Oct. 4 first round.
To prevail, he’s deploying a battle-tested strategy, casting his opponents as soft on crime and tainted by graft. It’s the same playbook his father rode to the presidency a decade ago.

His attacks in recent days have centered on tying Lula to a Supreme Court   judge under scrutiny over his relationship with Daniel Vorcaro, the former owner of Banco Master, the now-defunct lender at the center of a massive banking fraud.

The president has not been directly implicated in the scandal. But the Bolsonaros have long cast Justice Alexandre de Moraes as aligned with the leftist incumbent; the judge was among those who convicted Jair Bolsonaro of   attempting a coup after his 2022 reelection loss to Lula.
That line of attack has been complicated by Flávio Bolsonaro’s   own ties to Vorcaro. Police are now investigating those dealings for potential crimes including corruption and money laundering.
But allegations of misconduct have followed the challenger throughout his time in Rio without halting his ascent.
Flávio Bolsonaro denies any wrongdoing. Yet with much of Brazil’s political elite smeared by the scandal, his larger challenge may be convincing voters that he can match his father’s appeal.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and other US officials met with Anthropic’s chief compute officer, Tom Brown, to discuss   AI safety risks. Tensions between Anthropic and the administration were recently reignited by a 3,800-word essay posted by CEO Dario Amodei, who called for pacing development of the most advanced AI systems so researchers can better understand potential threats.

The US-Iran war has reached a crisis point for Saudi Arabia’s de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. The kingdom was spared the worst of the Islamic Republic’s counterstrikes against the US and Israel early in the conflict, but   that all changed when the Houthis started firing at the Saudis on a near-daily basis this month and drone strikes by pro-Tehran militias in Iraq forced it to close a key oil pipeline.

While Russia is developing AI for many spheres of life, including state services, improvements in industrial production and healthcare, the clearest sign its models aren’t competitive is that hardly anyone outside of the country uses them. It’s indicative of how President Vladimir Putin’s ambitious goal to build world-class AI is   falling short as the war in Ukraine, sanctions and the ideology of his regime cloud the chances of success.

Friedrich Merz canceled his trip to the UN General Assembly in New York next week, changing course as the German chancellor   faces growing opposition within his conservative party ahead of closely watched regional elections on Sunday. Separately, government bodies are surveying Germany’s healthcare systems and infrastructure to see how — or if — they would   stand up in a defense scenario.

In a little over a year on the job as Indonesia’s finance minister, Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa was outspoken and brash but ultimately unable to restore confidence among investors spooked by his boss’s policy unpredictability. Read this   deeply reported take on how the end came quickly for President Prabowo Subianto’s handpicked fiscal chief.

European Union head Ursula von der Leyen invited Canada to become the 27-nation bloc’s   first associate member during her state of the union address today, delivered with Prime Minister Mark Carney in attendance.

India’s economy is at an “  inflection point” that requires officials to rethink policies that powered growth over the past three decades, says Chief Economic Advisor Anantha Nageswaran, who added: “We need to raise our game in multiple respects.”

Hong Kong leader John Lee set out plans to almost double spending on innovation in the coming years and offered greater financial support for new parents, as the city seeks to   build new growth engines and stop a decline in births.
Swiss voters are set to   reject a proposal to tighten the country’s neutrality this month, polls show, preserving the government’s freedom to interpret the doctrine flexibly.
Sign up for the Washington Edition newsletter   for news from the US capital and watch Balance of Power at 1 and 5 p.m. ET weekdays on Bloomberg Television.

The Trump administration wants to   prevent China from catching the US on AI, but doing that will be difficult. The main challenge for the US is keeping China at bay without prompting Beijing to further restrict rare earths used in high-tech products like precision-guided missiles and drones. The Asian nation has continuously narrowed the gap with the US despite the curbs, as President Xi Jinping pours money into becoming self-sufficient on the entire tech stack.

The naval blockade Trump is using to try to force Iran into submission is   testing the limits of the American military, exhausting personnel and weakening Washington’s position elsewhere in the world. Along with a price tag of roughly $32.5 million a day, the fleet stopping Iranian-linked vessels in the Strait of Hormuz represents more than 30% of the US Navy’s warships, some of which have been at sea for several months.

items.title: South African Court Confirms Exclusion of Election Candidates
body: South Africa’s Electoral Court upheld the exclusion of some candidates from a local-government vote scheduled for Nov. 4, putting the country’s biggest political party at risk of losing control of several town councils.

More than 142,000 people were nominated to contest 10,526 municipal seats by the time the process closed on Aug. 28. While 2,274 names were captured, they weren’t properly submitted on the Electoral Commission of South Africa’s computer system, rendering them ineligible to run.

The African National Congress blamed the omission of some of its candidates on a technical glitch and filed a lawsuit challenging their exclusion, but the commission said due process wasn’t followed. The Electoral Court ruled in the commission’s favor on Wednesday.
The ANC plans to appeal the ruling.

“We have consistently maintained that this matter is not about seeking preferential treatment for the ANC, nor about asking the Electoral Commission to change the rules for the benefit of our organization,” the party said in a statement. “It concerns the legal status of candidate information that the ANC maintains was captured into the IEC’s electronic system before the prescribed deadline.”
More than 29 million people have registered to cast ballots, with 546 parties fielding candidates for seats.

items.title: Kosovo Ex-President Thaci Gets 25 Years for War Crimes
body: Kosovo’s former President Hashim Thaci was convicted of war crimes and sentenced to 25 years in prison in a ruling that is likely to send shockwaves across the Balkans.

The panel of judges at a special, European Union-backed court in The Hague found the wartime political leader of the Kosovo Liberation Army guilty of illegal and arbitrary detention, cruel treatment, torture and murder. He was acquitted on six other counts related to crimes against humanity.

The former president was the KLA’s political leader during the 1998-99 war with Serbia, when the ethnic Albanian guerrilla force fought for independence. NATO intervened with a 78-day bombing campaign in 1999, after which Serbian forces withdrew and Kosovo came under international administration.

Thaci, 58, later became prime minister, serving when Kosovo declared independence from Serbia in 2008, and was elected president in 2016. He also played a central role in US and European-backed talks with Belgrade aimed at normalizing relations between the two sides. Serbia still refuses to recognize Kosovo’s independence.
Read More: Kosovo Counts Down to War Crimes Trial of Former President Seen as Hero

The conviction is likely to carry significant political and symbolic weight in Kosovo, where the KLA is closely tied to the struggle for independence and many of its former commanders later became leading political figures.

It will also quash speculation about Thaci’s potential return to politics to challenge struggling Prime Minister Albin Kurti amid a slowing economy and delays in implementing reforms required to join the EU.

Crowds in central Pristina chanted “shame, shame” after Judge Charles Smith read the verdict. Thaci’s co-defendant Jakup Krasniqi also received a 25-year sentence, while Kadri Veseli was sentenced to 18 years and Rexhep Selimi to 13 years.
Kosovo Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca described the verdict as a “truly sad, unjust and undeserved decision for the four KLA leaders” in comments to reporters in The Hague.

The ruling establishes Thaci’s individual criminal responsibility rather than assigning guilt to the KLA as a whole. Kosovo’s parliament created the court in 2015 under international pressure to investigate allegations that crimes committed by some KLA members had not been prosecuted.

Thaci has been detained in The Hague since November 2020. He can appeal the verdict and sentence. He is also awaiting a verdict in a separate case over allegations that he obstructed court proceedings and interfered with witnesses. He denies those charges.

items.title: Indian and Pakistani Warships Collide, Refueling Tensions
body: Arch rivals and nuclear-armed neighbors India and Pakistan traded blame over a collision between their warships at sea, summoning each other’s top diplomats to lodge “strong” protests and adding another point of friction between the duo.

The incident took place Tuesday, according to accounts from both sides. A government official in New Delhi told reporters via text message on Wednesday that the Indian warship was on a routine surveillance mission in international waters in the northern Arabian Sea when the Pakistani vessel approached at high speed. The official asked not to be identified because the information isn’t public.

Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry said in a statement late Wednesday that its navy was conducting a biennial exercise in its exclusive economic zone when the incident occurred, describing the Indian Navy’s action as “highly provocative and unacceptable.”
Both countries said they had summoned each other’s charge d’affaires.
The incident was “unacceptable and unprofessional conduct of Pakistani naval units at sea,” India’s Ministry of External Affairs said in a statement Wednesday, adding that no “major damage” occurred.

Pakistan said it told India’s envoy “to convey to the government of India that Pakistan strongly rejects this belligerent Indian action.” It urged New Delhi to “adhere strictly to international law and bilateral agreements, particularly those aimed at preventing incidents at sea.”

Ties between the two countries — which have fought four major wars since independence in 1947 — have remained tense since an armed clash last year took them to the brink of another conflict. That was triggered by the killing of 26 people, mostly Indian tourists, in the Indian-controlled part of Kashmir. New Delhi branded it a terrorist attack and accused Pakistan of involvement, charges denied by Islamabad.

This week’s naval incident comes as the US-Iran war and near-closure of the key Strait of Hormuz disrupts global energy supplies, heightening concerns over security and freedom of navigation in waters around the Arabian Sea.
