items.title: ARS/USD: Argentina's Milei Defied by Governor Handing Out Own Money
body: Lea en español

One of Argentina’s most outspoken opposition governors is bringing back a local currency that can only be spent inside his province, doubling down on an interventionist economic model just as President Javier Milei tries to convince investors that the country has embraced free markets for good.

Governor Ricardo Quintela is handing out chachos, as the notes are called, to roughly 80,000 public workers and other beneficiaries in La Rioja, a small, impoverished province set along the eastern edge of the Andes mountains. Workers will receive a bonus payment of 50,000 chachos a month — equal to about $33, or nearly 10% of the local average wage — through the end of the year, reviving an initiative to prop up consumption that Quintela, a prominent Peronist party leader, first launched in 2024.

The return of the chacho, which circulates at a one-to-one exchange rate with the peso, exposes a stubborn reality lying just beneath Milei’s transformation of Argentina. He may have managed to slash bureaucracy, stabilize the inflation-ravaged economy and unleash a commodities export boom, but growth in the broader economy remains tepid and new jobs scarce, leaving many Argentines feeling left behind.That leaves political space for the interventionist model, long promoted by the Peronist opposition, that he’s trying to eradicate.

Mired in default since 2024, La Rioja embodies that alternative approach in its starkest form. There are more than three public-sector workers for every formal private-sector employee, according to national government data, making the local government the main engine of growth. The province runs a sprawling network of state-controlled companies and has shunned Milei’s flagship investment incentives while neighboring regions have drawn commitments for more than $15 billion of mining investments.
Quintela has described the chacho as an “act of rebellion” and threatened to reverse Milei’s reforms if the Peronists manage to defeat him in elections next year.

“Investors need to be warned: Peronism is going to review absolutely everything,” he said in a radio interview last month. “Whatever needs to be nationalized, we will nationalize. Whatever needs to be expropriated, we will expropriate. We’re going to take it back.”

Milei seems unperturbed. “Peronism always proposes spending more,” the President wrote on X after the province announced the return of the chacho. “And it always proposes paying for these delusions by printing money.”

The provincial leader has pumped about 4 billion chachos into circulation, worth roughly $3 million, over the last month. Legally, he could go much further: local lawmakers have authorized as much as 85 billion pesos ($50 million) through December this year.
So far, he is alone in his efforts.

While other provinces have also historically issued notes, mainly during crises like the US-peso peg collapse of the early 2000s, La Rioja is the only one to do so in the last 20 years. But for investors pouring money into Argentina on the basis that Milei’s market-friendly shift will outlast his presidency, the revival of the local notes makes La Rioja more than just an eccentric holdout.

“These aren’t unthinking outbursts,” said Lucas Romero, who runs Buenos Aires-based political consultancy Synopsis. “There is a clear intention to provoke with disruptive proposals that are antagonistic to Milei and stir market fears.”
Keeping that political risk alive, he said, works in Peronism’s favor, and could pressure Milei heading into the 2027 election.
Barely 20 minutes after Juan Barrionuevo received his 50,000 chachos, they were gone.

The public-school saxophone teacher, who drives an Uber on the side to support his monthly salary of 1 million pesos ($650), collected the colorful notes at a park. He then drove to a gas station and spent the entire amount on about half a tank of fuel.
“At least I can put them to work,” he said. “People aren’t thinking about the economy at large — they’re thinking about their own pockets. Isn’t the peso just a piece of paper too?”

Barrionuevo is among thousands of Riojans being handed the notes at an unlikely assortment of places: public parks, sports centers, tax offices, and even branches of the state-controlled electricity distributor.

Outside one such branch one afternoon in late August, several dozen people stood for about an hour to collect their chachos. In a province where the average monthly income is less than $400, few can afford to dismiss extra money.

Some merchants, like Gustavo Pairetti, won’t take chachos as payment at his empanada shop in La Rioja city since the suppliers he buys meat, cheese and cold cuts from don’t accept them. But the notes don’t tend to stay in workers’ wallets for very long.
It’s a pass-the-chacho economy: Workers use the notes to buy goods, while merchants use them for provincial obligations, like taxes, or hold them until designated redemption windows open.

“People get rid of them right away, buying what they couldn’t afford before,” said Juan Keulian, president of La Rioja’s Center for Commerce and Industry. “The chachos help revive retail sales a little — just a little — because business is deeply depressed.”
“It is also a message,” added Ricardo Herrera, La Rioja’s secretary general. “It is the path we have chosen to counter Milei’s model of an absent state.”

Since taking office, Milei has moved swiftly to shrink the state, slashing spending enough to deliver Argentina’s first annual budget surplus in 15 years. Cuts to discretionary transfers and public works in the provinces were a key part of the adjustment, and while the overhaul helped stabilize the economy and won plaudits from investors, it hit particularly hard in places like La Rioja, where federal funding and public-sector wages underpin much of local demand.“La Rioja isn’t poor. It has been impoverished from the 1980s to the present,” said Gabriela Rodríguez, a local lawmaker who opposes Governor Quintela, pointing to what she described as the province’s undeveloped economic potential following roughly four decades of Peronism rule.

The chacho is also deeply symbolic — named for La Rioja’s iconic caudillo, Angel Vicente “Chacho” Peñaloza, who defended the province against forces aligned with the central government in Buenos Aires. In a 21st century twist, each banknote carries a QR code linking to a website attacking Milei’s government for withholding federal funds that La Rioja says it is owed.

La Rioja has the lowest average individual and per-capita household incomes in all of Argentina, according to the national statistics agency. As of June, nearly a quarter of household debt was delinquent — the highest in the country, according to a report by consulting firm EcoGo and Buenos Aires-based Austral University.

“If there’s a decline in economic activity among public employees, we all get to feel it,” said Leonardo Guzmán, who has run a furniture business in La Rioja for more than four decades. “The chachos are undoubtedly the result of bad economic management. We’re talking about a province that can’t pay with real money.”
He accepts them anyway.
“I’m part of this province and sometimes you have to play by the rules,” Guzmán said. “Someone was paid in chachos. What fault is it of theirs?”

items.title: Los chachos vuelven a La Rioja en desafío al modelo de Milei
body: Read story in English

Uno de los gobernadores opositores más críticos de Argentina está reintroduciendo una moneda que solo puede gastarse en su provincia, redoblando su apuesta por un modelo económico intervencionista justo cuando el presidente Javier Milei intenta convencer a los inversores de que el país ha abrazado definitivamente el libre mercado.

El gobernador Ricardo Quintela está entregando chachos, como se denomina la moneda, a unos 80.000 empleados públicos y otros beneficiarios de La Rioja, una provincia pequeña y empobrecida situada al este de la cordillera de los Andes. Hasta fin de año, los trabajadores recibirán un bono mensual de 50.000 chachos, equivalente a unos US$33, o casi el 10% del salario promedio local. La medida reactiva una iniciativa para apuntalar el consumo que Quintela, un destacado dirigente peronista, lanzó por primera vez en 2024.

El regreso de los chachos, que circulan a un tipo de cambio de uno a uno con el peso, deja al descubierto una realidad persistente bajo la transformación de Argentina impulsada por Milei. Aunque ha logrado reducir drásticamente la burocracia, estabilizar una economía golpeada por la inflación y desatar un auge de las exportaciones de materias primas, el crecimiento del resto de la economía sigue siendo débil y escasean los nuevos empleos, lo que hace que muchos argentinos se sientan abandonados.
Esa situación deja espacio político para el modelo intervencionista promovido durante años por la oposición peronista y que Milei intenta erradicar.

En default desde 2024, La Rioja encarna ese modelo alternativo en su forma más extrema. Hay más de tres empleados públicos por cada trabajador formal del sector privado, según datos del gobierno nacional, lo que convierte al gobierno provincial en el principal motor de la economía. La provincia administra una extensa red de empresas estatales y ha rechazado los principales incentivos a la inversión de Milei, mientras regiones vecinas han atraído compromisos por más de US$15.000 millones en inversiones mineras.
Quintela ha descrito el chacho como un “acto de rebelión” y ha amenazado con revertir las reformas de Milei si los peronistas logran derrotarlo en las elecciones del próximo año.

“Hay que avisarles a los inversores: el peronismo va a revisar absolutamente todo”, afirmó Quintela en una entrevista radial el mes pasado. “Lo que sea necesario nacionalizar, lo vamos a nacionalizar. Lo que sea necesario expropiar, vamos a expropiar. Vamos a recuperar”.

Milei no parece inmutarse. “El peronismo siempre propone gastar más”, señaló el presidente en X después de que la provincia anunciara el regreso de los chachos. “Y siempre propone pagar estos delirios con emisión de dinero”.

El líder provincial ha puesto en circulación unos 4.000 millones de chachos, equivalentes a aproximadamente US$3 millones, en el último mes. Y podría ir mucho más lejos: los legisladores provinciales han autorizado  la emisión de hasta 85.000 millones de pesos (US$50 millones) hasta diciembre de este año.
Hasta ahora, nadie ha seguido su ejemplo.

Aunque otras provincias también han emitido sus propias monedas a lo largo de la historia, principalmente durante crisis como el colapso de la paridad entre el peso y el dólar a comienzos de la década de 2000, La Rioja es la única que lo ha hecho en los últimos 20 años. Pero para los inversores que están destinando dinero a Argentina bajo la premisa de que el giro promercado de Milei perdurará más allá de su presidencia, el regreso de los billetes locales convierte a La Rioja en algo más que un caso atípico.

“Son expresiones que no parecen ser salidas de exabruptos dichos sin ser pensados”, señaló Lucas Romero, director de la consultora política Synopsis, con sede en Buenos Aires. “Hay una clara intencionalidad en producir esa provocación, en expresar ese tipo de propuesta disruptiva, antagónica a Milei, para ganar protagonismo en la discusión pública”.
Mantener vivo ese riesgo político, señaló, favorece al peronismo y podría aumentar la presión sobre Milei de cara a las elecciones de 2027.
Apenas 20 minutos después de que Juan Barrionuevo recibiera sus 50.000 chachos, ya no le quedaba ninguno.

Este profesor de saxofón de una escuela pública, que además conduce un Uber para complementar su sueldo mensual de 1 millón de pesos (US$650), recogió los coloridos billetes en un parque. Luego condujo hasta una estación de servicio y lo gastó todo en aproximadamente medio tanque de combustible.

“Más allá de que sea una cuasimoneda, si me sirve para pagar, para mí es útil. Al menos lo puedo poner a trabajar”, comentó Barrionuevo. “Nosotros, la gente común, no estamos pensando en la macro, sino en el bolsillo de cada uno y vivir el día a día. El peso es un papel también, ¿no?”

Barrionuevo es uno de los miles de riojanos que reciben los billetes en una inusual variedad de lugares: parques públicos, centros deportivos, oficinas de impuestos e incluso sucursales de la distribuidora eléctrica controlada por el Estado. Afuera de una de esas sucursales, una tarde de fines de agosto, varias decenas de personas hicieron fila durante aproximadamente una hora para retirar sus chachos. En una provincia donde el ingreso mensual promedio es inferior a US$400, pocos pueden darse el lujo de despreciar dinero extra.

Algunos comerciantes, como Gustavo Pairetti, no aceptan chachos como medio de pago en su tienda de empanadas en la ciudad de La Rioja porque los proveedores a los que compra carne, queso y fiambres tampoco los reciben. Pero los billetes no suelen permanecer mucho tiempo en las billeteras de los trabajadores.

Es una economía de “pasarse el chacho”: los trabajadores utilizan los billetes para comprar bienes, mientras los comerciantes los usan para cumplir obligaciones provinciales, como el pago de impuestos, o los conservan hasta que se abren períodos específicos para canjearlos.

“Los chachos van a servir porque la gente se los saca de encima inmediatamente y compra lo que no pudo comprar porque no le alcanzaba la plata”, señaló Juan Keulian, presidente del Centro Comercial e Industrial de La Rioja. “Esto sirve para reactivar un poquito —un poquito no más— las ventas del comercio que estaban muy deprimidas”.

“Es también un contrapunto. Un mensaje de contrapunto de modelo”, añadió Ricardo Herrera, secretario general de la gobernación de La Rioja. “Es el camino que elegimos nosotros para contraponernos al modelo de Milei, un modelo de ausencia del Estado”.

Desde que asumió el cargo, Milei ha avanzado rápidamente para reducir el tamaño del Estado, recortando el gasto lo suficiente como para lograr el primer superávit presupuestario anual de Argentina en 15 años. Los recortes a las transferencias discrecionales y a las obras públicas en las provincias fueron una parte clave del ajuste y, aunque la reestructuración ayudó a estabilizar la economía y recibió elogios de los inversores, golpeó con especial fuerza a lugares como La Rioja, donde los fondos federales y los salarios del sector público sostienen gran parte de la demanda local.

“La Rioja no es pobre. Se ha empobrecido desde la década de 1980 hasta la actualidad”, señaló Gabriela Rodríguez, legisladora local opositora al gobernador Quintela, al señalar lo que describió como el potencial económico desaprovechado de la provincia tras aproximadamente cuatro décadas de gobiernos peronistas.

El chacho también tiene una fuerte carga simbólica: lleva el nombre del emblemático caudillo riojano Ángel Vicente “Chacho” Peñaloza, quien defendió a la provincia frente a fuerzas alineadas con el gobierno central en Buenos Aires. En un giro propio del siglo XXI, cada billete lleva un código QR que enlaza a un sitio web que ataca al gobierno de Milei por retener fondos federales que, según La Rioja, le debe.

La Rioja tiene el ingreso individual promedio y el ingreso per cápita de los hogares más bajos de toda Argentina, según la agencia nacional de estadísticas. A junio, casi una cuarta parte de la deuda de los hogares estaba en mora, la proporción más alta del país, según un informe de la consultora EcoGo y la Universidad Austral, con sede en Buenos Aires.

“Si hay una baja en la actividad por parte del empleo público, lo sentimos todos”, señaló Leonardo Guzmán, que lleva más de cuatro décadas al frente de un negocio de muebles en La Rioja. “Indudablemente el tema de los chachos es el resultado de una mala gestión económica. Estamos hablando de que la provincia no puede pagar con plata real”.
Aun así, los acepta.

“No es que esté de acuerdo, pero estoy inserto en esta provincia y hay veces que tenés que jugar con lo que te ponen adelante”, sostuvo Guzmán. “También entiendo que a alguien que le pagaron con chachos... ¿qué culpa tiene?”Traducción editada por Paulina Munita
Nota original: Argentine Opposition Leader Mints His Own Money to Defy Milei

items.title: The US Can Slow Down AI and Stay Ahead of China
body: When Chinese leader Xi Jinping visits Washington next week, artificial intelligence will be near the top of the agenda. The dialogue that the US and China began earlier this year has gained urgency as fears of out-of-control AI have spurred calls for a slowdown in innovation at the frontier.

But as the US debate over AI regulation intensifies, consider this: A pause by American labs will be meaningful only if paired with Chinese restraint. The US faces a difficult choice about whether to seek that restraint primarily through diplomacy or coercive pressure.

America’s increasing AI anxiety is a three-legged stool. Fears of economic disruption — loss of white-collar jobs or a rise in inequality — have been growing. So have concerns about community disruption — for example, the effects of data centers on local communities. Now, anxieties about existential disruption are surging, as AI agents go rogue and leading researchers warn that unchecked innovation could endanger humanity.

Some such fears may be overstated — a recent analysis by The Economist found that AI’s impact on employment is mostly positive — but calls for stronger regulation are getting louder. Even top AI executives agree that the advent of recursive self-improvement — the ability of advanced AI models to create more capable successors — risks a situation in which humans lose control. Over the weekend, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for a three-part approach to “pacing the frontier.”

The first step involves frontier AI firms giving access to third-party safety evaluators. The second involves negotiation, among frontier firms in democratic countries, of common safety standards and limits on AI progress. The third part requires bringing autocratic countries, namely China, into this framework.

Chinese compliance with any AI slowdown is essential, for safety and strategic reasons. Rogue Chinese AI could impact humanity just as catastrophically as rogue American AI. US labs are generally thought to have better safety records than their Chinese counterparts, because they are more exposed to the transparency of a democratic society.

Moreover, a unilateral US pause could bring strategic self-harm. “Whoever wins AI wins,” President Donald Trump remarked; the last two presidential administrations have bet that superior AI will give the US a decisive economic and military edge.
By some estimates, top Chinese models are only a few months behind top US models. A unilateral US slowdown would put America’s primary source of advantage in the AI race at risk.
Some analysts disagree: They claim that a unilateral US slowdown is sufficient, because China will then lack new US models to distill, or reverse-engineer.

It’s true that China has managed to be a fast follower in part through large-scale distillation campaigns. But it’s hard to claim that Chinese progress is purely, even primarily, the result of distillation. Given the rapid rate of technological progress, even if the Chinese can’t distill new US models, they could still achieve breakthroughs with dangerous geopolitical consequences.
A pause among democracies requires Chinese reciprocation. There are two options for getting it.

The first is to negotiate a mutual frontier slowdown, perhaps using the nascent AI dialogue to be led by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng. That seems attractive, but it’s likely to be terribly difficult.

Chinese officials see US calls for an AI slowdown as an effort to pause the race while Washington is ahead; state-run media have called it a “containment” strategy out of the “Cold War playbook.” A mutual AI slowdown might also be hard to verify — and the risk of Chinese defection would be substantial, given Beijing’s track record of violating international agreements.

The second option is harder edged. It involves a concerted export-control offensive. The US would close loopholes that allow Chinese labs to access high-end chips through the cloud or overseas subsidiaries; more aggressively combat smuggling and evasion; tighten restrictions on the sale and servicing of advanced semiconductor manufacturing equipment; and reverse Trump’s earlier loosening of curbs on sales of sophisticated chips.

The goal would be to starve China of the computing power it needs to train and deploy frontier models — to unilaterally impose a Chinese slowdown that allows the US to preserve its lead even as it paces its own progress at the frontier. By maximizing US tech leverage, this approach might also strengthen America’s negotiating position — unilateral pressure could, perhaps, provide a path to mutual restraint.
It is hard to imagine a serious US strategy for combining AI safety and AI advantage that doesn’t include a stronger export-control regime. But the dangers of this approach are real.

China won’t simply accept an onslaught of US tech coercion; it will likely hit back with rare-earth export controls and other retaliation. The superficial easing of tensions that Xi and Trump have engineered over the past year would likely collapse. Uneasy détente could give way to a fiercer, less-constrained cold war.

Trump, for now, denies that any such decision is necessary: He derides calls for an AI slowdown as a “hoax” and labels those pushing for one as fools and traitors. But this dilemma can’t be skirted forever. America’s AI anxiety isn’t fading — and neither is the question of how best to deal with Beijing.
Brands is also a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, the author of The Landscape of Power: Geography and the Rise and Fall of Nations, and a senior adviser to Macro Advisory Partners.

items.title: AI Trade Faces Midterm Risk as Trump, Politicians Fight Over AI
body: US midterm elections were already shaping up to be a key risk for AI-related stocks amid a backlash against data centers. But with a growing number of lawmakers from both parties sounding the alarm on the need for AI safety regulations, the stakes have only gotten higher.

Optimism about AI has powered the stock-market rally for the better part of four years amid soaring spending on computing infrastructure. That trade, however, is on shaky ground after Anthropic PBC and OpenAI both pledged to slow development of their most advanced models following a series of warnings from within the industry about its ability to control the technology.

The Philadelphia Stock Exchange Semiconductor Index, better known as the SOX, tumbled nearly 6% on Monday, its worst day in more than two months. Former President Barack Obama called for AI policy to be “at the center of our public debate,” in a statement Monday evening. Meanwhile, senators including John Thune, Ted Cruz, Bernie Sanders and Amy Klobuchar have all proposed a range of policy measures aimed at addressing AI safety concerns.

President Donald Trump, meanwhile, has remained steadfast in his view that new guardrails for the technology are unnecessary. During an impromptu call on Monday to Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang, who was on stage at a technology conference, Trump dismissed concerns about AI dangers as a “hoax.”

That divide ahead of the midterms means “the narrative will be that if Democrats have more control, this is a reason to be more cautious about AI going forward,” said Aniket Shah, global head of Washington, sustainability, and transition strategy at Jefferies. “Investors will use that as a moment to sell.”

AI-linked stocks had been under pressure even before the chorus of calls for safety regulations. The SOX has fallen 22% since hitting a record in June, with all but four of its 30 members down by more than 10%. The index rose as much as 1.9% on Wednesday.

The pullback has been spurred in part by backlash against AI and data center construction, which has sent sales of semiconductors and other computing gear soaring. Polling data show that opposition to new data centers has become a bipartisan issue, with voters concerned about their impact on the environment and electricity prices. Democrats taking control of the senate could trigger a stock selloff of more than 10% into the end of 2026, Bank of America strategists said last month.

Democrats appear to be more interested in drafting AI regulations and betting markets suggest their probability of taking back control of both houses of Congress is growing, Wells Fargo chief equity strategist Ohsung Kwon wrote in a note to clients this week.

“We’re increasingly getting nervous about the AI trade, seeing 2027 as a potential peak capex year,” Kwon said in an email to Bloomberg News on Tuesday. “The news over the weekend added another layer of uncertainty.”
The biggest risk from the midterms is a hit to investor sentiment, rather than concrete policies that would result in a slowdown in spending on AI by the largest tech companies, said Jefferies’ Shah.

Trump will still wield veto power after the election, making it harder for Congress to push through sweeping changes. And there are strong incentives for policymakers to avoid draconian restrictions, Shah said, in part because of how important AI is to the economy.

What markets do have to reprice is the chance that Democrats will get a boost in November as they line up on the politically popular side of the issue, according to Matt Gertken, who leads geopolitical and US political strategy at BCA Research.

If Democrats manage to take back both houses of Congress, there’s at least some chance Trump would sign AI regulations into law, according to Gertken. And a bigger midterm victory would raise the odds that Democrats win unified control of the government in 2028, Gertken said.
“It’s like clouds forming on the horizon,” he said. “You’re going to have to get your rain jacket and your umbrella, but you’re not going to necessarily cancel all your plans yet.”

While there is some debate over whether the midterms will be able to spawn broad-based change, the overwhelming message from politically focused strategists on Wall Street is that AI will be a core issue in the 2028 presidential election.

Vice President JD Vance, who is the favorite to be the Republican nominee for 2028, said he’d like Congress and the administration to come to a “consensus” on regulations. House Speaker Mike Johnson, meanwhile, said Congress “potentially” will need to impose guardrails on the industry, though he cautioned it would likely take time to fashion legislation with broad enough support to pass.

“A bunch of Democrats being for something that Trump’s against, that doesn’t matter that much,” Evercore ISI strategist Sarah Bianchi said. “What will be more impactful to the market is realizing that even a Republican president might do some of this stuff.”

items.title: Tata Board to Mull Asking Chandra to Stay On Amid RBI's IPO Push
body: The board of Tata Group’s holding company will meet Thursday to discuss how to handle a listing mandated by India’s central bank, including if outgoing Chairman Natarajan Chandrasekaran should be asked to stay on.

A last-minute addition to the meeting agenda is a discussion of the Nomination and Remuneration Committee’s recommendations, according to people with knowledge of the matter. The so-called NRC is expected to recommend asking Chandrasekaran to reconsider his decision to step down, the people added, asking not to be identified discussing internal matters.
The Reserve Bank of India’s refusal to relax listing rules for Tata Sons Pvt. has turned what was meant to be a routine board meeting into a high-stakes discussion on the way forward.

Chandra, as he’s commonly known, said last month that he plans to step down when his term ends in February, forcing the group to prepare for a leadership transition. His planned exit followed months of friction with Tata Trusts Chairman Noel Tata over the listing issue and capital allocation across the sprawling conglomerate.
A Tata Sons representative did not immediately respond to a request for comments.

Tata Sons had sought an exemption from the listing requirement to avoid tighter regulatory scrutiny and expanded public disclosures. A public float would force the holding company to reveal far more about the finances and governance of the group’s sprawling businesses — from steel and autos to software, airlines and consumer goods — and could dilute the influence of Tata Trusts, a group of charities that control the company.

After rejecting Tata Sons’ plea for an exemption from an initial public offer, the RBI also filed a caveat in the Bombay High Court to ensure its position is heard before any order is passed should Tata Sons seek legal relief, the Economic Times reported. The newspaper first reported the possibility of the NRC asking Chandra to reconsider his decision on Sunday.

“Tata Sons and Tata Trusts should work towards an IPO of Tata Sons rather than pursue prolonged litigation or alternative structures aimed at remaining unlisted,” InGovern Research, a proxy advisory, said in a Sept. 16 report. “The RBI has shown that it is tenacious by having filed a caveat in the Bombay High Court.”

The Tata Group values its current ownership structure, arguing that it allows the business to take a long-term view across its portfolio without public-market pressures. The group, with $185 billion revenue, controls over two dozen listed companies, and is also key to India’s high-end technology ambitions — having committed to producing the first homegrown semiconductor chips.

The RBI’s public-float mandate aligns with long-standing demands from the debt-laden Shapoorji Pallonji Group, Tata Sons’ biggest minority shareholder, which has been pressing for a listing to unlock value from its 18.4% stake.

Besides giving liquidity to SP Group and other listed Tata companies that hold a stake in Tata Sons, a listing will give capital flexibility to raise funding and “subject the Tata Trusts’ special rights to greater scrutiny,” according to InGovern Research.

items.title: Extreme Movie Screenings Are Testing Film Fans' Comfort Levels
body: There are 15 minutes until the clock begins, but Jake Molter has no doubt. “We’re gonna make it,” he says.

It’s a Friday evening in the middle of August, and the 24-year-old Brooklyn artist stands beside his three friends inside a small, basement room at Metro Private Cinema in Manhattan,   a luxe warren of screening rooms opened by the founder of Alamo Drafthouse. They’re preparing to embark on what some moviegoers might consider psychological torture: a 36-hour screening marathon of It Ends, in which four friends are stuck in the liminal horror hell of a never-ending road. Distributor Neon calls it a “challenge.”

The 87-minute flick from director Alex Ullom will loop continuously for two teams of four, each trying to remain in the theater longer than the other, no internet or outdoor breaks allowed. Participants get 25¢ for every minute they stay inside — up to $540 — and if the entire group completes all 36 hours, each member receives a $500 bonus.

This particular quartet of twentysomethings has come ready to win. They’ve brought changes of clothes, a deck of playing cards, noise-canceling AirPods to help with sleep, and a couple downloaded movies to stream when they need a break. (This was decidedly not an option for the characters of It Ends). Molter even arranged to get out of a mandatory work meeting the next morning. Across the hallway, another team is sizing up the room (four seats and a dining room table) and the competition, while a Mediterranean feast of lamb and branzino gets rolled in, along with bowls of Clif bars and water bottles.

The group still has some questions and concerns. Veronica Gilligan, 24, who entered her and Molter’s team into the social media contest, asks a Neon employee, “If I want to take, like, a mirror selfie in the bathroom, is that allowed?”

Molter is mostly concerned about his sleep schedule and the lack of sun, but nobody wanted to pass this up: The chance to make some sizable cash, disappear into a movie theater with your friends, test the limits of your own endurance and, most of all, find out whether you can beat the strangers in the room next door. “Originally I was like, ‘I don’t know, that sounds hard,’ But then I’m like, ‘I will literally never forget this experience,’” says Molter. He also appreciated that the marathon made thematic sense. “I wouldn’t do this with a movie that was actually supergory and scary,” he says.

The Endless Screening is one of several immersive endurance competitions that small and mid-size studios have crafted recently to create viral social media engagement and draw attention to their respective films. “It made sense to do that marathon because of the endlessness of it.” Last year, Lionsgate hosted a “treadmill” screening for director Francis Ellis’s dystopian thriller The Long Walk, challenging theatergoers to walk 3 miles per hour on small, individual treadmills for the full duration of the movie. The studio did something similar for this month’s rock-climbing thriller Fall 2: Deadpoint, placing invited participants on wobbling elevated platforms and “testing their balance and endurance as the tension builds onscreen.”

For genre fans, these specialized screenings offer the rare opportunity to step deeper into the realities and experiences of characters onscreen — to withstand the psychological exhaustion and “trapped” nature of an action hero or horror protagonist and turn an otherwise regular movie night into a highly gamified, shareable, memorable interactive event.

“This is something where I will forever have this relationship with this movie, whereas with everything else, it’s like, ‘I see it and I’m done.’” Molter says of It Ends. “I’m not just experiencing what they’re experiencing physically. I’m in their heads.”

To  capitalize on this year’s filmgoing resurgence after years of  declining attendance among US adults, studios and theaters have been getting more creative about attracting audiences and making the experience of watching a film more than simply sitting in the dark. Through the last decade, 4DX has been shaking seats, spraying water and blasting air at audiences. Microcinemas around the country  have offered taste-alongs( at prices up to $215), serving the food that characters are eating onscreen in real time. A24 leaned into smell for a free, invite-only New York screening of 2024’s Heretic, pumping the scent of blueberry pie into the theater during a pivotal scene involving the pastry.

The Rocky Horror Picture Show, a pioneer in participatory screenings since the late 1970s, has long offered people an excuse to perform amid a roomful of strangers, reciting lines and tossing props at midnight showings that have been running for decades. Lionsgate tapped into that same communal instinct last year with free, word-of-mouth screenings of The Housemaid in 18 US cities that  encouraged audiences to break plates during Sydney Sweeney’s “I love gravy” line reading, then join in on a collective scream cue.

Alison Foreman, a film writer and reporter in Los Angeles, can lay claim to helping conceive the studio’s treadmill event. After attending a press screening of The Long Walk, she was so inspired by the Stephen King adaptation, in which teenagers must continuously walk at 3 mph or be shot by a military escort, that, in a post-screening survey, she suggested a more physically demanding way to watch it. A couple months later, the studio invited her and 60 other fans to try out her idea.

Inside the Culver Theater, Foreman stepped into an auditorium filled with newly installed exercise equipment flanked by actors dressed as drill sergeants who barked out the promotional screening’s rules and regulations: If any of the invited participants (a mix of influencers and industry-adjacent guests) hopped off or couldn’t maintain the designated pace, they’d get kicked out of the theater. Like the movie’s plot, though much less deadly, the real-time simulation quickly became anxiety-inducing when a woman beside Foreman stumbled for a moment on her treadmill and received a stern warning.

“There is just something so poetic and beautiful about watching people grapple with the concept of a very serious challenge while you’re grappling with even a low-level challenge,” Foreman says. “The movie hit me exactly as hard, if not harder than my first screening, and I think that is hugely because of the context.”

A  viral recap video attracted 24 million views in a day, all but guaranteeing a repeat. For Fall 2: Deadpoint, about two women who survive a mountain rock slide that leaves them stranded on a fragile plank 3,000 feet in the air, Lionsgate dressed up the same Culver Theater auditorium to resemble the movie’s Thailand jungles and encouraged 18 harnessed competitors (hand-picked by the studio based on their social following) to stay mounted atop raised, narrow boards as various elements such as wind and water challenged their balance.
“By the time we got to the end my legs were absolutely fried,”  said one contestant, posting as @4k_filmss on Instagram. “I was literally shaking. I’m surprised I made it through.”

“We wanted them to feel at least a taste of the exposure, instability and thrills that our characters experience,” says Briana McElroy, Lionsgate’s executive vice president for digital marketing. “If that creates conversation online and gets someone else curious enough to search and ultimately see the movie, that’s obviously a great outcome. But it starts with creating an experience people genuinely want to talk about.”

According to Suzanne Scott, associate professor in the radio, TV and film department at the University of Texas in Austin, these immersive, interactive screenings tap into the next stage of fandom, which can kick in even when the characters are unfamiliar. Fans still crave the feeling of knowing them, inhabiting their world and experiencing the story alongside others.

“They pride themselves on endurance — learning all the trivia, watching and rewatching all of their favorite media objects, standing in line for tickets for 10 hours to get in to the content they want,” Scott says. “There’s a desire to feel a closeness to characters that those sorts of events facilitate, and that just sitting and watching a movie does not.”

The challenge of scaling these experiences beyond dozens of fans highlights the community aspect. “You could watch The Long Walk on your phone on a treadmill right now, and it’s not the same thing,” Foreman says.

When Molter and Gilligan and their group emerged victorious early Sunday morning, beating the other team by about 24 hours, the experience had transformed into something almost emotional. (The group remained determined to finish the entire challenge even after learning they’d outlasted their opponents.) They experienced a lot together — a surge of initial adrenaline, a visit from the director, Facetimes with the cast, and lots of sleep deprivation — and passed much of the time drawing, playing cards and occasionally reciting various passages from the film they’d committed to memory.

At a certain point, Gilligan says, sounding exhausted over the phone the next afternoon. “it was like time and space didn’t exist.” Along the way, Neon representatives, on-site for most of the competition, had rewarded the group with little surprises (bacon, egg and cheese sandwiches for making it through the first night), but the mental strain got tougher when most of the theater employees left on Saturday night, Molter says. “We were very separated from the world.”

He admits there was something special about being disconnected from his phone for so long — to the point he felt he’d become friends with the characters onscreen. “We were all together the whole time,” he says, “and we kind of just had to make our own fun, which was actually really nice.” The group planned to use some of their cash prizes on an oyster dinner, a chance to commiserate and reflect (in daylight) on their claustrophobic weekend.
Even after watching It Ends 25 times in a row, Gilligan says she still has stamina for more: “I kind of want to go to the movies tomorrow.”

items.title: Romania Set to Curb €10 Billion Foreign Debt Sale Plan
body: Romania’s officials in charge of debt management told investors the country will likely scale back its eurobond issuance plan for this year as it boosted borrowing on the domestic market, according to people familiar with the matter.

The Black Sea nation won’t sell more eurobonds until a new government is formed and there is greater clarity on the political situation, treasury chief Stefan Nanu said at a meeting with investors in London, the people said, asking not to be identified because the talks were private.
The Finance Ministry in Bucharest had no immediate comment when contacted by Bloomberg News.

Romania has raised about €5 billion in international bond markets so far this year through euro- and dollar-denominated tranches, against an original external borrowing target of €10 billion. Official data also show that the country completed roughly €2 billion in private placements. The country has been one of the most active borrowers in foreign currencies in eastern Europe as it sought to finance a large budget deficit.
Read more: Investors Look Past Romania Risk to Pocket Junk-Like Yields
The country’s hard-currency bonds gained across the curve after the report, with notes maturing in 2051 and 2053 among the top performers in emerging markets.

Romania’s markets were jolted by a political crisis following the collapse of a coalition government in May over austerity measures. While the government has curbed the budget deficit more than expected so far this year, the fresh political turmoil has raised concerns over further fiscal improvement in 2027.
President Nicusor Dan has scheduled fresh talks with the country’s main political parties this week, aiming to designate a new prime minister and break a four-month-long deadlock.

Romania narrowly avoided having its debt cut to junk grade at Fitch Ratings in July and Moody’s Ratings also affirmed its score last month. S&P Global Ratings, which similarly assigns Romania the lowest investment grade, with a negative outlook, is expected to publish its review next month.

items.title: Tata Sons IPO Order Backs Reclusive Tycoon's Long-Running Ask
body: The Indian central bank’s refusal to relax listing rules for Tata Group’s holding company delivered an outcome long sought by the conglomerate’s biggest minority shareholder, though the road to going public is far from smooth.

The Reserve Bank of India’s decision came months after reclusive billionaire Shapoor Mistry, who helms the debt-laden Shapoorji Pallonji Group, published an open letter to the regulator seeking a listing of Tata Sons Pvt. to help unlock value for the group’s 18.4% stake. Valued at about $31 billion by Bloomberg Billionaires Index, nearly three-quarters of Mistry’s net worth is coming from the Tata shareholding.

Executives close to SP Group also held meetings with Indian government officials in recent months to press their case, according to people familiar with the discussions, who asked not to be named because they’re not authorized to speak publicly. The executives convinced some senior government officials of potential contagion risk if the construction giant were ever to default, the people said.
Representatives of the RBI, India’s finance ministry, Tata Sons and SP Group did not respond to a request for comment on the regulatory decision last week and what led to it.

The RBI’s decision does not give a timeline for the Tata Sons IPO, which could help resolve SP Group’s broader financial challenges. A potential legal wrangle between Tata and the RBI could stretch this out even further.

The contagion concerns stemmed from the scale of SP Group’s recent bond sale — it was one of India’s largest private credit transactions — where the construction giant raised about 151 billion rupees ($1.6 billion), with global investors including Farallon Capital Management, Davidson Kempner Capital Management and Cerberus Capital Management each buying roughly $175 million to $200 million of the bonds.

The investors were encouraged by prospects that the engineering group could eventually monetize its Tata Sons stake, potentially unlocking billions of rupees in liquidity, according to a July report. Deal terms reviewed at the time indicated an 18-month timeline for monetizing the stake either through a public listing or some other arrangement.

RBI published a list of systemically important shadow banks in September 2022 that included Tata Sons, with a three year timeline to list. While that deadline expired in September 2025, the regulator continued to consider Tata Sons’s petition for an exemption from this list. A year later, the regulator declined to grant a waiver in a relief for the SP Group.

Barely days after sending a letter quashing Tata Sons’ request for an exemption from the listing requirement, the RBI filed a caveat in the Bombay High Court to ensure its position is heard before any order is passed, the Economic Times reported.

In an April statement, Mistry had sought to convince the Indian regulators that a Tata Sons IPO is essential to unlock value for investors, calling it “not merely a regulatory compliance but a necessary evolution.”

“Despite the round-one win awarded to the SP Group’s by RBI’s decision, multiple bouts remain before its debt woes see a clear conclusion,” said Utkarsh Sinha, managing director at boutique investment banking firm Bexley Advisors. “At the heart of SP Group’s desire to list” is their need to monetize their Tata Sons equity.

At the same time, the government could not ignore the implications for the Tata Group, one of India’s most prominent corporate houses, the people said, suggesting there may be room for Tata’s concerns to be taken on board.

The Tata Group, with $185 billion revenue, controls over two dozen listed companies that make everything from salt to luxury cars and offers financial services in India. It is also key to India’s high-end technology ambitions as it has committed to producing the first homegrown semiconductor chips in the western Indian state of Gujarat.

Tata Sons has been contesting its classification as an upper-layer non-banking financial company — a designation that requires such entities to list under RBI’s regulatory framework. The holding company for Tata Group — which owns brands ranging from Jaguar Land Rover and Taj hotels to Tetley tea — has argued that it is not a typical NBFC and should not be subject to rules designed for large lenders, according to the people.

A listing is also seen as problematic for the Tata Group because it could dilute majority shareholder Tata Trusts’ control over Tata Sons, expose the holding company to tighter regulatory oversight and investor scrutiny, and potentially alter the balance of power within the conglomerate, people familiar with the group’s thinking said earlier. Tata Trusts, led by Noel Tata, own 66% in Tata Sons.

People familiar said the situation drew comparisons with another shadow lender, Shanghvi Finance, which was placed in the upper layer alongside Tata Sons in 2022 but avoided the listing requirement after repaying its borrowings and surrendering its registration. Still, in Tata’s case, the people said the regulator was firm that norms governing top tier NBFCs could not be eased.

While the RBI considered Tata Sons’ request for a listing exemption in depth, and its reasoning that it does not accept public deposits, the people said the central bank ultimately chose to stick to the rule.

A RBI circular in May this year made it clear that a shadow lender could not de-register if it deals directly with customers in its day-to-day business. This is not the case with Tata Sons, but it is with Tata Capital. While Tata Sons has pared its own debts, its affiliated companies, including wholly-owned subsidiary Tata Capital, are still raising money from individuals and institutions.

All eyes are now on the critical Sept. 17 board meeting of Tata Sons, where the board directors are expected to focus on the RBI’s directive, the company’s stance to comply or contest this ask and potentially discuss Chairman Natarajan Chandrasekaran’s continuity, the people said.

Chandra had last month announced his decision to step down at the end of his term in February after months of friction with Noel over the listing issue, as well as capital allocation within the sprawling Tata Group.

Besides giving liquidity to SP Group and other listed Tata companies that hold a stake in Tata Sons, a listing will provide capital flexibility to raise funding and “subject the Tata Trusts’ special rights to greater scrutiny,” InGovern Research, a proxy advisory, said in a note Wednesday.
“Now is the time the Board of Tata Sons bells the cat once for all to achieve the best outcome for all stakeholders,” the note added.

items.title: Philippines' Duterte Appears Before ICC After Yearlong Absence
body: Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte made his first public appearance in more than a year on Wednesday at the International Criminal Court, where he’s awaiting trial for alleged crimes against humanity.

Duterte was seen attending live-streamed court proceedings, wearing a dark coat, a white shirt and headphones, with his chin resting on his hand. The presiding judge acknowledged his presence, and said he can leave the court anytime.

Duterte has been out of the public eye since March last year while detained at The Hague for charges over his anti-drug campaign that killed thousands. His arrest was facilitated by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s government after their clans’ political alliance collapsed.

The 81-year-old ex-leader has denied the charges against him. Duterte has been skipping hearings for the past months, saying he’s “old, tired and frail.” However, an ICC chamber in January said he’s fit to join pre-trial proceedings.

items.title: Merz Wins Backing From German Premiers as Pressure Mounts
body: Chancellor Friedrich Merz won backing from a powerful group of German state premiers, defusing for now a challenge to his 16-month tenure as his conservatives brace for deeper losses in a pair of regional elections on Sunday.

Merz’s ruling Christian Democratic Union has been reeling since the party was routed this month in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt by the anti-immigration Alternative for Germany, putting the insurgent party in position to lead the first far-right regional government in the country since World War II.

Much of the blame has centered on the beleaguered chancellor, who has failed to win public trust with a comprehensive reform program, giving rise to speculation that he could be replaced as head of government, potentially by one of CDU state leaders. The declaration on Wednesday strengthens Merz’s position ahead of the Sunday votes.

Restoring trust in the CDU will require “listening and taking political action, not in debates about personnel,” all eight CDU state leaders wrote in a joint declaration seen by Bloomberg. Signatories included Hendrik Wüst, the leader of North Rhine-Westphalia, who had been touted as a potential successor as chancellor.

“People can trust us to tackle their problems. As state premiers, we want to — and will — do our part, together with the chancellor,” they said in the statement, which was first reported by Deutsche Presse-Agentur. The CDU leads governments in half of Germany’s 16 states.

The German leader canceled a trip to the United Nations General Assembly in New York slated for next week, with his office saying his presence in Berlin will be required. He’s also convened a meeting with the CDU party leadership for Sunday evening in Berlin as polls close in the two states, a gathering that usually takes place the day after regional ballots.
Read More: German Far Right Expects Power in Eastern State Sooner or Later

Merz, who told party members that he was “deeply shocked” the day after the Saxony-Anhalt contest, said that the party would take stock after the two further elections this month, adding “there will have to be consequences.” Still, he’s made clear that he’s determined to hold on to power and drive through his reform agenda.

But the calculus could change if the party suffers another setback. The worst-case scenario would be a bruising defeat in the Baltic coast state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, where the party is polling in the single digits. Should it fail to meet a 5% threshold to enter state parliament, it would mark the first time the CDU is ejected from a regional legislature since the federal republic was founded in 1949.

The city-state of Berlin, where the CDU has led a government since 2023, also goes to the polls. Merz’s party risks falling behind the anti-capitalist Left party, though could potentially form a government in the German capital.

In New York, Merz had been scheduled to receive the Henry Kissinger prize and deliver an address to the UN. Instead, he’ll meet with the broader CDU leadership on Monday and with lawmakers from the party’s bloc in the Bundestag on Tuesday.

The state premiers referenced elections next year in France, Italy, Poland, Spain and Greece, signaling that they have no appetite for political instability in Europe’s largest economy that could trigger an election at home.

“That makes a stable and strong Germany in a united Europe all the more important,” the declaration said. Another conservative state leader, Markus Söder of Bavaria, who leads the Christian Social Union, has previously said he has no plans to challenge Merz. The CDU and CSU campaign and caucus together on the national level.

items.title: UK Long Bonds Are Struggling Even as the Government Sells Less
body: The UK’s strategy to prop up its long maturity debt by selling less in the wake of the Liz Truss-era crash is failing to pay off.
Instead the country’s borrowing costs have continued to climb since that meltdown in 2022, taking 30-year bond yields to the highest since 1998. They’re now only a whisker away from 6%.

The move comes despite the UK’s debt agency giving investors much of what they’ve asked for, shifting sales away from long maturities in recent years to match weakening demand from pension funds. And while the Bank of England has still been selling long bonds from its portfolio, a report this week said it may halt that to ease the pain on borrowing costs.
Yet the prospect of even lower supply has done little to settle what’s become one of most sensitive major sovereign bond markets.

“Unfortunately some of it is muscle memory,” said Fred Repton, senior portfolio manager at Neuberger, when asked about the hangover from the Truss era. “It’s starting to look a little bit precarious frankly, the level of yields and the cost of refinancing that is now continuing to increase.”

Bloomberg Economics estimates that, along with inflation, higher borrowing costs will now knock about £16 billion ($21.6 billion) off the government’s £23.6 billion buffer against its fiscal rules, which state that tax must cover all day-today spending in 2029.
Read more: UK Chancellor Healey Vows Fiscal Rigor in First Big Speech

Markets will be scrutinizing the BOE’s comments on bond sales at its policy decision Thursday, and then will focus on the spending policies of new Prime Minister Andy Burnham in a budget due next month. Truss’s plans for unfunded tax cuts in 2022 exacerbated worries about the UK’s fiscal stability, sparking a rout in long maturity debt.

The problem is that policy changes since then are being overwhelmed by forces extending well beyond gilts. Fears of an inflation shock from the Iran war and a global surge in corporate borrowing to finance the artificial-intelligence boom are keeping long-dated yields elevated across markets, limiting any relief from lower local supply.
Read more: Why High Yields on Government Bonds Are Causing Alarm: Explainer

The shift to shorter-dated debt sales by the UK Debt Management Office has been substantial in recent years. The weighted average maturity of UK government debt has fallen far faster than that of global peers, dropping to about 11 years from more than 18 years in 2020.
“When oil is heading higher and higher day on day, then their power is limited,” said Matthew Amis, investment director for rates management at Aberdeen Investments.
The DMO declined to comment, beyond pointing to robust operational results and recent innovations on gilt tenders.

For years, Britain’s defined-benefit pension programs meant demand for long-dated and inflation-linked bonds was near-insatiable. Now many of those UK pensions are fully funded, removing buying support from the market.
“Previously the DMO’s decisions were impacting the market, but now the DMO is more reactionary to where the market is,” RBC strategist Megum Muhic said. “The causal relationship has flipped.”
He said that in the current environment even a halt to the BOE’s sales of long-dated bonds would probably have only a marginal impact.

On Thursday, the BOE is expected to release plans for the next cycle of so-called quantitative tightening, where it reduces its balance sheet. It’s come under fire for selling long maturity gilts at a loss, costing the government billions, and is predicted to reduce the pace at which its portfolio is unwound.
Read more: Bank of England’s Dovish Majority Tested by Oil Price Surge
The BOE already shifted its approach last year, moving away from an even distribution of gilt sales across maturities and skewing them toward shorter-dated debt.

For long-end gilt yields to fall materially, investors say it would probably take something more dramatic. One route would be aggressive BOE monetary-policy tightening that decisively curbs inflation. Another would be a sharp deterioration in the global economy that achieves much the same through weaker growth.

So far, investors are not pricing a marked deterioration in UK fiscal risk. The premium of 30-year gilts over comparable swaps — one gauge of concerns about government borrowing — has been broadly steady this year, even with a change of prime minister.

The first budget by Burnham’s government on Oct. 28 still has the potential to rattle gilts even further in comparison to its developed market peers, according to ING Groep NV strategist Michiel Tukker.
“Near term fiscal spending, that’s the thing that will really freak out markets more and add even more upward pressure on rates,” he said.
Read more: Unusual Calm in UK Pound Is Red Flag to Traders Before Budget
