items.title: Pangram AI Detection Tool Tries to Prove Tech Deception Can Be Caught
body: If students in Joseph Reagle’s Communication in the Digital Age class last spring planned to have Claude or ChatGPT do their assignments, they found out early in the semester it might not go well. Reagle told everyone that, among other checks, he planned to run their writing through an artificial intelligence detector called Pangram.

Reagle, a former Massachusetts Institute of Technology research engineer who’d been a professor of communication studies at Northeastern University for 15 years, had recently discovered AI misuse by students almost by mistake. He’d assigned another class to contribute to Wikipedia, telling them the work had to be substantively their own and not a chatbot’s. But Wiki Education, a nonprofit helping with the assignment, used Pangram to review the submissions and detected multiple apparent violations of Wikipedia’s ban on AI content. Some students seemed to have just copied and pasted AI output.

Undisclosed AI was popping up everywhere by then: legal filings, research papers, newspapers and especially the internet. Much of it was so terrible that Merriam-Webster had named “slop” — bad AI content — its word of the year. Methods of spotting AI had until recently been unreliable, though, and the best-known detectors, from companies like Turnitin LLC and Grammarly, often made mistakes. Pangram was gaining a reputation among tech insiders for being the rare product that actually worked.

The startup behind the detector, Pangram Labs Inc., said that in testing, it caught AI in 99.98% of documents where it was present, with a false positive rate — when real writing is mistaken for AI — of just 1 in 10,000. Reagle often doubted companies’ claims, but he trusted Wiki Education and found outside research that deemed Pangram effective. He decided to pay out of pocket for it and use it alongside other methods, such as reviewing students’ draft histories. He’d give zero credit to assignments he concluded had relied too much on AI. And if students doubled down when confronted, he’d refer them to the university office dealing with code-of-conduct violations.

Pangram wasn’t yet mainstream, but it soon would be. In March, the New York Times’ Alexandra Alter reported that it had flagged AI in more than three-quarters of a horror novel called Shy Girl that was soon to be published in the US by Hachette Book Group. The book’s author, Mia Ballard, said an editor she’d hired had added the material, not her. Hachette still canceled publication. After that, people deployed Pangram to turn up all kinds of alleged AI use: in major newspapers’ articles, LinkedIn posts, the script for a YouTube video from the influencer Hank Green, even small portions of Pope Leo’s encyclical. (Green confessed; the pope didn’t comment.)

In nerdy corners of the internet, Pangram experimentation became a kind of parlor game. Come up with 100 random words, and Pangram correctly called them human. Prompt a chatbot to do the same, and Pangram caught it. Write an essay in Russian and use AI to translate it into English, and Pangram would recognize its human origins. Have a chatbot craft the Russian version before translating it, and Pangram identified the AI roots. One person had a chatbot invent a conversation between a dog and a cat — “Bark. Meow? Bark.” went one exchange — and posted it alongside Pangram’s assessment: “100% of this text is AI.”

This past July, with the detector’s profile rising, Menlo Ventures announced a $9 million round of seed funding for its maker — at a valuation of $50 million, according to someone familiar with Pangram who requested not to be named because the details aren’t public. The following month, about 222,000 people used the tool, up from 7,000 the previous August; revenue rose 24-fold across the same period, though the company remains unprofitable. While a vast majority of users were running the detector for free — Pangram offers 2,000 words of checks per day at no cost, plus a free browser plug-in that can scan online text in real time — increasing numbers paid for a premium version starting at $20 a month.

The company had a small but growing list of institutional customers too. The University of Chicago and Wellesley College signed up. Major publishing organizations began testing it. Substack integrated Pangram into its app so readers could scan any post. “We’re sick of slop and we don’t want substack to turn into LinkedIn,” Chris Best, the chief executive officer, posted bluntly on X.

But a backlash had also been growing. “While Pangram is accumulating the power to end reputations and careers, the tool does make mistakes, perhaps to a greater extent than is currently understood,” the Atlantic’s Matteo Wong wrote in May. A few months later, Wong’s colleague Will Oremus wrote about Pangram flagging AI use in a recently released high-profile novel, the Simon & Schuster romance bestseller Daggermouth, by H. M. Wolfe. Wolfe denied it all and suggested Pangram had been mistaken, and Simon & Schuster stood by her. Substack writers, meanwhile, were complaining about the potential for witch hunts.

All this comes at a high-stakes time for Pangram, and for anyone concerned about an impending slopocalypse. The company is pitching its product to universities, school districts, publishers, law firms and consulting firms. It’s also close to finalizing a Series A funding round at a higher valuation, according to the person familiar with the company. But if it’s to win over everyone with an interest in halting the flow of chatbotese into human thought and communication, it will have to answer an existential question: Can we really trust Pangram to tell the difference?

Pangram’s founders, Max Spero and Bradley Emi, have been close since moving in across the hall from each other their freshman year at Stanford University. They bonded over their competitiveness at board games and a shared habit of staying up all night. Emi expected to become a physics professor, and Spero hoped to found a startup. Instead, the gravitational pull of Silicon Valley drew them both into AI jobs at major tech companies: Spero at Google, at one point, and Emi at Tesla Inc.

Then, four years after the pair graduated, OpenAI released ChatGPT, and Spero made a prescient prediction: With the high cost of producing text suddenly falling to basically nothing, people would end up buried in synthetic babble and would need to sort it out from authentic communication. He played around with some existing AI detectors, and they seemed awful. Studies bore this out.

Detectors at the time essentially gauged a text’s variety and unpredictability — supposed signs of human authorship, since chatbot output tends to be uniform. But that approach didn’t work well for non-native writers with smaller vocabularies and less varied styles or for AI text that people had modified even slightly. Spero wanted to solve the detection problem, and he invited Emi to help. They floated the idea to friends at AI labs, who told them, “Don’t do that. It’s probably not possible,” Emi recalls. But Spero felt that the complexity made it an exciting business bet.

Plus, Emi had a novel approach in mind. He’d worked at Tesla under an AI legend, OpenAI co-founder Andrej Karpathy, who would later join Anthropic PBC. Karpathy impressed upon Emi that an AI model’s success often relies on the size and diversity of the data used to train it. Emi wondered if he could apply that principle to an AI detection model. But training one wouldn’t just require lots of diverse writing from people. It would require lots of diverse AI output as well — a challenge given the maddening sameness of what chatbots produce.

Emi came up with a method he called “synthetic mirroring.” He’d gather the required human documents, then prompt the models behind commercial chatbots to generate paraphrased versions of each one. That way, the material would be varied enough, in keeping with its human provenance, while still carrying the stylistic quirks of AI.

In the fall of 2023, Spero and Emi quit their jobs and started what would become Pangram, each investing $20,000 of their savings. Spero was living in New York and Emi in Cambridge, Massachusetts, so Emi traveled back and forth to Spero’s apartment, where they worked at an 8-foot folding table.

Before long, they were stuck. The mirroring was doing what they’d hoped, but only to a point. When they tested the model on samples of both human- and AI-generated texts, it kept tripping on edge cases in which real writing sounded chatbot-esque. It happened a lot, Emi says, with BuzzFeed articles from the pre-ChatGPT era. So he fed the difficult cases back into the training data, crossing his fingers that the model would get better at assessing them.

That December, Emi tested a new iteration; when he saw the results, he immediately messaged Spero. The new model, he wrote, “crushes it on all accounts.” Within months, their internal testing was finding almost complete accuracy, with minuscule false positive rates (including for non-native English writing).

Spero and Emi released Pangram in July 2024 — and were met with near-total silence. “Like, crickets,” Spero recalls. The founders had raised a $1.25 million round of pre-seed funding, but they still hadn’t hired anyone else, and they’d only recently moved from Spero’s folding table to a coworking space nearby. The closest thing to marketing they’d done was to post on X and update a research paper they’d published months earlier on the preprint site arXiv with a link to their website.
Reddit communities focused on evading AI detection noticed Pangram, though. A few people tried it out, and soon they were starting to panic a little.

Tuhin Chakrabarty noticed a post about Pangram on Reddit in the fall of 2024. “I’ve just come across the killer ai detector, am depressed,” its title read. The poster had tried and failed to fool Pangram. Chakrabarty, who’d just finished a Ph.D. in computer science at Columbia University, considered AI detection impossible. But he gave Pangram a shot, and it worked. He read the arXiv paper and was more impressed still. “It came across to me as something very credible,” he recalls. He started integrating Pangram into his research; over time, he and Spero became friends.

By 2025, Pangram’s name was appearing in academic papers, not just from Chakrabarty but from more established names in the field. Mohit Iyyer, a computer science professor at the University of Maryland at College Park, co-authored a conference paper that called Pangram’s accuracy “near-perfect.” Researchers at the University of Chicago’s Becker Friedman Institute for Economics published a working paper finding Pangram to be the only detector they tested with a low enough error rate to be useful: “Near zero,” they concluded.

Spero and Emi felt validated, but AI users were getting more sophisticated. Some would manually edit synthetic prose to rough up its telltale sameness, maybe with the help of free “humanizer” tools. Others would feed rough drafts to chatbots and request makeovers. Pangram’s black-and-white approach, tagging text as either human or AI, was starting to seem limited.

That summer, having raised another $2.7 million, Pangram hired Katherine Thai, a Ph.D. candidate in computer science at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, as an intern; after graduating, she stayed on as a research scientist. Thai had studied English as an undergraduate at Rutgers University, and her senior thesis was a close reading of the novelist Kazuo Ishiguro. (“A reader finds repetition, long-windedness, and a liberal sprinkling of qualifying adjectives.”) Now, Spero and Emi proposed that Thai get Pangram to detect what they referred to, diplomatically, as “AI assistance.”

This required, for one thing, imagining all the ways someone might ask a chatbot for help. Thai made a list with colleagues’ help, down to hypothetical prompts: “Make this an A paper.” “Rewrite this so it sounds good.” She asked chatbots to suggest other prompts and added those as well. Then, using fully human and fully AI documents along with AI-assisted ones, she trained a model to recognize when text reflected not just people or AI, but a commingling of both.

In the fall of 2025, a venture capitalist at Menlo Ventures named Deedy Das came across Pangram. He’d been looking for startups that could address problems AI was creating, including the proliferation of slop. (Menlo also funded the problem creators, of course; Anthropic is a marquee investment.) Das casually tested Pangram and came away impressed. “It’s shameful how small Pangram is,” he wrote to a friend; several less reliable competitors had higher market share. He reached out to Spero and arranged a call. When Pangram needed more money, Das told Spero, he’d be waiting to lead a round of funding. “The bet was that I really believe that technical differentiation matters here and that these guys have it,” says Das, who’s since been named a partner at Menlo.

In December 2025 the company released Pangram 3, the model Thai had trained to address the tricky middle ground of AI assistance. I discovered the tool around that time and started doing informal experiments with my own fiction and journalism. I never got a false positive. Once, while I was reporting on AI turning up in the New York Times and other newspapers, a source notified me that Pangram had detected AI in an opinion article I had myself published in the Times. Alarmed, I started formulating a defensive comeback before remembering that my article had quoted some exchanges with ChatGPT. Pangram had been right to flag it.

I did, however, notice Pangram mistaking material I knew to be AI-assisted for human-written. At one point my dad sent me an essay he’d edited with ChatGPT about a move he’d made to Florida decades earlier. Pangram called it human.

I wasn’t alone in testing the limits of Pangram’s abilities: A whole how-to genre was emerging, with people fooling the detector and documenting the steps online. Emi remembered Karpathy’s adage about data; he thought a bigger model might help. This February, Menlo Ventures led the promised round of funding, and Pangram’s founders put some of the money toward training a detection model six times larger than the existing one.

Over the summer, researchers at Belgium’s Vrije Universiteit Brussel published the results of a test of four detection tools in the International Journal for Educational Integrity. They found that Pangram was more than 95% accurate in spotting the ones that had drawn on AI, compared with 0% to 60% for the others. And it didn’t misidentify any human-written papers as AI-generated.

In July, Pangram released Pangram 4; it cut the false positive rate to about 1 in 24,000 in internal testing. I tested my dad’s Florida essay again, and this time Pangram caught the AI use. The company also unveiled a beta version of an AI detector for images.

Spero and Emi had set out to solve a problem no one had cracked before. On a technical level, they’d basically done it. But now they were discovering a facet of the problem that they hadn’t fully appreciated. Building an AI detector people will trust turned out to be not just a technical question — it was a cultural one too.

By summertime the bad press was piling up. First came Wong’s Atlantic article, with the headline “America Has a Pangram Problem,” in which he argued that even a minuscule false positive rate could lead to unfounded accusations. Spero and Emi had actually advised from the start that no one depend on Pangram results alone to determine AI use, and organizations using it tended to agree. Nonetheless, Wong’s concern was widely shared. That July, in another high-profile case, novelist Jerry Falade lost a $2 million book deal partly because of a Pangram finding. Falade denied relying on AI, pointing to the chance of false positives.

People who dislike AI in any form were also wary of Pangram. They compared it to the large language models whose content it detects, arguing that it, too, relies on the exploitation of natural resources, labor and creative production. There are definitely similarities between the models. However, Pangram’s is a smaller one that classifies content rather than generating it, a task that tends to require far less energy and water for servers than an LLM. It also hires US-based employees or contractors for menial tasks, steering clear of the kind of low-paid offshore labor that’s been used to build some LLMs. And while it trains its models on content from the internet and other sources, that material is licensed or in the public domain. Pangram also says it doesn’t train on the stuff people scan with its tool.

Still, the founders are far from the vanguard of the AI resistance. “AI itself is a very special technology,” Spero says. While he worries about the biggest companies’ concentration of power, he also sees AI as a way to help people accomplish far more than they otherwise could. He himself uses it to code. He even mentions that AI companies could use Pangram to help them distinguish between human- and AI-generated content in training their models. (On the question of whether that’s already happening, he declines to comment.)

While Spero accepts the principled objections to AI products, he’s grown less generous with another group of critics: people who take aim at Pangram’s effectiveness without evidence. Online, if someone made a claim that rang false to him, he might dig up that person’s writing and publicize how much of it Pangram deemed AI-generated — often, a lot. He offered a $100 reward to a stranger who claimed Pangram flagged a 30-year-old textbook as 100% AI, if the person would share the textbook itself. They didn’t. He put a copy of Daggermouth, the romance novel whose author denied AI use, on his shelf at home; he’d been quick to notice typical AI verbiage in it. (One character, for example, is called Elara — a name chatbots suggest so often that it’s become a meme.) “I’m an AI book collector,” he says wryly. “It’s a piece of history.”

Critics have cast Spero’s rhetorical campaign as mean-spirited and self-serving. Emi says his friend is generally good at taking heat, but when people make claims he knows to be improbable, “it’s hard for him to have a really thick skin.” Spero, for his part, tells me he isn’t trying to be mean or score internet points: “We’re actually in a critical period of norm-setting around AI content. If it is taboo to mention that others are posting AI-generated words as their own, then that will be where the norm settles.”

A lot of Spero’s campaign involved simply explaining how the product works. He’d point out, for example, that Pangram’s much-cited false positive rates are based on tests with documents of varied lengths. When people caught false positives on social media posts, he’d readily acknowledge that errors are more common with the shortest documents. But because mistakes generally fall significantly as the amount of text increases, Spero was steadfast in his skepticism about denials from novelists and from Substackers who get flagged repeatedly. Pangram’s internal testing places its false positive rate at essentially zero for books, and the Vrije Universiteit and University of Chicago studies reinforced this too. (I also asked Chakrabarty, now a professor of computer science at Stony Brook University, to try Pangram on 50 randomly sampled novels that had been self-published before ChatGPT’s introduction; he, too, found a false positive rate of zero.)

Spero also notes that basic grammar and spelling edits from an AI product typically don’t trigger a finding of AI — only more extensive changes do. In July, he posted a Substack comment acknowledging complaints about alleged false positives on the site. His tone was diplomatic, but he added that he hadn’t seen “much evidence so far that these are actual false positives, as opposed to cases of underdisclosed AI use.” Often, when a stranger made an unsupported claim about Pangram errors on social media, he’d write something like, “got any examples? dms open.” Half the time, he says, he doesn’t hear back.

It’s doubtful AI detection will ever be 100% foolproof; Spero and Emi both acknowledge as much. But people seem to be coming around to the idea that it can be immensely useful despite the occasional lapse. In August, a Nature article called out Pangram’s “remarkable results”; days later, Time named Spero one of the 100 most influential people in AI. Claire Von Schilling, a spokeswoman at Penguin Random House, the world’s largest trade publisher, reveals that it’s using Pangram to help identify potentially AI-generated content. (She specifies that such tools “are only one component of a broader editorial process.”)

How people end up using this technology, if it continues to be effective but imperfect, is an open question. Maybe at some universities, Pangram flags will be included in students’ files, with disciplinary action taken only if it keeps happening. Maybe some news organizations will summarily reject sloplike freelance submissions. Maybe more websites will share Pangram’s assessments with readers — as Substack already does — and let them decide how to treat the information. Maybe book publishers will rely solely on Pangram, if they’re convinced of the slim chance of errors for long documents. And maybe conscientious AI objectors will reject Pangram altogether.

At Northeastern last spring, Reagle did end up referring a few students for possible discipline. After the semester ended, he ran an informal experiment, giving Pangram hundreds of samples turned in for his digital communications class before AI chatbots existed. It got them all correct — fully human. Then he did the same with 50 samples each from several semesters after ChatGPT’s release. For the earliest batch, it detected AI in 6% of assignments; the figure peaked at 42% the semester before he started running homework through Pangram. Once monitoring began, the share fell back to 6%.

As a deterrent, his approach seemed to have worked. And yet the policing left him exhausted and demoralized. “It’s a very confrontational, oppositional stance,” he says. At the end of the semester, he received some of the worst teaching evaluations of his career.

Reagle recognizes that students will be graduating into a world saturated with AI content, and that employers might well encourage them to create it themselves. He’s grown so unsure about what this all means for communication — and how to teach it — that instead of faking it, he’s decided to retire early, at 55, after the coming school year.

No one can predict all the implications of a world filled with synthetic text, but some are coming into sight. People have started absorbing chatbot-isms into their lives: Parents are naming their kids Elara. Podcasters are using the word “delve.” Emi says he fears that, as humans sound more like AI, false positives could get harder for Pangram to avoid.

Over Zoom one night, I ask Spero about the future. He’s had a long day and says he hopes I don’t mind his multitasking, folding laundry as we speak; he seems both exhausted by a growing cascade of slop and energized by the challenge it presents.

As we discuss where it all might be heading, I start to grasp the extent to which AI language could corrupt communication and thought. “A lot of the AI content today is produced by humans who are just lazy, but in the limit, that’s not really what we’re solving for,” he says. Novels produced by Claude are not, to his mind, the biggest long-term problem. He lays out a future in which AI agents deployed by content farms outnumber people on the internet 1,000 to 1, disseminating mass-produced junk everywhere.

While Spero worries aloud about the loss of trust and connection that could ensue, my thoughts go to an even darker place. People are already absorbing chatbots’ linguistic tendencies — what about their ideological ones? Just a few AI companies dominate the US market, and their products don’t simply produce less varied language than people do — they also tend to generate a narrower range of ideas, disproportionately reflecting Western values. Some research suggests chatbots could even be biased toward AI itself.

If Pangram is successful, Spero envisions, we’ll be able to filter out synthetic content, leaving only the authentic communication. “The utopian idea is basically that we can still have the internet that we love that has connected billions of people, and we can also have this world where AI is a force multiplier in everybody’s lives, without polluting the commons,” he says.

In that light, Pangram’s eventual role could be like that of a spam filter. On occasion, a legitimate email might get routed away from our inboxes, but we generally consider that a reasonable trade-off. And if a human-authored article or novel reads like spam, we don’t mind rejecting it out of hand.
There’s another characteristic slop has in common with spam, though: The people generating it are persistent. And now they’ve got the chatbots on their side.

The day after my call with Spero, someone posts online that they’ve created a lab offering better AI-generated writing; they claim Pangram is labeling 86% of their output as human. “Our main goal is better writing, fooling AI detectors is just a side effect,” they say. I email Spero about it, but he sounds unbothered: New humanizers pop up all the time, and Pangram will improve its detection of this one if it gets any traction. “There is definitely a cat-and-mouse aspect of it, but that’s part of what we’re signing up for,” he writes.

Curious whether the cat is catching this particular mouse yet, I visit the lab’s website and try out the generator. To my eye, the stuff it produces is neither coherent nor grammatical. It’s clearly, mortifyingly, slop. I paste some examples into Pangram, hopeful. It calls them human. —With graphics by Susan MerriamRead next: How AI Is Changing the Skills MBA Students Need to Learn

items.title: John Wilson's 'The History of Concrete' Takes on $1.4 Trillion Market
body: The concrete world is so immense that most attempts to tackle the subject, including Robert Courland’s definitive 424-page book Concrete Planet, go big. They talk about how concrete is the defining material of modernity, how it spans the globe and civilizations, and how it contributes enormously to global warming (in the manufacture of cement) and coastal erosion (a byproduct of concrete’s insatiable demand for sand).

It’s easy to see why: The numbers associated with concrete are mind-bogglingly enormous. As Ted C. Fishman reported for Bloomberg Businessweek in his own 11,500-word story, it’s a market of $1.4 trillion per year; it accounts for more than half of all the stuff, by weight, that humans have created over the past couple of thousand years; and we collectively produce more than three tons of concrete per human being on the planet every year. China’s $167 billion Medog Hydropower Station alone is going to use an estimated 300 million tons of concrete by 2033.

The freshness of the documentary The History of Concrete, which opens in New York on Sept. 18, is that filmmaker John Wilson, whose TV series How To with John Wilson had three successful seasons on HBO, doesn’t go big.

Don’t be misled by its title: With the exception of a few seconds’ worth of the Pantheon and the Hoover Dam, and a quick shot of a highway interchange, this film isn’t designed to awe you with concrete’s world-transforming power. Courland’s book does get a very brief shout-out, but the movie’s focus, insofar as it has anything to do with concrete at all, is the way in which concrete fails us in our everyday lives. Think less planetary destruction and more annoying cracks in the sidewalk.

Wilson is a master at taking something quotidian, such as concrete, and using it as a jumping-off point for a discursive and digressive visual essay on the quirks and absurdities of modern life. The 102-minute runtime of this film, his first feature, allows him enough space that the main character in the movie (besides Wilson himself) doesn’t even appear until more than halfway through. That said, perhaps the real main character is you, the viewer — Wilson constantly refers to himself in the second person, a subtle way of making us feel as though the indignities he suffers through are our own, and that many of them are caused, one way or another, by concrete.

At one point, Wilson travels to Bellefontaine, Ohio, to drive down Court Avenue, the oldest concrete street in America; he finds it falling apart. (The burghers of Rome can be thankful that the Pantheon hasn’t had to endure decades of being driven on by two-ton pickup trucks.) He spends a lot of time in his own Brooklyn home, worrying about water leaking through the concrete floor of his basement or watching municipal workers fixing the sidewalk slabs in front of his window. His camera lingers on the yellow tape marking trip hazards, the disintegration of the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway, and the cracks marring the white concrete surface of Rafael Viñoly’s New York “skinnyscraper” at 432 Park Avenue. He interviews a woman who drops out of an endurance race because the concrete she’s running on was too hard; he also casts a skeptical eye on the pro-construction agenda of former New York City Mayor Eric Adams.

Wilson is a man who knows concrete, but, like much of the rest of the country, he doesn’t much seem to like concrete, which, as building materials go, is pretty unlovable, hard and unforgiving rather than organic and beautiful. Whenever he’s given the opportunity, he leaps at the chance to digress and turn to something completely different, like, for instance, a very touching and human story of an aspiring rock musician.

Of all building materials, concrete usually feels the most unnatural. In the hands of a master it can be transcendent — but those moments are the exceptions, not the rule, and even then they tend to be appreciated mostly by lovers of modernism. In our daily lives concrete construction often presents itself as a problem, something decaying and in need of repair. (The American Society of Civil Engineers estimates the amount of money needed to fix existing US infrastructure is $9.1 trillion; most of that is concrete in one form or another.)

Wilson talks a lot about how concrete construction lasts for only 40 years, a statement that obviously isn’t true (the Pantheon, which he visits in Rome, is nearly 2,000 years old) but that contains a kernel of truth: Concrete is so ubiquitous that the only time most people even notice it is when it’s broken in some way. A lot of the cheap concrete construction from the 1960s and 1970s has not been well maintained — it looks so impregnable, it can be hard to imagine how fragile and rust-prone it really is — which has led to concrete being associated in the public mind with stains and ugliness and disrepair. When something like New York’s pro-development City of Yes legislation arrives, the first reaction can often be “there’s too much ugly construction already, I don’t want more, not even if you call it affordable housing.” Zool Zulkowitz, a member of Manhattan’s Community Board 5, went so far as to call Adams’ proposal “the final dehumanization of the New York City streetscape.”

The History of Concrete is not a polemic — quite the opposite. But that’s precisely what makes it so interesting as a window into the often contradictory strands of public opinion on the subject. Wilson, in a previous show, took on the subject of scaffolding in New York, nearly all of which is ostensibly in place to protect the public from bits of buildings falling onto pedestrians below. Viewed from that angle, almost all urban buildings are inherently dangerous — and since that construction invariably involves vast quantities of concrete, all of which is going to age in an unpredictable manner, it’s easy to see where undercurrents of mistrust can originate.

The perennial fight between NIMBYs and YIMBYs is normally framed as a battle of abstract concepts. Terms such as urban density, housing prices, neighborhood character, carbon footprint, automobile dependency and more get thrown back and forth in debates that can get extremely heated. Underneath all that, however, is the lived experience of walking down a concrete sidewalk, passing concrete buildings and getting stuck in traffic behind hulking concrete mixer trucks with their instantly recognizable rotating drums. Wilson’s documentary is a useful reminder that most people would welcome less of all that, even if it’s necessary for us all to have somewhere to live.

items.title: Scaremongering About 5% Bond Yields Misses the Point
body: Investors and households are superstitious about round numbers, especially 5% yields on 10-year Treasury notes that influence mortgage rates and other borrowing costs. Rockefeller International Chairman Ruchir Sharma wrote in the Financial Times that the “AI bubble could pop” when the yield “decisively” breaches that level. Morgan Stanley’s Chief Investment Officer Mike Wilson recently described a rise above 5% as “the biggest risk to this consolidation turning into a correction” for US stocks.

Why can’t this economy and market handle a breach of 5%? Yields last eclipsed that level in 2023, accompanied by even more frightening commentary. Pessimists believed at the time that the economy was being sustained by a fading cash cushion left over from pandemic transfers and years of involuntary saving, and that we’d face a reckoning once the cash ran out. Projections of a late 2023 or early 2024 cash cliff never panned out. Rather than a meltdown, the intervening years have seen corporate profits, household wealth and the S&P 500 Index all surge to new records; debt service ratios remain relatively low; and the broad economy produce above-average growth.

Now, we’re right back there again. Yields on the 10-year note hit 5.04% on Tuesday (though they were hovering just under 5% at the time of writing), following a precipitous 1.12-percentage-point climb from recent lows in early March. As a consequence, 30-year fixed rate mortgages were quoted at 7.17%.

These yields aren’t easy for many people, nor are they good politics for Republicans ahead of this year’s midterms. Younger and less wealthy households are struggling to buy their first homes, with affordability near the worst in decades. Despite low unemployment, hiring is weak and could get weaker if businesses must pay more to borrow, hurting the same cohort disproportionally. That demographic is right to feel that the economy is letting them down, and they can reasonably blame President Donald Trump and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who vowed to bring 10-year yields down and has failed. Some part of that broken promise reflects the surge in energy prices caused by the US-Israel war with Iran, and another part is due to Congress’s failure to address the gaping budget deficit.

Higher market rates are, however, just as much a reflection of strong economic growth at the aggregate level — a perfectly normal feature of a humming, if uneven, economy. Ten-year yields averaged about 5.8% in nominal terms from about 1990 through 2007, and today’s 2.6% inflation-adjusted, or real, yields look close to average.

The difference is that we’ve emerged from the anomalously weak 2008-2021 period in which nominal growth was uniquely low and global central bank policy was extraordinarily accommodative. Now, the Federal Reserve and other monetary authorities are pulling back support, and artificial intelligence investment is booming, putting data center construction crews and equipment suppliers to work and enriching households with money in the stock market. Ultimately, that’s also supporting consumption. At this pace, yields probably won’t be coming down much in the foreseeable future. As my colleagues in Bloomberg Economics wrote recently, “Long rates are close to where fundamentals say they belong.”

There may well be considerable risks to the boom’s sustainability, but too-high Treasury yields are least among them. On the investment side, many tech hyperscalers and generative artificial intelligence companies report annual AI revenue growth of well over 100%. It’s almost laughable to think that a 1 or 2 percentage point move in borrowing costs might dissuade decision-makers from investing, especially in the context of a technological arms race with China. If anything will stop the boom, my money is on AI safety risks or a failure to adequately monetize the technology, rather than a modest increase in funding costs.

The 10-year yield is also a relatively small factor for household consumption today. Among households’ major expenditures are healthcare; energy and travel; and discretionary goods and services. The former (near 17.1% of personal consumption) is as rate insensitive as humanly imaginable, driven by an aging population and paid for with insurance. Consumption of gasoline and transportation services (5.5% of PCE by weighting) depends on developments in the Strait of Hormuz, not yields. And most components of the umbrella “other services” and “other nondurable goods” categories are similarly insensitive to yields. (That’s collectively another 16.6% of consumption and includes cellular service and internet, auto-pay categories that most households tend to set and forget.)

So where’s the the impact from longer-term yields felt? If the stock market were to crash as a result of the bond adjustment, that would certainly crimp consumption. But 10-year yields tend to compress price-earnings multiples, and recent history has shown that surging earnings are more than enough to compensate for a slipping price-to-earnings ratio. A stock market correction brought on by higher long-term yields would probably be a “near-term” affair, Morgan Stanley’s Wilson said this week. Higher rates, he added, “still look more like a strong-growth story.”

If bonds leave their mark at all, they’ll do so through the housing market, which has been in a slump for years. This has played out with people staying in their homes longer, rather than swamping the market with supply. The result is a long-lasting rut in turnover, rather than a housing crash. That might have affected the economy in the past through construction employment, but current circumstances are distinct: Thanks to data centers, construction employment is running at around 6% of private nonfarm payrolls, well above the 1980-2019 average.

These yields aren’t just survivable; they’re also an entirely normal sidecar of an economy with an encouraging growth outlook. Americans would certainly be better served by a healthier mix of growth (a bit more), inflation (a bit less) and fiscal largesse (a great deal less with a serious commitment to deficit reduction). But 4%-5% yields aren’t going away anytime soon, and we might even learn to tolerate them if they come hand in hand with a strong and sustainable expansion.

items.title: Rio's Crime and Corruption Are Shaping Brazil's Presidential Election
body: Framed by Rio de Janeiro’s lush green mountains and the fabled sands of Copacabana beach, Flávio Bolsonaro launched his campaign for the presidency declaring that Brazil had “lost its sovereignty” to organized crime.
It was a fitting location to deliver his core message aimed at unseating President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

Rio de Janeiro is a place of staggering beauty, and of equally grandiose dysfunction. A city consumed by crime, corruption and broken promises, it’s at once Bolsonaro’s base and a source of controversy for him, as well as the scene of the defining scandal of the 2010s that continues to shape voter views of the veteran leftist known universally as Lula.
Leia em português.

As the Oct. 4 first-round vote approaches, the federal campaign is turning on concerns about organized crime and a $10 billion bank fraud case that’s reignited a sense that Brazil is governed by corrupt elites. It’s all-too familiar for Rio, whose confluence of graft and violence — and the remedies prescribed for its ills — has become symbolic of the wider race to govern Latin America’s heavyweight nation, for both main candidates.

“Rio’s main problem is political,” said Mauro Osorio, an economist at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro who studies the history of the city and its eponymous state. “Everything else is a consequence of that.”
The Bolsonaro clan and the devotion they induce sit at the heart of that political story.

Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, won election after election in Rio on the strength of his famous last name, and now he’s attempting to parlay the brand of politics forged there into a path to Brazil’s top job. It’s a familiar script.

A decade ago, his father, Jair Bolsonaro, a one-time army captain and career Rio lawmaker, catapulted to national prominence and ultimately the presidency by railing against a rotten political establishment. Along the way, he left his mark on the city’s politics, building alliances with Rio’s power brokers and winning over millions of voters.
Even as the elder Bolsonaro sits under house arrest for attempting a coup after losing his 2022 reelection bid to Lula, support for the city’s premier political family endures.

“They are the country’s solution,” said Jorge Santos, 73, a retired mechanical engineer, among the crowds in Copacabana in mid-August as Flávio Bolsonaro opened his election campaign. “If he doesn’t win, we’re headed straight to the bottom.”

The contest showcases the dirty politics that became legend in Rio before spilling onto the national stage. With polls showing a dead heat going into the elections, Flávio Bolsonaro is leaning on the battle-tested formula his father launched in Rio and took nationwide: hammering opponents on crime and corruption.

His message has been complicated by his ties to former Banco Master SA owner Daniel Vorcaro, the jailed banker at the center of a massive financial fraud probe. Bolsonaro in May acknowledged that he’d sought funding from Vorcaro for a film about his father.

His is a pitch forged in Rio. The nation’s one-time capital draws throngs of selfie-snapping visitors with its golden coastline and intoxicating samba. But away from the beachfront enclaves, life is no Instagram reel.

Gangs control many of Rio’s working-class neighborhoods, including the orange-bricked favelas that climb its hills and ring the city. Public services are shoddy. And politicians elected on promises to restore law and order are often in cahoots with the crooks.
Rio’s top prosecutor minced no words after authorities dismantled yet another graft scheme in July, this one allegedly siphoning more than $15 million from public coffers.

There is an “institutional environment geared toward corruption,” Rio state attorney general Antônio José Campos Moreira said. “Numerous state structures, bodies that should provide services to citizens, have been co-opted by criminals.”

Brazilians have a simpler explanation: mar de lama — a sea of mud that has swept up people, parties, and political campaigns. No one knows this better than the cariocas, as residents of Rio are known.

Every Rio governor elected this century has ended up behind bars, impeached or barred from seeking office. The former head of Rio’s state legislature has been in jail since March on suspicion of obstructing an investigation into the assembly’s links to drug traffickers.
That culture of graft helped propel Jair Bolsonaro from the back benches of Congress to the presidential palace in the wake of Operation Car Wash, Brazil’s biggest corruption scandal to date.

The investigation, which kicked off in 2014, exposed systemic bribery centered on state oil giant Petroleo Brasileiro SA, or Petrobras, whose  Brutalist headquarters sits in downtown Rio. It sent titans of Brazilian business and politics to prison, including Lula, who served more than a year in jail on corruption convictions that were later quashed.

Even today, Lula, 80, remains tarred by the decade-old scandal that ran through Brazil’s second-biggest city. The fallout drained Brazilians’ faith in their institutions, preparing the ground for the country’s deep polarization, and priming the public for Bolsonaro’s outsider message.

Bolsonarismo “arose during a period of political decay, when Lula and the Workers’ Party had become mired in corruption,” Otoni de Paula, a Rio congressman and pastor who was once an ally of the former president, said in an interview.

In 2018, Jair Bolsonaro stormed to the presidency promising to make Brazil safer by showing no mercy to law-breakers. It was a message that had long resonated with Rio’s crime-weary voters, who had already elected members of his family to positions of power across the state.

“When they went national, they attracted voters out of conviction,” said Celso Rocha de Barros, a columnist for the newspaper Folha de S. Paulo in Rio. “But here in Rio, it was different. They already had a political machine.”

A native of the state of São Paulo, Jair Bolsonaro launched his political career in Rio after serving in the army. He built his profile by advocating for greater benefits for members of the armed services, a popular cause in the city with Brazil’s largest concentration of military installations. He later helped propel two of his sons into Rio’s corridors of power.

Flávio Bolsonaro, who spent much of his youth in the north Rio neighborhood of Tijuca, won election to the state legislature at age 21 and went on to serve four terms. His brother Carlos held a seat on Rio’s city council for nearly 25 years before leaving office last year.
Following his father’s lead, Flávio Bolsonaro, a lawyer by training, made a name for himself in Rio’s legislature by pushing for tougher penalties for criminals and a freer hand for police.

Homicides have broadly been falling in Rio, in line with a wider decline across Brazil, but crime and insecurity still cost the state more than $6 billion a year, according to a study by Firjan, Rio state’s industry federation.

Historians trace many of the problems facing the Marvelous City, as it’s known to its admirers, to the transfer of Brazil’s capital to Brasília more than half a century ago, which stripped Rio of government ministries and crucial drivers of its economy. Rio has been casting about for a new economic identity ever since. Political repression under the military dictatorship that lasted for two decades until 1985 spawned sprawling networks of patronage.
In time, that transformed Rio’s politics into what Osorio, the economist, calls a tropical version of southern Italy, where cronyism went rogue.
“What began as clientelism gradually became a mafia,” he said.

For all the Bolsonaro clan’s calls to clean up the system, members of the family have faced scrutiny over their own links to Rio’s underworld. Flávio Bolsonaro, in particular, has been dogged by questions about ties to alleged members of militias, armed groups with roots in law enforcement that control swaths of the city. He denies any involvement with militias.

Bolsonaro’s campaign did not respond to an emailed request for comment on past allegations of corruption and misconduct during his time as a state lawmaker, or on the Federal Police investigation into his relationship with Vorcaro.

Rio’s cops have long drawn scrutiny in Brazil and globally for their brutality. But the 2018 assassination of city councilwoman Marielle Franco by a former police officer with militia ties laid bare the nexus between law enforcement, organized crime and Rio’s political establishment, and so became a cause célèbre for the fight against impunity.
“Militias don’t emerge without politicians,” said Cecília Olliveira, director of Fogo Cruzado, an organization that tracks violence in Brazilian cities. “It’s a partnership.”

As a state lawmaker, Flávio Bolsonaro honored Adriano da Nóbrega, a former police captain accused of leading one of Rio’s militias, with the state legislature’s prestigious Tiradentes Medal and employed members of Nóbrega’s family on his legislative staff. He has said Nóbrega’s relatives were hired at the recommendation of an aide.

Even an apparent fainting episode in a live televised debate during a 2016 run for Rio mayor barely slowed his ascent. Two years later, as his father took the presidency, Flávio Bolsonaro rode a wave of voter anger at the long-ruling Workers’ Party into the Senate.

Questions about his time as a state deputy followed him there. In 2020, Rio state prosecutors charged Flávio Bolsonaro with embezzlement, money laundering and other crimes stemming from an alleged scheme to skim part of staffers’ salaries, a practice known in Brazil as a rachadinha.
He has denied the allegations. Higher courts later invalidated key evidence on procedural grounds, prompting prosecutors to drop the case before it went to trial.
In the Senate, Flávio Bolsonaro continued to champion the type of heavy-handed policing that drew applause in Rio. Back home, those tactics have only grown harsher.
Last year, Rio’s then-governor, Claudio Castro, a Bolsonaro ally, oversaw Brazil’s deadliest police operation on record, which resulted in the death of more than 120 people in a single day.

The stated goal was to capture leaders of Comando Vermelho, or Red Command, Rio’s dominant gang. But the operation terrified residents of Complexo da Penha, a cluster of favelas where much of the bloodshed occurred — even as it exposed the widespread support in Brazil for the type of shoot-first policing that has long been a fact of life in the city.
With drug traffickers still entrenched in Penha, residents like Thaís Barbosa, 32, a mother of three, are left wondering how to escape the crossfire.

As gun battles raged during the police offensive last October, gang members burst into Barbosa’s home to hide from their pursuers. The family was locked in a bedroom while officers swept through the neighborhood and eventually found their targets.

The police ordered the family onto the veranda while they dealt with the men. Barbosa recalls hearing gunshots and once the raid subsided her family took refuge at her sister’s home. Neighbors later found three dead on Barbosa’s concrete rooftop.
“There is nowhere left to run,” she said.
Across town in Copacabana last month, Flávio Bolsonaro was promising a way out, vowing to clamp down on gangs and clean up Brazil’s political system.
His larger issue may be simply convincing voters he can fill his father’s shoes. It’s a challenge he seemed to acknowledge during his stump speech.
“I know I look like him. But it’s hard to compare the son of Pelé to Pelé,” he said, referring to the Brazilian footballing legend.

Some in the crowd appeared to agree. Edison Sousa, 64, a retired metalworker, said he was confident Flávio Bolsonaro would win the presidency, but conceded that the rally was a far cry from the days when his father would pack Copacabana with supporters.
“Jair brought the people out,” he said. “This is another story.”

items.title: Flávio Bolsonaro desafía a Lula en Brasil con discurso de crimen y corrupción
body: Con las exuberantes montañas de Río de Janeiro y las legendarias arenas de Copacabana como telón de fondo, Flávio Bolsonaro lanzó su campaña presidencial con una declaración contundente: Brasil había “perdido su soberanía” ante el crimen organizado.
El escenario era perfecto para transmitir el mensaje central con el que busca desbancar al presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

Río de Janeiro combina una belleza deslumbrante con una disfunción igualmente monumental. Marcada por el crimen, la corrupción y las promesas incumplidas, la ciudad es a la vez la base política de Bolsonaro y una fuente de controversia para él, además del escenario del escándalo que definió la década de 2010 y que todavía moldea la percepción de los votantes sobre el veterano líder de izquierda conocido universalmente como “Lula”.

A medida que se acerca la primera vuelta del 4 de octubre, la campaña nacional gira en torno a dos grandes preocupaciones: el crimen organizado y una crisis bancaria de US$10.000 millones que ha reavivado la percepción de que Brasil está gobernado por élites corruptas. Es una combinación demasiado familiar para Río, donde la confluencia de corrupción y violencia —y las respuestas para combatirlas— se ha convertido, para los dos principales candidatos, en un símbolo de la contienda nacional por gobernar al gigante latinoamericano.

“El principal problema de Río es político”, dijo Mauro Osorio, economista de la Universidad Federal de Río de Janeiro que estudia la historia de la ciudad y del estado del mismo nombre. “Todo lo demás es consecuencia de eso”.
El clan Bolsonaro y la devoción que despierta están en el centro de esa historia política.

Flávio Bolsonaro, de 45 años, encadenó victorias electorales en Río gracias al peso de su famoso apellido y ahora intenta convertir el estilo político forjado allí en una vía hacia la presidencia de Brasil. La fórmula es conocida.

Hace una década, su padre, Jair Bolsonaro, excapitán del Ejército y veterano legislador de Río, irrumpió en la política nacional y acabó llegando a la presidencia tras arremeter contra un establishment político que describía como podrido. En el camino, dejó su huella en la política de la ciudad, forjó alianzas con figuras poderosas de Río y conquistó a millones de votantes.

Incluso ahora que Bolsonaro padre se encuentra bajo arresto domiciliario por intentar un golpe de Estado tras perder su intento de reelección en 2022 frente a Lula, el apoyo a la principal familia política de la ciudad perdura.

“Ellos son la solución del país”, dijo Jorge Santos, de 73 años, ingeniero mecánico jubilado, entre la multitud congregada en Copacabana a mediados de agosto cuando Flávio Bolsonaro inició su campaña electoral. “Si no gana, nos vamos directo al fondo”.

La contienda revive la política turbia que se hizo legendaria en Río antes de proyectarse al ámbito nacional. Con las encuestas mostrando un empate de cara a las elecciones, Flávio Bolsonaro vuelve a la fórmula que su padre puso a prueba en Río y luego llevó a todo el país: atacar a sus rivales con los temas del crimen y la corrupción.

Ese mensaje, sin embargo, se ha visto complicado por sus vínculos con Daniel Vorcaro, expropietario de Banco Master SA y banquero encarcelado que está en el centro de una enorme investigación por fraude financiero. Bolsonaro reconoció en mayo que había buscado financiamiento de Vorcaro para una película sobre su padre.

Su discurso político se forjó en Río. La antigua capital del país atrae a multitudes de visitantes que se toman selfies junto a su costa dorada y se dejan seducir por la samba. Pero lejos de los enclaves frente al mar, la vida dista mucho de parecerse a un reel de Instagram.

Las bandas controlan muchos de los barrios populares de Río, incluidas las favelas de ladrillos anaranjados que trepan por las colinas que rodean la ciudad. Los servicios públicos son deficientes, y los políticos elegidos con promesas de restablecer la ley y el orden a menudo terminan confabulados con los delincuentes.
El fiscal general de Río fue tajante después de que las autoridades desmantelaran en julio otro esquema de corrupción que presuntamente desvió más de US$15 millones de las arcas públicas.

Existe un “entorno institucional orientado a la corrupción”, dijo el fiscal general del estado de Río, Antônio José Campos Moreira. “Numerosas estructuras estatales, organismos que deberían prestar servicios a los ciudadanos, han sido cooptados por delincuentes”.

Los brasileños tienen una forma más sencilla de describirlo: mar de lama, un mar de lodo que ha arrastrado a personas, partidos y campañas políticas. Nadie lo sabe mejor que los cariocas, como se conoce a los habitantes de Río.

Todos los gobernadores de Río elegidos en este siglo han terminado tras las rejas, destituidos o inhabilitados para ocupar cargos públicos. El exjefe de la asamblea legislativa estatal de Río está encarcelado desde marzo bajo sospecha de obstruir una investigación sobre los vínculos del órgano legislativo con narcotraficantes.

Esa cultura de corrupción ayudó a impulsar a Jair Bolsonaro desde los márgenes del Congreso hasta el palacio presidencial tras la Operación Lava Jato, el mayor escándalo de corrupción registrado hasta ahora en Brasil.

La investigación, iniciada en 2014, reveló un amplio sistema de sobornos centrado en el gigante petrolero estatal Petroleo Brasileiro SA, o Petrobras, cuya sede de estilo brutalista se encuentra en el centro de Río. Llevó a prisión a prominentes figuras de los negocios y la política brasileña, incluido Lula, quien pasó más de un año encarcelado por condenas de corrupción que posteriormente fueron anuladas.

Incluso hoy, Lula, de 80 años, sigue cargando con el estigma de aquel escándalo de hace una década que sacudió la segunda ciudad más grande de Brasil. Sus secuelas minaron la confianza de los brasileños en sus instituciones, prepararon el terreno para la profunda polarización del país y dejaron al público más receptivo al mensaje antisistema de Bolsonaro.

El bolsonarismo “surgió durante un período de decadencia política, cuando Lula y el Partido de los Trabajadores se habían visto sumidos en la corrupción”, dijo en una entrevista Otoni de Paula, congresista y pastor de Río que alguna vez fue aliado del expresidente.

En 2018, Jair Bolsonaro arrasó en las elecciones presidenciales con la promesa de hacer de Brasil un país más seguro y no mostrar piedad con quienes violaran la ley. Era un mensaje que llevaba años resonando entre los votantes de Río, cansados del crimen y que ya habían elegido a miembros de su familia para distintos cargos de poder en el estado.

“Cuando dieron el salto a la política nacional, atrajeron a votantes por convicción”, dijo Celso Rocha de Barros, columnista del periódico Folha de S. Paulo en Río. “Pero aquí en Río era distinto. Ya tenían una maquinaria política”.

Oriundo del estado de São Paulo, Jair Bolsonaro inició su carrera política en Río después de servir en el Ejército. Se hizo conocido por defender mayores beneficios para los miembros de las fuerzas armadas, una causa popular en la ciudad que alberga la mayor concentración de instalaciones militares de Brasil. Más tarde ayudó a impulsar a dos de sus hijos hacia los círculos de poder de Río.

Flávio Bolsonaro, quien pasó buena parte de su juventud en el barrio de Tijuca, en el norte de Río, fue elegido para la asamblea legislativa estatal a los 21 años y cumplió cuatro mandatos. Su hermano Carlos ocupó un escaño en el concejo municipal de Río durante casi 25 años antes de dejar el cargo el año pasado.

Siguiendo el ejemplo de su padre, Flávio Bolsonaro, abogado de profesión, se hizo un nombre en la legislatura de Río promoviendo castigos más severos para los delincuentes y mayor libertad de acción para la policía.

Los homicidios han disminuido en Río, en línea con un descenso más amplio en Brasil, pero el crimen y la inseguridad aún le cuestan al estado más de US$5.000 millones al año, según un estudio de Firjan, la federación de industrias del estado de Río.

Los historiadores sitúan el origen de muchos de los problemas que enfrenta la Ciudad Maravillosa, como la llaman sus admiradores, en el traslado de la capital de Brasil a Brasilia hace más de medio siglo, que privó a Río de ministerios y otros motores clave de su economía. Desde entonces, la ciudad ha buscado una nueva identidad económica. La represión política durante la dictadura militar, que se prolongó durante dos décadas hasta 1985, también dio lugar a extensas redes de clientelismo.
Con el tiempo, eso transformó la política de Río en lo que Osorio, el economista, describe como una versión tropical del sur de Italia, donde el amiguismo se salió de control.
“Lo que comenzó como clientelismo se convirtió gradualmente en una mafia”, dijo.

A pesar de los llamados del clan Bolsonaro para limpiar el sistema, miembros de la familia han sido objeto de escrutinio por sus propios vínculos con el submundo criminal de Río. Flávio Bolsonaro, en particular, ha enfrentado durante años cuestionamientos sobre sus lazos con presuntos miembros de las milicias, grupos armados con raíces en las fuerzas de seguridad que controlan amplias zonas de la ciudad. Él niega cualquier vínculo con las milicias.

La campaña de Bolsonaro no respondió a una solicitud de comentarios enviada por correo electrónico sobre antiguas acusaciones de corrupción y mala conducta durante su etapa como legislador estatal, ni sobre la investigación de la Policía Federal en torno a su relación con Vorcaro.

La policía de Río ha sido durante mucho tiempo objeto de cuestionamientos en Brasil y en el extranjero por su brutalidad. Pero el asesinato en 2018 de la concejala Marielle Franco a manos de un expolicía con vínculos con las milicias dejó al descubierto el nexo entre las fuerzas del orden, el crimen organizado y el establishment político de Río, y se convirtió así en un caso emblemático de la lucha contra la impunidad.
“Las milicias no surgen sin políticos”, dijo Cecília Olliveira, directora de Fogo Cruzado, una organización que monitorea la violencia en ciudades brasileñas. “Es una asociación”.

Cuando era legislador estatal, Flávio Bolsonaro otorgó la prestigiosa Medalla Tiradentes de la asamblea legislativa a Adriano da Nóbrega, un excapitán de la policía acusado de liderar una de las milicias de Río, y contrató a miembros de su familia para integrar su equipo legislativo. Ha dicho que los familiares de Nóbrega fueron contratados por recomendación de un asesor.

Ni siquiera un aparente desmayo durante un debate televisado en vivo, cuando hacía campaña por la alcaldía de Río en 2016, frenó significativamente su ascenso. Dos años después, mientras su padre conquistaba la presidencia, Flávio Bolsonaro llegó al Senado impulsado por una ola de enojo de los votantes contra el Partido de los Trabajadores, que llevaba años dominando la política.

Los cuestionamientos sobre su etapa como diputado estatal lo acompañaron hasta el Senado. En 2020, fiscales del estado de Río acusaron a Flávio Bolsonaro de malversación, lavado de dinero y otros delitos derivados de un presunto esquema para quedarse con parte de los salarios de sus empleados, una práctica conocida en Brasil como rachadinha.
Él ha negado las acusaciones. Tribunales superiores invalidaron posteriormente pruebas clave por motivos procesales, lo que llevó a los fiscales a abandonar el caso antes de que llegara a juicio.
En el Senado, Flávio Bolsonaro siguió defendiendo la política policial de mano dura que era aplaudida en Río. En su estado natal, esas tácticas solo se han vuelto más severas.

El año pasado, el entonces gobernador de Río, Claudio Castro, aliado de Bolsonaro, supervisó la operación policial más letal de la historia de Brasil, que provocó la muerte de más de 120 personas en un solo día.

El objetivo declarado era capturar a líderes del Comando Vermelho, o Comando Rojo, la principal banda criminal de Río. Pero la operación aterrorizó a los residentes del Complexo da Penha, un conjunto de favelas donde se concentró gran parte de la violencia, y puso de manifiesto el amplio respaldo que existe en Brasil a una estrategia policial de disparar primero, desde hace mucho habitual en la vida cotidiana de la ciudad.
Con los narcotraficantes todavía atrincherados en Penha, residentes como Thaís Barbosa, de 32 años y madre de tres hijos, se preguntan cómo escapar del fuego cruzado.

Mientras los enfrentamientos armados se intensificaban durante la ofensiva policial de octubre pasado, miembros de una banda irrumpieron en la casa de Barbosa para esconderse de quienes los perseguían. La familia quedó encerrada en un dormitorio mientras los agentes recorrían el vecindario hasta que finalmente dieron con sus objetivos.

La policía ordenó a la familia salir a la terraza mientras los agentes se ocupaban de los hombres. Barbosa recuerda haber escuchado disparos y, una vez terminado el operativo, su familia se refugió en la casa de su hermana. Más tarde, los vecinos encontraron tres cadáveres en el techo de concreto de la vivienda de Barbosa.
“Ya no queda ningún lugar al que huir”, dijo.
Al otro lado de la ciudad, en Copacabana, Flávio Bolsonaro prometió el mes pasado una salida: combatir a las bandas criminales y limpiar el sistema político de Brasil.
Su mayor problema quizá sea simplemente convencer a los votantes de que puede estar a la altura de su padre. Es un desafío que pareció reconocer durante su discurso de campaña.
“Sé que me parezco a él. Pero es difícil comparar al hijo de Pelé con Pelé”, dijo, en referencia a la leyenda del fútbol brasileño.

Algunos entre la multitud parecían estar de acuerdo. Edison Sousa, de 64 años, un metalúrgico jubilado, dijo estar convencido de que Flávio Bolsonaro ganaría la presidencia, pero admitió que el mitin estaba muy lejos de aquellos días en que su padre llenaba Copacabana de simpatizantes.
“Jair sacaba a la gente a la calle”, dijo. “Esta es otra historia”.
Traducción editada por Malu Poveda.
Nota original: Rio de Janeiro Emerges as Crucible for Brazil’s Ugly Politics

items.title: Turkish Stocks Slump After Fund Default Heightens Investor Fears
body: Turkish stocks suffered sharp losses on Wednesday, after an asset manager’s failure to meet redemption requests sparked wider liquidity concerns.

The Borsa Istanbul 100 Index fell 6% earlier in the session, triggering a market-wide circuit breaker. Losses deepened to as much as 7.7% before the index pared some of the move to close 5.5% lower. The decline extended the benchmark’s two-day loss and marked its biggest such slump since March 2025.

The selloff came after Pusula Portfoy Yonetimi AS said Tuesday that some of its investment and money market funds were no longer able to meet redemptions requests after facing withdrawals worth billions of liras since the end of August.
Read More: Turkish Manager Fails to Meet Redemptions as Some Funds Crash

Investors have grown concerned about some funds after Turkey introduced ruleas aimed at reining in strategies involving concentrated positions in relatively illiquid stocks. According to financial data platform Fintables, a net 55 billion liras ($1.13 billion) were withdrawn from Turkish investment funds on Wednesday.

“Growing concerns regarding the soundness and liquidity of funds’ collateral appear to have heightened the risk that other funds and companies may also face difficulties,” BVeri Consulting founder and economist Banu Kivci Tokali told Bloomberg by phone.
“The deepening of the loss of sectoral confidence has played a significant role in the rising wave of selling in the markets” Tokali said.

The latest drop follows months of concern among some market participants over strategies used by certain investment funds, including concentrated exposure to relatively illiquid stocks. Strong returns at some funds and sharp gains in some equities had prompted debate over valuations, liquidity and trading patterns.
Read More: Turkish Funds Urge Action as Stock Swings Threaten MSCI Status

Turkey’s capital-markets regulator tightened investment guidelines at the end of August, with the new rules bringing certain limits and caps on particularly hedge funds’ exposures to related parties and concentrated investments.

After Pusula Portfoy said some of its investment and money market funds were unable to meet redemption requests, Tera Group, which had agreed to acquire Pusula’s portfolio management and securities businesses, said separately that the transaction hasn’t yet been completed and that it isn’t responsible for redemption processes.

“Defaults led to unease in the market, leading to increased demands for fund withdrawals,” said Alper Akalin, founder of financial advisory firm Akalin Finance. “Those withdrawal demands likely led asset managers to sell initially their more liquid positions, in this case index-member stocks, to meet requests,” Akalin said.

“These are all repercussions of the new guidelines introduced by the Turkish regulator. Some of the positions held by the asset managers, that would be expected to make most adjustments accordingly, are largely not very liquid stocks. So they’re opting to sell liquid holdings to balance cash positions,” Akalin added.

For now, the stress appears largely contained to the stock market. The lira was little changed as it traded less than 0.1% lower at 48.6571 per US dollar as of 7:18 p.m. Istanbul time. Turkish government bonds fell, with the yield on two and 10-year notes rising 76 basis points and 61 basis points, respectively. The five-year credit default swaps were up by 6 basis points to 236.

“Unless the liquidity problem broadens materially beyond the fund-management sector, we don’t see it altering Turkiye’s underlying macro, lira carry or sovereign-credit story,” said Tufan Comert, executive director of global markets strategy at BBVA.
“The main near-term uncertainty is how long the deleveraging and redemption cycle lasts and how far prices overshoot before liquidity conditions stabilize.”

items.title: Frasers Tightens Grip on Hugo Boss as CEO Murray Named Chairman
body: Frasers Group Plc strengthened its hold over Hugo Boss AG after its Chief Executive Officer Michael Murray was named chairman of the German fashion house.

The elevation of Murray, who is also son-in-law of billionaire Frasers owner Mike Ashley, follows months of pressure on Hugo Boss from its largest shareholder. After a takeover bid failed to give it a majority stake, Frasers made clear it still wanted to build a controlling position and also questioned the role of Stephan Sturm, who announced his departure as chairman on Monday.
Read: Hugo Boss Chairman Sturm to Step Down Amid Frasers Pressure

Hugo Boss, known for its pricey suits and underwear, is in the middle of a second turnaround plan since current Chief Executive Officer Daniel Grieder took the helm in 2021. Frasers is pushing more into luxury under Murray, and has long sold Hugo Boss products in its stores and online.

Hugo Boss has “significant untapped potential,” Murray said Wednesday, adding that his aim is to create “sustainable value for all shareholders and stakeholders.” Frasers declined to comment beyond the statement.

Shares of Hugo Boss were little changed in Frankfurt on Wednesday. Frasers shares fell as much as 4.6% in London, the most in two months on an intraday basis. They were up about 16% this year through Tuesday’s close.

Frasers’ growing influence over Hugo Boss has triggered fears among some investors about the loss of board independence. The retailer’s former company secretary Robert Palmer is also expected to join the Hugo Boss board.

“To ensure credibility in the capital markets and protect the rights of all shareholders, an independent supervisory board chairman will remain indispensable in the future,” Ingo Speich, head of sustainability and corporate governance at Deka Investment, said before Murray’s appointment.

Hugo Boss had advised shareholders not to accept Frasers takeover offer, which ultimately left Ashley’s company with a stake of close to 48%. In Wednesday’s statement, Grieder said Murray has “consistently supported the strategic direction” of his program and will work closely together with him.

items.title: Senegal Joins JPMorgan List of African Frontiers Set For New Bond Index
body: Senegal, the cash-strapped nation that recently agreed a $2.2 billion bailout from the International Monetary Fund and is seeking to rework its debts, is among African sovereigns included in a new frontier-markets bond index being introduced by JPMorgan Chase & Co.

The continent will account for almost 45% of the Government Bond Index–Emerging Markets Edge, with Egypt and Morocco representing the largest contributions from Africa by weight. Nigeria, Kenya, Uganda and Ivory Coast are among other issuers on the index from the region.

Senegal’s weight in the index is just 0.34%, compared with 8% for Egypt and Morocco. The West African nation is the continent’s most distressed issuer, with a sovereign risk premium trading at 1,639 basis points over US Treasuries, according to a separate index run by the Wall Street lender.

Since being locked out of global capital markets in 2024 after the discovery of billions of dollars in hidden debt, the nation has relied on the regional market for raising finance through local currency auctions.
Read More: Senegal Makes Request for Debt Treatment Under G20 Framework

It intends to exclude local currency borrowing from a debt treatment that it announced on Sept. 1, when it reached a staff-level agreement for a three-year facility with the IMF. It has since made an official request for the revamp to be done under the Group of 20’s Common Framework.

Senegal’s plan to ring-fence local currency debt has encouraged investors to maintain their support. The most recent debt auction held Sept. 11 raised $179 million. JP Morgan said it will include two local currency instruments from the West African nation which it values at $654 million in the index.

“The index is less about finding the next high yielder and more about defining the Frontier beta,” JP Morgan analysts wrote in a note to describe the index, which they said will track around $328 billion in debt across 425 instruments, spanning 26 markets and 24 currencies.
Read more: JPMorgan Adds Nigeria to Bond Index After Progress on Reforms

items.title: Sweden's Parties Stake Out Positions as Election Result Looms
body: Sweden’s political parties are laying out their starting points for talks to form the next government as they wait for a final election result to be confirmed in Stockholm.

Overseas and late-arriving advance votes were set to be counted on Wednesday with a final tally due either later that same day or on Thursday. Opposition parties headed by Social Democrat Magdalena Andersson held 176 seats versus 173 for the ruling bloc led by Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson — with 95% of votes counted.

If Andersson retains her preliminary lead, which experts say is the most likely final result, then tricky talks lie ahead as she tries to unite the pro-business Center Party and the Left Party around a common economic platform. Center has said it won’t back a government containing Left while the Left won’t support an administration it isn’t part of.

Even if Andersson’s opposition bloc is declared the winner early on Thursday, the ensuing period of political horse-trading could take weeks to resolve. In the last election, it took 37 days for Kristersson’s governing coalition to be formally sworn in, while in 2018 the process lasted 134 days.

“How can anyone think the Left Party is going to back down?” The party’s deputy leader, Ida Gabrielsson, wrote in a post on social media on Wednesday. “The Left Party made the biggest gains and has the most reasonable demand of all — namely, that everyone whose support is needed should be included.”
Gabrielsson also called on the Center Party to acknowledge to its voters the “logic” of the election result, which demands that they “pick a side and move on.”

Highlighting the potential impasse, Center Party secretary Hannes Hervieu told state broadcaster SVT that Swedish politics cannot “be divided into just two sides.” He added that, “we have been clear that we don’t want the Left Party in government. Rather, we want to work with the Social Democrats.”
Leaving parliament late Tuesday, Social Democrat leader Andersson told reporters she is “in continual contact with several parties.”

items.title: EU Unveils Social Media Curbs for Kids and Ban on Users Under 13
body: The European Union is working to ban social media for kids under 13 and restrict the use of technology and artificial intelligence services for older children, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in her annual address Wednesday.

“No social media under the age of 13. No personal account under the age of 15,” von der Leyen said. The bloc will permit 13- and 14-year-olds to have accounts with parental supervision and limited features, she added.

The comments come ahead of the presentation of a new EU Kids Act proposal on Thursday. The draft law would impose strict age-gating and age verification obligations on social media, video-sharing platforms, app stores, online games, AI companions and conversational AI chatbots, Bloomberg reported on Monday. Companies failing to meet the requirements could face fines of as much as 6% of their annual sales.
Read More: EU Draft on Social Media Limits Sees Fines of Up to 6% of Sales

The EU has been under pressure from member states to introduce bloc-wide rules as the global movement to restrict children’s access to social media gains steam. Individual EU members states have been planning their own limits in the wake of curbs introduced by Australia last year.
The Kids Act proposal still has to obtain the backing of European governments and lawmakers, a process that can take years.
