items.title: McLaren to Open New Car Plant in Rare Boost for UK Industry
body: McLaren Automotive Ltd. plans to open a new UK factory as the supercar-maker gears up for its first sport utility vehicle, a welcome boost for Prime Minister Andy Burnham just days after Jaguar Land Rover announced thousands of job cuts.

The company said it will create 1,000 new jobs by 2032, investing £500 million ($674 million) in the additional assembly facility and its headquarters in Woking, Surrey, where it makes its sports cars, as well as a carbon-fiber manufacturing site in Sheffield.
The location of the new factory is still being finalized, Chief Executive Officer Nick Collins said in an interview, though it’s exploring options elsewhere than Woking.

The news will provide relief for Britain’s beleaguered car industry and follows JLR’s plans to cut 4,000 roles as it tries to stay competitive. Separately, Nissan Motor Co. announced Wednesday it’s investing £170 million to build a new hybrid SUV at its Sunderland factory, Britain’s largest car plant.

High costs across Europe have piled pressure on the region’s carmakers, but the UK’s steep energy costs have made manufacturing particularly challenging. Burnham is trying to lift employment rates, especially among young people.
The investment will “create high-quality apprenticeships, jobs and drive growth far beyond their factory gates,” the prime minister said in a statement.

New Abu Dhabi-based owner L’imad Holding Co. is trying to reboot McLaren, which for years has been strapped for cash. The company had to tap its former shareholders for emergency funding on several occasions amid delays to its Artura sportscar. In recent years, it sought other ways to raise funds, including selling assets such as its heritage car collection and its advanced technologies arm, as well as completing a sale and leaseback of its Woking headquarters.

L’imad took control of the company recently after Abu Dhabi’s CYVN Holdings LLC transferred ownership to the other state entity, which also now owns Chinese electric-vehicle maker Nio Inc. CYVN had bought McLaren from Bahrain’s Mumtalakat last year. McLaren’s owner paid off its debts, Collins said, as he set about turning the company around, starting with reining in production volumes to match demand.
Read More: McLaren Sells Off Prized Vintage Supercars in Liquidity Crunch
The car industry in Europe is “changing, and the worst thing to do is to be in denial of that and wait for it to come to you,” Collins said.
The CEO now plans to broaden McLaren’s appeal beyond hardcore racing fans with the company’s first SUV, putting it in competition with the likes of Ferrari NV and Lamborghini.
“It’s very much a performance SUV,” Collins said. “There’s a lot of people who would love to take more than one passenger in their car or use it for different lifestyles or different purposes.”

The new model will be the latest in a long line of luxury and sportscar brands to start selling an SUV. “In the way we’re going to do it, there’s absolutely space for another one,” said Collins, who plans to grow in the US, already the company’s largest market.

Producing an SUV is a “no-brainer” according to Chief Operating Officer Michael Straughan. “We’re well known for rear-engine, rear-wheel-drive sportscars and supercars, but you’re almost capping what you can produce because of that,” he said. McLaren currently produces roughly 2,200 cars a year.
Read More: McLaren F1 Team Valued at More Than £3 Billion in Stake Sale
The company looked at building the plant in other European countries, but ultimately decided on the UK. The government isn’t providing financial support as part of the investment, Collins said.
McLaren also said it will make its own engines in the future, rather than outsource production.

The company is banking on increased consumer demand on the back of the success of the Formula One team. It’s riding high after securing the team title for the past two seasons, with driver Lando Norris winning the driver’s championship last year.

items.title: Gender Equality to Take 120 Years Even as Gap Narrows, WEF Says
body: Global gender parity remains more than a lifetime away for women even though the gap with men is now smaller than ever, according to the World Economic Forum.

The Geneva-based organization’s annual report on the matter, released on Wednesday, found that current progress means it will still take 120 years to reach full equality. That’s a marked improvement, and up from 170 years measured a decade ago, but it still means that no-one alive today is likely to experience it.

The WEF’s report combines indexes of political empowerment, economic participation and opportunity, health and survival and educational attainment to assess gender disparity across the world. The overall gap across 145 economies has narrowed to 69.4%, the best result recorded in two decades of such reports.

“Gender parity is achievable — economies at every income level have made progress, so the barrier is not a lack of resources,” said Saadia Zahidi, managing director at the WEF. “To accelerate, governments and employers need to learn from the policies that work and apply them faster.”

The category gaining the most ground in the last 20 years is political empowerment — even as parity there is almost two centuries away. There is now one female minister for every 4.3 male peers, up from 8.1 in 2006.
In parliaments, the ratio has moved from one woman for every 5.6 men to every three or so.

Politics is also the dimension showing the clearest signs of reversal, scoring lower than it did in 2016. The number of female heads of state peaked in 2022, the highest in half a century, and has since fallen back.
Women have advanced in other leadership roles. Within the C-suite, they hold 19% of chief executive officer positions and around a quarter of chief financial officer and chief operating officer jobs.

Even so, women remain particularly underrepresented in the most powerful corporate roles. They hold fewer than a fifth of those that typically lead to top jobs, while dominating positions such as chief human resources officer and chief people officer.

And within artificial intelligence, women remain in a minority at every level. Fewer than one in five AI engineers are female, and they are more concentrated in data annotation roles, which often pay less than engineering jobs.

“Progress toward gender parity in leadership has stalled for a fourth year,” said Sue Duke, managing director for EMEA & Latam and head of global public policy & economic graph at LinkedIn. “Based on the current trajectory, girls born today will not see equal representation at the top in their lifetime. And the issue is even more pronounced for women working in AI roles.”

On a geographical basis, Europe leads in closing the overall gender gap, followed by North America, while the Middle East and North Africa lag. That latter region had a later start but has steadily stepped up efforts to become the most reform-intensive part of the world in the current decade.
Iceland topped the report’s rankings for the 17th consecutive year, with 93% of the gender gap closed. It remains the only country to have eradicated more than 90% of its disparity.
LinkedIn’s Duke highlighted that in times of economic slowdown, there typically is a reversal in women getting leadership roles.
“Every time there is a hit, we will default to old patterns,” she said. “For years in row, women’s roles in leadership has not only stalled, but also gone backwards.”

items.summary_zh: 世界经济论坛报告显示，全球性别差距已缩至69.4%，但实现完全平等仍需120年。

items.title: EU Chief Asks Canada to Become Bloc's First Associate Member
body: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed Canada becoming the first associate member of the European Union, forging a novel transatlantic alliance as President Donald Trump tears apart the old one.
She offered the invitation during her state of the union address in Strasbourg, France, Wednesday, with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in attendance.

“In this new world, we must urgently reimagine our partnerships and build global coalitions for our resilience and democracies,” von der Leyen said. “I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada being the first associate member of the European Union.”

By creating a tailor-made title just for Canada, the EU is sending a powerful signal as a trading bloc that it can expand beyond its borders and reinvent itself in the aftermath of Brexit, when it lost an economic powerhouse. What this means in practice is another matter, with negotiations likely to take years. Significantly, it also suggests a path for the UK to re-stitch its ties with the EU, though with Canada ahead in terms of establishing what associate membership will entail.

Regular membership of the EU entails a lengthy accession process and comes with rights, like access to the single market, as well as financial, fiscal and legal obligations. There is no precedent for associate membership, and proposals earlier this year to offer a “membership light” to Ukraine faced backlash from many member states.

Certain countries like Iceland, Norway, Liechtenstein and Switzerland, however, have special arrangements with the bloc on topics such as the free movement of goods and people. Iceland two weeks ago rejected reopening talks with the EU over full membership.

Carney warned earlier this year that the “rules-based international order” was effectively dead and has made repeated calls for so-called middle powers to band together to oppose the pressure tactics and intimidation of the world’s dominant economies. Bloomberg reported earlier that the transatlantic allies were in talks to forge a new alliance to ensure their security.
Von der Leyen also discussed closer cooperation with Canada on manufacturing, tech, defense and energy, and cited the Arctic as a “flagship joint project.”

Carney’s government, economically shaken by a trade war with the US, has made a deeper EU partnership and other partners a top priority. After US-Canada talks ended last month, Trump imposed 50% tariffs on $20 billion of goods imported from Canada, and Carney soon retaliated with tariffs on a roughly equal amount of US-made products.

Canada’s focus is on concluding the ratification of CETA, the EU-Canada Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, an accord that was negotiated a decade ago but that still hasn’t been formally approved by 10 European countries, according to people familiar with the discussions.
Carney and von der Leyen held a meeting in Strasbourg. Afterward, his office said Canada seeks a “far stronger, more ambitious alliance in the future” with the EU.

“This includes critical minerals, defense industrial capacity, AI and compute, energy security, space, as well as financial services and payments,” the prime minister’s office said in a statement. “The leaders also discussed moving toward seamless digital trade in non-agricultural goods and a wide range of services.”
Outstanding issues with the bloc also include ironing out differences over EU’s carbon pricing tool on imported goods and its deforestation and pesticides rules.

Bloomberg reported earlier that EU officials see the potential to pursue a closer relationship with Canada than with the UK. The EU views Canada as successfully implementing a so-called sovereignty agenda on economic and defense matters — a campaign that could inform the bloc’s own push to cut foreign dependencies. Furthermore, Canada doesn’t have the Brexit baggage London carries.

“We already are looking at how to increase the trade, what we can do in research and innovation, how we can cooperate more in defense, and also how we can support each other in all the multilateral negotiations, if it comes to WTO and other trade negotiations,” EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic told reporters in Strasbourg after the speech.
Sefcovic said he would meet his Canadian counterpart, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne later Wednesday.
Canada, unlike the UK, has been granted access to SAFE, the bloc’s €150 billion ($173 billion) loan program for defense procurement.

Canada and the EU will be expected to make progress ahead of their summit in Montreal in October, at which they could sign a digital trade agreement that it’s been in the works, said the people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity.
“Europe and Canada believe in democracy,” von der Leyen said. “That power does not belong to the strongest, the richest or the loudest.”

items.title: Tiny Village Votes to Leave UK in Protest Over Migrant Housing
body: A tiny village in England voted in a symbolic referendum to secede from the UK over the government’s plans to house 1,200 male asylum seekers at a site nearby.

The local parish council at Piddington, a leafy village near Oxford with a population of 400, held the vote — which has no legal force — in protest against the Home Office’s plans to accommodate the migrants at a former military barracks half a mile away. More than 90% of the 300-plus people who voted opted to leave the UK, results announced Wednesday showed.

The UK’s asylum system has become a flashpoint for community tensions in recent years, with public concerns over the thousands of people crossing the Channel in small boats from France to reach Britain contributing to the rise of Nigel Farage’s right-wing Reform UK party.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he would be “relentless” in tackling small-boat crossings. And the Labour government has pledged to stop using hotels — at one point costing the government more than £8 million ($11 million) a day — to house migrants while their asylum claims are being processed, turning instead to sites like the one near Piddington.
Cabinet minister Lisa Nandy told BBC Radio on Wednesday that while the government is listening, “we’re not going to change our plans.”
“We do hear the clear frustration of the community in Piddington,” Nandy said. “I do want to reassure people that we are getting a grip on this.”

Local residents in areas like the Oxfordshire village have raised concerns about community safety, environmental impacts and the strain on local infrastructure from the influx of hundreds of more people. Women residents wrote to female lawmakers this month, raising concerns about safety. “Life’s not going to be the same again,” one woman from the village told Sky ahead of the result.
Council officials in Piddington said they decided to hold the vote after the government failed to engage with them over the issue.

“We do have obligations to people who come to this country seeking safety to house them, and for many many years, that accommodation has been largely, or sometimes exclusively, concentrated in some of the poorest communities in the country,” Nandy said, adding that “we are all going to have to do our bit.”

items.title: Zambia Stock Market to Debut Gold ETF, Sees Five Stock Listings
body: The Lusaka Securities Exchange will introduce its first-ever exchange-traded fund before the end of October, giving Zambian investors exposure to gold.

The fund is sponsored by South African lender Absa Group Ltd. and will list via introduction from the Johannesburg bourse, LuSE Chief Executive Officer Nicholas Kabaso said in an interview in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi.
Gold ETFs have seen a surge in popularity in 2026, driven by rising prices and broad-based demand across geographies. Total gold held by these funds has risen 1% this year to 100 million ounces.
The exchange has also lined up five company listings in the manufacturing, mining and telecommunications industries, Kabaso said on the sidelines of an industry conference.
“Potentially we might be listing two this year and then possibly push the other three to next year,” he said.
The initial public offerings are expected to raise about $1 billion, he said.
Majority state-owned mining investor ZCCM Investments Holdings Plc is considering selling a portion of its shares to meet local requirements of having a minimum 25% free float.

The LuSE’s all-share index has climbed 1.3% so far this year, giving it an overall market value of 124.5 billion kwacha ($6.36 billion). Top gainers include Airtel Networks Zambia Plc, Zambia National Commercial Bank Plc and Real Estate Investments Zambia Plc, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.
Demand for both fixed-income investments and equities among foreign investors has recovered following Zambia’s election in August, Kabaso said.

The Electoral Commission of Zambia declared incumbent Hakainde Hichilema winner of the ballot with nearly 61% of the vote, extending his rule of the copper-rich southern African nation to a second term.
“All these are coming obviously on the back of renewed confidence that there will be policy consistency and there is also going to be very few variation from the macroeconomic environment,” he said.

items.title: EU Plans Climate Insurance Pact After Hot 'Summer of Truth'
body: The European Union will set up a “climate insurance alliance” to better cover losses as global warming increases the frequency and intensity of droughts, floods and wildfires.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced the initiative as part of her state of the union address Wednesday, saying that with only a quarter of catastrophe losses privately insured, many costs fall on national budgets. A climate resilience framework, due next month, will map 100 of the most vulnerable regions in the bloc, she added.

The initiative comes after what von der Leyen dubbed the “summer of truth,” when a series of heat waves triggered wildfires across Europe and key rivers like the Rhine and Danube fell to record-low levels. The continent is warming twice as fast as the global average, threatening economic damages that could spiral into hundreds of billions of euros.
“There can be no repeat of this summer,” von der Leyen said. “Far too often, national budgets become the insurer of last resort. We need to take action to close this gap.”

The alliance will aim to increase insurance uptake, promote instruments that incentivize risk prevention and make sure that schemes are adequate to meet the growing challenge posed by natural catastrophes, a commission spokesperson said. The alliance would be made up of insurers, experts, investors and regulators, they said.
Read More: Europe’s Heat Wave Raises the Cost of Waiting to Adapt

Von der Leyen announced that the commission, the bloc’s executive branch, would put forward a European Water Initiative to combat waste, adding that key rivers, like the Danube and the Garonne were “disappearing before eyes.” A heat wave plan would be put forward, as well as proposals for a European firefighting fleet, she said.

With around 90% of some rare earths currently coming from China, the EU would also establish a European Corporation on Critical Raw Materials to stockpile key elements for clean transition technologies and defense, von der Leyen said. She pledged to accelerate the shift away from climate-warming fossil fuels, which have soared in price after the Iran war impeded flows of oil and gas through the Strait of Hormuz.

“Since the start of the conflict, imported fossil fuels cost us an additional €90 billion, without a single molecule of energy added,” von der Leyen said. “We need to double down on our affordable and homegrown, clean energy; be it renewables and nuclear.”

items.title: Russia's Richest Woman Sees Fortune Shrink On Drone Strikes
body: Tatyana Kim built Wildberries into Russia’s dominant online retailer, transforming it into a homegrown rival to Amazon.com Inc. and becoming the country’s richest woman along the way.

That changed this July, when Ukraine started targeting the firm’s vast network of warehouses, destroying about a third of its storage capacity and saddling the company with billions of dollars in losses.

A wave of drone strikes has hit more than 20 of the company’s facilities, destroying goods worth at least 550 billion rubles ($6.4 billion) as of the end of August. Rebuilding damaged warehouses will cost more than 200 billion rubles ($2.3 billion), according to research firm Data Insight.

Kim founded the company more than two decades ago while on maternity leave as a place for people like her — moms on a budget with limited time for shopping. She started out ordering clothes in bulk from a German mail-order catalog, scanned the pictures, and posted them on her website.
Her net worth has decreased by $1.5 billion this year to $6.4 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

Over the years she transformed the firm from a small upstart, in which she delivered products personally, into Russia’s largest online marketplace. It had gross stock turnover of about 6.1 trillion rubles last year, equivalent to nearly 3% of the country’s gross domestic product.

Wildberries’ massive warehouses — with some spanning about 250,000 square meters, roughly the size of 35 standard soccer fields, have become easy and recurring targets in Ukraine’s campaign against Russian logistics infrastructure as Kyiv expands its reach and intensity. Ozon, Russia’s second-largest e-commerce company co-owned by billionaire Vladimir Evtushenkov, operates a more dispersed network of smaller facilities which have also come under attack.

The war in Ukraine, now into its fifth year, has killed at least 1 million according to the Council on Foreign Relations, as well as displacing millions as Russia took over about 20% of Ukrainian territory.

RWB group, which includes Wildberries following its merger with Russ Group, said in an emailed statement that “despite the extraordinary nature” of the situation, it’s “taking all necessary measures to minimize the impact and restore normal operations.”

Ukraine’s targeting of Russian warehouses began after President Vladimir Putin’s forces repeatedly struck facilities operated by Nova Poshta, a critical part of Ukraine’s wartime logistics network that moves goods, supports e-commerce and delivers humanitarian aid, including to areas near the front line.

The war in Ukraine initially gave the platform a significant boost. As Western retailers formally pulled out of Russia, Wildberries became an even more important marketplace for everything from Zara clothing to smartphones and other electronics with some goods delivered to the country from abroad via parallel import schemes, without getting permission from brand owners.
At the same time, it has poured money into expanding its warehouse network, nearly doubling total floor space to about 5.2 million square meters over the last year.

While the drone strikes have wiped out a substantial chunk of Kim’s fortune, they’ve also had a knock-on effect on a key part of Putin’s wartime economy: the hundreds of thousands of sellers who rely on its platform. Burned inventories, slower deliveries, and increased logistics costs have all fed into consumer prices, already stretched by four years of war.

The attacks imperiled the businesses of thousands of third-party vendors who sell goods over the popular online platforms. More than 1 million sellers use Wildberries, according to its website. The company introduced additional support measures for affected merchants, including fixed payments for damaged goods and automatic three-month payment holidays on loans issued by WB Bank and WB Finance.

“This is a direct blow to small entrepreneurs,” said Alexandra Prokopenko, a fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. “Next, we’ll see businesses close, bankruptcies rise and investment activity decline. Many people have now felt the impact of the war and realized how it affects their own lives.”

Muscovite Tigran Arutyunov, 42, sold school bags, children’s toys and kitchen supplies on Wildberries. He said that he lost goods worth about 1.5 million rubles ($17,300), of which only 30,000 rubles was reimbursed and has been unable to retrieve his goods from Wildberries warehouses since the first strikes began.
Read More: Putin Says Ukraine 40-Day Strike Campaign Cost Russia 1% of GDP
Monthly revenue from his store has fallen by about two-thirds, forcing him to dismiss all his employees and take a part-time job as an ambulance driver to help repay his debts.

The entrepreneur said keeping part of his inventory in his own storage facility helped the business survive. He now plans to build his own sales website and has temporarily suspended sales on Wildberries, though he aims to resume them soon.

“The first support payments to sellers began on July 22. All inquiries and follow-up questions from partners are being reviewed on a case-by-case basis,” the company said in a statement. “RWB group is also implementing a comprehensive set of measures to support employees and contractors at the affected Wildberries warehouse facilities.”

Kim now has to move quickly to adapt Wildberries to a rapidly changing operating environment. The company cut commissions for sellers using its fulfillment-by-seller model, under which merchants store and pack goods themselves while Wildberries handles only delivery to customers. It’s building a network of partner storage centers, with facilities starting at about 100 square meters.

Operating them is more expensive than running large-scale warehouses, adding to the financial pressure on Wildberries. Little is known about the firm’s financial health and it doesn’t report full results under international standards. But in a statement earlier this year, it said that despite being in an active investment phase, the group ended last year with a comfortable debt level.
The company’s total debt could be close to 1.3 trillion rubles, including more than 500 billion rubles owed to state-run VTB bank as of the end of 2025, Russian news outlet The Bell reported.
For Kim, the upheaval means rethinking a business whose enormous scale helped make her Russia’s richest woman.

Within a year of launching Wildberries, Kim had begun hiring couriers to deliver orders. As the business outgrew her apartment, she rented space at a nearby research institute to store a growing pile of parcels and boxes, but demand kept outpacing the company’s capacity. As income from her company eclipsed that from the small IT business run by her former husband, Vladislav, he started helping more at Wildberries.
In 2024, amid her divorce, Kim found herself at the center of a scandal over a merger deal with Russ Group, the nation’s biggest outdoor advertiser, which Vladislav opposed.

A dispute between the former spouses escalated into a shooting outside the company’s office in central Moscow, not far from the Kremlin, when her ex husband tried to force his way into the building. Two security guards died.
Now, during the current difficulties, she’s appealing for calm.

“The only thing we, the Russian business community, can do now is keep a cool head, plan for the near future, adapt and transform,” she said in a video posted on Telegram in late July. “Entrepreneurs know how to do that better than anyone.”

items.title: South Africa Is Sleepwalking Toward a Gas Crisis, Businesses Warn
body: South Africa’s government has resolved the country’s recurring power outages and is racing to fix its crumbling water infrastructure. But, business leaders warn, it’s sleepwalking into another crisis — a “gas cliff.”

Combined, glassmakers, tile manufacturers, food processors and other industries that rely on gas account for 8% of the economy and 700 billion rand ($43 billion) in annual economic output, and provide 75,000 jobs. Almost all of their needs are currently supplied by Sasol Ltd., the country’s biggest petrochemicals company, from its fields in central Mozambique.

Sasol warns that in two years time there will only be enough gas coming from those fields for its own needs, leaving industries holding back their investments and clamoring for the government to find solutions.

“South Africa doesn’t do anything until it’s an absolute crisis. And this is one crisis that’s still too far away” for the government to take seriously, said Thomas Shaw, chief commercial officer of Ardagh Glass Packaging-Africa, the continent’s biggest glassmaker. “It’s frightening how much investment has been put on hold because nobody knows if there is going to be gas beyond 2030 and at what price.”

Attempts to get the private sector to build gas import infrastructure that would bridge the gap have been frustrated because there’s not enough demand from industrial users alone to justify the investment.

TotalEnergies SE, together with South Africa’s Gigajoule Group, has been planning a gas import terminal in Matola, but has been struggling to secure the demand needed to justify it since at least 2025. That terminal could link to existing pipeline infrastructure that runs to South Africa’s industrial hub of Gauteng, where the cities of Johannesburg and Pretoria lie.

“We need at least three years to develop a project like that,” said Magali Pailhé, head of Total’s exploration and production business in South Africa, adding that the company needs “the uptake to be able to secure the cash flow over a period of time and the reimbursement of the investment.”

Investing in gas-fired power generation would help make the economics of liquefied natural gas terminal projects stack up. The country has a few small plants, and while its long-term strategy is to encourage the building of more renewable power plants, its national energy plan also envisages the use of gas as a transition fuel, with 16 gigawatts of gas-fired power generation by 2039.

The government is currently considering bids from private investors for 2 gigawatts of gas fired power plants, but there’s no certainty as to when those will be built. National power utility Eskom Holdings SOC Ltd. is considering a 3-gigawatt plant in the eastern port of Richards Bay, which would require the construction of an LNG terminal, however there’s no pipeline to Gauteng from there.
South Africa also has reserves of gas onshore and offshore, but ocean exploration has been held up by legal challenges and disputes with environmental groups.

In August, Shell Plc was told by the country’s highest court that it wouldn’t be allowed to renew an exploration right off the country’s Wild Coast region, the culmination of a five-year legal fight with activists — just one of a number of court room battles that have been fought over hydrocarbons exploration off South Africa over the past decade. Requests by industry associations to have specialist courts set up to adjudicate on oil and gas matters to speed up the process have not been acted on by the government.

“The potential in terms of domestic resources is huge,” said Pailhé, who is also chairwoman of the Offshore Petroleum Association of South Africa. “But today the industry is basically stuck and cannot progress. We cannot even say if the resources are there or not as we cannot explore.”

Sasol has offered a stopgap option, but it comes with an environmental cost. The company has applied to the energy regulator to set pricing for methane-rich gas produced from coal. Methane is a significantly more powerful climate-warming gas than carbon dioxide.

Sasol’s chief executive officer  Simon Baloyi acknowledged the environmental concerns, but said they need to be weighed against economic and social considerations. “It’s a country decision where we have to say: ‘do you prefer to push 700,000 people out of a job?’” he said. “Because it’s purely going to boil down to that.”
Some industrial users aren’t convinced.

“It’s not a sustainable long-term solution from a security-of-supply, economic or environmental perspective,”  Julian Singonzo, managing executive for sustainability at Premier FMCG Ltd., South Africa’s biggest bread producer, said. “Sasol has indicated future MRG pricing at levels that are very expensive and potentially above imported LNG.”
Even so, Singonzo said, something has to be done. “Any disruption to gas supply would impact our ability to operate ovens efficiently and keep bread affordable and available,” he said.
Brandon Wood, CEO of South Africa’s biggest tile producer, Italtile Ltd., said the fuel is “critical” to its manufacturing processes and expressed concern about future supply.

The Industrial Gas Users Association Southern Africa, or IGUA-SA, a lobby group, has called for the office of President Cyril Ramaphosa to set up a task team to resolve the impending gas shortage, much as it did to resolve the electricity outages. “South Africa has no practical plan to replace declining gas supply,” the group said in a recent report.

There is a “a big void in terms of state coordination, policy positions and practical ways to tackle this issue,” said Jaco Human, IGUA-SA’s executive officer. “The government is simply not engaging.”

Vincent Magwenya, Ramaphosa’s spokesman, referred queries to the Department of Electricity and Energy. That department, and the Department of Trade, Industry and Competition, acknowledged questions from Bloomberg but didn’t respond.

items.title: Uganda Shilling Dips to Lowest Since 2024 as FX Demand Soars
body: Uganda’s shilling slumped to a 2-1/2 year low against the dollar, weighed down by a surge in demand for foreign-exchange in key economic sectors including energy, manufacturing and telecommunications.

The East African nation’s local unit weakened to 3,925 shillings per dollar in early trade before firming slightly to 3,910/dollar later in the session. Its previous lowest level on a closing basis was in March 2024 when it cost 3,924 shillings to buy the greenback.

“The move appears to have been driven largely by offshore investor positioning rather than domestic fundamentals,” Citigroup Inc. analysts said in a note to clients. “ We expect the shilling to continue trading in the 3,900-3,930 range until the global backdrop improves.”
Read more: Ugandan President’s Son Declares Bid to Succeed His Father

Still, it said domestic politics in the East African nation posed a greater risk. President Yoweri Museveni, 82, was reelected to a seventh five-year term in elections in January but his son Muhoozi Kainerugaba has since said he plans to succeed his father in the next elections.
“Combined with a less favourable coffee outlook and unresolved fiscal pressures, there is potential for a more sustained period of weakness,” Citi said.

In addition, the Bank of Uganda hasn’t intervened in the currency market to stem its slide and “has remained on the sidelines,” according to Richard Nsubuga, head of trading, corporate investment banking at the local unit of Johannesburg-listed Absa Bank Ltd.

Even the large pool of dollars sourced from commodity exporters, remittance inflows and state-linked institutional investors converting their dollar holdings has been “insufficient to offset the strong underlying demand for dollars and reverse the shilling’s downward trajectory,” he added.
“Offshore activity has been evident during the week with flows likely driven by a combination of stop-loss triggers and selective conversions of proceeds from bond sales,” Nsubuga said.

Uganda’s vibrant local-currency bond market has been a huge draw for foreign institutional investors. JPMorgan has identified nine instruments with an estimated market value of $9.4 billion that it plans to include in a new frontier index it’s set to introduce.

items.title: European Stocks Advance as Bond Yields and Oil Ease Ahead of Fed
body: European shares snapped two days of losses as a bond selloff and oil prices eased ahead of the Federal Reserve’s interest-rate decision later on Wednesday.
The Stoxx 600 rose 0.5% at the close in London. The index extended its gains as Brent crude dropped to $105 a barrel.
Elsewhere, utilities shares were the best performers, while miners also gained as metal prices advanced.
In single stocks, Soitec jumped 13% as JPMorgan Chase & Co. upgraded its rating on the French chip-materials supplier to overweight and more than doubled its price target.

European shares have struggled to gain traction since hitting a record in August as higher energy prices fanned inflation and growth concerns, sparking a selloff that wiped 4% of the benchmark’s value. That pushed the Relative Strength Index, a technical gauge that measures the velocity of price moves, close to a level suggesting the correction may have gone too far, too fast.

“Europe just flashed technically oversold for the first time since March,” said Carl Dooley, head of EMEA equity trading at TD Securities. “It feels like the short-term path for risk is once again higher.”
Bond yields eased ahead of the Federal Reserve’s interest rate decision after reaching multi-year highs. Investors are pricing a 90% chance of a hike at the central bank’s meeting.

“If we do get the hike, it will be important to see how the longer end of the bond market reacts to that,” said Bill Dinning, chief investment officer at W1M Wealth Management. He sees a 5.5% yield on the 10-year Treasury as a level that would put pressure on stocks.
Read more: Will Surging Bond Yields Halt the Global Stock Rally?: Explainer

Turkey’s Borsa Istanbul 100 Index fell 5.5%, prompting the exchange to activate a market-wide circuit breaker as an asset manager’s failure to meet redemption requests fueled concern about broader liquidity stress in the country’s investment fund industry.

The automotive sector was the biggest laggard in Europe’s benchmark index, weighed down by a Berenberg downgrade on the Jeep and Fiat owner Stellantis NV. UK housebuilder Barratt Redrow Plc rose 12% after its full-year results beat expectations.

items.title: UK Inflation Hits Five-Month High, Adding Pressure To BoE Policymakers
body: Morning, I’m Louise Moon from Bloomberg UK’s breaking news team, bringing you up to speed on today’s top business stories.
In the final crucial batch of economic data before the Bank of England’s rate decision tomorrow, inflation has risen to a five-month high.

Consumer prices climbed for a second consecutive month, rising 3.1% in the year through August, according to the Office for National Statistics. Motor fuel prices and air fares drove much of the increase, as energy costs surge amid the fallout from the war in Iran.
Services inflation, a key indicator of domestic price pressures, held steady, as did core inflation, which strips out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco.
The figures underline the dilemma facing the Bank of England: while underlying domestic price pressures appear contained, a fresh surge in energy costs is pushing headline inflation higher.

With the conflict in the Middle East showing little sign of easing, policymakers face a familiar problem - how long they can afford to look through an external shock before it starts feeding into the wider economy. More from my colleague Morwenna below.
What’s your take? Ping me on X, LinkedIn or drop me an email at lmoon13@bloomberg.net. Oh, and do subscribe to Bloomberg.com for unlimited access to trusted business journalism on the UK, and beyond.

Barratt Redrow, the UK’s largest homebuilder, cut its completions target for the year largely due to planning delays. It urged the government to take action to boost demand, particularly for first-time home buyers. Shares rose 6% with current trading better than expected.

Glencore has accused iron ore trader Radiant World and associated companies of sending falsified invoices to lenders. That’s as Radiant World filed a suit in Singapore against Glencore, seeking $2 billion in damages. Both mark an explosive end to a business relationship that for many years was very close.

Fintech Revolut has applied for a Swiss banking licence as it pushes on with global growth plans. That would give it a stronger footing in one of the world’s wealth hubs at a time when it has been making inroads into private banking.

Chancellor John Healey is considering raising taxes on slot machines in the budget, in a move that would target betting shops and adult gaming centres, reported the Financial Times. The gambling sector is already reeling from steep hikes at last year’s budget, which has led to shop closures and layoffs.

Plus, the UK should slash taxes on the rich and encourage the City to take more risks, according to a report by a think tank linked to Reform UK that’s set for publication next week and likely to guide the party’s economic principles. It will also urge a breakup of the Treasury, with responsibility for growth moved to a different department.
Here’s your daily snap analysis from Bloomberg UK’s Markets Today blog:
The fact that higher energy prices have driven the latest CPI reading higher is no surprise, in fact it’s exactly what most economists expected.
But that doesn’t make it easier to swallow. It takes the headline rate of inflation further above the Bank of England’s 2% target and sets the stage for a much tougher number to digest next month.

That’s because in August wholesale energy prices only went up slightly, with crude oil ending the month just over $90 compared to below $85 at the end of July. It’s September that’s seen prices really rocket, with crude screeching back up to almost $110 per barrel. Likewise natural gas futures have continued to rise through the month.

That means the broad impact of higher energy prices in August is only going to be augmented in September. And a new energy price cap coming in for households in October will push up bills from then too.

Today’s number may not have delivered any surprises for the Bank of England ahead of its decision tomorrow, but other than not being drastically worse than expected, it won’t bring them much comfort either. What it confirms is the headache the central bank faces, coming after yesterday’s soggy labour market data, in balancing a need to curb inflation without further throttling the economy.
— Morwenna Coniam
Check Bloomberg UK’s Markets Today blog for updates all day.

The Bank of England will decide on interest rates at midday tomorrow, and is expected to hold at 3.75%. Investors are watching closely for language around energy prices which have surged since the last meeting, reviving inflation concerns. Traders have pared bets on the BOE raising rates, but are still pricing in four hikes during the next 12 months.

The government’s independent climate watchdog says Heathrow should only be allowed to add a third runway if the industry pays the cost of decarbonisation by 2050, which could be passed onto flight tickets. In that time, expanding Heathrow would increase pollution by what percentage?
[Yesterday’s answer: A Malaysian state pension fund bought 10 Gresham Street, Moody’s City of London head office, in 2012 for £200 million. It is now on sale for £330 million.]

items.title: Europe Gas Swings With Traders Weighing German Stockpiling Moves
body: European natural gas flipped to losses from earlier gains as traders weigh Germany’s next moves to boost winter stockpiles, which could determine fuel demand from the county in the coming months.

Benchmark futures fell as much as 4%, following a sharp retreat in oil contracts. Earlier, prices had risen above €80 a megawatt-hour as market players were looking for more clarity on gas purchases from Germany — Europe’s biggest energy market — whose inventories are abnormally low.

Any signs that the country is stepping up buying could support prices at a time when global supplies remain tight. European gas jumped as much as 4% in early trading, after media reports that German Economy Minister Katherina Reiche had prompted the state-owned Securing Energy for Europe GmbH to buy gas to boost inventories. The company said in emailed comments to Bloomberg that it received no such instruction.

Germany is considering a plan to expand an existing tender that pays suppliers to guarantee that gas is available if the system is strained, according to people familiar with the matter. The government is discussing the measure, with a decision likely as early as Sept. 21.

Sharp price moves underscore the growing concern over Europe’s depleted gas reserves ahead of winter. Storage facilities across the region are about 68% full — way below seasonal averages — and in Germany the level is just 56%.  The German government has repeatedly said it won’t formally intervene to secure supplies, though it has held talks with state-owned energy companies about supporting stockpiling efforts, Bloomberg reported earlier this month.

The low storage is also rippling further along the gas curve. Contracts for summer 2027 are more expensive than those for the following winter, with the premium widening to a record this week. That leaves traders with little incentive to buy gas during the warmer months and put it into storage, raising the prospect of a third straight year of difficult refilling if global supplies stay tight.
Read More: Record Gas Spread Raises Risk of Another Low-Storage Winter

European gas prices have almost tripled so far this year — reaching the highest since December 2022 earlier this week — which stoked inflation and threatens the continent’s already fragile economic outlook. LNG demand from Asia is setting the stage for more intense bidding wars when colder weather sets in. Europe needs elevated prices to attract more seaborne gas cargoes ahead of winter.

There’s a risk European gas could approach €100 a megawatt-hour this winter — more than 25% above current levels — given sustained disruptions to Middle East supplies and Europe’s historically low storage levels, Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Patricio Alvarez said in a note. Further escalation of the conflict could even drive prices above €120, he said.
Dutch front-month futures, Europe’s gas benchmark, traded 3.1% lower at €77.60 a megawatt-hour as of 5:43 p.m. in Amsterdam.

items.title: Hong Kong Sets Out Gold Hub as Driver for Commodities and Yuan
body: Hong Kong’s plan to build a global gold hub will provide “an entry point” for trading other commodities and expanding the yuan’s usage on world markets, according to its first-ever five year plan.

The city will “fully leverage the role of gold as a strategic asset” by developing a one-stop gateway for storage, trading and clearing the precious metal, according to a document released Wednesday laying out the government’s priorities.

The plan involves building mutual access with mainland gold markets, including the Shanghai Gold Exchange and the Shanghai Futures Exchange, to increase the variety of yuan-denominated products. Hong Kong’s role in the London Metal Exchange’s global warehousing network for base metals will also help drive more commodities trading, risk management, and financing, the document said.

Hong Kong began trialing a new gold clearing system in July, marking progress in its ambition to take market share from traditional bullion centers like London. The People’s Bank of China is stockpiling more gold in the city, which is also inviting other central banks to shift their reserves.
Read More: Hong Kong Vows to Deepen Role as Premier Offshore Yuan Hub
A stronger connection between Hong Kong and the mainland is likely to help traders access the world’s biggest gold consumer. China strictly controls imports, while exports are largely prohibited.

The city “will offer all‑rounded support for more gold traders and financial institutions to establish their presence in Hong Kong,” as the government explores more “preferential policies” for the industry, the document said.

items.title: South African Inflation Expectations Dip Before Rate Call
body: A closely watched gauge of South African inflation expectations fell in the third quarter, days before policymakers meet to decide on interest rates.

Average inflation expectations two years ahead dropped to 3.8% in the third quarter from 3.9% previously, according to a survey released on Wednesday by the Stellenbosch-based Bureau for Economic Research.
The South African Reserve Bank’s monetary policy committee, which delivers its next policy decision on Sept. 23, prefers to anchor expectations around its 3% inflation goal.

The dip may provide the MPC with room to again hold its benchmark interest rate at 7% next week, to help support an economy battered by surging energy and fertilizer prices caused by escalating tensions in the Middle East. South African gross domestic product contracted 0.2% in the second quarter, snapping six quarters of growth.
The SARB previously raised rates 25 basis points in May to counter the inflationary impact of the Iran war, before unexpectedly standing pat in July.

The May hike “limits the need for further rate increases, especially against the backdrop of these lower inflation expectations” Johann Els, chief economist at PSG Financial Services, said. “There is concern about ongoing high oil prices and ongoing high inflation, but that would likely be temporary, and oil prices at some point will come down.”

In contrast, Goldman Sachs Group Inc.’s Andrew Matheny — who recently shifted his forecast to a hike from a hold, which he expects to result from a split vote with dovish dissents — doesn’t expect the softer reading to have a bearing on the upcoming MPC meeting.
“We think that the MPC will be mostly influenced by external developments including the Fed and oil prices,” he said.
The Federal Reserve is forecast to lift interest rates later on Wednesday.
Forward rate agreements used to speculate on borrowing costs are pricing in a 45% chance the MPC will raise rates by 25 basis points, compared with 56% on Tuesday.

SARB Governor Lesetja Kganyago said this month the MPC would continue to be measured in its approach to the aftereffects of polyshocks such as higher oil prices and the El Niño weather phenomenon that may reduce rainfall in the coming months, causing food costs to increase.
Since the last survey three months ago, inflation peaked at 5% in June and moderated to 4.3% the following month.

items.title: LNG Market Faces Extended Hormuz Outage, Japanese Shipper Says
body: Mitsui OSK Lines Ltd., a top Japanese shipping firm, doesn’t expect LNG shipments through the Strait of Hormuz to resume soon, signaling a prolonged disruption that could keep prices elevated and curb demand across Asia.

“As long as this situation continues, it’s almost impossible to carry the LNG cargoes” through Hormuz, Chairman Takeshi Hashimoto said on the sidelines at the Gastech conference in Bangkok on Wednesday. “At the moment, we are quite pessimistic about the near future.”

He said that a peace deal settlement among the parties looks “very, very difficult.” MOL, as the company is called, has stopped sending liquefied natural gas tankers through Hormuz, a strategic waterway that carried about a fifth of global supply before the conflict began.
Read More: A $7 Billion Gas Bill Sees Developing Asian Nations Sour on LNG

The disruption has pushed Asian spot LNG prices to their highest level since 2022, with the potential for further gains as winter approaches and heating demand rises. The price surge is already prompting many buyers in Asia to scale back purchases, Hashimoto said.
“People are saying that there are alternative energy supplies possible from the US, Canada, Australia or parts of Africa,” he said. “But obviously it would not be enough to cover demand.”

items.title: Monaco Set to Exit Dirty-Money List Along With Bulgaria, Ivory Coast
body: Monaco is among several nations poised to exit a global financial watchdog’s dirty money watchlist next month, marking a change in fortune for the city-state that’s home to the world’s highest concentration of millionaires and billionaires.

The French Riviera principality was placed on the Financial Action Task Force’s “gray list” in June 2024, bringing with it heightened scrutiny over shortcomings in its efforts to tackle illegal money flows. However, officials from the Paris-based monitor have since found significant progress, according to people familiar with the matter.
Bulgaria and Ivory Coast are also expected to come off the list, some of the people said, who asked not to be identified because the deliberations are private.

The official outcome isn’t due until the final day of the FATF’s next plenary in the French capital on Oct. 30 and no final decisions have been made, the people said. Listings are determined based on a consensus among the group’s membership, which includes the US, UK, European Commission, China, Japan and India.

The watchdog’s recommendations are closely tracked by global investors who are wary of conducting business in places found to be deficient in anti-money laundering regulations. Jurisdictions added to the list require closer monitoring, and the designation may cast serious doubt over the integrity of their financial systems.
A 2021 International Monetary Fund report found gray-listed countries experienced “a large and statistically significant reduction in capital inflows.”

An exchange-traded fund that tracks Bulgaria’s benchmark stock index was up 2.8% at 12 p.m. in Sofia. Monte Carlo casino owner Société des Bains de Mer also rose on the news, up by 1.8% in Paris trading at 11 a.m.
A spokesperson for the FATF declined to comment on the listing decisions.
What’s FATF, The Global Body Targeting Dirty Money?: Explainer

The FATF’s October plenary will mark the first under the presidency of British official Giles Thomson. Since assuming the role in July, he has placed a particular priority on combating fraud, including scam compounds.
Monaco’s expected delisting comes as the city-state is still reeling from a murder plot on its soil in late June, which triggered a large-scale manhunt.

Since arriving on the gray list, the principality has tightened laws and sought to show it can take meaningful enforcement actions. Earlier this year, its anti-money laundering watchdog fined UBS Group AG €6 million ($6.9 million) over a range of failings. Two other banks, including Julius Baer Group Ltd., have also been fined.
A spokesperson for the Monaco government declined to comment.
For Bulgaria, the original gray-list designation in 2023 came at the peak of the nation’s negotiations to enter the euro area.

The Council of Europe has long criticized the country, which regularly ranks among the European Union’s most corrupt. But more recently, FATF officials have praised improvements in risk-based supervision and market-entry controls for virtual asset service providers. In early September, Prime Minister Rumen Radev met with FATF representatives to discuss the nation’s progress.

Besides meeting all formal criteria, “we have another guarantee that puts us in a strong position to take Bulgaria out of this disgraceful list — and it is the political will and the actions taken by the Bulgarian government with regard to fighting money laundering, gray economy and corruption,” he told a government body in late August.

Elsewhere, the Ivory Coast’s progress on bank supervision and beneficial ownership verification has drawn plaudits from the FATF, which previously raised concerns about oversight and enforcement. Among the steps recently taken: a multi-year prison sentence handed out to a local influencer on money-laundering charges.
“It is highly likely that we have met all the conditions, but we are awaiting the final assessments,” said Amadou Coulibaly, Ivory Coast’s Minister of Communication and government spokesperson.

Ivorian dollar bonds maturing in 2041 rose for the first time in seven days by 0.3 cent on the dollar to 92.4 cents at 3:40 p.m. in London. Notes maturing in 2037 rose for the first time in as many days by 0.2 cent on the dollar to 106.1 cents.

items.title: EU Calls for European Security Council in New Defense Plan
body: The European Union proposed creating a security structure with like-minded allies to confront growing threats amid doubts about President Donald Trump’s commitment toward the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen floated a so-called European Security Council during her state of the union address in Strasbourg, France, Wednesday.

“Europe needs its own counter-hybrid playbook. We urgently need a consensus on how to respond to certain incidents,” Von der Leyen said. “The urgency is clear. And the principle is simple: Europe’s security is indivisible.”

The plan would create an emergency security protocol that, when triggered by member states, would activate all countries to convene and coordinate a European response. It would also create a format focused on security with partners like Ukraine, the UK, Norway and Canada.

The initiative comes as Europe grapples with a shifting geopolitical climate over the past few years as the US has threatened to pull back from NATO and China has become an increasingly important global player.

France and other member states have supported pan-European initiatives to regain control on security matters, including a European Security Council. The EU’s defense chief, Andrius Kubilius, has also been calling for setting up such format.

But the idea, which could group nations like UK, Ukraine or Canada, would clash with US-led NATO, the main provider of security for the continent. NATO has long bristled at what they perceive as the EU duplicating its structures without the actual war-fighting competences and procedures to back it up.

“Can we seriously afford to spend time, money and energy creating an alternative to NATO from scratch — and to do so within an entity that doesn’t even have defense within its remit?,” said Bartosz Grodecki, head of Poland’s National Security Bureau, an advisory body to the country’s president, stressing the increasing risk of Russian escalation in Eastern Europe. “I see this as a purely political declaration.”

items.title: Bond Traders Bet on Fed Delivering 25 BP Rate Increase
body: Good morning. Bond traders are piling pressure on the Federal Reserve to deliver a rate hike. Crypto’s long march into mainstream finance takes a step backward. And Germany delves deep to prepare for the possibility of war with Russia. Listen to the day’s top stories.
— Samson Ellis

Bond traders have piled into bearish positions ahead of the Federal Reserve meeting, betting that the Treasury selloff driving yields to their highest in almost two decades will continue. The benchmark US 10-year yield rose to its highest level since 2007 on Tuesday as traders braced for the Fed to hike interest rates in response to inflation worries.

Senators from both parties blocked a landmark digital asset market structure bill, denying the industry a chance to turn its newfound influence in Washington into fresh rules that could outlast the current administration. Crypto exchange Coinbase Global closed 10% lower, while Bitcoin also dropped.

Glencore has accused Radiant World and associated companies of sending falsified invoices to lenders, cutting ties just as the iron ore trader filed a suit in Singapore against the Swiss-based commodities group, seeking $2 billion in damages.

Swiss voters are set to reject a proposal to tighten the country’s neutrality this month, preserving the government’s freedom to interpret the doctrine flexibly. Two final polls ahead of a Sept. 27 plebiscite showed clear majorities against a right-wing initiative intended to enshrine a strict stance in the constitution.

At first glance, the hospital in the southwestern German city of Ulm looks much like any other. Patients sit in reception areas waiting to be called, doctors roam the halls looking at reports or their phones. Only the uniformed soldiers among the staff hint at military ties. Yet many meters beneath its busy wards lies a Cold War-era bunker that has suddenly become relevant again.

There are two certainties in life: death, and taxes getting the blame whenever rich people leave the UK, Paul J. Davies writes. Billionaire hedge fund manager Chris Rokos departing for Greece, where he’ll pay just €100,000 ($115,000) a year, is the latest to provoke a flood of recriminations. But these stories — and claims of an exodus of the super-rich from Britain — should be taken with a hefty dose of salt.

items.title: Investor Faith in Europe's Stock Market Shows Signs of Fatigue
body: Europe’s rally has become more concentrated this year, amplifying risks just as investors turn less optimistic about its economic outlook.

An underperformance against US stocks has deepened over the past month, despite Europe’s stronger economic surprises and worries about artificial intelligence spending by American tech giants. While oil above $100 increases the likelihood of interest-rate hikes in both regions, pricey crude is a bigger problem for import-dependent Europe. Meanwhile, crowding in a small number of high-performing themes has encouraged investors to broaden exposure.

Bank of America Corp. strategists including Paulina Strzelinska noted a “softer bull case” for Europe in the firm’s fund manager survey published Tuesday. Global investors are net 5% underweight euro-zone equities, flipping from net 6% overweight just a month ago. By contrast, they are a net 25% overweight US equities, not far off the 27% in the previous poll. Moreover, a net 8% expect to underweight Europe over the next year, the BofA team said.

For the majority of survey respondents, declining energy prices and easing inflation remain the key potential positives, while 43% of participants view disappointments in AI investment as the largest downside risk. No fund managers cited spending on AI, digital or data centers as a driver of European growth. Instead, they have pursued economy-linked sectors like basic resources, technology and industrials to capture the benefit of low interest rates and fiscal stimulus in the region. Exposure to banks remains elevated, but has dropped by half since last month, the survey showed.

This pattern is backed by data such as the euro-zone PMI manufacturing survey, which supports the case for cyclicals. The gauge has improved sharply over the past three years, and has been in expansion territory since February. Separately, European industrials geared to electrification and data centers have been in favor, benefiting from rising capex and low financing costs.

Still, the European Central Bank has turned more hawkish as elevated oil prices stoke worries about inflation. The central bank raised rates this month and the swap market expects three more hikes through April. Meanwhile, with investor exposure to defensive sectors relatively low, diversification could be ahead for Europe given the potential hit to economic growth.

“The geopolitical context is becoming an increasingly tangible obstacle,” said CIC CIB strategists Nicolas Bouthors and Maxime Garcia. “Rising energy prices are becoming increasingly problematic for growth and inflation, a situation which central banks, especially the ECB, will be unable to ignore.”

The strategists added that the earnings outlook is becoming more fragile because of the protracted Iran conflict and its implications on growth and interest rates. They expect 2027 profit forecasts to be cut by at least 5%. They favor sectors highly exposed to the risk of interest-rate volatility, such as banks and insurance, defensives like personal care, drug and grocery stores, as well as strong growth thematics like defense and electricals. Globally, they prefer US stocks, where exposure to the AI theme is higher.

Earnings growth in Europe is still running strong, but trails the US. Stoxx 600 profits are expected to surge 15% this year and 9.7% in 2027, according to Bloomberg Intelligence data. That compares with jumps of 27% and 19%, respectively, across the Atlantic. As a result, the European market has been losing its valuation discount cushion quickly, and now trades near its long-term average discount to the US market of about 20%.

“Our conviction on US equities versus Europe is intact: the US has a broad hegemony over global profits, it represents 65% of the total of OECD countries,” said Christopher Dembik, senior investment adviser at Pictet Asset Management. “That strength lies in the fact that US companies are currently present and dominant across all the AI industry’s value chain.”

items.title: India's SEBI Is Said to Ease Arbitrage Fund Rules to Aid Auction
body: India’s market regulator has given arbitrage mutual funds more flexibility in managing their positions, according to people familiar with the matter, seeking to draw a key source of liquidity into the struggling closing auction for stocks.

The Securities and Exchange Board of India has allowed these funds to temporarily carry unhedged positions of as much as 1% of their plans, said the people, who asked not to be identified because the details aren’t public. Arbitrage funds held a combined 3 trillion rupees ($31 billion) in assets at the end of August.

The relaxation is aimed at bringing liquidity into an auction that has struggled to attract enough players since its launch on Aug. 3. Arbitrage funds profit from price differences between the cash equities and futures markets, but requirements that they remain fully hedged have made it difficult for them to participate in the auction process.
Under the previous system, price swings in the final 30 minutes could create temporary gaps between cash shares and futures, giving arbitrage desks time to step in and close them.

The auction has shortened that window and increased the risk of a temporary mismatch. A fund may sell futures expecting to buy an equal amount of shares in the auction, only to find too few sellers in the cash market. The new 1% allowance lets funds carry that mismatch instead of staying fully hedged at all times.
Read more: Why India’s New Closing Auction Is Agonizing Traders: Q&A

The move adds to regulators’ efforts to tackle one of the auction’s biggest challenges: a lack of liquidity. Several institutional investors have largely stayed away, citing thin volumes that aggravate price moves and make it harder to set stable end-of-day prices. SEBI on Saturday also proposed sweeping changes to the closing auction framework, including a possible return to the previous method for settling derivatives on expiry days, after concerns emerged over sharp price swings.
Representatives for SEBI and the Association of Mutual Funds in India, an industry trade body, didn’t respond to emails seeking comment.
AMFI communicated the relaxation to asset management companies earlier this month, the people said. Funds seeking to use the allowance may need to communicate the change to unitholders, they said.

items.title: UK Inflation Rises to Five-Month High Before BOE Decision
body: UK inflation climbed for a second month as motor fuel prices jumped, according to official figures a day before the Bank of England announces its interest-rate decision.

Consumer prices rose 3.1% in the year through August, the highest since March and up from 2.9% the previous month, the Office for National Statistics said Wednesday. The increase was in line with the median forecast of economists.

The acceleration was driven by higher prices at the pump due to the ongoing war in Iran, as well as air fares during the summer holidays. Rising cost pressures pose a political threat to Prime Minister Andy Burnham who came to power in July pledging to improve people’s finances.
Burnham said later Wednesday that next month’s budget “is going to be challenging” amid rising inflation and elevated borrowing costs.

Domestic pressures remain subdued but are expected to intensify in the coming months. Services inflation, an indicator of domestic pressures, remained at 3.4% in August, the ONS said. Core inflation, which excludes energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, was also unchanged at 2.6%.
BOE officials meeting this week are expected to keep rates unchanged as a weak labor market has helped contain price pressures from the Middle East conflict so far.

However, that stance is becoming increasingly difficult to maintain as the war drags on. UK drivers now face the most expensive diesel and petrol costs since 2022, while oil prices are above $100 a barrel. BOE Governor Andrew Bailey also warned that new risks are coming into play, particularly for food prices, amid extreme drought in the UK and the looming impact of El Niño.

Most of the rise in inflation came from transport costs, particularly motor fuels which rose 6.9% in August, far more than the 0.4% gain a year ago. Airfares, a highly volatile component, jumped 6.2% on the month compared with a 2.1% rise a year earlier.

Annual food inflation was little changed at 1.1%, with prices climbing just 0.3% on the month. Downward pressures came from furniture and clothing and footwear where prices rose less than a year earlier.

Factory gate prices for those buying manufactured products also accelerated, climbing 3.7% compared to a year earlier. Refined petroleum products and coke contributed to the pickup to the highest annual rate since May. Fuel and raw material prices jumped 6.1%, a pickup driven by higher crude oil costs.

“Rising energy prices are testing the Bank of England’s wait-and-see approach” said Yael Selfin, chief economist at KPMG UK. “Higher energy costs remain the primary driver of rising inflation, while domestic price pressures remain relatively well contained.”
A Bloomberg Economics analysis found that household energy bills could jump by about 25% when the UK price cap set by regulators resets in January.

Such an increase would push CPI inflation above 4% in 2027, piling pressure on the Labour government to deliver fresh support for households at a time when the public finances are already under pressure.

Burnham administration’s therefore faces a difficult first budget in October. With the conflict in the Middle East spreading, the outlook has deteriorated sharply over the past month. Oil and gas prices are now above the adverse scenario the central bank set out at its last meeting in July.

While the UK economy has been surprisingly resilient since the start of the war, there are few signs that price pressures are spiraling out of control. The BOE’s own survey of households showed inflation expectations for the year-ahead dipped to 3.2% in August, down from 4% in May. A separate BOE poll of businesses found that wage settlements for 2027 will “broadly in line with or lower than 2026,” when they averaged 3.6%.

Burnham said the government “won’t take risks with people’s living standards” at the budget next month. Both the PM and Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey highlighted the Middle East conflict as a key challenge for households, in comments on Wednesday, with Healey singling out the impact of the war on “our bills, our weekly shop and at the petrol pumps.”

items.title: Hong Kong Bourse May Launch First Bond Index Before End-2026
body: The Hong Kong stock exchange is considering launching its first-ever bond index before the end of the year, according to people familiar with the matter, as the Asian financial center bets that the benchmark would boost trading activity in the world’s largest offshore yuan market.

The offshore renminbi bond index is expected to track so-called dim sum bonds with a minimum size of 1 billion yuan ($149 million), one of the people said, asking not to be identified discussing private information. Eligible securities would be required to be listed on the Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited and use its infrastructure, they said.

“We look forward to sharing more details of HKEX’s first bond index in due course, supporting the RMB internationalization journey and the continued development of a multi-asset ecosystem in Hong Kong,” a spokesperson for the bourse said when asked for comment.

During his policy address earlier on Wednesday, Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee said the HKEX’s Offshore RMB Bond Index will be a “reference for market trends and an underlying index for exchange-traded funds.”

Chinese authorities are amplifying efforts to bolster Hong Kong’s status as the top offshore yuan market in the world, tapping on growing investor enthusiasm for China’s currency as geopolitical tensions including the Iran war cast doubts on the dollar’s status.

In July, regulators expanded a program called Southbound Bond Connect, which allows mainland institutional investors to buy offshore bonds through Hong Kong, raising the annual limit to 800 billion yuan from 500 billion yuan.
Read More: PBOC Unveils Measures to Cement Hong Kong’s Yuan Hub Status

Momentum in the dim sum bond market has accelerated this year. Sovereign and corporate issuers sold a combined 876 billion yuan of offshore yuan-denominated bonds so far this year, up 34% from the same period a year earlier and a record for the period, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.
Bloomberg LP, the parent of Bloomberg News, offers index products for various asset classes through Bloomberg Index Services Ltd.

items.title: Paytm Bulls See IPO Price Back in Reach After Five-Year Wait
body: A turn in sentiment toward Indian digital payments pioneer Paytm is putting its initial public offering price back in sight for the first time since its listing.

The stock is about 22% away from its IPO price of 2,150 rupees apiece following a 54% rally this quarter. Jefferies and JM Financial have lifted their price targets to exactly that level, while Investec Securities and Emkay Global Financial Services see it reaching 2,300 and 2,400, respectively.

Paytm, listed as One97 Communications Ltd., is winning back investor confidence as improving profitability and a stronger operating outlook help put years of regulatory setbacks and losses behind it. The stock had slumped after a blockbuster IPO in November 2021, marking one of the worst performances for a large debut globally.

The stock jumped as much as 7.3% Wednesday, the most in more than five weeks, as analysts expect the firm to gain from a fee that merchants will now pay for receiving instant payments via a state-backed system.
A 0.4% levy will apply to payments exceeding 2,000 rupees ($20.8) to businesses through the Unified Payments Interface, or UPI which also supports peer-to-peer money transfers and bill payments.

Citigroup Inc. estimates the new rules will translate into 3 billion rupees ($31.3 million) in revenue from Paytm’s UPI app and as much as 7 billion rupees from its merchant-acquiring business. The stock is on track to rise for a fourth straight year after slumping 60% in 2022.
“Paytm trades at inexpensive valuations that are appealing when Paytm returns to growth, owing to potential for operating leverage,” Citi analysts Vijit Jain and Sanchit Chandna wrote in a note.

items.title: Saudis Pivot to Send More Oil Via Hormuz After Pipeline Shut
body: Saudi Arabia is ramping up prompt sales of crude from outside the Strait of Hormuz following the shutdown of the kingdom’s East-West pipeline, which halted cross-country flows to its Red Sea coast.

Saudi Aramco has sold about 20 million barrels to Asian refiners this week that can be picked up this month and next from just outside Hormuz, according to traders familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named. The buyers included Chinese state-owned and independent processors, and other importers in East Asia, they said.

The global oil market is focused on the fallout from the halt of the pipeline, which was the primary link that helped Saudi Arabia to circumvent the Iran war-induced turmoil in Hormuz. The conduit was shut last week after attacks, and there’s been no official word on when operations will resume. The rising spot sales via the Persian Gulf suggest that Riyadh is now seeking to pivot back toward its traditional route even as risks to shipping persist.
Read More: Saudis Seek to Boost Hormuz Oil Exports as Key Pipeline Attacked

Following the pipeline halt, Aramco has delayed deliveries from its Red Sea port of Yanbu, the conduit’s western terminus, to some European customers and at least one East Asian refiner. The extent of the delays wasn’t immediately clear, according to people familiar with the matter.

The spot cargoes sold by Aramco are for loading from the Gulf of Oman on a ship-to-ship basis over September to October, the traders said. That means while the crude volumes will still need to traverse Hormuz, buyers will not be responsible for that portion of the voyage given the pick-up location.
Saudi Aramco declined to comment.
